Set 25 years after a zombie outbreak, 'The Reapers Are the Angels' portrays the struggle of mankind as it attempts to build a new society decimated by death and consumed by hatred. Funnily enough, its not the zombies that pose the dominant threat to the new world, rather the survivors themselves (amongst who live inbreds, hunters, and criminals) who haven't learnt to live harmoniously without laws and governance. The protagonist, Temple, oozes classic southern gothic appeal and is instantly likable - the perfect heroin for the imperfect post apocalyptic time she lives in. Driven to the fight, Temple roams the USA encountering one band of survivor society to another and picking up some interesting wards along the way. The zombies are portrayed as little more than cattle (by some as a means food, others as a source of narcotic) adding a semi-original touch to a well used theme. Consistently fast paced, this is as good as a page turner I've ever read. 5 stars.

My all time favourite book!

The Reapers are the Angels isn't just a dystopian, zombie novel centred around a young, fearless girl. It's a big question mark towards morality in survival.

Poor Temple starts out like the little tomboy sister we want to protect, but goes on to become very troubled by her own thoughts and actions. She sees herself as evil which only makes you pity her and the things she has had to do to survive.

The characters in this story are all grey, nobody is 100% good or bad and this is what makes it so amazing. Everyone's POV is understandable. The world-building is phenomenal; Bell is able to describe a scene with all senses so accurately you almost feel like you're really there. The "meatskins", and their various names, are described so well that it can turn your stomach to imagine them and their stench.

I am very certain this book would make a killing being made into a film and I'd be first in the cinema to view it.

Absolutely fantastic story. And one I'd highly recommend.
If you like The Stand, zombies, even Blood Red Road, strong female characters, self-discovery which goes hand in hand with rich characterization, post-apocalyptic settings, let's see, oh yeah, don't mind a bleak, haunting, terribly depressing yet deeply moving story, then I'd definitely give this gem of a book a try. Bonus, it's beautifully written.

Temple (aka Sarah Mary Williams) has never known a world unpopulated by meatskins (zombies). To quote Moses Todd(the man who is dedicated to hunting and killing her) Temple knows about the forces of things, and she understands America the Beautiful, and she is unafraid, except of herself.

Imagine if Cormac McCarthy wrote about heroines instead of heroes and about zombies instead of the Mexican border and you would have The Reapers Are the Angels.

A poetic, elegant amd passionate zombie book. Yes, it is worth reading.

Zombies, much like vampires in recent years, have seen a resurgence in TV, film, novels and comics. Therefore finding something new and interesting can seem like an impossible task, but Alden Bell has accomplished it with style. The story takes place after a zombie apocalypse, and the closest story it resembles to me is The Walking Dead, a long running comic series from Image, which is currently being made into a TV series by Frank Darabont. Unlike The Walking Dead, the world has been like this for 25 years and the main character, Temple, is a teenager, so this is all she has ever known, which makes for an interesting and unique perspective. Enough time has also passed that humanity has clawed back small portions of the land, barricaded sections of cities and small communities, but Temple is a traveller. When she was younger she tried the sedentary life, with something resembling a normal life, but the inevitable happened and staying on the move seems safer. She’s spent so long living with a shadow at her back that it has irreversibly changed her into an older, more brutal version of the girl she might have been if she had been born many years before the fall. The most poignant example of this divergence comes when she meets someone her own age who has grown up in a fenced community and the differences between them are shocking, touching and very telling.

The story follows Temple’s journey across this rugged new version of America, where the wolves lurking at your eye corners are now shambling zombies or meatskins as Bell names them. Creatures driven by primal urges and instinct, to be dealt with if required but also pitied because of what they have become and who they used to be. In many ways the story is not about zombies at all, but humanity, how it adapts and copes with adversity and how, even in an utterly ruined world, the greatest threat to an individual comes from their fellow man.

The Reapers are the Angels has strong echoes of I Am Legend by Richard Matheson, in the haunting beauty of the story and the horrific turn of events that come out of the blue. Temple, like Neville, is driven by demons in her past which are gradually revealed as the story progresses. These terrifying and crippling memories are another spur that keep her on the move, forever in search of something intangible, a refuge from the madness and even from herself. They eat away at her and she believes she doesn’t deserve a comfortable life and that she will never be forgiven by God for what she’s done. When the story begins she is at peace, living a very simple and isolated life, but she cannot hide from the world forever, or from herself, and unfortunately the world catches up and she is forced to move on.

Temple does whatever she has to in order to survive; scavenging food, weapons, cars and gas to stay on the move, killing meatskins and finding safe places to sleep at night to avoid being bitten and turned. This is a hard life that would take its toll on anyone and on a young girl surviving by herself it has many effects that most people can’t see and don’t understand.

The main relationship in the story is a complex one between Temple and a man named Moses Todd, who is in fact her worst enemy. Both of them live by a code, a set of rules in a world without laws, and when Temple breaks one of Moses rules, he becomes her implacable nemesis. At the same time he is not driven by anger, because he understands why she committed this crime, as he sees it, but if he lets it slide, if he ignores it then he might as well not bother with any rules and live like a savage. There has to be a line somewhere and she accepts it and doesn’t hate Moses either. So he swears to pursue her to the ends of the earth and kill her for what she has done and that decision makes sense to both of them. Moses is also the only person who understands Temple because he is a survivor like her, one who has spent more time on the road that sat still in one of the new communities. It is a fascinating and very unusual relationship, but one that somehow makes sense in a world gone mad. In different circumstances they could be friends or allies, but there’s no going back and no pretending in this world. They accept the truth and the world as they find it now and get on with it.

For all the walking dead, the murder, destruction and desolation, there is beauty in this shattered world. Real joy and brief moments of peace for Temple come in finding something amazing amidst the horror, which to her, means that God is still there watching over everyone. He shows wonderful things to those who keep looking and keep believing, but it also means he is still judging everyone by their actions, which is the splinter in her mind that can never be removed.

Another fascinating element in the story is what has managed to survive the fall and the passage of twenty five years. Music, literature, technology, art, history, much of it is now obsolete or irrelevant to most people. Entertainment still exists in the communities and even on the road, but it too has morphed into something else. With no TV or radio broadcasts Temple makes her own music, half remembered tunes passed down orally or mangled versions of real songs that have changed over the years as if passed through a meat grinder.

The style of the text is simple, clean and unpretentious and the story moves along at a solid pace. There are some quiet moments of contemplation, lulls amidst the storm in a chaotic world, but I was always conscious of the shadow at Temple’s back and had the feeling it couldn’t last very long.

The Reapers are the Angels is a haunting, beautiful and engaging story full of moments of horror, where very few of these come at the hands of zombies. It is also a very powerful story about humanity and one that I can see myself reading again. Like I Am Legend I think it will become a classic of the genre and one against which others will be measured.

The Reapers are The Angels by Alden Bell

Born into a crumbling society plagued by zombies, all 15-year-old Temple knows is to kill or be killed. When she is assaulted at a safe house, she murders her human attacker, Abraham Todd, and runs from his vengeful brother, Moses. Temple soon acquires a traveling partner, a slow mute by the name of Maury, and begrudgingly takes responsibility for his care, remembering a young boy she swore to protect but couldn't save. Fleeing Moses, the "meatskins," and her own battered conscience, Temple still finds moments of simple joy in the brutal world. Bell has created an exquisitely bleak tale and an unforgettable heroine whose eye for beauty and aching need for redemption somehow bring wonder into a world full of violence and decay.

Alden Bell's The Reapers are The Angels is the perfect combination of Charles Portis' True Grit and the classic zombie flick Night of the Living Dead. If you are a fan of the highest quality literature, thought provoking themes and the supernatural than there is nothing lacking in this book. I often pick up a book, hoping for something new, something unexpected, only to be disappointed with another piece of drivel. Now don't get me wrong I'm not above drivel *cough*Twilight*cough* but the quest for quality adult literature is an ongoing one. In fact, I often feel like Don Quixote himself, always trying but never succeeding. For once my high hopes were rewarded with a thoroughly enjoyable and at times profoundly disturbing story.

Reapers follows a young girl named Temple who has learned that not only isn't it safe to live in the world because of the "meateaters" but sometimes because the other surviving humans are the worst monsters of all. At the beginning of the book she is living alone on an isolated island, sleeping in an abandoned lighthouse and fishing for food. We are immediately given the sense of desolation that she feels, her language is unsophisticated and she is harder than anyone should have to become. But Temple was born into this world of horror and death, this is where she belongs and the only thing she knows. In the manner of a true survivor she can find beauty in the simple things around her and even in the very monsters that threaten her life.

Bell tells a simple tale. A girl is forced to leave her island and travels with the dream of someday seeing Niagara Falls Along the way she meets many different kinds of people and monsters, until in the end she must face what it ultimately means to be human. In Moses Todd Temple finds her counter part: a man as hard on the outside as she is on the inside. Their stories are intertwined and the relationship between them is romantic without any of the complications of sex. Perhaps romantic is the wrong word, what they feel is more like the mutual respect of an honorable enemy or perhaps a brother. There are no shocking twists or sudden revelations. There is no deep mystery. What there is, however; is a story so eloquently written, full of so much truth, that you almost expect to walk outside and see "slugs" slowly lumbering toward you.

So what does it mean to be human? When we look at our lives what separates us from the "meatskins" who go about their days simply reacting and moving on instinct? Are we only surviving or is there something more to being human, something beyond eating, breathing, working, plodding through life. For Temple there is. There is something sacred and precious about life; there is a plan and God has seen to it that we're all in the place we're supposed to be. Even id we don't understand God is a "slick" God and he knows what he's doing. Temple has seen the very worst of what people are but she has also seen the beauty of miracles.

Temple is a difficult character to relate to. She's tough and hard. She handles herself in a way I'd like to think I would should zombies take over the planet. She kills with precision, both zombie and human when necessary. But she is broken. The world that she lives in is a terrible place and it has been her mother, father and mentor through life. She knows nothing else. Responsibility and honor guide her through a world with no rules. The small havens of normalcy she finds feel as alien to her as the outside world of Reapers would appear to us; she will never belong there, but there is nothing in the world that matters more to her than the safety of those who do.

The Reapers are The Angels is a mature book, the violence and gore are intense and the lessons in it are hard learned. It's the moral though; that I think takes an adult mind to truly grasp. Concepts of sacrifice, family, and morality are rarely conveyed as profoundly as they are in Reapers. Bell has managed to give us the perfect Anti-Heroine in a world without heroes in a time without hope. Temple takes us on a journey through the worst parts of human nature only to show us that in the end, all that matters is what you hold inside of you.

I was very disappointed with this book. I don't usually give negative reviews but..this was the first book ever to make zombies look...well like kittens! They don't appear scary at all. Nor does the world- I love scary end of the world books and this one really wasn't that! In the least! It was sad but in a people way...and the ending just ruined it. I saw there was a second book so I decided to read it- I dislike stories of only one book as it does take many, I believe, to truly get drawn into the world and into others reality in these books...and this...short and sad- And truly did not build the world or anyone's lives well. It was very hard to like the heroine- It was more gore than anything and not scary. The one creatures were sort of scary BUT it didn't even delve into it at all!

Also I agree with the others- NO Quotations so I constantly had to decide if someone was talking or not- And truly a LOT of things did not make sense- No running out of food, no one seems scared of zombies?? SO WEIRD! And the lead character does NOT even STICK to her character! One minute she is strong and wants to be on her own- The next she is imploring and even begging people to take her in- even though even BEFORE she gets there she doesn't want to be trapped anywhere more than a day with OTHERS- Huh? Then why is she begging them to let her in for a night? If she is so self sufficient and dislikes others..why in the heck does she want to stay there? And throwing in the sex with the boy who didn't even leave with her was RIDICULOUS- She doesn't seem the fast and loose type- She just never sticks to her character- And the world is very unbelievable. I normally love most dystopian and zombie novels...but this was..not scary, not believable- Heck give me a freaking zombie apocalypse now if I can just have whatever I want and yet not be scared! Live where i want- and there is still food,water etc. HECK the world seems about perfect instead of horrible,LOL!- No more working for anything and you can have whatever you want?? And not be scared?? REALLY! And you can sit and wait for very slow moving "animals" and just shoot them, even up close? Like fish in a barrel or turtles- That is what the zombies seemed like- Big turtles! RIDICULOUS!!!!

Seriously- And also why does everyone seem like rednecks or that the are from the 18-1900's ??? :/

Also why does she need to borrow cars or anything?? Seeing as there are a ton for the picking and gas is everywhere? JUST UNREAL! Give me a freaking break. WORST book! This is my first truly negative review. Truly

SPOILERS!!
Beautiful and atypical zombie story with a great heroine. I found this book extremely sad

This is the first book I've ever come close to regurgitating the "can't put it down" cliche for.

If Cormac McCarthy wrote zombie novels, they would be just like this. I cannot think of a higher compliment I have ever paid a piece of writing.

Synopsis:
Zombies have infested a fallen America. A young girl named Temple is on the run. Haunted by her past and pursued by a killer, Temple is surrounded by death and danger, hoping to be set free.
For twenty-five years, civilization has survived in meager enclaves, guarded against a plague of the dead. Temple wanders this blighted landscape, keeping to herself and keeping her demons inside her heart. She can't remember a time before the zombies, but she does remember an old man who took her in and the younger brother she cared for until the tragedy that set her on a personal journey toward redemption. Moving back and forth between the insulated remnants of society and the brutal frontier beyond, Temple must decide where ultimately to make a home and find the salvation she seeks.

I would first like to say I received this book from the Henry Holt publishing Co. in exchange for a fair and honest review.

I feel bad for Alden Bell who had the misfortune of having his post-apocalyptic tale published on the heels of Justin Cronin’s The Passage. It is hard to avoid comparison. Both deal with a world overrun with the walking dead, though in this book the plague are zombies.
I love post-apocalyptic novels, have for over 25 years. Ever since Stephen King’s The Stand came out I have been fascinated by the tales of collapsed societies and how people deal with their new reality. These books can be studies into the human condition if well done.

I do not think this book was well done at all. It was not well researched nor was the back story of how zombies came into being ever flushed out. Both are very important if a book is to be believable. Characters have to be likable for me to enjoy a book. I did not like Temple at all.

The main character, Temple is a young uneducated self sufficient teen. I could have liked her had we not witnessed her killing another human and calling a mute mentally impaired man “dummy” several times. In the second chapter Temple comes across a large human colony where she is warmly invited to stay. She is warned not to visit the “4the neighborhood”, the part of the colony in which the single, rough men live. Of course Temple visits, playing cards late at night with them. When one tries to force himself on her she kills him. I am not saying she deserved the almost rape, but she could have handled it in a less fatal manner. After all there are only so many humans, and had she could have run out of the room screaming “rape.” Others would have come to her aid. Instead the killing leads to the victim’s brother chasing her throughout the book bent on revenge. The relationship between the two is creepy. On one had he wants to kill her, on the other he seems to be the only one who “understands her”. It reminds me of a classic abusive relationship. Other reviewers see this as a mentor/nemesis relationship, but it left me unsettled.
Since the back story is not explained we readers have no idea what kind of infrastructure is in place and why some towns have electricity and why some are leveled. In an absurd scene Temple not only finds a car that starts right up (this after sitting for 25 years) she stops at a gas station to fill it up. If Bell had done his homework he would have found out gasoline goes bad after six months. 25 year old gas would be worthless. There is more to complain about, but this is a review not a
paper. I used this as example of how poorly researched the book is.

Bell may have used the zombie/post-apocalyptic setting to tell a deeper story. Temple is on the run, not only from a killer but from her past. Redemption seems to be the theme, yet I could not get passed the poor research, absurd scenes and a unlikable main character. The end is supposed to be tragic yet I had the feeling Bell had no idea how to redeem Temple. Other reviewers seem to love this book, but I cannot recommend it. Read it if you love zombie carnage, but pass if you like well researched, fully believable stories.

An uber-capable young woman wanders through the American south-east decades after the Zombie Apocalypse.

First, from a writing standpoint, this book is technically well written. The prose is very professional and clear. The dialog, descriptions and action are all well done. I particularly liked Temple's Southern cracker vernacular. Some of which was very humorous. In places the prose may be a little baroque, but I enjoyed the filigree.

Plotting was less well done. This is a "Road Novel", but with Zombies. (The journey propelled the plot.) It vaguely reminded me of The Road, that famous example of Road Novels in an apocalyptic setting. Generally, the stops were well thought out, with the notable exception of

I had severe issues with the author's post-apocalyptic 'world'. It was just technically wrong, in foolish ways. The story is set 20+ years into a Zombie Apocalypse. The world should be in an advanced state of returning to nature. (Reading The World Without Us is a good reference for this.) However, in the story the unmaintained roads are mostly clear and the unmaintained electrical grid is still up and running in several places.

In particular, the electrical grid(s) is not automated or robust enough to survive that long a period of neglect.

There is also a plentiful supply of stranded working vehicles to commandeer, along with gasoline available at working pumps. A car or truck left standing for just 5-years has four flat tires and a dead battery. Untreated gasoline has a maximum shelf-life of about 2-years. Its unusable after that period in a modern engine.

The backdrop of the story is written 'as-if' the world is only 9-months into the apocalypse, instead of the intended 20+ years. Temple's journey just wasn't credible.

Characters were a mixed bag. Subordinate characters were OK. In places, even very good. The Moses character was real good. However, the story was written from the POV of Temple, an illiterate, 15-17 year old girl, the Warrior Princess of the Wasteland.

In the beginning, I thought the use of this character was a true inspiration. Then the author took her in the wrong direction. As the story developed, Temple revealed herself to be wise way beyond her years. There was no character growth; yet she was fully grown. I'd expect her to be 50-years old and not 15. For example, despite her charming dialog, the illiterate Temple, had an internal dialog with the vocabulary of a MFA. She knew the meaning of 'nuanced' and 'connoisseur'! I found myself to always be at odds with this split-personality.

This story had its points, but its flaws consumed its advantages. I suspect the author had literary pretensions when he started writing this book. He wanted it to be like Station 11 . And, it could have been, but he failed. He could not artfully disguise himself as his protagonist: a 15-year old, girl, without letters, kukri wielding, Buffy the Vampire Slayer (of Zombies). Also, in this day of the Zombie apocalypse in popular mass media, how could a serious author render the collapse of civilization so carelessly?

I won't be reading the other books in the series. There are better Zombie stories to read out there. I'd recommend trying, Patient Zero for better Zombie horror.

The Reapers are The Angels by Alden Bell is an excellent novel. This is an important statement because of the one word I did not say, and that word is “Zombie”. Because this is not just an excellent zombie novel, but just an excellent novel. Period. Alden Bell has combined the dark and disturbing genre of “Southern Gothic” with the, to be honest mediocre genre of “Zombie” fiction. What he has created is a character and a world that is both disturbing and comforting in its familiarity.

Temple is 15 years old and was born 10 years into the zombie uprising. She has never known a world without zombies. She was “raised” in an orphanage that was overrun by zombies while she was still a very young child. Because of this she has had to grow up on the road wandering the southern states. Uneducated in the traditional sense, Temple is unable to read or write, but is knowledgable in the skills necessary to survive in the zombie world.

The southern gothic aspects lend themselves in surprising ways to the novel. Temple is an odd mixture of ignorance and brilliance. Although uneducated, Temple is not ignorant. The novel is told mostly as an internal monologue, out of necessity, as she is alone, or with a mute, developmentally disabled, companion for most of the novel. Her thoughts are complex and much, much more mature than her 15 years. As she travels, Temple comes to a city that is trying to make a stand in a complex of high rises. While there she is attacked by a man and kills him in self-defense. Because of this, the man’s brother swears he is going to kill her, and the remainder of the novel is her attempts to evade this man named Moses Todd. They meet several times during the novel and it is obvious that they feel a connection to each other. Not in a sexual way, but as kindred spirits. At one point Temple and Moses are talking and Temple explains that she killed Moses’ brother because he attacked her and that he was not a good person. She does not tell him this in a begging way but just explains it. The funny thing is Moses admits that his brother was not a good person, but it does not really make a difference because family honor demands he avenge his brother’s death.

The relationship between Moses Todd and Temple is the driving force of this novel. The reader reads page after page of them meeting and sparing, and, at least in my case, hoping they will find a way to solve their differences without one having to kill the other. There are several times in the novel where Temple could have killed Moses Todd, but she chooses not to do it because he had not done anything to her yet, and she understands why he is seeking revenge. I get the impression that she approves and would do the same thing in his shoes. The southern gothic theme of duty and honor are the major theme of this novel.

This novel is beautifully written, and the reader will feel they are traveling with Temple. Her sense of overall contentment with this world that most would find unbearable is a wonder to behold. She sees the miracle of Gods work all around her. Her faith is unbreakable, and on the surface seems so simple, but is in fact so profound that it almost boggles the mind. She feels that God puts people where they are meant to be. In the very beginning of the novel, Temple is at a light house in Florida, and one night she sees a school of glow-in-the-dark fish. This is an example of Gods wonder. Everything that happened in her life led her to seeing these fish. Call it fate or God’s will, but Temple does not rail against her life or wish things were different. The ending is truly horrific, but left me with a sense of hope I had no right to feel.

This review has not done this book justice, just read the novel, you won’t be sorry.

5 of 5 stars

"A knockout! A fresh take on the zombie novel, with a heroine you can't help but root for as she braves the land of the living dead and the dead living, pursued by a foe more dangerous than the beacon of redemption flickering ahead." --Tom Franklin

This book didn't quite meet the mark for me, it didn't get my hyped up or anxious at all(ok maybe only one or two scenes, scattered here and there) like i expected it to. The synopsis wasn't bad tho, haha. However, i kinda like the ending, but at the same time disappointed/shocked. (SPOILER ALERT!) I didn't expect her to die in the end, seriously did not see it coming, at all. So yeah, it came as a pretty big shock.

The whole book was generally slow-paced - mostly describing about the barren landscapes and all the slugs(term for zombies)around Georgia, Statenville, and all the other places she's been to thru'out the book - and let's just say she's been a nomad all her life..so you can imagine how much of the book was on description. It got so bad that i skipped 20~30 pages of the back part and read the end where there was this teeny climax.

The strong heroine really struck a chord with me - she knew how to kick ass>D (really well, i might add. Liked it) She didn't see a world that was beautiful, and i thought, it was THIS world that she was missing. And yeah, this world is beautiful, if you see past the conflicts and stuff around the world. Maybe our world isn't so different from her slug-infested one after all, what with all the poverty, starvation, diseases and conflicts. And if i were her, i would've died a long time ago already.

There were random spurts and bits of romance parts in there, with the Griersons and (surprisingly) Moses Todd. Todd struck me as an unshaven man well into his forties..And the main girl, Temple, is only fifteen! So when it was clear he liked her, which was after she died, i was left shocked and like saying "PAEDO!" But after i got that out of my system i felt quite crappy for them. Things could've really worked out well for both of them since both were survivors with an attitude. Or well maybe not, since both of them have such an odd relationship - what with Todd's obligation to kill her for killing his brother.

The world Bell created is a rather bleak and scary world to even imagine living in, with a nice story and successful twist(which i just spoiled for some readers:P i warned you tho...), it did give me a little satisfaction for finishing the better part of the book. But i'm giving it a 2 out of 5 because i don't think i'll even consider touching it again..It's just not my type:)

Tho this book probably won't make my top 20 fave books, it left me thinking of a lot of things and with mixed emotions - mainly sad that the main girl died-.- By right, it should have been a successful book, but the process of reading it was rather laborious, if i must say. Too much description.

Well, those who has a liking for zombie novels can give this a try.

PS. Is it, i don't know, universally recognised to write dialogues the way Bell does it without the "double quotation marks"?

I consumed this one quickly much as a pack of "meatskins" might attack a stack of human pancakes. I was so hungry for something NOT for young adults, though I couldn't help myself weighing this one for possible purchase for a school library, but there are a couple of scenes that might be over the top, most notably the near rape of our young heroine, Temple, who also calls herself Sarah Mary Williams, as part of her determined navigation 25 years after the start of a zombie apocalypse. She was born into a world "of the living dead and the dead living," to quote Tom Franklin, an author whose blurb appears on the back of this novel Tom Franklin.

We meet the fifteen year old in isolation at a lighthouse on a small island in the Florida Keys, a sanctuary she knows is ending when a broken--but still snapping away--zombie washes up on its shore. Haunted by the loss of a man who befriended her and the boy Malcolm, who might or might not have been her brother, who taught her some of the skills of killing and surviving that have her still among the living who walk the earth, rather than the dead. In mourning for Malcolm as well, whose story comes only in hints throughout most of the novel, Temple finds beauty where she can, like the flashing fish who swim around her ankles in the surf, and she doesn't blame the meatskins for following their nature: They are a fact of life for her, and she can't much settle in the enclaves of safety and community that she stumbles on. In one large Florida group, a man attacks her. When she kills him in self defense, she makes a permananet enemy of his large, imposing, tracker brother Moses, who dogs her escape at every turn. In her flight, she picks up a stray, a 30-something "dummy" she can't just abandon. Her dream of seeing Niagra Falls must wait while she attempts to reunite Maury with the relatives whose names are written on a scrap of paper in his pocket, a note Temple must have someone read for her, as her education was interrupted by zombies overrunning the orphanage.

A memorable character with an even-keeled way of looking at a mad world, presented in often moving language. My complaint: he is too much a fan of Cormac McCarthy, hence the lack of quotation marks to aid the reader. Luckily, he hasn't sworn off commas as much as his mentor. Remniscient, in some ways, of The Road, this one has more rockin' zombie action and some serious downhome Southern cornbread flavor. Southern Gothic, Flannery O'Connor, blah, blah, blah. It was good if a little self-conscious.

I hummed and haahed between 4 and 5 stars for this - clearly I really enjoyed it. I enjoy most post-apocalyptic media in general, although admittedly the zombie craze is not my favourite (excluding The Walking dead comics & tv series) - I usually prefer the post nuclear or plague types. In a way this had the feel of the plague types though as it had gorgeous descriptions of the world 'after' and less of the 'hide / run away / escape' that zombie books often have - I'm into the whole empty world / few survivors thing. The zombies themselves are not even remotely the focus of the book, which is probably how I prefer it (see again, The Walking Dead).

I very much enjoyed the play between the two main characters - Temple and Moses - and thought they were both well visualised and believable. It's basically a series of Temple's encounters as she travels the world that remains, and her thoughts and musings, and they were a great, interesting little series of vignettes of how the world has progressed. Yes there's some 'sillyness' and suspensions of disbelief - this does seem to be a book you either 'get' or don't get and hate it - lots of 5 star or 1 star reviews. Having read some of both, I do see both sides, but am happy to, personally, dismiss the faults and quibbles. I had no problems with the lack of speech marks, as it wasn't a difficult read, and I've not read enough Cormac McCarthy to be annoyed by that (only The Road, duh) and I had no problems with believing that gas may remain in some distant out of the way petrol stations or that some electricity generators would still work - after all it's only 25 years after, not hundreds. We are, after all, reading a book where most of the people in the world are zombies. Suspension of belief required.

I'm one of those people who are bright but not intellectual, if you see what I mean. Although I know I should enjoy the classics, I often don't, and since becoming a mum and having no peace of mind to sit down and concentrate on a book without interruption, I've probably got even worse at being able to enjoy books that you have to concentrate on, as I can't enjoy it when I'm being constantly interrupted or asked for things. I mean, there's not that many intellectual 'clever' p-a books...so taking that into consideration, I didn't find the prose 'purple' just thoughtful, didn't realise it was trying too hard, just felt like a young girl in a hard life that was far too empty of distractions. When you're alone with your thoughts...This book was an easy read but a an exciting and thoughtful one. Had no idea it was a young adult book but I'm in my mid thirties and it didn't bother me. It seemed to have fairly adult themes but then I grew up reading Judy Blume so who am I to judge? :D

The Reapers are the Angels:

This book was so beautiful, so amazing in every way, I wanted to re-read it right the moment I finished it, and that is one intense feeling I never had for a long time. The Reapers are the Angels is my first zombie novel, and on and on I keep thinking, why did I skip this?

If you haven’t read it yet, don’t look at the reviews- the good or the bad- just go and read the damn book, you’re wasting time reading my review here. If you’re looking for a dark, intense, bloody, suspense, action-packed, this is it. This is the one, and you won’t find another one like this. Trust me, I’m still searching out there. If you are looking for a light-humor, zombie book, go read – “Warm Bodies.” This is a book with a serious, dark tone and yet beautiful.

The main character, Temple, is fifteen years old. But, this is not – I repeat – Not a young-adult novel. I’m not sure why people are tagging this as such.

Temple's thoughts and words turned into drugs for me. I want to know what she sees, how she feels, what she does in a certain situation. And when the book ended, I felt like I lost something in me. And I keep thinking, I want more- more of Temple’s thought, eyesight, her world. I think I’m obsessed and not in a pleasant way. The kind that keeps me awake at night, and I wonder if I’ll get better, cause I haven’t had a decent sleep since I finished this novel.

Little girl. Little girl. Little girl. (Don’t mind me, I’ve gone nuts)

I love how Temple sees the beauty in her forsaken world. Her opinion on god, her thoughts, and the way she thinks is just so realistic, and amazing, you forget you’re just reading a book. Temple was born into this world, she doesn’t know much about the previous world. A time where there wasn’t a hoard of zombies crawling and dragging their rotten body through cities and towns. A time where little girls at the age of fifteen did not bash zombies’ head and swing blades.

I can keep writing on and on about how good this book is, but you will never know unless you read it. And if you skip this book, because either the cover wasn’t cool-looking enough, or the book review didn’t sound interesting to you. Well... You're missing out and you don't even know it!

Now, I'm going to go hear the audiobook, and god forbid if someone disturbs me.

I am baffled. How can a book about zombies be beautiful?

I am awestruck by the beauty and grotesqueness of it all. Beginning a book set in a world infested with zombies with a scene as beautiful as luminescent fish beneath a powerful moon, genius. I didn't feel like the characters were just shallow representations of real-life people, just words on a page. I became invested in who they were, and where they were going. A necessity if I am to gain anything from a book (I think I say that over and over again, but it is so true).

It probably took me far too long to recognize this parallel between...no not parallel...connection between the beautiful and the gruesome. At one point Temple says, "beauty and evil are on opposite sides of a wall like lovers who can never really touch," but I honestly don't know. How can a character who is written into that world -- who is able to actually see beauty in that world -- feel that way? It was hard for me not to lose myself in thought while I read, thinking about how nothing is ever as simple as good or bad, beautiful or ugly, evil or pure. Beautiful things are beautiful because they have flaws.

Is it dangerous though, getting caught up in the beautiful things in life, losing awareness of reality? Bad things happen in Temples life when she becomes unaware, and that seems important. It is an importance that is beyond me though. I don't know what it is...

One thing that I could not quite piece together, what was the purpose of Millie, Maury, and Malcolm? I get that Malcolm was her maybe brother, and that moment is fundamental to who her character becomes. I don't understand the purpose of the hard to understand charges...are they a representation of some sort of purity? Surely not...Millie does not evoke that image for me, perhaps in some sort of childlike innocence, but not even that. She tries to be a caretaker, unless she was just treating them as play-things. Do they maybe represent a bridge, a connection, to that pureness that Temple feels like she doesn't have?

Oh! And, I loved Moses (speaking of connections). I loved how connected he was with Temple in this really weird and twisted way. (Should I spoiler this?) I love the resolution of the end scenes. They were poignant, but not really in a way I am used to. I felt sort of shell-shocked and awed at the same time.

Also, I would love to write about the gaze as it pertains to this book. Does that make me a total nerd?

Do you like reading zombie books? Neither do I. They aren’t my top pick. They are always full of gore. I can handle gore, probably better in literary form than in movie form. But it’s not my favorite thing. Although I did love Pride and Prejudice and Zombies. Well this book is definitely a zombie book. But it’s more than that too. If I said that this is a zombie book with heart, would that be too cheesy? Because I think it’s an apt description.

It’s beautifully written. The main character, named Temple (a girl who seems a lot older than her fifteen years) is from the south. The narration and her voice have a southern accent. Kind of like Huck Finn I guess. I bet Alden Bell read Huck Finn before he wrote this book. Anyway, here is a small sample of the writing,

See, God is a slick god. He makes it so you don’t miss out on nothing you’re suppose to witness firsthand.

That’s another thing. Most, if not all, post-apocalyptic fiction I’ve read ignores God. He is either no where to be seen, long forgotten or given up on. This book brings God in from the first page. It also seamlessly blends in evolution. I love that the characters all talk about God. I keep wondering if setting this book in the south is why God still exists in the minds of the characters. Anyway, people in this novel even go to church. Not our main character, of course, but other people do.

Now for the problems. Every book has them. This book is set 25 years after a zombie infestation began. 25 years. There are times in the novel where Temple runs into an abandoned store and gets supplies. It’s a small thing but so unbelievable for me. I would think that the packages of cheese crackers she grabs would be either long gone in 25 years or really bad. People still also had electricity. How is that possible? Is it? I don’t know but it seems strange that there would still be electricity if no one is around to work in the plants. The setting, the way it all played out, it wasn’t really that original. There wasn’t a lot that was completely new. It was worth reading, for me, because of the style. It was beautiful and haunting. I just finished reading it, but I can already feel it haunting my brain. I was even thinking in a southern accent for at least an hour after I read it. But, I Hated the ending.

Even with all it’s problems, I would still give this one a solid 4 stars (out of 5). If you like zombies, then this is definitely a book worth reading.

Actual Rating: 3.5

Let me begin by saying, this book was not what I was expecting. I found that I wasn't over-excited to hurry and finish so I could find out what happens. It was more like I couldn't wait to find something else to do. In other words, it was a slow read for me. What I found though, I didn't hate the book.

The Reapers Are the Angels, tells us a compelling story about survival through the eyes of fifteen year old Temple. Alone in the world after a tragedy struck, she travels the decaying world seeking only ways of surviving. For Temple, there never was "a time before the zombies", so she knows not of the ways of generations past. For her, zombies are as normal as birds flying. I found that I really liked Temple, she's a strong, resourceful and fiercely independent young woman who's just as flawed as any human being. And just like everyone, she's got demons she'd rather not acknowledge. Her personal journey takes her to others, communities of people bent on rebuilding their world, hunters roaming the lands and finding, special ways of surving, and a family lost in their own world, refusing to accept anything beyond the perimeters of their property. But growing up in a world where the dead are living and the living dead, Temple knows it's best to keep moving and not look back.

This book was more spiritual, than urban fantasy. It was a story of survival and redemption, there's zombies and an apocalyptic world, but that's just background noise... and that's where I hit a road block in my reading. I couldn't get past that, the story itself is amazing, Alden Bell does a great job in painting this dying world, and the characters are so vivid and real. The actions Temple takes in order to survive, so gruesome, violent, horrific, and cringe inducing. It was less fantasy and more realism, and honestly I'm not use to these type of books. I gravitate more towards paranormal romances, urban fantasy books, where the line between real and fiction isn't blurred.I will say, though, that the ending was a shock ;)

The book, I recommend to anyone who's interests are that of realistic fiction. It's not bad, I've read great reviews about it, and a Goodreads friend of mine highly recommended it.. Believe me when I say, it's not the book, it's me. Lol :]

Who balances out the world? Is there some sort of crazy checks and balance system that a higher being tallies up? Things that seem unfair to us.... are they actually pre-destined?

This book is serious and dark. It's also compelling, haunting, an old melody that you remember from long ago, yet are missing notes. The lead character had me at her first conversation with a meatbag. Here's this 15 year old girl who's been surviving since she knew what a zombie was, and she still has humanity in her. I suppose that's what makes all great people, that even in times of direness, of blood and unfairness, that spark of humanity of what's right and then what should be done. That line is usually blurry and not easy to spot. Temple thinks she's evil. She kills, even for survival, taking another creature of god is evil. She kills to protect, someone dies who she fails to protect, and yet it is still killing. She knows that her organs and heart are made up of twisted bits that have grown since her brother Malcolm died.
The journey she finds herself on can be one of many things. It's for survival yes, yet also an engaging one about who she is and who she kills to protect. An enemy seems to be the only other one who understands the gravity of life and death, of nature and god. Though he swears to hunt her down for killing her brother, their exchanges are philosophical and deep. I teared up at the end. It was as if my brain couldn't figure out whether the ending gave Temple what she wanted, what she needed, or nothing. She sees the strings that attach fate and miracles. Maybe she got her own.

It's really a novel that will stick with me. The type of narrative it is sort of blunts the readers to the violence, not hearing her voice from her, but from a third person, yet everything happens in real time. I think that not explaining why there are zombies actually made the novel more realistic. We were thrown in to a spot in time of Temple's life, she's not going to be thinking about how it started, for her it always was. This is one that I will pass on to a select few who I believe will appreciate it as much as I did.

*also reviewed on amazon*
One of my top 2010 books (I adore this one)

Reviews seem to go back and forth on whether or not this is actually a YA novel, so I thought I'd give this a shot despite not being a fan of YA in the slightest. To be fair, the first few chapters pulled me in. I wanted to like this, really. I've yet to find a good post-apocalyptic novel with good female characters. This book promised that, plus a change from the typical urban setting. Unfortunately, there are a few issues:



I know I'm tearing into this book more than it deserves, probably. It was just so disappointing after how much I enjoyed the opening chapters.

I was really looking forward to reading this, it looked awesome and maybe I would have liked it better if not for one of the scenes in the beginning of the book: "They stumble out of the utility closet, three of them (..)They must have fed recently, so they will be strong. And they are between her and the stairs."
How did they get in there? And if they were put in there, who puts three zombies in a utility closet, that are apparently at their strongest?
And did they have a snack with them in there, since they've all recently fed or to be fair they could've snacked of each other. AS they are later on revealed to do when in a tight spot (pun intended).
Three zombies don't randomly wander into a closet and lock the door after them, they don't hang out there till someone happens to come into the room and they certainly don't lay in wait in an old meth lab, in a basement, in a utility closet!
I know for many this would be a detail, but it annoyed me so much I kept thinking about it throughout the book, it wouldn't have annoyed me if the main character had thought about it, but it was apparently a natural occurrence.
To me it seemed like a bad scene from a video game.
Other than that, I thought it was a good take on how society could be, some in secure groups and some as drifters. And I liked Moses and mostly I did actually like Temple.
But another thing annoyed me and that was the lack of "" around the dialogue. I kept getting reminded I was reading a book, since I had to go back a lot and see if it was something she had said out loud or just thought, because it could be either or. I first gave it one star, but I'm going to up it to two, since writing this review has reminded me of its better points. I also liked the mutants and the fish...
Edit: You know what I take it back; one star it is. After reading some other reviews, I realize how unresearched it actually is (gasoline etc) and the editing is nonexistent. I just didn't realize the other things because i was obsessing over the plot hole... This book has made me angry! It could have been fantastic, if the work had been done properly! GAH!

See my other reviews at Never Enough Books

For over twenty-five years, humanity has survived in small meager enclaves, guarding against the plague of zombies that have infested America. Among the survivors is a young woman named Temple, who prefers to travel the blighted landscape than stay still. She doesn't remember a time before the zombies but she does remember the old man who took her in and the younger brother she once cared for.

Moving across the brutal frontier, Temple is haunted by her past and soon becomes pursued by a killer. Surrounded by death and danger she must search where to try and make a home and find the redemption she needs.

This is one of those books that it rather hard to describe. While many categorize it as a sort of post-apocalyptic zombie novel, in truth that barely begins to describe things. Yes, the setting is a post-apocalyptic America; where an unnamed event has decimated the land; and yes, zombies do play a part in the narrative. Yet, there is so much more.

The Reapers are the Angels is coming of age story as well. Temple, our narrator and main character, is barely a teenager searching for a place to call home. Every place she finds herself, events occur and Temple finds herself leaving either by choice or by force. All the while she is trying to come to terms with events that occurred in the past that set the story in motion.

There are some who might have issue with the narrative style of The Reapers are the Angels. It has a very stream of consciousness feel which can be disconcerting at times. There are no actual quotes to indicate when a person is speaking, sometimes leaving the reader wondering who has said what.

Much as I enjoyed The Reapers are the Angels, it is doubtful I will be reading the subsequent books in the series. Certain events occurred, which I will not reveal due to spoilers, that rather ruined the ending for me.

Though the book itself is rather slim, I found it to be a good read. I would recommend it to those looking for something to entertain and perhaps make them think, but know that you might be disappointed too.

La lectura de este libro me dolió mucho. Luego de esperar tanto por su distribución a México, luego de por fin haberlo encontrado en El sótano (literal y figurativamente), luego de haberme maravillado con las reseñas y críticas ovacionantes, me topo no con un mal libro, sino con una enorme tristeza.

Al principio supe que Alden Bell tomó el camino fácil de los best-sellers al apuntar hacia la tríada de venta: Un tema de moda, un héroe de ensueño y un mercado meta asombrable. Pese a ello, pienso que se necesita una buena novela profunda y original que arrope con justicia a la figura del no-muerto. En la prelectura, La ira de los ángeles afirmaba serlo, pero no.

Antes que nada debo advertir que La ira de los ángeles y The Reapers are the Angels son dos libros totalmente distintos. La traducción de Adolfo Muñoz García (un nombre que nunca olvidaré) parece venida de un asistente de tallerista preparatoriano: Muletillas constantes, cambios de personajes y vocablos irrisorios hicieron de la narración un tropiezo tras otro. Pensando que la traducción era fiel a la posible mediocridad original, conseguí el texto en inglés y comparé ambas lecturas. Señores, para ser traductor hace falta mucho más que el certificado de Harmon Hall.

Pero tienen razón, ¿qué culpa tiene el libro de la traducción eshpaniola (sí, así es la traducción, eshpaniola)? Habría que ser justos con Bell y reconocer su trabajo. Original, aventurero y con ganas de hacer vomitar al lector, la historia de The Reapers are the Angels parece buena opción si de holocaustos zombies no sabes nada. Y digo parece porque con la traducción de Muñoz García no se puede tener certeza de que los disparates ahí descritos sean realmente como se habían imaginado.

En definitiva, es un libro que le prestaría a mis neófitos alumnos para que vean tripas y canibalismo en un libro sin el menor pudor, y ya. La ira de los ángeles no cumple con ninguna otra función que no sea la de demostrar de qué manera un narrador puede estorbar en la historia.

I didn't like this book from the beginning but I thought I would finish it before I made a comment about it, as it's hard to judge a book before you've read it completely. It wasn't SO bad, I guess, and a few points were actually well-thought, but it wasn't a really pleasant read either.
It should also be said that I didn't read the original edition, but the french translation instead.
Nevertheless, have a list of what bugged me:

- The only black people we meet are a butler and a maid happily working for a family of white people, in a big and rich residence. Really? I mean, *really*? We don't get to know a lot about them either, they're just on the background, taking care of the house and the family. I'm sorry, did this Apocalypse thing rewind the USA to their Segregation phase?

- God. Lots and lots of religious references, shoved down the throat. I actually don't mind religious characters at all, they're characters just as good as any other, and yes, I can see how a Zombie Apocalypse can call for some return to Faith. But it was poorly handled and became really soon irritating, from my modest atheist point of view.

- The "show don't tell" rule is applied for the world itself, but not for the characters. A lot of conversations between the hero and any other character is spent to describe how we're supposed to percieve the hero ("you're like this" or "i'm like that").

- Also, everyone approves of the hero and thinks she's great. Even the man who hunts her down to kill her.

- The writing-style was flat, as was the rythm of the story, which always makes it harder to get into the action.

Thoses are the main points. Some others were actually more interesting, like how the hero didn't know how to read or how nobody really knew nor cared about what's appropriate anymore. (The hunters eating zombie for dinner on a regular basis, for one). You don't expect the ending either, so yay for the surprise, but the hero dies and it actually feels good, so that tells something about how unlikable she is.

Holy cow. I have debated whether to go four or five stars, and for now am settling with five. The writing is incredible. It is like Henry James or Flannery O'Connor. I seriously could not put this book down and neglected my family for a day and a half until I finished. Then it took me a few hours to re-enter this planet. This book will completely suck you in.

In some ways I loved this book, and in some I hated it. The main character, Temple, is 15 years old, but this is not a YA novel. She is just roaming, existing with all her demons inside, trying to do the right thing, but not sure what exactly that is. Temple is very much a realist. She has never known a time before zombies, and she is not angry or dramatic. She accepts the world the way it is. She wants to stay alone, she wants to be uncaring and a loner, but finds herself unable to do this.

The book is so bizarre because on the one hand, it's so intellectual and thoughtful, and on the other hand completely gory and disgusting.

The only places I had to suspend my disbelief: The hillbilly family was a little bit of a stretch for me, but I decided to let it go. I am also not sure a Coke is still good 15 years after it was created. I also found myself wanting to know more about the communities in California rumored to exist. I also wanted to know if the whole world was affected in the same way.

The ending made me want to blow a gasket, or pop a vein in my forehead. Not sure what else to say so I don't spoil it for someone.

Cleanliness Factor: A lot of gore, however, I thought it was done in a matter-of-fact way rather than gratuitously. But it is definitely there. Two brief sexual encounters. Not very graphic, but they are there. I skipped over it pretty easily. One has to do with a not-nice man finding her and wanting to take advantage of her. One scene with a string of f-bombs--other than that the language was clean, as I recall.

This was easily the most gripping book I've read in a while. I don't go looking for zombie stories but when I find one it better be far and away beyond excellent. This was better than excellent. I was surprised by the beautiful language in what is really a bleak and brutal story. There was something transcendent in the way things were described. This was not your run-of-the-mill disaster story. There are no white hats and black hats, just people who know how the world works now and people in denial - and all kinds of predators in between, not just the dead.

Temple was one of the most refreshing female characters I've ever read. Stopping just short of making her a feral child, we're presented with someone who is practical, resourceful, intelligent and pretty handy in a fight - all of which works for me! There's no illusions about the sort of world she's grown up in but at the same time she manages to see beauty even in the rot and ruin of a dying world. Her outlook on life is surprisingly optimistic and while she fights altruistic urges, she's not so hardened by the need to survive that she won't protect those who need it. Her personal moral code is interesting. I one particular instance I would have 'fixed his wagon' rather than letting a threat continue. I actually like her more because she didn't.

Perhaps one of the strangest things was the complete lack of speech marks. This served to make us feel that we were always deep inside her head even during a conversation. I think it worked but it took getting used to.

Every character was well rounded and satisfying. The end was brutal, visceral and right - though I'm sure it will put some noses out of joint. I'd love to read more in this world. And I don't particularly like zombies!

This was awesome. I loved it and wish I had it to read all over again. If you haven't discovered it yet, set aside some time - you're in for a treat.

I'm not sure I can express the enormity of this book. When I first saw the cover I knew it was no ordinary zombie post-apocalypse novel, but I had no way of knowing the depth at which it would touch me. The Reapers are the Angels can easily stand beside novels like The Road, Earth Abides, and A Canticle for Leibowitz, as a modern day classic.

Yes, there are zombies and yes, there are scenes with blood and mayhem, but those take back seat to the human condition. The Reapers are the Angels is a character driven story that reads more like literary fiction than genre fiction. Temple, the main character is not a survivor of a forgotten world, she was born into a dying world.

It's a given, Temple is no ordinary fifteen year old. There were times I forgot she was fifteen. The suffering she's seen and experienced has aged her well beyond her twenty's. If you are squeamish about a fifteen year old participating in ADULT situations, then I warn you now this may not be the book for you. But if you delve into her character and realize this is not our world, then her actions are far less shocking. As her story unfolds I found myself grieving for her pain and hoping for an ending I knew could not happen.

Alden's take on a world ravaged by the walking dead is not necessarily original, but the perspective, twenty-five years after, is not one commonly approached. So often with zombie fiction we see the beginning, the trigger but not the outcome. The effect the devastation has on the survivors Alden's world varied from those hiding in small groups to those trying to retake cities. Every bit kept me engaged and fascinated.

I'm putting The Reapers are the Angels on my "keepers for life" stack of books.

Surviving post-apocalyptic America with fierce courage and an unwavering appreciation for everyday miracles, a 15-year-old girl battles zombies and evades a man with a score to settle as she leads a mute traveler across the country to a family she hopes is still alive.

Tormented by shame and regret, Temple lives alone in a lighthouse on a Florida island until a "meatskin" washes up on shore, threatening her self-imposed isolation. Armed with a gurkha knife, the only gift she has ever received, Temple returns to the mainland and does what it takes to survive, even if that means slaughtering zombies who attack her at every turn, fighting off a depraved family of mutants, and briefly taking comfort in the arms of a battle-weary army veteran with secrets of his own. After she kills a man in self-defense, she finds herself on the run from his vengeful brother, Moses Todd. Her road trip quickly evolves into a quest for redemption when she meets Maury, a 35-year-old mute who needs help finding a safe home. As Temple and Maury travel toward Texas, Moses pursues the pair relentlessly, forcing them to make one narrow escape after another culminating in a terrifying final confrontation with an unexpected twist. While the plot centers around the chase and the action is violent and gory, lyrical storytelling creates a mesmerizing, suspended-in-time effect. Temple is an unforgettable heroine who finds slivers of beauty brightening the darkest corners of a crumbling world. Her heartbreaking story of survival and resilience amid brutality and decay is brilliantly told by Bell (pseudonym for Joshua Gaylord, Hummingbirds) in this outstanding novel.

Really enjoyed the book. Didn't care much for the writing style. When writing dialogue between characters, no punctuation was used. I didn't know if Temple was thinking something or actually saying it at times. It was very distracting. I was surprised to see that this was published by a major publishing house because of that issue. Having said that, this book was completely different then any I've read. Surrounded by death and the hopeless of those around her, Temple views everything as part of the bigger picture. On her own since 13 and at two different times in her life, responsible for those less able then her, she is uneducated and has the killing ability far beyond her years. She has a no nonsense way about her, that blindly accepts her fate and always keeps in mind how much worse it could be. She is in a constant moral battle with herself, knowing that the things she does to survive are not necessarily good things. She is a very religious person, but we never find out where that moral compass comes from. She doesn't remember her parents and lives in a world where there is no place for religion in most peoples eyes. Yet she sees it in almost every small thing she encounters. She accepts her fate as "God's Will" and is resigned to live her life, knowing that He puts her exactly where she is meant to be. The ending was not at all what I expected, and I imagine many will be turned off from the entire book just because of the ending. I didn't care for the ending so much, but hey, life sometimes doesn't work out like you planned it either. Overall, great read. I hope Alden Bell writes some more. I would be interested to read it.

I always have my eyes open for a good looking apocalypse novel. I am obsessed with The Walking Dead (more so with the show than the comics - but I have read the first Compendium). I love when end of the world stories are done well, and I especially love a good survivor story. Problem is, I have been extremely disappointed by zombie-novels in the past and am no longer quick to jump into one (I especially know to stay away from YA zombies). "The Reapers are the Angels" just looked too good to skip out on though, and as soon as I stumbled upon it, I ordered it from my library.

I wasn't sure if I liked it at first. It's very different -- not what I was expecting at all. The story takes place about 25 years after the dead stopped staying dead and started eating people, so we never see that initial panic and confusion. Instead, we see the damaged way in which society has attempted -and essentially failed- to put itself back together again. But we see it through a 15 year old girl, who has personally never known anything else, so there is a muted edge to it all. We, as readers, need to accept it and jump right into our heroine's story - which, it turned out, was easy to do.

Temple was strong and admirable. She struggled with her morality and her ability to inflict violence, with ease, on those who threatened her. At first I was not sure how I felt about her, but she grew on me very quickly -- even with the at times annoying, "God is great" talk.

"The Reapers are the Angels" is a refreshingly unique look at the second half of an end to the world. And in no way your average bloodbath zombie novel.

I was really in love with this book. So much violence and beauty, all depicted in the same breathless tone. I came to care deeply about the hardcore, ass kicking, unsure of herself, fifteen year old heroine, Temple. I loved how she was never afraid, and never assumed, never judged, and never (well, mostly never) got caught unprepared. I loved how a little fifteen year old girl could unerringly defend herself against the zombies (meatskins, slugs, creepers...), and against some really scummy people too. I loved how she does what she needs to, then feels awful later. I loved how she does the right thing, even when she doesn't want to. I loved how most people she meets are truly good people. I loves this hideous depressing (but joyful and beautiful) world the author created for us.

But I really really didn't like the ending. It just completely threw me right out of the book. I felt like e author had come up with a great beginning and a great ending, and while he was busy writing the great middle of the book he went off the rails, and ended up someplace else, some place where his original ending didn't really work. But he was really devoted to his original idea, so he used it anyway. And the sound in my head at that moment was the sound you would hear when playing a record and the. Suddenly dragging the needle right across the vinyl. Schreeeeeeeeeech! Wrongness.

I don't understand how this can be a series. What else does he have left to say in this fantastical world he created for us?

By far the best zombie novel I've read. But it's literary fiction with zombies, not a genre book.

Its main character is a teenage girl, but don't let that convince you it's YA. As you can see by some of the one-star reviews here, the language is confusing to ... certain teens, shall we say. Some words have three syllables, so be forewarned. 8/

I liked this a lot (4.5 stars worth) despite three problematic-for-me things. It is in present tense, which I don't like (but can get beyond, if there are other matters to compensate). It has dialog but no quotation marks, which I can seldom get past (but did here). And there are at least fifty references to God, and as a non-religionist, I'd usually be turned off by that. Here, I'm fine with it. I believe in Temple's beliefs and respect them. And if you're a serious, philosophical-type believer, this book should appeal to you for that.

What's good about it is very good: the beautiful language, the elegiac tone, and the wonderful main character, whose moral struggles in a decayed world are moving and thought-provoking.

The driving force of the book is less the plot than that you'll be wondering what happened to Malcolm a few years ago, knowing it's going to be the emotional climax of the book. But the external plot--a road trip through a PA landscape and getting "the dummy" back to his his home--and that backstory inform each other and build a sort of resonance. I suspect I'll be thinking about this one for awhile.

Go "look inside" and see if it's for you. The first five pages will tell you.

3.5 stars

Basically: Temple lives in the middle of the zombie apocalypse and is on a quest to kill as many of them before they get her. There are still a few safe places in the world and when she stays the night in one of them, a man tries to force himself on her. When she manages to get away , she gets to deal with his brother, Moses, who lives according to some old code of honour and wants revenge, so not only does she need to make her way through the zombies, she also needs to stay ahead of Moses, because both are out to get her.

Okay, so I had no idea this was going to be about zombies, but I don't even care. Temple is fantastic and more people should know about her. This is so frustrating, because I want my brother to read this one, so we can talk and talk and talk about the goodness that is Temple and The Reapers are the Angels, but the moment he hears (post)apocalyptic he runs. Somehow he associates it with 1984, which apparently was not a very pleasant experience for him.

This worked as a standalone, but apparently the series goes on, and the sequel(s) is/are focused on Moses. Not sure how I feel about that.

***4.5 stars***

Maybe you ain’t so interested in miracles. But still and all, you can cherish a miracle without deserving one. We’re all of us beholden to the beauty of the world, even the bad ones of us. Maybe the bad ones most of all.

This is so much more than a post-apocalyptic, dystopian, zombie novel.

I’ll be honest: I highlighted the crap out of this book. It was just so beautifully written. It’s gritty and visceral. It’s ugly and dark and sad. But underneath the darkness of it all there is a sense of wonderment, that even when the world has gone horribly wrong there is still beauty to be found. That hope for something better, for a life better than what we’re born into, can exist. And maybe, just maybe we can make it there.

The story is portrayed through the eyes and mind of Temple, a 15 year old girl who is on her own in this new world. I was amazed by Temple. She’s just such a fantastic character. She was hardened by circumstances beyond anyone's control, staying alive by her wits and blade alone. However, under that tough visage was a little girl, still able to marvel at God and man’s creations. She was someone who could look at the grotesque and think, “Miracles’re sometimes hidden by unpleasing looks.” It was really pretty astounding. I could see through her eyes that the world was an amazing place, even with all the death, and rot, and decay, and I was mesmerized viewing the world through her lens.

Her story is one worth reading.

The very first thing I noticed is the lack of quotation marks around the dialogue. I suppose it's a style choice of the author's and whether or not it works is left up to the reader. I eventually got use to it. I did switch back and forth from reading and listening to the audio book. By the way, the narrator, Tai Sammons, is amazing. Her voice is the voice of Temple. Superb performance.

As for the book? I loved it. Loved it. It's so well written. At first, I was a little thrown that this wasn't written in first person because it's told through Temple's voice. It's through her eyes that we view this post-apocalyptic world overrun by zombies, yet it's told in third person? I was confused at this choice, but once I finished reading it, I understood why, and for those who are perceptive will know the reason right away. (But I won't spoil anything for anyone.)

This isn't a "light read" by any stretch of the imagination. It's dark, and at times profound, and occasionally I even found myself laughing. The dialogue is sharp and to-the-point.

I am in awe of Temple, the main character. The way she looks at the world and sees what is and not what she fears or what she wants. She's bad ass, broken, but hopeful and truthful. Her entire journey was so interesting to me. A 15 year old who is more at home alone, on the open roads, surviving, so comfortable in her skin, and yet afraid of the violence she is capable of.

Well done.

This was a book suggested by "A good story is hard to find" podcast and this was just an excellent novel.

I haven't been impressed much within the Zombie genre, but there are intelligent and well-written ones like World War Z. I liked this novel even more since while Zombies play a large part of the plot, the story transcends being just a Zombie novel and is just great story telling of the human condition.

Temple a 15 year old girl who never knew a world without "meatskins" goes on a journey that brings her in touch with different groups and of course constant danger. Temple is more than just a warrior, but someone with a deeper context and one with her ideas of God and meaning and that she takes the world as it is. This book is just so well written with interesting characters that range all over the place and goes far beyond just the "how would people adapt" scenario.

One quirk of this book is that it is written totally without quotes and so all the dialog is inline. This doesn't really distract from it since you can almost always pick up who is saying what by context - it was just a little jarring to me. For me the term "meatskins" never grew on me as a term that people would come to use a dominant term for the living dead, but that is an extremely minor quibble.

Just a great book even for those who want nothing to do with the Zombie genre.

This book has definitely left a mark on me... but how to describe it?
This book doesn't so much focus on the zombies, more that they are part of the setting - just a way of life. It's more about a young girl coming to terms with carrying a terrible guilt.
Temple is an illiterate girl in her mid-teens making her way in a dead land. Once there was family, but now she is alone. Temple's journey is an interesting one, where she finds she can't relate to other people and would rather be alone on the outside, knife in hand, fending off the 'meatskins' than to be trapped within a community of survivors. After a mishap sets her on the run from the community she has found, she is pursued by a man desiring vengeance. There is an understanding between the two that should he catch her, she will die despite the fact that she has his respect and recognizes her as a kindred spirit of sorts.
Temple finds a simpleton, Maury and takes him under her wing aware of the possible problems he will cause and that he will slow her down. She soon makes it her mission to get him home and in this journey, she discovers more about herself and learns to care again.
The book was so unexpected and I suppose this is why I will remember it.
The writing style was probably the let down for me, but the ideas and emotions that are conveyed made this well worth the read.

The Reapers are the Angels is one of my all time favorite books. It is a brutal yet exquisite story of survival and transcendence. Temple is a teenage girl who has survived the end of civilization. She has grown up after and it is all she has ever known. Some people are broken or they have used these circumstances as an excuse to surrender to their most selfish impulses. Other people live unable to face reality or in their dreams of rebuilding a new civilization. Many simply live continually in fear. Temple however is different. She is a true spiritual warrior who sees beauty and God in almost anything. She lives in and accepts the present and the only thing she truly fears is her own capacity for violence. She certainly is not broken and she lives by her own code. She meets a man, Moses Todd, who will become her enemy and hunter and yet they will share the bond of kindred souls. Moses Todd respects and understands her, but will he spare her? Can Temple survive this new brutal world on her own? Can one kill ruthlessly and yet remain at all pure or good?

I will read this book again. It is a story of survival, resiliency, violence and deep spirituality. Alden Bell is brilliant. I'm not sure where this story came from, but I hope he keeps writing more like this one.

Temple was born after the dead rose. The few comforts of this desolate world are all she's known. There was a time when she had family -- a found uncle who guided her, a boy who was her brother -- but for now she is alone, moving forward to a destination even she doesn't yet know.

OH. MY. GAWD. This book. Just don't.. like just stop reading this and go get it.

Bell's writing is so taunt that you just move forward page after page, as Temple moves forward to place after place, and you want so badly for her to get what it is so badly she is seeking, even though you can see she already has so much more than what she knows. Many have compared the temperance of the writing -- the pace, the place, the stoic resignation of what is instead of what could be -- to Flannery O'Conner's Gothic sensibilities and I can't help but echo that comparison. The devil of this book is in the details, the ones that got to Temple and the ones that will get to you, of the beauty in the world that is insistent on staying, even after the dead have risen to take its place in the rightful order of things.

I read this book in two short moves and two long bursts and recommend you carve out a similar block of time for yourself. The story doesn't take kindly to those who rest too long.

This book is a win/win proposition on all fronts. Not only does it tell an entertaining and gripping story, but it also presents unforgettable characters against an interesting background. And to top it all is superbly well written.
