Temple has wandered America, a vast land emptied of most people by the zombie apocalypse that took place 25 years earlier–10 years before Temple was born. Still, she is able to find beauty in the world that surrounds her, and doesn’t begrudge the “meatskins” for doing what it is their nature to do. However, when Temple accidentally kills a man who attacks her, she finds herself on the run from his brother: a large man who has found his new singular purpose in life. On the way, Temple befriends a developmentally disabled mute, who she comes to need just as much as he needs her. As she runs from the man who is hunting her, she also works to discover herself and the good she believes she has lost.

The Reapers are the Angels is a strikingly beautiful, poetic novel of a young woman finding her way in a world rife with both danger and beauty. What’s remarkable about Temple is the way she views the world. She finds miracles in the nature that surrounds her, and, although she could be angry that she was born into a world full of the walking dead, she takes life as it is for what it is, without wishing for it to be otherwise. Her way of speaking is old fashioned and has a rhythm to it, like the dialog in the Coen brothers’ True Grit. This book is a pleasure to read for the writing alone.

Temple’s antagonist, Moses, is a mesmerizing character himself. He sees avenging his brother’s death as something he must do, something he is fated to do like an actor in a script. However, he’s honorable to Temple, and respects her even while wanting to kill her. I found his relationship with Temple to be surprising, and not at all like the usual vengeance-driven villain.

The Reapers are the Angels isn’t a young adult book–it’s an adult book that will most likely appeal to a wide audience including young adults. It is horror, containing violence (mostly involving the living), sexual content, and questions of good and evil. However, for all of its darkness, this is still a hopeful book that has a strangely uplifting quality to it. I highly recommend it to zombie lovers, horror aficionados, or anybody just looking for a smart, well-written story.

In The Reapers Are The Angels we meet Temple. A young girl (fifteen, so not that young) who is living in a post zombie-apocalypse world. The book is about her journey as she travels across the ruined United States while being hunted by a man who wants her dead.
The premise itself isn’t exactly original, we’ve all read zombie apocalypse books before, and this story doesn’t break too much new ground as far as the zombie mythos goes. But that’s okay in the long run, because the zombies in this story aren’t really the antagonists so much as background dangers, they take a back seat to the other human survivors, and the story itself.
What does make this book stand out amongst the zombie fiction crowd though, is the language. It’s beautiful. The way the author describes Temple’s thoughts and feelings really pulled me in. They aren’t too gimmicky, and don’t sound like an old person rehashing what they think teens talk like these days, no, it actually feels like the thoughts and philosophizing of a young girl who’s grown up in a dark and deadly world. A girl who’s experienced loss and had to do hard things. The descriptions, too, are marvelous and several times I found myself just soaking in the text itself.
Take for instance the tag line, which is also the first line in the book, ‘God is a slick god. Temple Knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe.’ The book is filled with lines like this, lines that hook into you and grab on.
Not only that, but I enjoyed the other characters as well. As I said above, Temple feels like a very real person, and just about everyone she encounters feels the same. Some are wicked, others are kind and gracious, but none feel one dimensional, stereotypical, or fake, and the book is filled with them. Even the antagonist is likeable in his own way.
Now, the book is aimed at older teens, and it is gruesome at times, and is always harsh, but the undertones of beauty never fade. I’d highly recommend this book to anyone who likes YA, zombie fiction, apocalypse fiction, or just is bored without something to read.
It may just be post-finishing-a-book excitement, but this is one of the most enjoyable books I’ve read. So dig in.
-Jeff

The Reapers Are the Angels is a YA novel by Alden Bell from Holt.

Book Blurb:

Zombies have infested a fallen America. A young girl named Temple is on the run. Haunted by her past and pursued by a killer, Temple is surrounded by death and danger, hoping to be set free.

For twenty-five years, civilization has survived in meager enclaves, guarded against a plague of the dead. Temple wanders this blighted landscape, keeping to herself and keeping her demons inside her heart.

She can't remember a time before the zombies, but she does remember an old man who took her in and the younger brother she cared for until the tragedy that set her on a personal journey toward redemption.

Moving back and forth between the insulated remnants of society and the brutal frontier beyond, Temple must decide where ultimately to make a home and find the salvation she seeks.

My thoughts:

Temple does not remember a time without the ‘meatskins’. Those dead things that won’t stay down without a bullet or sharp object to the brain. Temple also doesn’t remember her parents. She’s sure she must have had some - but she doesn’t know what happened to them.

She’s been on her own for a little while now. Moving from place to place - trying to stay out of the way of the meatskins. Trying to find what beauty is left in the world.

But not everything is beautiful - and not all survivors are trustworthy. When Temple is placed in a dangerous situation she does what she must to stay safe. Killing comes easy - whether man or meatskin.

Temple actions - however justified - have consequences and now she is on the run. And being pursued - not by the meatskins - but by a flesh and blood man out for vengeance.

I enjoyed The Reapers Are the Angels. It is written a bit oddly - not a quotation in the whole book. Once I wrapped my head around that I was okay.

This book fascinated me. I’m not sure if it was due to Temple’s young age or the ease with which she dealt with whatever life handed her. The ending made me angry though - really.

I give The Reapers Are the Angels 4 out of 5 stars.

Tenemos a Temple, una niña de 15 años que no conoce otro cosa más que aquel mundo podrido donde los muertos se levantan. Desde su nacimiento, ha tenido que sobrevivir día a día. Tiene que ser la más fuerte si quiere ver otro amanecer. Pero no solo tiene que luchar contra los zombies, pues también tendrá que luchar con los humanos lascivos que quieren aprovecharse de su supuesta juventud. Temple ha sabido librarse de ellos con bastante facilidad, hasta que se topa con Abraham, quien no está dispuesto a desaparecer tan fácil hasta que Temple lo elimina ella misma.
Por desgracia para ella, Abraham tiene un hermano psicópata llamado Moses, quien está dispuesto a cruzar medio continente con tal de vengar a su sangre.


Y así empieza la historia de estos dos, aunque Moses esta decidió a matar a Temple, entre ambos surge una extraña rivalidad que tiene matices de hermandad… (Algo así como la rivalidad de Goku y Vegeta xD), ambos son cazadores que viven con sus propios fantasmas y remordimientos, ambos viendo más la belleza del mundo a pesar de los muertos vivientes.
Durante su huida, Temple conoce a bobo, un hombretón en sus 30 y algo de años que tiene algunos problemas mentales. Hasta que conoce a bobo, Temple no se había permitido querer a nadie, y aun con el hombre junto a ella, insiste en negar ese lado humano suyo que aun puede amar a alguien.

Y bueno, pienso yo que leer el recorrido oscuro que Temple recorre, para algunos sonara horrible. Es decir, seguir a esta chica de 15 años que se ve obligada a matar todos los días para vivir, no es una idea muy agradable, pero la verdad sea dicha toda la historia es simplemente genial. Son de esas historias que te gustaría leer eternamente sin llegar al final.

El autor no escatima a la hora de describir las escenas. O sea que, vemos sangre y más sangre por todos lados pero no, a pesar de que no soy fanática de la sangre y las tripas, no me pareció grotesco ni mucho menos. Creo yo que una buena escena de acción debe ser bien detallada para que el lector no se pierda y entienda todo, y eso es lo que este autor logra

.
Así que, tienen que leer este libro si no quieren que aparezca un Zombie frente a ustedes y se beba su cerebro con un popote del McDonald :)

Temple es una quinceañera nacida una década después de la aparición de los primeros zombies y se ha pasado los últimos años viviendo en un faro, hasta que llega el día en que los zombies comienzan a acercarse y le toca mudarse. A pesar de su corta edad, ha convivido desde siempre con estos seres, por lo que sabe moverse entre ellos perfectamente. Acaba llegando a un refugio donde la acogen encantados, pero uno de los hombres, no sabe aceptar un no por respuesta y Temple se resiste, ocasionando la muerte del atacante.
Tras este desastre no le queda otra cosa que abandonar el refugio y huir. El problema, es que Moses, el hermano del asesinado, sale tras ella en busca de venganza.

Nada más comenzarlo me vino a la mente que el autor tuvo que inspirarse si o si, en La carretera de Cormac McCarthy, tanto por la lúgubre ambientación con la que nos muestra un mundo oscuro, sin vida, donde lo peor no se esconde dentro de los muertos, sino en los vivos. Además, de valerse de una narración en tercera persona que nos mostrará el camino de nuestra protagonista pero sin adelantarnos nada, sino haciendo que la acompañemos, acomodándonos a su ritmo y descubriendo las cosas poco a poco. Los sentimientos tampoco son expresados de forma directa, y la mayoría tendremos que ir sacándolos gracias a la observación de los actos de los diferentes personajes.

La incertidumbre es algo que caracteriza esta lectura desde el principio. Aunque la temática sea de zombies y la realidad que nos muestra el autor sea cruda, no por ello nos encontraremos con escenas sangrientas o desagradables. Todo ello queda en decisión del lector quien decidirá si dejar que su imaginación vuele por esos derroteros o no.

El final...qué final...oh god!Tenía las mismas probabilidades de acertar como de fracasar en mis intuiciones...pero ninguno iba a ser un final que me fuera a gustar sentimentalmente hablando. En su línea, el final es oscuro pero con ciertos tintes de luz que deja un reguero de esperanza...para la humanidad.

No es la típica historia de zombies a la que estamos acostumbrados, más bien, los zombies son una excusa para poder mostrarnos un mundo decadente y oscuro, dónde lo más peligroso que podemos encontrarnos es a nosotros mismos.

What a fantastic little zombie novel. This is one of those books that rises above its genre material, like Christopher Buehlman's excellent Those Across the River.

You can tell Alden Bell writes non genre books, and I'd say this one compares well to Cormac McCarthy's The Road, although this one is a lot less bleak than the McCarthy's novel. It has a similar theme of survivors in a post-apocalyptic world travelling to another place.

I enjoyed Bell's take on the world, it was fresh and new. Love that his protagonist was not bogged down with memories of the past because Temple was actually born into the new zombie world and so has never known a world without them. She doesn't view zombies as evil creatures that destroyed civilization but rather just a part of life -- another dangerous animal like a bear or a wolf but ultimately she isn't terrified of them or trying to set up some semblance of an existence that resembles that of life pre-zombie.

It was interesting to see this novel almost as a travelogue through a zombie infested America through fresh eyes. In fact, the country is almost as much a protagonist in this tale as Temple herself. As she travels through and describes the buildings she sees and the people she meets as well as places she wishes she could go, you feel the same wanderlust that Temple herself feels, a desire to go and see all the 'wonders' of the world before they are reclaimed by time and the earth.

There's a lot of action in this book - Temple's no shy flower scared of everything, but a capable young woman who is just as dangerous if not more dangerous than the teeming masses of zombies. Bell keeps the pace moving along quite well with lots of action between the ruminations to keep zombie lovers satisfied.

I highly suggest this to anyone who likes a good post apocalyptic novel or zombie novel but want something a little different from the norm. Definitely a very satisfying read.

3.5
This book has really stuck with me. It was disturbing and not in the way you would necessarily expect. It's about a 15 year old girl trying to survive in a zombie apocalypse. Honestly, the zombies are kind of background noise but there are some pretty gruesome descriptions. The protagonist may be 15 but I do not think I would classify this book as YA at all. It was very very gritty.
I fell in love with the main character Temple, she's an earnest sort of character who's tough because she's had to be. She's not the stereotypical ~amazing badass~ which I appreciated. The author did a really good job showing you just how tragic it is that this little girl is having to grow up in constant survival mode. It was really heartbreaking and disturbing. But there were light moments as well, Temple cracked me up a few times with her insights and just the purity only kids have. The author portrayed a teen pretty well in that sense.
Some favorite lines:
"You must get a great deal of attention from the young men."
"Usually the kind that needs beatin down."

"Temple, I've been livin off the land for years. I ain't gonna die."
"Sooner or later you are. I just don't want you standin next to me when you do it."

There was one thing that just crossed the line completely for me

I mean this isn't the greatest book ever, there wasn't really any world building, no answers to why the zombies were there in the first place and it was sort of aimless honestly but it was emotionally engaging in a way not many books are. I would even consider rereading it just because I liked Temple so much. All in all, I would recommend this book. But beware there's no quotation marks, wtf was up with that?

After my disastrous re-reading of a popular zombie novel last year, I started to get more scared about re-reading books that I’d loved the first time around. But I felt that I needed to read The Reapers are the Angels again before moving onto the next book, Exit Kingdom – and I’m glad to say that re-reading it was so worthwhile.

Temple is a loner – she lives in an abandoned lighthouse, removed from the remnants of human civilisation. Born after the zombie apocalypse she has never known life to be anything other than a constant fight for survival in a world where one wrong move could be her last. She’s a fighter, brutal and unforgiving, but underneath her tough exterior is a girl who struggles to understand herself – her motivation, her feelings and her remorse are all shoved behind a tough exterior. And I loved her right from the beginning. Despite her struggle with demons both inside and outside, she’s an unforgettable character.

The Reapers are the Angels is more about the human side of the zombie apocalypse than the undead side – relationships are fragile, built on moments and chance, and Temple has experienced that first hand – it’s made her hard and seemingly cold. And yet as she moves through a landscape that is full of danger, parts of her humanity start to seep through – despite the fact it puts her at more risk of being hurt than when she existed only for her own survival.

Apart from Temple, what makes this book so outstanding is the writing. It’s so beautiful, so melodic and so captivating that at times I actually forgot I was reading a post-apocalyptic zombie novel and just lost myself in the words. In that respect, The Reapers are the Angels is definitely more unique than most other zombie novels – although it’s terrifically gory and intense in places, the writing is what really held my attention.

There is nothing I didn’t enjoy about this book – from the characters to the writing to the plot and pacing, it worked perfectly for me, even the second time around.

This book cured me of my fear that I am unable to read anything zombie-related that doesn't employ humor, although now that I think about it, the (extremely likable - gives Katniss Everdeen a definite run for her money) heroine is fairly sassy in a laughing-in-the-face-of-death sort of way. Alright, maybe I am unable to read anything zombie-related that isn't funny in the least, which explains why I gave up on Aftertime and why I so disliked Forest of Hands and Teeth. The thing with writing about zombies is that everyone gets so worked up about how Serious they need to be about portraying Endtimes, or maybe they're self-conscious about writing about zombies (who knows?), but this book not only tackles the post-apocalyptic scenario, it also unapologetically ruminates about Good and Evil and god's design every chance it gets, and somehow almost pulls it all off. I didn't get the motivations underpinning the main conflict of the novel - at the outset, yes, but not by the end - but it may be my ignorance of Southern gothic conventions. Maybe it just had to be that the two sides would be opposed... still, I would have liked to have bought the whole struggle between the protag & her chief adversary hook line and sinker (does labeling something "allegorical" necessarily entail suspending more than the usual amount of disbelief?) The language took some getting used to - I get that Bell's trying to convey a mood, but it veers towards self-indulgence at times (especially hard to swallow that a 15-year-old girl who's been chiefly on her own might speak in such a florid manner - not that she would have such big thoughts, but that she'd be able to articulate them so perfectly)... still, I eventually got into the writing/overall tone enough that I found myself humming the creepy Robert Mitchum song in the movie where he's a child killer. So yes, four full-fledged stars for this book, which kicks the ass of every zombie story I've read lately, with the possible exception of the Walking Dead comics...

Turns out zombie stories can be more than gory 2D character, plot-driven action or parody add-ons to classic tales. Bell has written a story where the living dead are both real and metaphor. If you’re looking for action or parody, you can miss the richness of the metaphors and the mirrors: life and death, male and female, civilized and uncivilized, rule-bound and chaotic, care-giver and cared-for, father and daughter, god and godless.

Temple is a 15 year old girl who cannot remember her parents. She remembers living in an orphanage for awhile, but then it was overrun by zombies. For a long time she lived in the wild with a younger boy who may have been her brother. They lived with a kindly man for a few years until he was bitten by a zombie. Now the younger boy is gone and Temple wanders post-apocalyptic North America with a dignity and morality so often missing in stories of survival and the decay of civilization.

Sadly, for all the good Temple is and does, she thinks herself evil and seeks redemption. Temple is able to take care of herself against the best of enemies with all the skills heroes possess. She still has a vulnerability, a child-like quality, an innocence that caused her to be vulnerable to self-retribution that pained me and invited me to worry for, care for her and feel protective of the zombie slayer.

The richness of this story is not just in contrast to the usual thinness of these stories. It is a stand alone masterpiece that will mostly go unappreciated only because of the genre to which it’s been relegated. Too bad. It’s a rich emotional adventure described by Publishers Weekly as “an exquisitely bleak tale and an unforgettable heroine whose eye for beauty and aching need for redemption somehow bring wonder into a world full of violence and decay.”

I'm a big fan of Cormac McCarthy and clearly Alden Bell is as well. It'd be diplomatic to try and find a way to say this that doesn't sound mean, but I can't: trying to write like McCarthy doesn't make you McCarthy. Far better to find your own voice.

Perhaps I should have just taken this for a quick airplane read (because that's how long it lasted me) but I couldn't shake the feeling of low-rent McCarthy wannabe. It was there on every page, in every sentence spoken by Temple. The plot is a combination of The Road and Blood Meridian - a trudge through barren lands with a hulking philosophizing killer trailing behind.

... except add zombies, which makes it inherently goofy.

Okay, I'll give this much to Bell - he knows how to keep it simple. The plot is established quickly: hulking killer wishes to murderize our protagonist. It's obvious that the book will end with those two meeting up one way or another. The pages in-between fly by and there are no real surprises to be had, no plot twists to throw you off the trail. It was just ... I don't know.

Here, this is blunt: do you like Coca-Cola? Can you taste the difference between Coke and the grocery store's generic brand? Would the generic taste better if it were in a can that looked a whole lot like Coke? Generic soda is fine, it is what it is. I don't dislike generic soda for existing. I only start to dislike it when it knows what it is but tries to be something it's not.

This book is not deep or wondrous but through its language it sure does try to paint itself as such. Perhaps it is the absolute pinnacle of zombie books; I'm not overly familiar with the genre. I just couldn't stop comparing it to something better because every sentence was practically begging me to, but falling far short of the mark.

I should read more carefully the synopsis from now on...

A very beautiful post- apocalyptic zombie novel...

I was impressed...

I first learned about this book at the Philip K. Dick awards. It was nominated this year and they read a part of it. I really liked what I heard, and it was actually my second favorite of the six they read that night. It lost the award to The Strange Affair of Spring Heeled Jack, which I haven’t read yet, but plan to.

Reapers is a an amazing zombie story, filled with gruesome scenes and blood squirting gore. But more than anything the best thing about Reapers is the deep emotional connection that the writer creates to the protagonist. The writing is superb and I loved it, despite the fact that the novel is written in present tense. I normally run shrieking away from all present tense novels, and this one is the first one that I have ever liked. I think that is due to the incredible skill of writer, Alden Bell.

It’s a story about a girl named Temple who has grown up in this zombie post apocalypse world, where the slugs and mutants rule, and humanity is a scrabbling minority barely surviving and struggling to take back their world. Temple has survived on her own so long that she doesn’t trust too many people, and although life has made her tough and hard, she finds it difficult to shirk responsibility for others. She thinks of herself as evil because of the things she’s had to do, but really she is better than most of her fellow human beings who instead of banding together, in a lot of cases are turning on themselves.

I loved this book, but I ran into a couple plot choices that I personally didn’t enjoy. I can’t go into the details without spoiling the book. I still like it despite those choices, and recommend it to anyone who likes zombie stories or scifi. It is zombie genre evolved and grown up. A serious book about what makes people tick inside.

The protagonist is fifteen-sixteen, but content-wise it's not a YA novel. If Faulkner were to collaborate with George Romero, it might come out like this. The language is often as beautiful as the action is graphic. It's not for the squeamish.

Zombies are a permanent part of the American landscape, and have been longer than teen-aged Temple has been alive. She accepts them as part of her world, something to avoid or confront as the moment demands, like mosquitoes or the weather. When she confronts the walking dead, they don't rise again. But she takes no joy in it. However brutally she acts, though, there is an undertone of empathy. We meet her as a momentary idyll comes to an end, when a "meatskin" washes ashore here previously unbreached island off the Florida mainland. Her return to civilization brings encounters with survivors who have adapted to the new world in various ways (isolation, community, hunting, greater humanity, greater inhumanity). Temple picks up an enemy and an innocent charge early on, which frame the story. There is honor among combatants, and though I didn't completely buy the relationship arc between Temple and Moses, it has enough resonance to accept. The action is confined almost entirely to the American Southeast, and the comparisons to Faulkner are deserved. Bell's language truly is magical at times, and the themes drawn from the New Testament parable of the Wheat and Tares are allowed to unfold naturally.

I don't read much zombie fiction, and for films I tend to stick with the comedies (Zombieland, Shaun of the Dead). A friend recommended this, and though it's not my usual fare, I found it worth the read. Recommended, with the content caveat.

My favorite book of all time. I have always loved the post apocalypse world, whether it will the Fallout style nuclear waste land or the zombie infected world. The main character is Temple who I find completely fascinating. She is fourteen or fifteen but able to carry her own in combat, as well as survive in the wasteland.

If you read this book you have to look past the zombie apocalypse and see the loan road/wandering soul theme that carries the book. Temple is a girl who has no family or friends, she bumps into a group of survivors but things go bad *I will leave out spoilers* and she is on the run.

Later she finds a mansion that seems unaffected by the zombie world. The people inside are safe and not in danger, they welcome her in. Its the point where you realize that even though there is danger all around her, there is still beauty in the world and you have to see it. Shortly after this my favorite part of the book is "you know what's out there but you still want to find it". I take it as we knows what's in the world but we still want to experience it for ourselves while we find our purpose.

Temple later finds her purpose when she meets a handicap man, who is able to be swarmed by zombies. After meeting him and saving him, she knows his family is dead so she takes him under her care. This is her purpose that she has been seeking.

I'm bad at avoiding going around spoilers so I will just leave it with the man chasing her finds out he has a purpose as well. He realizes that as much as he hated Temple, he saw her as a daughter of sorts. So when she dies he buries her and takes over protecting the handicap man. I feel like this is the symbolism that two people's paths can be intertwined regardless of how different they are.

I re-read the back of this book and wondered why I thought I would like it. It must have come recommended on Amazon in one of those "if you like this, you'll love..." blurbs. I couldn't imagine why I bought it. But I told myself to give it a try, and I began reading and couldn't stop. The first sentence, "God is a slick god" hooked me, and the lyrical writing kept me engaged. The back cover says it's like a Flannery O'Connor novel with zombies, and to some extent the southern gothic tradition is evident, but it read to me more like a western, and the zombies were placeholders for all the other antagonists you would rather fill in. It's dystopian literature for sure, but rugged and raw and desolate like a western. While it's all of these things, it is also hopeful in an odd, serene way.
The characters are odd, but brilliantly written. Temple, the protagonist, has a strong, original voice, and if I find it surprising that a man wrote her experiences so well. She rings true. Maury, the mute, is an odd addition, but read it and he fits in. And Moses Todd is also well written. You pull for the girl, even though you know what is going to happen almost from the beginning.
There are some really beautiful lines in this book, and I'm sorry that I didn't mark them all. Like the rest of the first line: "God is a slick god. Temple knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe." There were so many others that I can't even find them all as I skim back through the book, but I will add them later.
I highly recommend this book, highly.

When I give 5 stars to a book it doesn't necessarily mean it is without flaws. It means that it soars above the few small bumps and stumble stones that once in a minor second paved moments in the plot, it means I am fully in awe of the world that just unfolded in front of me, that I am soaked by its imprints, marvels and frights.
"The Reapers are the Angels" is a tale, an allegory, a road movie, a zombie story, a saga, a search. It is about the end of life as we know it and not the end at all, it is about order, about belonging, about loss, about God, about philosophy, about evil, about humans, about living. It is perfect for me.
Yes, within the world building I encountered a couple of scenes that could make one wrinkle noses a bit. But, really, if those tiny, tiny moments bothered you, it means you have missed the impacts of this journey, its characters, its strives, its soul. This book deals -among other things- with questions of religion and faith, and I loved every exploration of it. There is no preaching in it at all, it was fascinating to read about this perspective on religion. It will by no means change my personal beliefs but it was incredibly interesting, like reading about a foreign culture.
The strong and unique heroine Temple and Bell's writing are the core strengths but there is so much to dive into here, so much to love and ponder about, so much to sink your teeth into and lick up the blood. And honestly, it really has been a while since an ending had pulled me out from under!
Powerful, that is the word I want to end this review on, this one was powerful!

The Reapers are the Angels is Alden Bells first novel and what a great career start! I bought this after cruising GR listopia for Best Zombie Books for some ideas on what I wanted to follow up Breathers with since it sparked a zombie phase. Although I'm still not sure if this is a YA novel or not but either way it's got my vote.

Two and a half decades after to world we know today crumbles into a chaotic life and death dance with the undead, in this book their called meatskins or slugs. The theme is fight or die only now it's not just the meatskins your trying to survive but each other however few and scattered the living are. Temple a 15 year old girl with a much older soul was born into this world of death, decay and corpses. Temple travels the continent alone by choice, meeting other people, seeing the beautiful miracles all the while living at the end of her knife and wits. Through chance she stumbles upon a community living in highrises in a downtown city but when she is endangered she acts on instinct killing a warrior of theirs, she leaves in a hurry knowing the warriors brother will hunt her down. Thats all I'm saying now read the book already.

This story is amazing in the fact that even in all the horridness Temple found pleasure, peace and saw the beauty God created for her. It's pretty awesome that thru all the ugliness we as a people still find the strength and drive to keep looking to the future. My heart went out to Temple, to be so alone and so self critical yet such a fighter, she truely was a badass with a blade, and yet kind hearted and understood 'the code' of mankind.

Reapers Are the Angels does what few novels in the over-saturated zombie and post-apocalyptic-genre have: It actually distinguishes itself from the pack. Part of this I attribute to plot, part to Alden Bell’s ability to spin a hell of a good sentence.

Bell knows how to set our teeth on edge, he knows a thing or two about what makes a good story tick, but he also knows the value of an impeccably good turn of phrase. Stylistically, he stands on his own—although I sense that he may have well-worn copies of Blood Meridian and The Road on his nightstand. Unlike Cormack McCarthy, though, Bell strikes me as someone who has a lot more faith in human dignity.

Reapers Are the Angels gives us the ubiquitous zombie story, but approaches it in a fresh way. We don’t witness the outbreak, follow society's collapse, or have idyllic flashbacks of what life was like before contagion. Instead, our story begins at least a decade and a half after "it" happened, which actually makes the presence of zombies, oddly, less menacing and more a source of inconvenience and disruption. Sure, bad things happen. People die and some of these scenes are rather chilling. But characters like Temple and Mose are neither sulking nor overly-sentimental types.

Our protagonist, Temple, may be fifteen years old, but I’ll be damned if she’s not one the toughest, smartest and most believable characters I’ve come across in a long time. I could offer a synopsis of the plot, but I think other reviewers have captured it well enough.

Long story short: I highly recommend this one and am looking forward to reading more by Alden Bell.

1. The title is amazing. Seriously. What a great title.
2. My boyfriend thinks the cover is amazing, but he's wrong. The cover is too low-contrast to be appealing, and it's also totally misleading. The girl on the front appears to be hiding from the world. Does that sound like our protagonist? Not so much. Pretty sure the whole point is she's the last wide-eyed thing left after the zombie apocalypse.
3. Our protagonist is fascinating. Sure, she reads like an adult man's imagining of a teenaged girl, but that's the way of novels written by men about teenaged girls. She is, in any case, a young lady worth traveling with for a few hours. Violent and conflicted and brave and curious and occasionally surprisingly generous.
4. I like the dialect, and the atmosphere generally. It's lonely and claustrophobic and expansive, all at the same time. Extremely effective.
5. As others have pointed out, the plot holes here are gaping and go completely unaddressed. There is absolutely no way that this story can take place 25 years after civilization collapsed - maybe 4 or 5, tops. (Seriously, have you ever encountered a car that can run after sitting untended for 25 years? Ever? Or tried to eat 25-year-old packaged food? Or drink a 25-year-old Coke?) However, I'm willing to let it go, because that distance is necessary for Temple to operate the way she does. She's able to see the world the way she does because she's never known it any other way. I'm willing to suspend my disbelief in order to take a look at the miraculous.

I struggled with this one for a while. One of the things I noticed about this story is that many people enjoyed the strong, female heroine. I really wanted to like her as well, but ultimately could not accept her as a fully formed character. For one, she did not feel like a strong female character to me, but rather a strong male character with a girl's name. I'm not fond of the idea that, to make a strong female character, she must remove everything feminine about herself. Even as a tomboy I didn't find her believable, though I realize some may disagree with that. Aside from my doubting Temple as a strong female, I found her unbelievable in other ways. I didn't buy her "illiterate philosopher" routine. Pages and pages we had to listen to her trying to explain the universe. I suppose that, on their own, overly philosophical and warrior princess are not bad character traits, but that was simply all there was to her. I'm not sure I ever liked her, felt for her, sympathized with her enough to care about either her diatribes or the perilous situations she found herself in because I always knew she would be on them like James Bond or Indiana Jones. When we finally do get something like real emotions from her, it's too late, and they, too, are unbelievable.
Overall, the book is beautifully written and especially stands out in the genre, but I wanted a character to like, not an archetype.

A literary zombie novel set in the American South twenty-five years after the start of a zombie apocalypse. Fifteen year old Temple wanders the country looking for safe places to stay. She encounters occasional outposts of civilization but finds that she never fits in for long. After killing a man who tried to rape her, she has to flee from his brother Moses, who is another wanderer as dangerous as she is. On her way through Georgia she rescues a mentally-disabled man and takes on the mission of delivering him to relatives in Texas while still staying ahead of Moses.

My problem with this book is mainly in the setting. It takes place many years after the zombie apocalypse, which is atypical, but the world itself seems like one where the collapse has just happened. Electricity still works in many places, even completely uninhabited ones, there are working cars sitting on the side of the road with plenty of fuel to be found, and abandoned stores are still full of edible packaged food.

The book is very well written though with a lot of beautiful language. I enjoyed Temple as a character, even if she did seem to have a vocabulary well beyond someone who is totally uneducated. I enjoyed it as an attempt to bring a different style of writing to what is often a fairly standard type of story.

What to say about this novel...? I guess I can start by saying that for the first few chapters, I really wasn't enjoying it. Structured very similar to "The Road", the kind of incidental storytelling really wasn't grabbing me at first. "This is nothing like 'The Passage'" I thought, since this was a recommend on Amazon for those who enjoyed that particular book (which I wholeheartedly did). But...something happened on the way, as they say, and after a few more chapters I found myself hooked. While Temple may not be the most nuanced of all characters, she is pretty darn close. But what really grabbed me was the prose. The world is described, usually by Temple's thoughts, in aching and poetic detail. This is one beautifully written book. It brings to mind the honest and poignant conversations from some of the great Westerns of the past decade or so, men and women of violence who still have a way with words that cuts to the very heart of the matter. It's not really a horror book, though there are horrific elements in it. I really don't want to discuss anything else about this book, not to avoid spoilers so much as to leave the trail untouched, and the sights fresh and new. This really is one you should read for yourself, maybe with a glass of wine or when it's storming outside. Highly recommended for any fan of literature, not just zombie fans.

This read like McCarthy's The Road with sprinklings of Charles Portis's True Grit, attempted rape of a minor, sex with a minor, shotgun blasts of religious reference and allegory, and, last but not least, zombies. If that's your cup of tea, go nuts.

However, while all that content might tickle your post-apocalyptic funny bone, the contrived nature of the plot and the extremely boring "antagonist", Moses, might make you wonder if you've accidentally wandered into a young-adult fiction book of the month selection. There is viciousness and graphic content galore in this story, yet the basic conflict, a chase, lacks any semblance of maturity or realism. Fresh off experiencing the otherworldly chase between the Kid and the Judge in Blood Meridian, to me Bell's story seemed to lack a suitable justification for the conflict even while plying you with tautological exposition.

Some of the set pieces were phenomenally colorful and unique, and I can see it serving a film adaptation well. The author makes you ask some great questions about life and hardship, and that alone was worth the quick read.

All in all, not terrible, but pales in comparison to the storytelling in The Road, which this novel unfortunately must be compared to. Similar themes and plot devices are also used in, and to much better effect, The Last of Us (video game) and Seraphim Falls (film).

Have you ever read a book that you'd be hard pressed to describe to another person, but makes perfect sense within it's own pages? That'd be this book. Temple is only fifteen years-old and all she's ever known is a life filled with fighting, death and zombies. We join her in her travels and get intimate glances at what has happened to the world and the changes to what is left of humanity.
Temple fights a lot of her memories because nothing can be taken for granted. She hides herself and what she could have been because if she didn't she'd be zombie fodder. As people gather in clusters of form some semblance of a city or town she knows she'll never find a place among them. It was tough to read about her life and the snatches of memory she chooses to share. I wasn't a fan of the ending, but the interactions between her and another character had me shaking my head and hurriedly reading the next paragraph to see these two and their Old West-style showdown would unfold.

This is Temple's story. A fifteen year old girl, who is wandering through a post-apocalyptic world filled with Zombies. We never find out what happened to change the world in such a drastic way but that isn't really the point of the story.
Temple is tough, can fight and has seen and done things most other people would have nightmares about. She has no family left and has travelled for many years through a declining America, shunning the small communities that have sprung up all over the place. Life might be safer in a protected area with people around but that is not what Temple wants. The few times she tried, she was soon itching to get back on the road.
When we meet Temple, she is full of self-loathing for something that happened a few years ago and for which she blames herself. She is sad and angry, but also vulnerable and is one of the few people who can still see the beauty in the world around her. We accompany her on the road, fighting of Zombies, meeting people and acquiring a very human nemesis, who will do anything to kill her.
This is a book about a girl's search for redemption. It is bleak, yet beautiful.

Wow, just wow. I didn't see that ending coming....

Alden Bell, first and foremost, thank you for zombie-YA-Fiction with a smart, theoretically deep, bad ass heroine on a mission with played down romance.

Temple had guts, man. Crazy guts. She was a good person whether or not she thought she was. She cared and she took the little bits of happiness for all they were worth. She never tried to sabotage a good thing and I really liked that about her. She wanted to make good choices. Sure, she had internal strife but it wasn't all she thought about.

I loved listening in on her thoughts. She was illiterate, she couldn't read, but at fifteen, she was far from stupid. It's like how the people of yester-year spoke with such large words but were still considered stupid by today's standard. I found myself looking up some words because I didn't know what they meant.

The perspective of the book is truly written observantly (I can't think of the proper term) which was different. But made for an easy transition when it was needed.

All in all: A truly wonderful read. Kudos to Mr. Bell.

However, my main problem with the book, was with the main story line, which includes grown adult Moses stalking Temple through multiple zombie infested cities and states because he has a grudge against her, a literal child, for killing his brother, who he readily admits is a bad person, during his attempted rape of her…like, what the actual fuck? Twenty-five years after the zombie apocalypse, a fifteen-year-old girl named Temple travels through the wastelands of America, seeking beauty, meaning, and purpose. She also happens to being fleeing a man whose brother she killed.

Wow, that was some trip. It was interesting to see someone's perspective on what the world would be liked decades after zombies. It's desolate, sad, yet still beautiful and moving. This was an amazing book with some of the most striking imagery I have read all year.

My only complaint is Bell's penchant for run-on sentences and refusal to use quotation marks. I want to recommend this to Christy, but she will so have to overlook the liberties taken with grammar.

Still, it is definitely worth the read. This is only the second book I have read this year that I would really like to see as a movie. As long as Hollywood doesn't mess it up. Reminded me of The Stand, Pitch Black, The Road and the Dark Tower. Yet, it is completely different from all of these at the same time...

"Temple speaks. She tells the woman that she has done bad things - things God would not like - and that sometimes she wonders if God could be angry at her, and if she would know the difference between a blessing and a punishment because the world is wondrous even when your stomach is empty and there is dried blood in your hair.

She tells of how you have a special amazement for all the beauty in the world when you are evil like she is - probably because beauty and evil are on the opposite sides of a wall like lovers who can never really touch.

She tells of the people she has killed, she lists the names for the ones she knows and describes the others, but she can’t remember them all, and she knows she shouldn’t forget things like that and she would write them down except that she can’t read or write because when she was supposed to be learning her letters she was busy hiding in a drainage ditch because her foster home got eaten up by meatskins."

This author owes a clear debt to Stephen King, who is quoted (from Pet Sematary) at the start. That said, this has its own clear voice, and the protagonist is simply fantastic. At times, I felt this a little much for believability/immersion in the story/being able to set aside fictional coincidence and run with it, but the imagery here is great, the dialogue is wonderful, the scenes are sharply drawn for the most part, and there's enough backstory given to get you close to the protagonist, but not so much that it ruins the mystery. This was a great beach read but it's also one I will put on the shelf to eventually read again. My initial comment, too, may make this sound like a horror novel, but though it has zombies, really, it's road trip book/story about a teenage girl on her own (who's forced to mature quickly in some ways but who is still clearly childlike). The horror in the book is not the point, and the gore here doesn't get out of hand, so it's realistic and engrossing as a story without being a typical shlocky horror read or slash-fest. Well done.

There are dozens of different zombie stories out now. But not all of them work. The concepts might be interesting, but the story sometimes falls flat. I found Bell's story to be just the opposite. Are there zombies? Sure, they're there, but they'd not the focus. Has civilization collapsed on itself turning mankind back to a more primitive way of living? Yup, that's accounted for. But what I truly liked was how Bell's novel reminded me of The Road. That same kind of haunting bleakness that not ever author captures. It was rather, for me, a merge of that, The Walking Dead, and in some fashion bits of The Stand. (I believe Maury made me think of that, but it wasn't a big issue.) Whether those works influenced Bell or not, I couldn't say, but if they did, he certainly used them to an advantage. It's a human story with the ruin of what we know as civilization as the background. I found it more sad than particularly gross (though it is violent and there are gross things). Regardless, probably one of the better zombie novels I've read. Definitely up there with World War Z.

The Reapers Are the Angels is a Western. It happens to be set in a post-apocalyptic near future overrun by zombies, but other than this detail, it is a Western. It has a standard Western revenge/mission storyline, it echoes the typical Western musings on guilt, purpose and desperation, religion and morality, and the contrast between civilization and life in the wild, it's written with the lilt and language of the American South, its atmosphere is the bleak yet hopeful one of the frontier, and so on and so on. It is not, as far as I can determine, an innovative or exceptional example of the genre. Stylistically, it has one feature of note. Alden Bell writes dialogue without the punctuation of dialogue, which on one level makes the conversations seem appropriately dreamy and fatal, and seems mildly annoying and pointless on another equally valid level. Every story ever told ends up getting retold in every setting ever imagined. If the combination makes sense and the writing is competent, fair enough.

Wow. This book was unexpected. I loved the "voice" of the main character. And more than that I loved her ability, in a horrible world, to see the miracles that surround us, even when everything looks desperate. I thought it was a stroke of genius to have Temple, the protagonist, be a child born into a world where the "normal" state of being was dangerous and nasty. What would it be like to have no other memory of what the world "used to be" or "ought to be." In the midst of all the awfulness, Temple still has the ability to believe in a God who is a "slick God" - a god who, she believes, showers people with miracles if only they knew how to look. The one thing that Temple lacks is the ability to judge herself rightly, leading to a mistaken belief that she is evil at heart. And *that* she is not.

Like Flannery O'Connor, the author uses grotesques to illustrate the points he is trying to make. Southern to the core, or so it seems to me, the story very much illustrates Flannery's "God haunted" South.

Distrubing, dark, but worth the read.

Je ne sais pas trop comment parler de ce livre, parce que je l'ai trouvé très fort, très puissant, que je me sens toute petite face à la beauté âpre qui s'en dégage, et que j'ai du mal à trouver les mots pour exprimer tout ce que je ressens.

C'est un roman post-apocalyptique avec des zombies, oui, mais franchement, c'est beaucoup, beaucoup plus que cela.

D'ailleurs, les zombies se font très "discrets", dans le sens où ils ne sont vraiment pas la préoccupation majeure des personnages. Il faut dire qu'ils sont lents, comme la plupart des zombies, et que depuis 25 ans qu'ils ont fait leur apparition, les survivants de ce monde savent exactement comment les éviter et leur échapper.

On ne sait rien de ce qui est arrivé il y a 25 ans, ni pourquoi il y a eu soudain des zombies. Ce qu'on sait, en revanche, c'est que le phénomène n'est pas terminé, dans le sens où les gens qui meurent continuent à se relever sous forme de zombies si on ne leur coupe pas la tête.

Mais comme je le disais, le vrai sujet de ce roman est ailleurs.

Pour moi, il est dans la vision que les survivants ont de ce monde devenu si différent et, plus accessoirement, dans les différentes façons de vivre qu'ils ont adopté. Il y a les gens qui se sont regroupés en mini-sociétés, ou en groupes encore plus petits, retranchés dans des enclaves protégées, il y a les chasseurs (de zombies), et il y a les solitaires, qui n'appartiennent à aucun groupe et parcourent le pays, dans une quête personnelle. C'est le cas de Temple, jeune fille de 15 ans, qui sillonne les routes de l'Amérique, en quête d'une rédemption que jusqu'à présent, elle s'est refusée à elle-même, écrasée sous le poids d'une énorme culpabilité.

Au cours de son périple, Temple fait plusieurs rencontres. Certaines sont agréables et représentent un répit dans sa solitude. Mais Temple n'est pas du genre à se lier très longtemps, et elle repart très vite sur les routes.

D'autres rencontres seront franchement dangereuses et l'obligeront à se battre pour défendre sa vie ou celle d'un autre personnage qu'elle a pris sous son aile, se sentant malgré elle obligée de le protéger alors qu'elle voudrait juste être seule dans son errance.

Temple est vraiment un personnage à part. J'ai été très étonnée par sa maturité et sa force. En même temps, quand on est obligé de se débrouiller sans aide dans un tel monde depuis toujours, ce n'est pas étonnant de grandir très vite. Mais son habileté au combat est vraiment surprenante et limite effrayante, y compris pour elle. D'ailleurs, cela fait partie du poids qu'elle porte sur ses épaules. En effet, elle s'est persuadée que si elle est si redoutable quand elle manie sa machette, c'est parce qu'elle porte le Mal en elle. Ce que nous, lecteurs, ainsi que tous les autres personnages, savons être totalement faux. Mais comme je l'ai dit plus haut, elle est convaincue d'avoir commis un acte si horrible qu'elle ne peut qu'être mauvaise, forcément, et pour elle, aucun pardon n'est possible pour cet acte. L'histoire nous dira de quel acte il s'agit, et si, comme on s'en doutait, sa part de responsabilité est beaucoup moins importante qu'elle ne le pense (et surtout, si elle est largement excusable, compte tenu de son jeune âge à ce moment-là), on peut comprendre pourquoi elle, elle ne se le pardonne pas.

Parallèlement à ce côté assez sombre, elle a une autre facette, très humaine, très ouverte aux autres, qui montre qu'au fond d'elle, il y a une bonté qui ressort malgré elle, même quand elle voudrait être dure. Enfin... quand je dis "ouverte", je pense surtout à sa façon de voir les autres. Pour elle, tout être vivant (ou non-vivant) fait partie de ce monde, est une "créature de Dieu", dans le sens de "créature de la Nature". Si elle existe, c'est que ça doit être ainsi, rien n'existe pour rien. Et de ce fait, elle n'éprouve aucune haine pour personne, même pas pour ceux qu'elle est obligée de tuer. Cette sorte de philosophie de vie, dans un tel roman, est à la fois déconcertante et extrêmement apaisante.

Par contre, niveau bavardages, elle est plutôt renfermée, la fillette. Mais malgré cela, il y a quand même de nombreuses discussions entre Temple et d'autres protagonistes, dont tous ne sont pas forcément ses amis (et c'est un euphémisme), dans lesquelles il est beaucoup question d'apprécier la beauté du monde, de la roublardise de Dieu, de choses que l'on doit faire, parce que c'est comme ça que ça doit être... même si, souvent, les autres parlent bien plus qu'elle. Encore une fois, toutes ces réflexions et considérations donnent une sensation de sérénité, d'acceptation, que l'on ne s'attend pas à trouver dans un livre de ce genre, surtout avec une héroïne de 15 ans, mais qui lui donnent toute sa profondeur et sa beauté.

Côté personnages secondaires, l'auteur sait nous les dépeindre en quelques phrases, que ce soit physiquement ou psychologiquement. Tous ont un passé, des blessures intimes, et tous recherchent quelque chose, ou rêvent de quelque chose. Tous ont leur importance à un moment ou l'autre dans la vie de Temple, et tous m'ont beaucoup marquée.

Ce que j'ai ressenti tout au long de ma lecture était vraiment très fort, et résonne encore en moi aujourd'hui. Empreint de poésie et doté d'un aspect forcément sombre, étant donné le contexte, il n'est pas désespéré pour autant. Les personnages de ce roman ont appris à vivre dans ce monde qui est désormais le leur, et ils en ont tiré des leçons de vie, une certaine acceptation, et c'est cela qui m'a le plus marquée.

J'ai eu la très nette sensation d'être devant un grand livre, pour ne pas dire un futur classique de la science-fiction.

Conclusion : Une histoire sombre mais où brille une lueur d'espoir et une certaine sérénité, avec des personnages forts et une héroïne atypique, à la fois attachante et étonnante. Un roman puissant et poétique à la fois, à la beauté sauvage teintée de violence, qui m'a profondément marquée.
