I picked up this book on sale and because I read a review of it that I really liked. And I liked the book. The story is about a girl Temple, born after the world is taken over by zombies. I loved the character- she was realistic but in a zombie cowboy sort of way- very human, with regrets and guilt over her young life. I think the thing that turned me off the most was her need to be forgiven and her spiritualistic desires. It wasn't these kind of concerns themselves that turned me off, a situation like this would certainly have many turn towards a greater power- but where were these values and beliefs instilled? Growing up in an orphanage and having those who raised her eventually killed- where did these beliefs come from? These desires were so strong, I needed them better explained, so the ending didn't quite work for me. I admired Temple as a young hero and her resiliency definitely had me reading, but I was left with empty questions that didn't sit well with me.

Proof positive that the soulful, emotionally resonant post-apocalyptic zombie road novel is not an oxymoron.

I agree with many of the comparisons made between Alden Bell's style and the likes of McCarthy, Faulkner et al. Alden Bell uses the blighted, zombie ridden post-apocalyptic landscape to render his storytelling with the kind of mythic, Old Testament gravity that one expects from those types of writers.

I really enjoyed Temple's emotional journey in this novel. Despite all of the devastation and horror around her, Temple doesn't hate the world and is driven by a sense of purpose and duty that transcends her personal needs. And yet, she carries a secret burden which damns her to a life of solitude and the endless highway. And she can handle a Gurkha knife like nobody's business. "Meatskin Tango" is one of the many phrases from this book that will live in my memory for a long time.

The mutant hillbillies were a nice touch too.

Highly recommended.

This was my third time reading this book and it remains utterly fantastic. It's a zombie book, but the zombies are incidental. They start out more central to the plot but as the book continues the zombies fade into the background. It's more about a girl trying to survive in a dog-eat-dog world, but it's a world she's always known, so she isn't bothered by it. She's killed a man and is being pursued by his brother, seeking the revenge that he believes is his duty, even though, in the depths of his soul, he actually likes and respects her. It's about being stuck to your fate, but facing it with grace.

Everybody should read this.

(Note: I have just finished reading this book for the fourth time and it only gets better with rereading. The ending made me cry this time. I don't think it's done that before. I am seriously considering going out and buying 12 copies and just handing it out to everybody I know.)

(5th time at least. Still my favorite. All the stars.)

Recommended by a friend who likes to send books with strong female heroines. It was definitely entertaining to read now that zombies and zombie apocalypses are in style. I finished in about two sittings/one day.

I didn't recognize the Biblical reference when I first read. Now that I do, I think it's a pretty loose one -- although if I had to explain, I would say that Temple's life contrasted against the other survivors she encounters could be a modern expression of the separation of wheat and tares. She herself is unsure of her standing in good and evil (not even standing with God, I don't recall this being a theme) up until her death.

I liked the post-apocalyptic element and the depiction of how dark the human heart actually is when the comfort of the world is snatched from us (the community in the skyscrapers) or how weak the mind is, wanting to reject reality and live in denial... unable to face the Truth (the rich family living in oblivion behind their gates).

*Note from before: Highly recommended by George. Not sure it's my cup of tea though. I'm halfway, and I've lost my interest in it. I'm going on to Fearless Fourteen, but I'll come back to it after that.*

This was definitely not my cup of tea in a lot of ways, but it was horrible and beautiful, and I couldn't help but get sucked into it. It focused not on the zombies so much, in fact they're pretty much just in the background. Instead, it focused on the people, and particularly the evil in people. The narrator does a wonderful job, the writing was wonderfully lyrical. But my scalp prickles when I hear or see something gross, and it sure was prickling during the end of disc 3, and most of disc 4. Yuck. There is no happy ending, which makes it definitely not my cup of tea, but the journey was enjoyable enough that it still gets full stars.

Zombies..... Not much more needs to be said. You either like them or hate them. I think you can see by my review which side I'm on. Here's the synopsis anyway;

Zombies are the order of business in an apocalyptic future world. Temple is a 15-year old girl who is thrust into a world where self-preservation is a way of life. Desolation is everywhere and she must strive to stay alive amongst the threat of zombies as well as desperate and depraved people. Temple is a strong female character who finds another survivor and treks across the country to stay alive.

The Reapers are the Angels is a 2011 Alex Award winner (Books written for adults that may be enjoyed by Young Adults). The theme is a bit heavy and is best read by older YA readers. The female lead character is very strong and because of that this book may appeal to female fans of horror.

Temple, 15 ans, a toujours connue un monde dominé par les zombies. Chaque jour elle lutte pour survivre et cherche un sens à sa vie sur une terre vide où subsistent peu de survivants. Alors qu’elle se réfugie parmi un groupe de survivants, un incident survient et elle se retrouve alors traqué par un homme qui a juré de la tuer.
Les Faucheurs sont les anges est un curieux mélange de réflexions philosophiques, de zombies, et de courses poursuites aux allures de road trip à travers l’Amérique. Les personnages sont intéressants, le ton du récit plutôt mélancolique est surprenant pour ce type de roman et les zombies, contrairement à la plupart des histoires sur le même thème, servent l’intrigue mais n’en sont pas l’élément central. A recommander pour ceux qui cherchent une histoire poétique et réaliste sur fond de fin du monde et/ou qui ont aimé la Route de Cormac McCarthy.

I never actually finished this book. First off, the authors says something in one paragraph that could be cut down to about five words, which really distracts from the story. Second, I know NOTHING personality-wise about the main character, Temple, and I got through about one-fourth of the book. In all honesty, I find Temple like a blank slate. There is literally nothing to her personality. The thing that drives me nuts about the book, even above the lack of character development, is the fact there are NO quotation marks. NONE. How the hell am I supposed to tell who's talking in a conversation without them?! Considering the writing style sounds sometimes like someone is talking when there isn't. I just found it tiring and cumbersome to read, and I started to dread trying to keep reading it, so I have given up before I give myself a massive headache.

Please, read this book! If you’re looking for a typical zombie novel never mind because this isn’t it. In this one the zombies are merely a part of the scenery for the most part. The writing is so incredible I found myself backing up and rereading sentences and paragraphs often just to enjoy them again. I never do that! I saw reviews that are critical of some aspects of the story pertaining to how things would be 25 years into a zombie apocalypse, but I don’t think that matters. I also don’t have a problem with the author’s choice to forgo some punctuation such as quotations marks for dialogue. It’s a choice, and it’s consistent. Honestly the writing is just so good that I will recommend this book to many people. I will probably read it again after a while, another thing I very rarely do. It’s simply beautiful and poetic.

Solid 4-star zombie yarn right up to page 123, when The Family, a group of <input type="checkbox" class="spoiler__control" aria-label="The following text has been marked spoiler. Toggle checkbox to reveal or hide." onchange="this.labels[0].setAttribute('aria-hidden', !this.checked);" id="7ace17b4-dcbb-433c-8a2e-c63a52d9302e" /><label aria-hidden="true" class="spoiler" for="7ace17b4-dcbb-433c-8a2e-c63a52d9302e">juicing, hillbilly saquatch zombies with exoskeletons of bone</label> shows up. I don't know why Alden Bell felt the need to throw this wrench in the works. It didn't really fit in with the rest of the novel and it wasn't necessary to move the plot forward. Maybe he had the image of this particular bugbear banging around in his head for a few years and he just had to get it on paper. Maybe he thought he needed to do something that would distinguish his zombie novel from all the others. That would be a shame because he had already done so with the unique style of the novel, his engaging protagonist, and his skillful handling of the zombies themselves.

I had a hard time rating this book. It's pretty gruesome at times, and has a sad, dark feeling throughout and personally I don't like to read books like that too often. But. . . BUT, the writing was so incredible, and evocative that I felt I was living everything right with Temple (which is not a pretty place to be). And honestly I think that any author who can create a character like Temple, who is so compassionate and brave even though she is so broken from choices she's made in her past, deserves a high rating. Temple was the absolute best part of this book, she's a character you can't help but care about.

This book did make me feel, deeply and it is not one I'll be forgetting any time soon.

I am blown away by this book. I think this is considered YA and I typically have a difficult time with the language and general immaturity of of characters in YA novels, but this book is VERY different. The young protagonist, Temple, is just 15, but has lived on her own for years since zombies attacked her orphanage as a young girl. Temple was born after the world was taken over by Zombies 25 years prior, so this is the only life she knows. Temple has a shocking maturity level for her age, but most of all she retains a surprising sympathy towards the slugs (zombies), even though they have killed loved ones in the past.

This book is not your mindless zombie apocalypse novel, it is full of substance and philosophy-most definitely a worthy read.

Zombie novels are fun. We all know this to be true. But it's a rare zombie novel indeed that stretches beyond the realm of 'beach read' into something, Lord help me, approaching literature, and this one does it. Even the formatting choices (most notably the absence of quotation marks for speech) aid in bringing the reader into the intense atmosphere of the world Temple lives in. And it's Temple's particular view of the world, this corrupted, "meatskin" infested world, that is so completely engrossing. She is a fifteen year old paradox: a vulnerable warrior, a loving loner, a visionary pragmatist. Temple is, in other words, a marvel, and it is a delightful thing that Alden Bell has imagined her into existence.

Poetic and gruesome and thought provoking and truly unexpected, this was a wonderful read for a bazillion reasons. Having read a few zombie books already, it bring something new and fresh and DEEP to the genre. I particularly loved the nature V nurture argument it poses, or shall i say that Temple posed again and again; was she truly evil or a victim of circumstance?

Temple was such a refreshing lead character, uncertain of herself yet resolute when it counts (who can forget that one scene in the mutant town :O) and caring, yet rational enough to make the intelligent choices so many female protagonists lack. Forget the amazing story line, the slew of memorable characters and the impressive prose, if you want one reason to read this book then Temple is enough.

Got about halfway though this book before stopping, don't know if I will bother to pick it back up. Hate the way that it's writen, not to even think about the fact that half the places have working - power, water, ect ect - or even that the main charater justs stops by stores - mostly untouched by anything or anyone - and gets snack foods and cokes when shes hungery..
For a post end of the world book, or even a zombie book, i find it a fail..
**Edit 9-25-10**
Finished the book after putting it down for a while. Easily the worst book I have ever read. Don't read it unless your just looking to take a nap..

This book is not a light read.

While I thought that it was well written, it didn't sit well with the rest of the story. Too much about the setting - dark atmosphere and I find the writing too flowery for a book involving an illiterate main character.

Also, didn't enjoy the main character, Temple and the storyline just went on without any depth. I find myself struggling to keep up with her journey. There wasn't much violence or gore as I expected from a zombie book but fairly portrayed some good moments I thought was exciting. Personally, "The Reapers Are the Angels" is not a memorable read for me.

This book's ending was so disappointing it motivated me to write this review. The story starts strong, but by the end my suspension of disbelief was long gone due to all the "deus ex machina" it took to sustain and wrap up storylines. I kept hoping the end would salvage the book, but that sent mixed messages and seemed like a cheap gimmick to generate a "surprise ending." I liked THE ROAD (which this book is VERY similar too), but this story's initial promise sours by the end. Overall it's just an okay "zombie" book (due to the engaging start), but I'd say look for other books if you value your reading time and/or dislike muddled endings.

The Reapers are the Angels started out amazing.
The description of a zombie was really detailed, and quiet gruesome.
I loved it, and was hoping it would stay that way.

Unfortunately, it sort of lost me after that.
I was confused at a lot of points, and was bored.
There was flashes of stuff that i liked, but they didn't come very often.

I didn't know what to think of Temple. Sometimes i liked her, but other times she really annoyed me.

It had a promising start, but didn't live up to it.

I know that a lot of people really enjoyed this book but sadly I am not one of them. The writing of this book really bothered me. The fact that there were no quotes bugged me. I found it confusing at times. Maybe I will give it another try one day.

I also noticed in the beginning that she quoted Stephen King. As the book goes on I noticed that Maury resembled Tom Cullen from Stephen Kings "The Stand" The way they describe him reminded me so much of Tom Cullen. The way that Temple refers to him as "Dummy" reminded me of how Julie Lawry
( the crazy lady that they meet when Tom is sick ) speaks to him.

Who would have thought?... A zombie tale that literally made me cry, and not because of the horror and gore. Just to make things clear, there is no trace of romance in the story. I would call it an emotional psychological thriller with zombies in the background. It's rare to find a heroine as believable as Temple, independent and self-sufficient on the surface, but eliciting so much empathy from the reader because of her internal struggles, honesty and kindness which she would never actually acknowledge she possessed. I wish the ending could have been different, but I did get Moses as well. I just wish he could have changed his mind...

Book Plug: Jayden Tuthill
11/1/15

This is the story of temple. Temple is one of the rare survivors of an zombie apocalypse or slugs. Temple is trying to make her way through this with her ghurka knife and pistol. She has been around these zombies for a long time with lots of experience she has to try to make it through this although this virus has been around for 25 years.


If you liked Hatchet you would like this book because its a very descriptive, brutal, and a great survival story.

I received this book from a Secret Santa....it is definitely not the type of book that I would have chosen for myself. I really liked it!! I was so surprised. I think what held my interest most was the main character...a fifteen year old girl named Temple. She was one tough little cookie, and could really kick some zombie ass. Along in her journey from Florida towards the west coast, she meets a variety of non-meatskins (normal people) a colorful cast of characters that are for the most part, likable. If you are a Zombie novel fan, then I recommend this one.

Very Good!!!

Well, I casually stared this book at 3:00 in the afternoon, and I just finished it. Talk about a gripping plot (and my lack of self control). I was in the mood for a light zombie novel, and this one fit the bill. This is definitely NOT rated PG-13 due to the level of gore, but I guess that is to be expected when zombies are overrunning the earth. I really loved the main character of the book, and was surprised to find that the writing was at times very beautiful (in between decapitations).

I generally don't dig anything with zombies in it, but I was motivated to read this as part of a horror novels challenge. And I'm glad I did because it's an amazing book. It's difficult to imagine how a post-apocalyptic setting with zombies can be so horrifying and so heart-breaking at the same time; go no further, "The Reapers are the Angels" manage to do exactly that. I loved every page of this unique, magnificent novel. I loved the strangeness of it, the raw quality of the language and its beauty, the characters, the inevitability of the ending. Overall, an amazing read.

I was really wanting to like this book but it was really just 'meh'. First off, the writing was truncated, choppy and difficult to follow. The total absence of quotation marks when people were talking really ruined it for me. Half the time I wasn't sure who was speaking, or when speach transitioned into thought and visa versa. The story line might have been more interesting if I wasn't so distracted by the bad Grammer and flip floppy writing style. I stopped reading this book 2/3 of the way through, just wasn't enjoyable.

Wow.

I did not like the first half of the book. In fact, I almost gave up on it. But I put it down and came back to it a couple days later. And holy crap. Very intense, very powerful, very much of I don't quite know what to say about it yet.

Well, I take that back. Reading this book when you are somewhat sick and nauseated is NOT a good idea lol. I did have to skip over some of the gore. But Temple...damn she's one hell of a character!

A post-apocalyptic zombie novel, said to be modeled on Southern Gothic horror. (I think that means there's a lot of religious references, but they aren't cloying). There's nothing strikingly original here, but it is elegiac, involving, and the writing is a notch above what the genre usually offers. I cared about Temple, the fifteen year old protagonist who grew up in this ruined world, and her wrestling with whether she is good or bad, but there was no earth-shaking meaning in the novel.

i'm a sucker for post-apocalyptic novels, zombies, and kick-ass female protagonists. so it's no surprise that i enjoyed this. in parts, the book reminded me of other post-apocalyptic novels, like The Dead-Tossed Waves and The Road. the main character is bad-ass and can convincingly take care of herself in the blighted world. although many parts of the book were typical of the genre, there were several plot twists that added enough interest to make this an engaging read.

In THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS, Temple, a young woman, helps a mentally retarded man find his home, seeking redemption in the process, while a killer hunts her, seeking revenge. The setting is sometimes oddly unrealistic and the poetic voice at times a little overworked, but it is a beautiful book–that rare literary zombie novel–that questions whether one must choose between survival and morality during the apocalypse. A must read.

To be honest I had to give up reading this book as I couldn't cope with the lack of speech marks. I found myself having to reread the conversations once I realised someone was talking, which ruined the flow of the story for me. The story was interesting enough (at least the bit I read), but not interesting enough for me to force myself to read the rest of it. If a new version is printed which contains quotations the I'd probably read it then, but it wouldn't be top of my list.

Je ne sais que penser réellement de ce livre. L'écriture me donne l'impression d'être saccadée et part parfois dans une direction un peu trop religieuse avec toutes les références à Dieu.
L'histoire ne m'a pas convaincu même si elle avait du potentiel. Ce livre m'a fait pensé à un mélange d’essentiellement 2 livres que j'ai pus lire précédemment en ajoutant la petite touche de l'auteur mais qui n'a pas suffit pour m'emporter dans cet univers.

I'm not sure what to think of this. There was beauty and horror. Terrible, awful, brutal violence.

Seriously, I'm completely flummoxed here. I don't know what to say. There is such an awful landscape to this story. Yet there are moments of small miracles, of kindness and humanity, and those are so stark that they're terrible too, in the midst of all that ugly.

A very quick read, but man, will it leave an impression.

Temple is one of the survivors of the apocalypse and lives amongst the zombies and the others that remain. She is 15 and has learnt to fight, she does not fear the ‘meatskins’ (refreshing), in fact she has more problems with other folks! Brilliantly written in the dialect of Temple I found this to be very enjoyable with great 3D characters and an unpredictable story. It is not like other zombie stories but I don't care I loved her kick ass attitude!

Meh...it takes a lot for me to not like a zombie book. This is written in the style of a western, so that right there turned me off. There's a plot development halfway through the book that is very weird and not at all explained that was the final straw. I was hanging on until that point.

And can we all agree that you can be edgy and literary and still use quotation marks? I was irrationally annoyed by this throughout the entire book.

I made it about a third of the way into this book before giving up. The lack of proper punctuation was irritating - I refer to when someone was speaking, the usage of "" was not used. I would not say this is a YA novel, but it read like it was written by one. Perhaps because of the age/lack of education for the main character, that he author wrote in that particular style. I don't know. I just found it irritating, and too 'dumbed down' for me.

"Through the tiny broken-out place in the window above, she sees a touch of movement. She focuses on it, watching it inch along, little more than a finger shadow against the daylight. It’s a green caterpillar, and it pokes its way through the hole in the glass and along the sill of the window.

And she thinks:
Ain’t no hell deep enough to keep heaven out."

A really solid zombie apocalypse story. I loved Temple and her fierceness, determination, and not-taking-any-of-it attitude. The ending was unexpected, in a good way. This one leans gruesome and gory, but like all good zombie tales, it's really a story about humanity and what keeps people alive and driven to survive.

Side note: I didn't realize Bell was Megan Abbott's husband, which was a neat little fact to find in the author's 2-sentence bio.

Very Underappreciated!!!Enjoyed the story. (post apocalyptic zombie). loved the voice of a mountain man poet coming out of a young woman. there are some technical issues with the end days but i chose to let them go. if you're that person(s) who knows that gasoline spoils after around a year or so and has a problem with someone refueling 25 years after the fall and driving on you will be irritated. I let the little stuff go and enjoyed what was done so well.

Recomiendo este libro ya que para mi es original, al no haber leído nada de zombies antes, y el autor es muy arriesgado al crear este mundo con mucho lujo y detalle y a una protagonista valiente y fuerte que nos demuestra que se puede encontrar la belleza en la vida. Espero que le den una oportunidad.

Lee mi reseña -> http://vivimosentrepaginas.blogspot.c...

I really liked "The Reapers are the Angels". The main character, Temple, is only 15, but she is tough as nails. Temple has never known a world without zombies, a world without hardship and fighting for survival. She is wise beyond her years, although she can't read or write. And despite everything, she still has a kind heart.

I'm going to miss that girl. Finishing the book was like losing a close friend.

Protecting yourself is a big thing in the post zombiepocalypse world - Temple have developed a style of self-protection that dictates lying, avoiding creating bonds to other people and always being on the move.

The book echoes this by only letting us read the story as told by Temple, and it gives it the feeling of distance that she has to the World - so read it if you aren't afraid to be alone with the zombies.....

I enjoyed this book so much. Until I didn't. The writing was stellar. The protagonist, Temple, is up there with the best girl narrators - Scout Finch, Ellen Foster, Elvis from Rabbit Cake. Kind of a female Huck Finn with mad fighting skills. So the resolution of her story arc felt like a betrayal of her, and of the reader. I don't require happy endings to books, but this was beyond unsatisfying. I have no interest in reading on in this series.

Una muy buena historia corta, donde la protagonista y el antagonista tienen una dinámica muy interesante, además de parecerme que tiene una cierta vibra al estilo Fallout. En mi caso como me tocó escuchar el audiolibro la experiencia fue muy agradable dada la voz que eligieron para narrar hizo un muy buen trabajo para darles personalidad a los personajes.

Si quieren una historia corta de zombies con una prota femenina rebelde adolescente, los invito a que le den un vistazo.

I absolutely LOVED this book. Alden Bell does an amazing job of bringing his characters to life-from Temple, the main character, to the zombies or "meatskins" themselves. Add to this an amazing portrait of a ruined american landscape written with beautiful prose, and you have a fantastic novel.

One of the best I've read in a very long time!

I didn't pick up this "zombie novel" expecting poetry or profundity, but it turns out that The Angels Are the Reapers, like Cormac McCarthy's The Road, isn't about horror/sc-fi tropes as much as it is a philosophical exploration of guilt, responsibility and redemption...an amazingly good, elegiac and sorrowful novel...

When I started reading The Reapers Are the Angels, I was pleasantly surprised. I don't believe I have ever read a zombie book which is so very well written! I was so caught up in the quest of 15 year old Temple for truth, knowledge and beauty. I felt so much sympathy as her anger could turn
Temple into a lethal weapon. A GREAT read!

As far as zombie apocalypse fic goes, this book is one of my faves so far. The story follows Temple, a teenager on her own in a zombie filled world. Throw in a mute, mentally challenged man that Temple takes charge of, a family of socialites holed up in their estate, scary redneck mutants and a few other interesting characters and you've got yourself a great story.

A beautifully well told story that takes place 25 years after a zombie outbreak, detailing the life of a 15 year old orphan girl who only knows one thing: survival. Rich prose written in a style similar to Cormac McCarthy with a lead character that reminded me of Mattie Ross from True Grit. Even if you're not a fan of zombie lit, give this one a chance. I think you'll enjoy it.

recommendFor: People that don't mind a robotic MC
text:
2/5 stars

If only I could have emotionally connected Temple. Maybe then I would have found this book as beautiful as others did. This book did have some good lines in it. I'll give it that. It's too bad I felt so alienated from the MC that they made me feel absolutely nothing in the end.

Coldness and disappointment. Those are the feelings The Reapers Are The Angels left me with.

recommendFor: anyone who likes the inner struggle of "The Walking Dead" series
text:
This was a beautifully crafted zombie apocalypse story. Yeah, I know, "beautifully" shouldn't be in the same sentence as "zombie", but it's true. Bell wove an impressive tapestry starting with believable emotional characters, a desolate stage for them to play on AND absolutely NO quote marks for dialogue (they would've gotten in the way).

Thanks, Michelle, for the awesome recommendation!

Probably the best book I've read this year. Imagine Cormac McCarthy writing the zombie apocalypse through the eyes of a 15 year-old girl, except with the focus on the beauty and freedom of life on the road rather than bleakness and inhumanity (though there's a fair bit of that along the way as well). Can't recommend it enough.

Really really good. Wonderful writing and great characterization. Temple has got some serious charm and her interplay with the character, Moses Todd is deep and complicated. Really creative integration of the living dead to develop an atmosphere and a framework to tackle some bigger questions about how we find meaning in our lives.

Ta książka była okropna. Styl pisania beznadziejny, fabuła nudna, zakończenie nieciekawe, jedyne co było ładne to opisy. Bardzo długo ją czytałam, nie mogłam się zebrać do tego, żeby czytać więcej niż 2 strony dziennie. Całość wygląda jak opowiadanie napisane przez nastolatka na lekcje języka angielskiego.

This was great. Really enjoyed it. A lovely "gothic western justice novel", True Grit with zombies, as this reviewer described it: http://www.goodreads.com/review/show/... Go read that review, it pretty much says it all.

This is a beautiful story. I was looking forward to it because I love post-apocalypse stories and zombies stories. This is so much more than that. The people are incredibly real, the journies riveting.

Without a doubt this is one of the best books I've read all year. It's beautifully written, high readable, has characters that are relatable, and world-building that is believable. Plus it's got zombies. Need I say more?

An interesting twist on a zombie novel. Zombies are far from the scariest thing in this book. Even more frightening and unsettling are the explorations into how scary humans can be and if there is redemption for even the wicked. Very well done.

It's a incredible gripping novel. I loved Temple and how strong she was. It's taken from her point of view. Not too many zombie books or films take it from the point of view of someone who has grown-up in this way of life. The action is on point, well-thought out and paced nicely.

Yeah it's a zombie novel but the voice and writing style transcends the typical zombie novel. And yes the lead character is 15 but there is nothing YA about this book. The prose is, well.....beautiful. It feels weird saying that about a PA zombie novel, yet it fits. I can't recommend it enough!

Oh! I just figured out why I loved this book so much. Its like "To Kill A Mockingbird" but with zombies. Poetic and descriptive. And characters that you grow to love and don't want to ever leave. I know it sounds crazy, but that's what I am feeling.

Put the Thesaurus down slowly and no one gets hurt .. geez. This entire book carried on with such discord between Temple's simple Southern speech and the flowery, "intellectual" narration. Liked Temple well enough and kept waiting for the story to be worth it, just never happened for me.

combines Joyce Carol Oates, Flannery O'Connor, the lightest touch of Scott Fitzgerald, and a dab of A Choir of Ill Children.


just read Karen's review. I'm not even going to try with this one.

I really like the zombie story with a western feel. Temple is a strong girl and could probably kick most 15 yrs old butts. I absolutely hated the end of this book, but in a good way. Didn't see that coming at all and it was just so sudden!

Read about zombies, dream about zombies. Held onto this one cause I was afraid it wouldn't be any good. Read it last night and couldn't put it down till the end. Really good YA dystopian read. Just got the 2nd book yesterday and will have to read it over the weekend.

Vivid, violent, philosophical. This book was so much more than I anticipated. Alden Bell is an amazing storyteller; his words rich with imagery. His dystopian world sucks you right in and spits you out, changed and heartbroken.

This book was a sleeper. Probably one of the best zombie books that I ever read. I could not put the book down with a fifteen year old girl reminding me of a combination Uma therman in Kill Bill and John Wayne from True Grit. Fantastic read.

i don't want to tell anything about this book It makes me so sad in 225 pages I will keep it maybe even reread it Won't say it was amazing (it's a zombie world and i don't really care for this sort of stories) but i really happy to have read it

Literate, atmospheric zombie thriller that wanders through themes of vengeance, mercy, humanity, and providence. Characters are drawn so boldly that I'm sure I'm missing their deeper typological significance. Not for everyone, but I was fascinated.

So this was way outside my usual fare and I'm not sure zombies are really for me. That being said, Temple was pretty kick ass. I did love how snarky, ballsy and capable she was. All of these stars are for her.
I really enjoyed this book. I haven't gotten to read in quite a while, but this one captured my attention and kept it the entire time.
Temple knows no other world than this one, ravaged and desperate, plagued by meatskins and unnamed evils. From the title to the last line - beautiful, with a hard, hard edge.
Loved it. Shed a little tear at the end, even! Definitely not your average zombie novel. Find my full review here - Linkylink
Superb. Stumbles once or twice, but it still wins the race. Lush with style, a honed focus, and sense of purpose that together explode the notion of genre. Pastiche in all the right ways.
This book was very atmospheric. It really reminded me of a female teenage slingblade in post appoc zombie world. I thought it was about to deep for me. Glad I read it.
I found this story stiff and completely unbelievable. I could give examples, but pretty much every turn in the story, I had trouble with.
Best gothic postapocalyptic teen girl zombie novel ever.
Utterly gorgeous language--not for the squeamish, though (but then, zombie books don't tend to be, do they?)
Solo por ese inicio no le doy las cinco estrellas. Un libro al que le podrán encontrar muchos peros, pero que simplemente es muy bueno, claramente, no para todo público.
I was on board until the mutants turned it into a comedy. Then it all just felt goofy and I felt goofy for being invested.
This book is so fine. Could not put it down, looked forward to picking it up. Made you think about life, the future, how it could be.
Very cool book. It's as if Cormac McCarthy wrote a book that was equal parts True Grit and zombies. Dark and erudite, it's a refreshing change from the normal pulp undead fare.

My Reaction:
I had a mixed reaction to this book.  It was very well written-- much more elegantly (if not realistically) presented than your average zombie novel.  I admired the strength of our young heroine, Temple, and was always interested in what would happen next.  And yet... Something was missing.  Emotion... I didn't have an emotional response.  For whatever reason, it left me, if not quite cold, at least a little cool.  As a result, I have to give a half-hearted review.

Caveats aside, I would recommend the book to fans of zombie/post-apocalyptic fiction who are looking for something less pulpy, more literary.  Though in some ways it seems like YA literature, some of the rough language and themes (not to mention the violence) make it inappropriate for younger readers.  Best for only the oldest teens and up, imho. 


Tidbits:
--  I liked Temple best in the very first section of the book and somewhat less as the story went on.  (Not a good sign...)

--  Temple drags out some odd words for a girl who apparently has had so little formal education.  (She's street smart, but illiterate.)

--  It's always interesting to see how characters in a zombie novel label the zombies.  (Seems like they very rarely call them "zombies".)  In this book, we have "slugs", "meatskins", "creepers", and "gobblers".

--  Temple was born into the zombie-infested world.  She doesn't know anything else, and so she's more at home in the new landscape than are adults who remember how things used to be.  She's exasperated with people who sigh over the past and creep through the present with fear and loathing-- or act like they expect the world to somehow change back, if only they wait long enough.  She, instead, is the ultimate pragmatist.  The world is what it is; she's alive now, and she accepts her reality with no qualms.  That's a fascinating perspective, and one I don't think I've seen addressed in other zombie books. 

--  Not a huge fan of the present tense in fiction.  Eventually, I got used to it, but I still don't love it.  Similarly, not impressed by the lack of quotation marks. I mean, why?  It just makes the book more difficult to read.  (Of course, I think e.e. cummings was pretty ridiculous for eschewing capital letters.  My tolerance for nonsense is low.)

--  The Biblical references... Not sure I have much to say about them.  Ta-da.  They were there. 

--  "In her own experience, she's learned that happiness and sadness find their own level no matter what's biting you, mosquitoes or meatskins."


Temple holds everyone out at arm's length, and it's hard to be emotionally invested in a character like that.
Well this was a surprise. It's like Cormac McCarthy wrote the novelization for Dawn of the Dead.

text:
In many ways, I'm still processing this book, so my apologies if this review sounds a little disjointed, rambling, and/or underdeveloped.

I loaned this book from a classmate of mine after expressing my disappointment in Zone One, which is basically the only other major "literary" zombie novel and the one that I'd had to read for a class on monstrosity in fiction. She'd read this one for the same class a couple of semesters back and said it was much better, loaning it to me for the summer. I have to say, I can't remember ever being so grateful to borrow a book in my life. (In an attempt to be balanced, though, I should probably add that a part of my delight might stem from the simple fact that it isn't Zone One.)

There's just so much this book covers, and very little of it really has to deal with zombies. It reminds me of something that the teacher for my class on monstrosity once said, which is that zombie books usually aren't really about zombies. There's the decay of the Old South, family, destiny, God, the deconstruction of society, and redemption, and it's all squeezed into a fairly slim novel with a relentless pace. I finished it in 2-3 hours reading non-stop on a road trip. I started off wanting to read one chapter, then another, then to get to the 50 page mark, and before I knew it I was halfway done and decided to just finish it because there was no way I was putting it down.

I'm still thinking of how all the themes interconnect and how everything ties into itself, and it's been several weeks. I particularly love the relationship between Temple and Moses Todd and how there's this tragedy to their interactions, with both "getting" each other on a level that no one else really can, to the extent that their relationship resembles a sort of twisted father-daughter scenario, but also being deadlocked into a situation where they have to go against each other.

Twenty-five years after civilisation collapsed due to the appearance of the 'meatskins', a young woman named Temple has found solace living on an island off the south coast of Florida. When she finds a meatskin on the beach, she realises that her sanctuary is no longer secure and she strikes back north to the mainland. As she journeys through the former southern states of America, she finds herself a charge and a mission, but she also makes a remorseless enemy of someone who could have been an ally.

Alden Bell's second novel (but his first genre piece) is an intriguing book. It's a post-apocalyptic novel with zombies, but zombies who are almost incidental to the plot. The undead are presented as more of a nuisance than a major menace, only really dangerous in large numbers in contained areas, otherwise they can be outrun or out-maneuvered easily. Humanity has adapted to their presence and life continues, albeit at a different, more isolated pace.

With the zombies more of a background menace than an actual threat, the narrative focuses on Temple, a teenage girl who's grown up knowing nothing other than the world as it is. She is one of the first of a new generation of dispossessed, to whom avoiding meatskin packs and executing bitten friends is a way of life. This way of life on the road, contrasted with a more comfortable life in the sealed-off enclaves, engenders a certain amount of camaraderie and mutual respect between the wanderers. At the same time, there is plenty of scope for conflict, for rivalries and murderous grudges. This also gives the book something of the feel of a Western, with zombies standing in for hostile native tribes and where towns again represent outposts of light in a hostile wilderness (there's even a dangerous train journey through zombie-infested territory at one point which could have come out of a Western, zombies excepted of course).


The focus of the story is the grudge between Temple and Moses Todd, another wanderer on the road with his own code of honour that he feels he must adhere to or lose himself. Temple is established through flashbacks and stories about her life that she tells others (some stories more reliable than others) and is a fully-rounded protagonist. Moses, whom we only meet in chapters from Temple's POV (which make almost all of the book), is well-established through dialogue and his actions as he pursues Temple relentlessly across the American South, and part of the tragedy of the novel is that these two characters could easily have been allies and comrades if events did not drive a wedge between them.

Bell's prose is rich, evocative and intelligent, a genuine pleasure to read, although an odd quirk is his decision not to use speech or quotation marks (or the use of a hyphen sometimes favoured by older writers). This results in bursts of confusion as it is sometimes unclear if we are reading Temple's thoughts, some description of passing scenery or actual dialogue between her and another character, and becomes mildly irritating at the book continues. Another issue is inconsistent levels of education in the characters: Temple knows how to drive and maintain a car and is aware of the principles of aerodynamic flight, but doesn't know how to read or write (a facet which adds nothing to her character but is purely a contrived situation to delay her decision on where to go next as she can't read the directions someone he written down).

The Reapers Are the Angels (****½) is a superior post-apocalyptic novel whose literary ambitions are intriguing and impressive, if not altogether successful. The novel is available now in the UK and USA.

Ashley: Temple… Temple, is her name- Dude, for like TWO paragraphs I thought they were talking about an ACTUAL Temple and I was WICKED confused

Smash: For real?

Ashley: YES!! I had to re-read the first few pages several times… I’m fairly certain that the ‘literary genius’ of this novel was totally lost on me. ;)

Smash: Heh. I’m not sure I would go that far. ;) However, I loved the name choice. Throughout the book, she reminded me of a sturdy temple, refusing to fall.

Ashley: Really? Dude, I was too freaking irritated throughout Reapers to concentrate much on the story… What ‘perspective’ was this told in? Have you ever read anything without the use of quotations??

Smash: No, and it was wicked annoying. You had to really focus to know when something was being spoken. I am not sure why the author chose to go that route. However, the story was definitely from Temple’s perspective, and an interesting perspective it was!

Ashley: That it was!! But, you know that ‘focusing’ isn’t so much my strong suit… ;)

Smash: And while it is mine, I seem to lose it around you. :D

Ashley: Hehe!! Alright, so I honestly think that this would have been an AWESOME book- if I could have gotten past the problem I had with the whole NON-quotations thing… Why not write the dialog like EVERY other book in the world???

Smash: It was definitely hard to get past. I tell you though; I was drawn into the story from the start though. Temple was fairly young and had been on her own for a very long time. Not a lot of contact with other humans, and she has survived. I really admired her strong wit and backwards smarts. She was a tough cookie.

Ashley: My thing is… the dead rose- What? Like 25 years prior to this story right? WHY is there so much food left? Why are there so many stores, museums, landmarks, malls… EVERYTHING, left untouched?

Smash: Great point, and it isn’t one I even thought about! She did seem to have it easy while traveling, stopping at abandoned stores for her favorite crackers, which should have been spoiled and a pile of cheesy mush by then.

Ashley: See? I may not be the sharpest tool in the shed… and all that. But, it’s the little things that bug me! Like the fact that she could barely string a coherent sentence together, then used words that I had to look up in the dictionary! Like: shoal. WTF? No one knows what ‘shoal’ is! And palaver, and cartograph… I DO know what these mean, but with her limited speaking ability- you’d think she wouldn’t have such a broad vocabulary!

Smash: That’s one of the things I loved most about her though! She was wise beyond her years. Simple minded but sharp. She was hella fierce but you caught glimpses of her compassion. She tended to reason her way through everything, and I was constantly amazed by her positive outlook: “But you gotta look at the world that is and try not to get bogged down by what it ain’t.” That chick went through serious Hell and continued on like it was another day at the office.

Ashley: Okay, so what’d you think of Moses? I liked him, dude. Does this make me wicked insane? This guy tracks her with an intense sadistic passion across what is now America with the intent to kill her under any circumstance… but I liked him!

Smash: Personally, I would recommend this to zombie fans. As you’ve stated in the past, there are so many different types of zombie books. This is one of the most unique, and I think people should read it just cause. :)

But, you knew after you read it and I hadn’t that this wouldn’t be one I’d LOVE, didn’t you? I go more for “gore and blood” or “hilarious awesome” in my zombie books… rather than… uuuuuh? text:
Well here we are in October, when I get all seasonal and pack my queue with horror, paranormal and otherwise intense books. I'm taking the safe route and giving this book 3 stars. From page 1 this story reminded me of The Walking Dead, during the wandering-around seasons prior to reaching the Alexandria Safe-Zone.

This book follows a couple of weeks in the life of 15yo Sarah Mary Williams (aka Temple) across post-apocalyptic America. Because "the event" happened 25 years before, Sarah Mary has no memory of life "before" and seems well-adapted (very well) to solitary nomadic life.

While I didn't hate this book, it's difficult to describe what I thought of it. Let's see if I can make sense of a few things:

- There are excellent passages that are so poetically, beautifully written... but the story doesn't want to go anywhere. Sure, there are some objectives to accomplish, but basically it's about a girl who's just trying to lose the hangers-on she keeps running into, get back on the road alone and start going nowhere again. I guess I like books with unifying goals, so maybe this one's just me.

- There are absolutely mystifying turns in the story that are beyond weird and stretch belief - I know, it's ridiculous of me to state this but I can't help it.

- At one point Sarah Mary kills a man in self-defense and gets herself a dogged antagonist, another nomad type name Moses who lives by the same awesome code as Sarah Mary: a kind of "right thing to do" philosophy, sprinkled liberally with a lot of "reckon so" responses. This "right thing to do" stuff lends itself more to the laws of survival; a that's-just-the-way-things-are kind of view. It's not necessarily anything you or I would agree with, but I really enjoyed reading anything Sarah Mary and Moses had to say.

The book finishes in a way I both expected, and didn't. It wasn't a satisfying ending, and I think if I stick with a book all the way through it kind of owes me a satisfying ending, be it happy or sad. Overall not great, not terrible.

I recently created a ranking of the best zombie books ever written, based on popular opinion. Through a highly "scientific" process, I reviewed nearly two-dozen best zombie novel lists on websites like Audible, Book Riot, Bustle, Epic Reads, Goodreads and LitReactor. I then created a master list based on the overlap. (A "best of the best," if you will.)

In addition to being one of my personal favorites, The Reapers Are the Angels appeared in numerous "best of" lists and articles. And because I first read it many years ago, it's high time I posted a review of my own.

This is a literary take on the zombie genre. It fits into the Southern Gothic style popularized by authors like Flannery O'Connor, and employed by contemporary writers like Cormac McCarthy and the HBO series Sharp Objects.

I say this because some readers might be put off by the writing style in this novel. Other readers, like myself, might thoroughly enjoy it.

My advice is to read a sample of the first chapter. If you like the writing style -- and you're also into zombie apocalypse novels -- you'll probably love this book. If the find writing style and character voice off-putting, you can move along to the next one. No harm, no foul.

But don't get me wrong. "Literary" does not mean boring. The Reapers offers plenty of thrilling and gruesome goodness, as we've come to expect from modern zombie apocalypse fiction. But it also takes its time with character development, backstory and inner reflection.

Again, some readers will appreciate this, while others will not. You just have to know what kind of reader you are.

And speaking of characters, young Temple is one of the most memorable characters I've encountered in zombie fiction -- or fiction in general, for that matter. I still think about her from time to time, as if she's a real person. Crazy.

The takeaway: This is a coming-of-age zombie thriller with a tough female protagonist, written in a style rarely seen in the post-apocalyptic genre. It offers memorable characters, heartfelt moments, thrills and chills, and an ending that will stay with you long after you finish the book.

"But one day, when the world gets back to the way it’s supposed to be."

"What do you know about the way it’s supposed to be? You ain’t that much older than me. You were born into the same world I was."


Bizarrely, this is one of the first post-apocalyptic books I've read since the pandemic began, so certain lines have a curious resonance. The part that is different about this zombie adventure is the timing: a generation or so in, when there are kids who've not known a world different from what's given at the start of the novel - and when the main character we're following isn't some bloke waxing eloquent about the good old days.

I'm not sure there was enough to keep me reading this series, if it ends up a series (as the "Reapers, #1" naming system here implies), but it's fine as a piece of short fiction. Stylistically, it's more like "Young Goodman Brown" or an annotated travelogue for the times than anything with significant plot or character development. The problem I have with these is that it's a "this happened and then this happened and then this other thing" - things are barely connected. The lack of quotation marks is an annoying trend but I guess I just had to be in the right mood to finish reading this one. The third-person limited POV makes it particularly weird when the writer suddenly wants to wax eloquent - when the rest of the time, it's us riding along with the main character's thoughts, those interludes seem jarringly purple and inauthentic.

One week--it was the fastest I've read a book in a long time. The times that I had to put it down, I couldn't wait to get back into the story of Temple and Malcolm and Moses and Maury and the mutants and Earth despoiled by hungry meatskins/slugs (what Bell's characters call the zombies).

Bell writes in a very reflective, philosophical way, and his prose is poetic and beautiful. He uses alliteration, assonance, internal rhyme, meter, etc., so fluently he makes it look easy. But even now, as I write this review trying to emulate his beautiful style, it is NOT easy. Bell is a gifted writer who's honed his skill razor-sharp.

I loved the protagonist of Temple, alias Sarah Mary Williams (which, as I just found out by looking it up, is an allusion to Huckleberry Finn). She is a fierce and fearless fifteen-year-old (OK, now I am starting to do better emulating Bell!) who is haunted by the thought, not of meatskins/slugs eating her as she sleeps, but that she is an evil person. The questions Bell raises through her character, particularly is it possible to survive in a blighted, zombie-infested world without committing moral evil, are thought-provoking; and, though a world of zombies is (hopefully!) farfetched, this question has great relevance for us, for the lives we live.

While this book overflows with artful and beautiful quotes, there is one more than any other that blasted me right out of my seat: "All of a sudden, there is no hurry. There will be time for everything. For the breezes that blow and for the rainwater drying in the gutters... For the big things, too, things like beauty and vengeance and honour and righteousness and the grace of God..." This book isn't "Christian," and I am not sure what Bell believes personally about God, but for me as a Christian, The Reapers are the Angels (itself an allusion to Matthew 13:39) helped me think about profound questions like where is the grace of God in blight (the COVID-19 pandemic, for example) and even more, since the grace of God is everywhere, blight or no, where is the grace of God right now in my life--like Temple's "Miracle of the Fish"--that I am overlooking?

I don’t even know where to start formulating in my brain the many reasons why I couldn’t enjoy this book, so let’s start with the obvious one - why no quotation marks for characters speaking? Just, why? It didn’t make it more chilling, more telling of the post apocalyptic era or more consistent with the inner musings of the main character. Nope. All it did was serve to confuse me and make me check each sentence to be sure it was actually a conversation and not all happening in Temple’s head. A terrible idea which I just can’t understand.

The purple prose is issue number two. I’d seen this book described as having beautiful writing, sucking me into the desolate and barren wasteland filled with dribbling zombies (there’s barely any zombie action, but that’s by the by). But no, instead it felt like deliberately flowery sentences with unnecessary use of overly long and rarely used descriptive words which I can only assume were chosen to make the author appear more original or intelligent? Who knows, not me!

I also disliked some/most of the decisions the main character made. There is an attempted rape scene, for example, within this book, and the character holds her own, but then proceeds to immediately trust a bunch of strangers through the night who offer her alcohol and a promise that they won’t touch her. Seems legit.....I just can’t believe Temple would be so trusting after such an encounter.

But to top it all off, this book is so very boring. Nothing happens for at least the first 150 pages. Absolutely nothing. Unless you enjoy the idea of reading about a girl wandering around a wasteland years after a zombie apocalypse. Generous use of electricity and an endless supply of gasoline though....go figure.

I don’t know. I’m so frustrated but what I can only describe as the most disappointing book I’ve read in quite some time. Maybe the style just wasn’t for me.

What's up with the lack of quotation marks in this book? It's a pain in the ass to figure who is talking to whom, and when someone is just thinking to themselves.

I'll admit it - it was the lovely, rather strange title that drew me in. I didn't know it's actually a Bible verse, Matthew 13:39 (good choice to use a version that says "reapers" instead of "harvesters"). So, I'm not quite sure how it actually ties in with the story.

This isn't so much a zombie story as it is a survival story. The zombies just give the protagonist something to run from and provide a sparse backstory to explain why she's alone. The zombie apocalypse started 25 years ago. Temple is 15 years old. She's illiterate and likes cheese crackers. Oh yeah, she's also got almost Herculean strength and foxlike wiles as she has no trouble defending herself or getting out of sticky situations (or figuring out how . That is kind of where the author lost me. We're supposed to believe that her "uncle" (a man who took her and another orphan boy in and raised them as his own) trained her to be so proficient in weaponry and self-defense.

I just didn't like Temple.

However, I did like her story. She's on a sort of mythical quest to help an innocent person. Her journey serves as a convenient way to show how people live in this terrible world - a less than utopian commune, playing Gone With the Wind, living like hobos, or in the most creative zombie twist I've read in a long time .

It's an easy read and perhaps worth it just for the freakish aspects, but it does not really come together and kind of leaves the reader hanging.

4,5 / 5

The Reapers Are The Angels, by Alden Bell, is a book about Temple, a young girl who is forced to travel through an post-apocalyptic, de-civilized and zombified America. As usual, I will avoid going into too much detail describing what this book is about, you can read that up there ^. Instead, I will go straight into my review. Quick summary?: This is an amazing book, with an unusual writing style, exceptional setting and a unique protagonist!

Format:
In my e-book version, the book had 190 pages. It contained 3 parts divided in 16 chapters of relatively medium length (~20 pages). The narration is in 3rd person perspective and almost entirely in the present tense apart from some memories.

Characters:
The main character in this novel is of course Temple (or Sarah Mary Williams). She is a young girl living alone in a hostile environment. She is fierce, a true warrior and survival is her forte.
“Amid the hot stench of fresh offal, she rises to her feet like the dreadful ghost of a fallen battlefield soldier, her hands tacky with the thick pulpy dregs of death splayed wide.“

She is a real pragmatist but at the same time she’s looking for beauty wherever it can be found, she likes to dream and wonder and hope; after all she’s still a kid. We always know what Temple thinks and feels and we quickly get attached to a seemingly cold and thorny character.
There are many recurring secondary characters, and Bell has them really fleshed out well. We come to understand them, like them and accept them as part of Temple’s social environment, which admittedly is a very scarce one.
Needless to say Bell’s characterization is superb and spotless. The whole novel depends and builds on it and it is part of the reason why this book provokes such an intense feeling throughout.

World building:
This novel’s other major strong point is Bell’s world building, or rather his depiction of a post-apocalyptic America, plagued with “zombies” or something of the like. You see, we learn that slugs (the novel’s “zombies”) have overrun the states and are everywhere from the first pages. But these are not your ordinary scary threatening zombies. On the contrary, they are hardly “living”, moving slowly and relatively harmless in most cases. Still, they are the reason that the typical western civilization has completely collapsed and there’s hardly any form of society anywhere. The setting is desolate, empty and harsh but there are constantly overtones of nostalgia and beauty in the descriptions of each corner and sight.
“A country of foolishness and wonderment and capital and perversity. Feeling like God at supper in the sky, horizons pink and blue, a frontier blasted through with breath and industry, like God himself could suffocate on the beauty of the place, could curl up and die at beholdin his own creation, all the razor reds of the West and the broke-down South always on a lean, elegantlike, the coyote howl and the cannibal kudzu and the dusty windows that ain’t seen a rag of cleaning since.”


Plot, story & pacing:
The plot is the novel’s first hurdle, demanding of the reader to keep reading at its absence. There’s not really a grand mystery here, neither an ultimate goal. The story is more like a road-trip, an adventure that might or might not have an end or a purpose. But this is not the main strength of the book and was probably never intended to be as that spotlight is shared already by characters and setting. Still though, after a while we want to know things such as who is Maury and where does his story lead? What’s the deal with Moses? And of course, what’s going to happen to such a restless spirit if and when she deals with the problems she has consciously adopted for her own?
“It just comes from thinkin too much. That’s why you can’t slow down for long. You gotta keep your brain tired out so it don’t start searching for things to dwell on.”

As for the pacing, truth be told, the book starts slow, bluntly requiring of the reader to just keep on turning pages purely on blind faith, and honestly, maybe it takes up to the half-point until I was attached to the characters so much that I got hooked up and couldn’t stop reading. But maybe that’s too much of a request or too late, and I won’t blame people for dropping this one before they realize they have a true gem in their hands.
As a sidenote, I’m pretty sure there’s a lot of allegory and symbolism in this story... but unfortunately it was lost on me. I know it’s there, I can feel it but I can’t connect the dots and make the connection. Regardless of this, I still enjoyed the book immensely and think that it didn’t subtract from my satisfaction.

Writing:
Bell’s writing was the first thing that really stuck out to me. Initially I found it jarring and needed quite some time to get used to it. Also the use of present tense is something that I haven’t been used to and felt strange at the beginning. It didn’t take long however for me to change my opinion and accept it as part of what gives this book such a strong atmosphere and tone. In a way, it’s blunt, rough and direct, kinda like the world depicted therein and the protagonist’s personality. But while the language may intentionally be imperfect, the imagery conveyed by it is beautiful, showcasing Bell’s imagination and perspective. Make no mistake, this is a dark and cruel novel full of griminess which Bell often shoves in your face.
“And when it was finished, her clothes soaked through in blood and bile and crusted with graying tissue, she wiped from her face the gore she had ripped from the bodies of the dead—the issue of her own feral cannibalism—and only then was she able to open her eyes full to the stinging, punishing orange light of the failing day.”

But it is often in the contrast and antithesis of the elements presented that one can understand where the beauty is and feel the emotions that Bell intended.
“See, God is a slick god. He makes it so you don’t miss out on nothing you’re supposed to witness firsthand.”


Conclusion:
In conclusion, this is a book that surprised me in ways I was not expecting. With such an amazing setting, so attachable characters and unique language and writing style, I can recommend this novel to anybody who would like to read something different and captivating. This was one of those books that made me feel sad when I realized I was nearing its ending because I wanted more! Alden Bell is an author who now has my full attention and I will be looking forward to reading more of his works in the future.

4,5 / 5

The Reapers Are The Angels follows Temple (alias Sarah Mary Williams), a late teen/ young adult on her journey of survival, self discovery, and redemption. Her story is hopeful and heartbreaking, inspiring introspection. In this post apocalyptic world, you’ll discover: zombies, zombie-human mutants, found family (and found and found and found….), train rides, a little bit of brief spice, and a whole lot of beautiful imagery amongst devastation and ruin.

Favorite quotes:
“In the history of the planet, there ain’t never been a kid like you before. A kid who’s seen the things you seen. A kid who fought the same fight you fought. You’re a new thing altogether. A brand new thing.”

“Sometimes you gotta bust apart to get yourself put back together.”

“Ain’t no hell deep enough to keep heaven out.”

“Her thoughts go to sorry places. She thibks of God and of the angels who will decide whether or not she enters heaven.”

“She hold it (a memory) in her palm like a captured ladybug and thinks, Well ain’t I been some places, ain’t I partook in some glorious happenings wanderin my way between heaven and earth. And if I ain’t seen everything there is to see, it wasn’t for lack of lookin.”

“And she turns her back on the lost and the dead and the trampled down, she leaves them to their airy graves, and she and the big man next to her look upward at heaven and find there not just gates and angels but other wonders too, like airplanes that go faster than sound and statues taller than any man and waterfalls taller than any statue and buildings taller than any waterfall and stories taller still that reach up and hook you by the britches on the cusp of the moon where you can look and see the earth whole and you can see how silly and precious a little marble it really is after all.”

There are hundreds possibly thousands of post apocalyptic novels. It is very hard to find a decent zombie novel though....Until now!!!!

The Reapers are the Angels is set roughly 25 years after the dead started returning to not so dead. The book focuses on Temple a young girl roughly 15 years old but with the experience of one who is much older.

Temple is a 15-year-old girl who has survived the zombie apocalypse. We join her story on an island, where she is living in a lighthouse and thinking about God and the way that the world is full of miraculous beauty and wonder even as it is filled with the most unspeakable horror. It is a theme the novel examines thoroughly and that Bell manages to mirror in beautiful prose, stunning even as it describes scenes of gore and horror.
“And, too, a carnival of death, a grassy park near the city centre, a merry-go-round that turns unceasing hour by hour, its old-time calliope breathing out dented and rusty notes while the slugs pull their own arms out of the sockets trying to climb aboard the moving platform, some disembodied limbs dragging in the dirt around and around, the hand still gripping the metal pole—and the ones who succeed and climb aboard, mounting to the top of the wooden horses, joining with the endless motion of the machine, dazed to imbecility by gut memories of speed and human ingenuity.”

Temple knows what it takes to survive. At the first sign of trouble she moves on. She has no emotional ties, just takes what she needs and goes. The story follows her progress across America. The people she encounters and the incidents she endures. Each of these episodes are intriguing and well portrayed. Whether it be communities in denial of the world around them, or mad mutants who feel they are superior you get the sense of desperation and loneliness of Temple’s plight.

Running alongside this survival, a carefully revealed back story is revealed that hints of a past family where Temple was happy.

Temple herself is a great character. She is hard and cuts herself off from getting close to other humans but at the same time displays a good sense of loyalty and at times subtle tenderness. It keeps her character fresh and the reader interested.

If surviving the zombies (slugs) wasn’t enough. Temple is also constantly looking over her shoulder for a man determined to kill her. It is this relationship that is the strongest part of the novel. Despite their hatred for each other, the two begin to recognise that they understand each other better then anyone else they have come across.

The focus of the story is the grudge between Temple and Moses Todd, another wanderer on the road with his own code of honour that he feels he must adhere to or lose himself. Temple is established through flashbacks and stories about her life that she tells others and is a fully-rounded protagonist. Moses, whom we only meet in chapters from Temple's POV , is well-established through dialogue and his actions as he pursues Temple relentlessly across the American South, and part of the tragedy of the novel is that these two characters could easily have been allies and comrades if events did not drive a wedge between them. The dynamic is interesting and plausible and concludes in excellent fashion.

Though the zombies provide a sprinkling of the novel’s horror, they are portrayed as innocent animals, following their instinctual drives, doing what their bodies tell them. It is the people who are the real monsters, and Temple battles with her fear that she is a bad person because in order to survive a zombie apocalypse, you have to do some bad things. Temple’s voice throughout the novel is distinctive, yet realistic, simple though often beautiful and wise.

Take this passage from a memory Temple has about showing her little brother a large statue in a ruined city post-zombie plague. He has just asked her who built the incredible, enormous metal statue:
“I don’t know, she said. It makes people feel good to build something big. Makes people feel like they’re making progress, I reckon.

Progress towards what?

It don’t matter. Up higher or down further. As long as you’re moving, it don’t matter much where you’re goin or what’s chasin you. That’s why they call it progress. It keeps goin of its own accord.”

Bell's prose is rich, evocative and intelligent, a genuine pleasure to read and by the end of The Reapers I was deeply attached to this complicated, intelligent, road-savvy woman, to the way she spoke, and to the style Alden Bell had attached to her story. It so easily could have been Just Another Road Trip at the Zombie Apocalypse. But it turned out to be so much more. A philosophical discussion of progress, of adaptation and context, about living your life now with no excuses, and about trying to distinguish right from wrong. The Reapers Are the Angels turned out to be a deeply moving story and as both the prose and the main narrative drives came to a climax on the final pages, I found myself with goose bumps on my arms.

The Reapers includes a number of women, it is positive about a female teen’s sexual desire. Temple likes sex, and when she wants it she seeks it out with partners she finds attractive. When men try to rape her or sweet-talk her into sex, she clearly says no, though sometimes she has to say it with a fist or the large knife she carries around to kill zombies and assholes. We can assume that there is rape happening in this world by the frequency at which men attempt to rape Temple, but it isn’t a world filled only with rapists, and we have the satisfaction of seeing a woman kick ass instead of being forced into sexual acts.

Temples sidekick Maury, a large, silent, mentally handicapped man who travels with Temple as she tries to find his relatives. Through most of the book she only refers to him as “dummy,” in an affectionate way, although think a few people will take offence to this term. Maury is sweet, innocent, silent, mentally handicapped man who does not speak. His size and description were strongly reminiscent of Lennie in Of Mice and Men, a comparison which fits well with the themes of Temple’s story arc.

Alden Bell has struck the correct balance between portraying the horror or the situation and concentrating on the human elements of the story.

This is one of my all time favorite books & Temple my favorite character. I genuinely could of kept reading & reading. I didn’t want to ever end & have to say goodbye to Temple.

“Words have the power to make things true if they're said right.”

I don't know if I consider myself an emotional reader. There are books I read that contain very emotional passages and events that I wind up leafing through because I just cannot make myself care. So I don't think I am super sensitive and weepy. But then there are books that I cry to. Books that leave me shaken long after I closed the last page. Books that ruin a day and a half of my good mood because I grieve over the events the characters are subjected to, like they were my own close friends. So I don't know. Maybe I am a sucker for a sad read, and my water works do have a hair trigger, even if I don't want to admit it to myself.

That said, I read half of this book with tears blurring the words. There were chapters where I had to stop and put down the book and blink the moisture away so I could continue with the story. This book took my heart out, smacked it a few times with a hammer and then shoved it back into my chest cavity. I am still sad and mad over what happened and how things ended.

This book wasn't all dark gloomy depressing moments. In fact, most of it was about the beauty of the world and the goodness of the people that inhabit it. Even the protagonist was an upbeat sort of person, considering the situation she was in. Maybe this acceptance of the world, both good and bad, is probably what makes all the horrible sad moments that much more powerful and impactful.

It will probably be weeks before I shake the gloom this book put me under. I know there is a sequel, but I don't know if I am ready to start it yet. I need to heal. But once I do, I will be chasing that same feeling of anguish this book gave me.

Such a bummer. I really wanted to like this. I'm a big fan of post-apocalyptic novels. I loved the idea that this was written from the perspective of someone born in that world without any experience with prior civilization. So the first few chapters did it for me in that respect. I didn't mind the vernacular writing once I got used to it and didn't even mind the use of no quotation marks - the author did a good job of making it obvious who was speaking. The world building is where it started to crumble. I absolutely couldn't wrap my mind around what type of world this was when the main character somehow has easy access to junk food and bottled water 20+ years after the end of the world. I couldn't suspend my disbelief that entire cities like Houston were essentially untouched. Not rebuilt, just perfectly fine and deserted. But where it really fell apart for me is in the plot. I just didn't buy it. Any of it. The whole familial revenge cat and mouse chase mechanic is obvious and tired. I hate that the absolutely bizarre introduction of mutant humans hopped up on drugs made from zombie brains (seriously, what?) bears any importance on the plot whatsoever when it was just a few pages of exposition that made very little sense. But most of all I hate that the entire plot essentially starts because of a sexual assault. Authors please just stop with this tired out trope, we're over it.

One bright shining star of all this: Maurie. Best character ever. If the book had just been about him and Temple traveling around meeting people and hanging out, I would have been on board and much more likely to forgive the weird 'is this or isn't this a post apocalypse situation' details.

I give this 3.75 stars. I liked it, it was my first zombie book and well it was pretty good. I watch the Resident Evil movies and love them and well this book puts in mind of the movie although different in story line.. The meatskins is what they are called in this book which have took over every town and state which Temple who is just trying to survive runs into some trouble and the story goes from there short, fast and the ending not what you would expect in books today but glad it was what it was a good ending.. He makes it so you don't miss out on nothing you're supposed to witness firsthand"
(Page 4)

"Goodbye, you good old tower, she says. Keep standin true.
