Absolutely fantastic read. I was quite surprised at how much I enjoyed this book. First, it's a dystopian fantasy involving zombies. What fun! Second, the writing is very different and I was a bit taken aback by the fact that quotation marks were not used to mark dialog. This is the second book I've come across that skipped quotation marks and the first time I put the book back on the shelf. I didn't realize this book was written that way until I was already into it a bit but this time, it didn't slow me down or confuse me at all.

The main character is a 15yo girl who is on her own in this frightening new world. She has grown up knowing nothing else and is a product of this new world, illiterate, a wanderer, a philosopher, tough but damaged by all she's experienced. She has found a bit of a refuge in a lighthouse off the coast of Florida, but the "slugs" have found her and it's time to move on once again. As she travels north, she discovers a small oasis of civilization that a few have carved out of the devastation. A brief stay proves to change the course of her life and she inadvertently gains an enemy who will not stop hunting her until he's gotten his revenge. However, he's never met a girl quite like her and knows that they are the same, they understand each other, down to the marrow. But that doesn't mean she shouldn't die.

As a fan of The Walking Dead and Fear TWD on AMC, I thought I would give zombie reading a little try. This was the first book I picked up in this genre and it fell flat.
The main character Temple was okay, I didn't like or dislike her. My main issues was the fact that the story takes place 20 some odd years after the zombie apocalypse and yet gas pumps are working, stores have not been cleared out of goods, and tools seem to still be ripe for the picking. I realize the irony of saying this since, but I just found some of it a little hard to believe. This is where maybe a little more backstory could come into play. More details on how the power grid is up and running certain places, why water seems to run freely from faucets, how come supplies are not completely looted? Instead the author spends paragraphs detailing feelings of Temple and her wrestling with dark thoughts of her past.
There is one part of the book that essentially had me give up on even remotely enjoying it..caution this is a spoiler...The Mutants. I mean really? I can handle the dead walking around and eating people, but this was so beyond fathomable.. even for a zombie book. To top it off the ending was both terrible and predictable.
I know I am not in the majority here, but this book does not reach beyond two stars for me.

Womp womp!

From just a summary, I should have at the very least enjoyed this book. Southern gothic zombies with a strong female character with some almost Swiftian encounters with different societies but... I am so disappointed. I'm actually quite surprised this book has as high of a Goodreads rating as it does, considering how much I hated it.

The biggest issue (and man, is it devastating) is how problematic it is in so many different ways. I'm used to Southern Gothic being a place where you examine the grotesque but Bell doesn't know how to handle it. There is an ableist representation of someone with an intellectual disability, multiple examples of people mourning an antebellum south in a positive light, very few characters of color, and repeated sexualization of a 15 year old girl, including one where it was painted as a positive and consensual relationship. So many parts of this book were uncomfortable for no discerning reason.

In fact, so many things happen in this book for no real reason. Bell starts a lot of interesting ideas and plotlines and... then does nothing with them. It's really disappointing to read something that actually hooks you and then nothing comes of the build up. Even the ending felt weird and like it belonged to a different book entirely.

The zombies are basically just a McGuffin here to set the plot spinning, so don't think of this as a "zombie novel". This novel packs both an emotional and intellectual punch that far outweighs its modest length. In the end it's a people novel, a novel about living in the world as it is, not as we wish it to be, and a novel about a certain kind of person in the world that was made. The ending is somewhat brutal... but then, so is the reality of the book. And our reality beneath the veneer, for that matter.

There are few novels that will make me just sit back and say, "Whoa. That was something special." This is one of them.

Note - though the main character, Temple, might appeal to some YA viewers, this is a very violent and sad novel that might be upsetting to younger YA readers. Also may be upsetting to some literalist viewers who are, like, "why do gas stations still have gas ten years after the zombie apocalypse?" and such, the novel is powerful as metaphor but the kind of people who obsess about the details of Star Trek warp drives and transporter beams will be greatly annoyed.

Disclaimer: I got about halfway through this book and couldn't finish it.

I really wanted to like this book. The premise seemed interesting and I love the idea of a Zombie book with a badass female character as the lead. I borrowed this book from my library and literally dropped other books that I was reading to read this one the minute it became available.

From the first paragraph, I could already tell I wasn't going to like this author's writing style. No quotation marks to signal that a character is speaking, so I had to go back several times to make sure that the characters were actually speaking to each other and not thinking to themselves. Then, there was the author's incessant use of the word "and", as if commas were only a thing that existed before zombies.

I started to get particularly disgusted with the book when sexual assault was used as a plot device. I tried to trudge a bit further, got halfway through the book, and just had to NOPE the fuck out of there. So glad I did not spend any money on this book.

Where to start. This book has seemed to get raving reviews from so many people and I just struggled to finish it. The storyline was there but the writing in my opinion was just poor. I struggled at times to differ between what was thought and what was being spoken throughout the book with the non existent quotation/speech marks. The fact that the main character Temple has not known of life away from the post apocalyptic and has never had an education of any kind, yet has bipolar like vocabulary. One moment she's talking slightly hillbilly the next like she's reading straight from a thesaurus, the overuse of calling the mentally challenged Maury "dummy" (shit are those things quotation marks?) which is a constant cringe moment for me reading it all the time.
All in all I'd rate it 2 1/2 stars and will probably not read the prequel of Moses' story, especially when half the time I just wanted to get this book over and done with halfway through, even with the niggling urge to find out what happens in the end. I'm sorry Alden I just couldn't get into your writing style.

There were times while reading this where I wondered if the imitator would surpass the master (Cormac McCarthy's THE ROAD). In the end, this didn't surpass, but there were long stretches where I thought it might. Still a 4.5 star read.

At times the prose goes a little florid, but most of the time it works and evokes the THE ROAD without feeling like satire--it just works. The times it goes over the top are short and easily read past. And rather than just being a copycat book, this book brought something different to the table. The story felt more direct, the characters more fleshed out, and the dialogue more interesting, and yet it did all that while keeping that Faulkner/McCarthy prose. So overall, I was able to forgive the imitation and even praise it's ambition. This was a fantastic story, with a great character, some true horror, and great writing.

The only thing keeping this from being 5/5 is the ending. It's...well, not the best. It was only the last 5 pages or so though, so I can round up to 5 stars on goodreads.

What a fantastic read. The language is eloquent, the story tragic and the characters memorable.

I read alot of dystopian fiction and this was a welcome break from the norm. The focus here isn't on the blood and the chase, instead it's an exploration of morality on a world where morality is dead. The lines between good and evil are thoroughly blurred as our young protagonist attempts to weave her way through life. Temple is both endearing and terrifying and as a reader we can share her sense of loneliness and uncertainty.

What I also loved is that the author isn't afraid to piss off his reader. Knowing this was part of a series you might expect the author to keep certain people alive but no, he tells the story he wants to tell and the ending is, in that sense, perfect. I think a lot of authors would have rushed the ending and tied up all of the lose ends, but this would be a mistake.

I'm off now to read the next installment, which I believe is a prequel, and I can't wait to get stuck in and devour the words right off of the page. Highly recommend

I enjoyed this book more than I thought I would. Having read dozens upon dozens of zombie books, author Bell still managed to breath new life into the genre by way of his characters - mainly our protagonist, Temple. The journey she takes, along with her back story, felt real and organic. Smoothly paced scenes always kept the story interesting, and anything involving the antagonist, Moses Todd, made the book even better.

My one big problem with the story was how advanced and mature Temple was for fifteen years old. Without ever having learned how to read, she had an incredibly intelligent vocabulary. The phrases she used were well beyond her years and was a struggle at times for me to reconcile her age with her supposedly young character. With that aside, I would still recommend this book to any zombie fan. However, be advised this story puts more emphasis on character than action. Think of The Walking Dead more than Dawn of the Dead. Plus, it had a very dark, satisfying ending.

I "inherited" this book in a classroom library. Picked it at random to read. Will pull this from my shelves as I feel it is inappropriate for my junior high classroom audience.
The vernacular doesn't pardon the "would of, could of" instead of "would have" or even "would've" that is throughout the book. The lack of quotation marks takes some getting used to differentiating thought from speech, but it's do-able.
**spoilers below** here's what I didn't like - for my classroom, you may have a differing opinion, that's fine.
15 year old Temple hacks her way across a zombie wasteland of America. She meets up with other survivors, gambles for drugs, takes said drugs, murders a would-be rapist (he's pretty graphic explaining what he wants from her), gets part of her finger hacked off and stitched up, meets up with a mentally disabled man (calls him dummy), has sex with a 35 year old man and then kills the man's father upon his request.
Meanwhile, zombies get hacked to pieces and she travels. It wasn't a great book, it wasn't the worst I've read.

More a 3.5.

Still on my zombie kick and found this in a list of books in that genre! I really enjoyed the narrative of this one, though I seemed to trail off a bit at times. The overall world is interesting and more established than some zombie novels that start at the beginning. And surviving is only part of the plot as the protagonist, Temple, first finds herself the target of a man whose brother she kills and then discovers purpose in returning a developmentally/intellectually disabled man, Morrie, home... from Georgia to Texas.

I feel that the author put some suspense into details that were withheld from the reader, which was both interesting and frustrating-- but I enjoy more dramatic irony than others might. Overall, the most fascinating part of this book went deeply unexplored as the protagonist passed through an inbred family that had started injecting themselves with zombie... brain matter? I feel like fans of Resident Evil: Biohazard would especially like that touch as well as the overall southern gothic vibe the book has.

Es lamentable que no le haya dedicado el tiempo necesario a este libro, realmente se lo merecía. Leer de 10 a 15 páginas diarias de tan solo 290 que tiene... es una vergüenza. Pero igualmente lo disfrute bastante. Honestamente son pocos los libros sobre zombies que he leído en mi vida (quizás unos 3 o 4) y este lo considero uno de mis favoritos, es un libro sencillo pero conmovedor. Y no se esfuerza es describirte un mundo que (come on) ya todos sabemos como es.

Si hablamos de algo que no me gusto serian los mutantes (dueños de la luz o algo asi), me parecieron algo fuera de lugar, pero imagino que le dieron un aspecto diferente a los típicos libros sobre zombies.

Me gusto muchisimo la manera de escribir de este autor, es algo profunda pero no llega a ser poética como tanto detesto en los libros.

Insisto, libro corto, buen escrito, algo gore y ESTA LLENO DE ZOMBIES!! What else?

This is a very interesting addition to the zombie genre with a strong narrator. But I can't recommend it because of a very dangerous idea that runs through the novel. Early in the story, Temple is hunted by a lecherous man who tries to rape her. Temple is forced to defend herself and ends up killing the man. For the remainder of the novel the dead rapist's brother--knowing full well his brother's character and that he died trying to rape Temple--pursues Temple in order to avenge his POS brother's death. The brother is written like he is honorable and in fact he is a horrible person who is essentially saying that Temple should have let his brother rape her. He ends up causing the suffering and death of Temple and I just can't pretend that the way he is written is okay. The brother is just as bad as the dead rapist, but the author fails to understand this. So I don't recommend this book due to the fatal flaw of victim-blaming and making rapists enablers seem noble. Absolute rubbish.

Apocalyptic stories have always been a type of story that I have been particularly drawn to. And I found that The Reapers are the Angels fits right into that category. The Reapers are the Angels is the first book in the “Reapers” series and is written by Alden Bell, a pseudonym for Joshua Gaylord.

It’s hard to start the review of The Reapers are the Angels because there are so many things still running around in my head. All of it good stuff to be exact.

The first thing that I must say is that there are quite a few zombie stories in modern fiction but I haven’t come across one that is told in the way that The Reapers are the Angels is being narrated. The way that Alden Bell writes the whole story of it is really unique. For starters it really puts you in the place of Temple (the main protagonist) herself and how she is navigating through the fallen America. And even more so is the close relation there is to the world that we know ourselves and makes the impact of the story that much stronger. It just feels like the events in The Reapers are the Angels couldn’t happen to us right now. I really liked the world that was created, on one level it gave me a certain laughs when things went well with Temple, the chills in certain encounters and a heart breaking moment in the end. The Reapers are the Angels is a work of fiction but has a very strong emotional side to it, that makes it an truly unique book to read.

In The Reapers are the Angels you follow the main protagonist Temple, a young girl, who lives on her own in what is left of America filled with zombies. Especially the cover of the book did produce a delicate image of Temple, and the introducing chapters, with her living her own life in the lighthouse only further added to this. Her life starts of “easy” if you can say it, she is doing quite well for her own, but she finds it enough and ventures to the mainland, and from this point on you are readily introduced to the fallen America. This really enlarges the whole scope of the story. What you also see in Temple once she is on the mainland is her rough and bold side, the first encounters with the slugs (that’s how she calls the zombies), are quite vicious and brutal. Next to this is that Temple is quite young, under the twenty. The world that she knows is normal to her, she has never known the world before it all happens, and how she reflects on several things that happen in the world really add much depth and a certain feeling of compassion to her characters. It’s like you just want to hug her and say everything will be ok, but on the other hand she probably won’t need it.

Though the focus is on Temple for most of the part there are some other characters that are pretty interesting to read about, especially here the relation between them and Temple is nice feat. The first one is Moses Todd. Temple meets up with Moses in one of the safehavens and from this point onwards Temple life changes much. Moses has a certain believe and I think he is actually quite a psychopath, with what he says and what he does. Only convinced that what was done was unfair and he has to exact his own justice/revenge on Temple. His introduction to the story added a great secondary element. Secondly there is Maury, who Temple refers to as dummy since he can’t speak. Though Maury isn’t that stupid. The first few chapters when you read about Maury remain a bit unclear as to how the story of Maury will unfold, but later on it does become clear and Temple helps Maury to get home. What was in particular nice to read about that both Temple and Maury are a bit impaired by one thing or another they are able to find a way to communicate and continue onwards. This really gave an humanly touch to The Reapers are the Angels.

The story of The Reapers are the Angels has a very interesting concept and this is a book that really lets everything come together; the characters, the setting and the storyline. As soon as Temple is on the mainland, she ventures from safehaven to safehaven and in her travels Temple, makes some wise and maybe unwise decisions. In one place Temple makes a powerful enemy which forces her to run for her dear life. This chase next to Temple’s quest, that she later accepts are combined to give a certain sense of panic and fear to the storyline and a great pacing overall. How this all came to pass just comes to show that the America in The Reapers are the Angels is really destroyed and people have different opinions, it feels that sometimes society is hardly there, same as for some morals and ethics of specific people. Overall the storyline is very strong and you get a good feeling of how that version of America should look like. And as the story progresses there are a few twists and turns that really hit me. The ending of the book is on one part pretty sad and left me a bit struck right there. It made me feel sad. However it does give a beautiful ending to The Reapers are the Angels.

The Reapers are the Angels is a recommendation for everyone, even if you’re not totally into the zombie genre, this is still a book that you will quite enjoy. The writing style of Alden bell is just amazing, its rich and really engages you in the book. The whoel concept of the book, not turning this into a hack n slash zombie book but highlighting the effects on the nation and how several characters now navigate through it was really done quite nicely and does come to show that this is a versatile genre. The ending of The Reapers are the Angels made me blink away, it was something unexpected but does produce a very nice ending. I can highly recommend this book to anyone, you will be amazed.

originally posted at http://thebookplank.blogspot.com/2013/07/the-reapers-are-angels.html

Well-crafted and with wonderful dialog. Temple is a great character, interesting and complicated and wiser than her 15 years. The story had me hooked from the first line, and I found Temple's voice compelling. I enjoyed how the author portrayed the dialog of this wasted world, and the characters found within it.

The book doesn't shy away from showing the truly awful, but there are miracles and goodness along the way as well. As a story set after the zombie apocalypse is well underway, it could have fallen into hackneyed tropes and well-worn convention of "just another zombie novel," but it never does that.

Perhaps it's an indication of how much I really enjoyed the book that I'm giving it only three stars - because, from a purely subjective point of view, I absolutely and thoroughly hated the ending.

The prose in this book is good - poetic, but it actually works (at least for me! I know that some people beg to differ). I wasn't sure at first if it was going to be too much for me to handle, but it was fine. I got drawn into the protagonist's voice within a few pages.

I took the story at least partially at face value, but I appreciate the allegorical interpretation of the story that some of the other reviewers have discussed and think that considering it on a more metaphorical/non-literal level adds some depth to the novel. That said, I don't have anything new or insightful to add to that discussion, so you should read other people's reviews if you want to think more about

Finally, the zombies shape the world of the novel immensely, but it's not really about the zombies, if that makes sense. No need to be super into zombie fiction to appreciate this book!

God is a slick god. Temple Knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe.

The world was falling away, the hunger irresistible in the veins of those who wander long past their endings. A young girl, only between 15-17 is left alone in a scary new world, her named, Temple, and she is figuring out how to handle her own, when it seems everyone is at one another's throats. Fighting through the hoards, the human instincts take over, where justice isn't valued until its an eye for an eye, a lesson Temple will learn the hard way. After killing his brother, Moses Todd sets out to have a one last stand battle against Temple, when one of the mutants, Millie pouts a bullet to Temple's chest. In a fit of rage, Moses repeatedly slaughtered the girl, angered at the death of Temple.

Astonishingly good. Imagine if Cormac McCarhty wrote a zombie novel: this is it. Temple has instantly become one of my favourite narrators- she has all the mesmeric strangeness and shocking insights of Merricat in Shirley Jackson's We Have Always Lived in the Castle. And Moses Todd is almost memorable as The Judge in McCarthy's Blood Meridian. The world-building is spare and efficient, the pacing is breathless and the emotional impact is overwhelming. There are moments when (like McCarthy) the baroque language becomes slightly overwrought, the philosophising too heavy-handed, but these are brief glitches in what is otherwise a genuinely stunning novel and, in my view, a phenomenal achievement. I can think of few books that have had a greater impact on me in recent years - a profoundly wonderful novel that should be much more widely known.

This was wild. This was another zombie book so you know I'm on board!
As usual this book required suspension of disbelief, but that's par for the course with zombie fiction. This one wasn't keen on world building. Who cares why there are zombies? Who needs to know about the infrastructure of the world? Not me, we have adventures to get to!

Join an MC who has grown up in a zombie filled world. She's basically Clementine from the Walking Dead video game, except maybe crabbier. She's like Clem, but a sociopath.

This was a road trip book, so if you don't like those this won't be your thing. The beginning didn't impress me but as we got more bonkers I grew more invented. Plus we had a frenemies dynamic with a guy who is hunting her.

I do plan to do a full review on my channel so keep an eye out for that!

This introspective zombie novel follows made-for-this-world Temple as she makes her corpse-strewn way across the U.S., headed north. Towards what, she's not sure. Maybe Niagra Falls. Maybe not. Maybe just steady moving, seeing some things she hasn't seen before. She generally avoids staying long in places people have settled; where there's a false sense of safety; where folks drop their guard and start hoping for things to go back like they were "before". Temple was born in this world and she lives in it with the "slugs" just fine. It's what's in her head that needs managing. That's what keeps her moving, as much as anything else. Temple's peculiar yet rigorous sense of right and wrong, of proper balance in this world, are central to the novel's theme and trajectory.
Fascinating read. For its execution and faithfulness to theme I rank it with Zone One and World War Z.

I've been looking for the perfect zombie novel for some time. Perfect for me, anyway. A zombie novel about an regular person with their own quirks and personality, who happens to be stuck in a zombie apocalypse, and I finally found it in this novel. I love that the main character had a personality, didn't always get things right, did her best to survive and follow her compass, and actually the z-word was never mentioned, which I kinda liked too. I was always kept guessing about the plot, and was never able to predict what would happen. The dialogue was fresh and the characters distinct from one another. The ending was a surprise.

I highly recommend this to others, and I'm sad it was a library-borrowed book, because now I have to try and find myself a copy for my own bookshelf. Let the hunt begin!

Ce qui semblait être une dystopie futuriste plaisante s’est révélée être un pool décevant. On suit la jeune Temple, orpheline, qui se démène pour survivre dans un monde post apocalyptique peuplé de zombies, ou de limaces comme elle aime dire. Temple est née après la chute du monde tel qu’on le connaît actuellement, elle n’a donc aucune connaissance de notre monde, ne sait pas lire ni écrire mais elle sait manier la machette comme personne.

L’histoire est plaisante et tient la route mais quelques détails m’ont un peu dérangés : Temple a 15 ans donc le monde a chuté il y a au moins 15/20 ans mais l’électricité fonctionne toujours ? Les stations services sont pleines ? Les magasins sont encore remplis (et ne parlons pas des DLC des produits) ? Si on met ces détails de côté, l’histoire reste plaisante et se lit assez rapidement

Twenty-five years after the zombie apocalypse, a teenage girl travels the wastelands trying to find a home while trying to come to terms with her past. This is definitely not your ordinary post-apoca zombie book. It’s thoughtful and introspective, and sometimes even oddly poetic.

The world-building is mostly realistic, except perhaps for one section (which I won’t spoil, but which I felt was unnecessary.) And Temple is a fascinating protagonist who struggles to reconcile her dual nature: the killer that does what is necessary to protect herself and the people she reluctantly comes to love, and the philosopher who sees beauty in a school of fish or the night sky. She’s only ever known this desolate world and so she has only her own moral compass to guide her. I loved following her on her journey.

A haunting and exquisitely written mashup of Faulknerian Gothic horror and the zombie novel. Normally I am not even slightly interested in the zombie genre. But Bell's zombies are more of a backdrop for the generally depressed state of the post-Apocalyptic south (the main character starts in Florida and never makes it further north than Georgia or further west than Texas). Our protagonist is a bad-ass fifteen-year old who travels as a migrant, avoiding the sluggish hordes and giant mutants with her gurkha knife by her side. Early on, her act of self-defense leads to her being relentlessly hunted by an inversely kindred spirit. Bell's atmosphere is perfect, his dialogue taught, and his descriptions vivid. And that ending - oy. Looking forward to reading the next one.

2.5 stars; NOT a ya book: there’s the 15yo MC having sex; cussing; gory in places; offensive language about an intellectually delayed young man (retard, dummy)

After an ending like this, I feel like this book really wasn’t worth reading. It could have had so much more depth...was she dead and in purgatory? Was she a rebel guardian angel? Nope, none of that...just a young girl wandering place to place fighting off zombies. Some of the conversations were deep, and made me think, but the story goes nowhere.

She’s a young girl who acts like she’s at least 10yrs older. This book culminates with the MC bringing Maury back to his home in Texas. From there, the story ends rather abruptly.
The title means nothing. The reapers aren’t angels. Such a bummer. I don’t plan on reading book 2.

3 1/2 * first off, hated hated hated the ending. now that i've gotten that off my chest, i liked what bell is doing, (showing us the future of a zombie apocalypse, where the monsters, although still dangerous, have mostly rotten into mere annoyances) but by setting the story so far into the future of the disaster, he's set himself up with a conundrum in that he still wants to use technology that wouldn't be working by then (gas, electricity, satellites). i know it's silly to ask for logic from a zombie story but you have to keep some scientific reality. i got a nice "river tam" vibe from temple. although the writing got a bit adjectivey for me, i was willing to forgive it for the action scenes. the plot seemed a bit random at times. all in all, i enjoyed it - a solid read.

It was predictable
Boring
And have a tons of plot holes
The writing style is also not it. There was no use of punctuation mark its kinda hard to tell sometimes whos speaking who,bthe only thing that help me indicate it is when theres a "ask by" or "says by-" 🤷‍♀️
Also the fact that shes 15 and going at it with someone who is twice her age is 😬 a big no

I skip a lot of dialogue and a chapters and yet i still understand what was happening, i honestly no need to a scene that was felt unecessary and long for me

And the part i find more ridiculous is when if u got bitten by a zombie u will get infected and turn into one but it was ok if you eat them? Lmao idk where that logic holds but eh whatever this is fiction everything is possible i guess even tho it doesnt make sense

I enjoyed reading this, and finished it greedily months ago, but for some reason I can barely recall any of the prose that is not related to significant plot beats. I think I know why too, zombie novels just aren't that good. There are a few, which you've probably already read by the time you're googling "zombie novel hidden gems," and with the bar being so low, the only way is up.

This is most assuredly a decent read for post apocalyptic undead fans. There will be some readers who will fall in love with the protagonist, and sincerely, good for them, for their mileage and lasting impression will be better than mine.

If you want a decent and entertaining zombie novels for a few ours, this has got you covered.

I listened to the audiobook so I didn't experience some of the issues others had. This book definitely has a lot of issues moving the time line up about 20 years solves a lot of them. I'm very surprised by this zombie book being rated so high. Even with a timeline fix, I found myself daydreaming through a lot of the flowery writing that honestly didn't fit the setting. I feel like the story that was told in flashbacks was a better idea than the story we got. Temple is our protagonist apparently the only thing this 15 year old girl can't do is read. Gambling, drinking, sex, shooting guns, knife fighting, and hand to hand combat come as natural to her as 007. It's bland and boring trying to be more than what it is if you have read it save yourself some time Don't!

Amongst the plethora of vampire and zombie re-imaginings that has infested the publishing world over the last few years, Justin Cronin's 'The Passage' stands as a high-water mark. But now it has a serious rival in the shape of 'The Reapers are the Angels'.
A poetic 'alternative' to Cronin's epic, it centres on the journey of one young woman, Temple, in her journey through a strangely altered, apocalyptic landscape, it's less about the zombie plague than about how 'normal' people adapt, or, more pointedly, fail to adapt, to this new world. Temple's survival strategy of coldness and detachment is mitigated by her attempt to do one good thing in this new world, but it turns out that being a good person isn't easy.

As a non-native speaker the language used to describe ordinary stuff was absolute garbage and unnessesarily "old fashioned way of saying something". lot of gimmick sentences.

The athmospere was 6/5 beautiful once you got around the fancy words. The zombies were well written and this writer really did them how they should be done.
Story had good and bad parts, not gonna spoil it. though it had some wierd things going on. + There is some inconsistencies in what really could be working and what absolutely would not work after 25 years of no maintenance.

still 3/5 because of the good worldbuilding if you let reality out the window and the fact he got zombies right. + some of the stuff was original so that was also a huge plus.

Kind of hard to rate this one, but overall this was a good read. I for one enjoyed the writing style, and it should be noted that I listened to the audiobook, whose performance I thought was quite wonderful. This book was chock full of vivid similes and interesting themes, while balancing the violence beheld in a post apocalyptic zombie world. My biggest issue was with the story beats. I really liked the characters but it felt episodic in a way I didn't really care for. I wanted to know more about certain things while not caring for other things that were dwelled upon. It felt like the kind of story that only means something if you can find a pre existing backdrop to allegorize it, and personally that's not a search I much enjoy.

Rounded down from 3.5

Temple, la protagonista principal, es una adolescente de quince años que no alcanzó a conocer el mundo antes de que se transformará en un mundo lleno de zombies. Viaja sola, sin la necesidad de asentarse con grupos de sobrevivientes, a pesar de que se encuentra con varios en su camino. Luego de encontrarse con un grupo y matar a un hombre que intenta violarla, Moses Todd hermano del hombre que Temple asesina, la persigue en busca de venganza. En su camino de escaparse de Moses, Temple se encuentra con grupos, personas, zombies, mutantes que van marcando el camino de la aventura. No me gustó el final, en lo personal creo que podría haberse convertido en un libro para realizar una bilogía o trilogía.

I'm not a huge fan of zombie stories. Usually people try to do human drama with too much zombie plot, or try to detail a zombie apocalyptic world with too much human drama.

Reapers are the Angels are not like this. Temple's story is a perfect balance. She needs the zombies because that's the world she was brought into. But the zombies don't need her. And they're both fine with that.

This is star-crossed enemies' story between two BAMFs who understand each other in a way that not even the reader could ever hope to. You won't find Sigourney Weaver doing a headshot mid-barrel roll, but you'll be read through a chunk of poetically bleak descriptions made out of metaphors and similes - which is my cup of tea.

While the story itself is not so much bad, there are aspects to the reality I could not get past. It is at least 15 years post zombie apocalypse and cars are still driving, the power grid still works in places, and areas still have running water. In reality gasoline lasts about 3 months at best without a fuel stabilization. Tires have not dry rotted? Who is maintaining power plants and water facilities. Small details have a way of turning into major plot holes.
From a writing perspective, the lack of punctuation around dialogue makes this somewhat difficult to read. Who said what? Let me go back, over and over.

1.5 Stars

I hate to give books 1 star unless I can't even bring myself to keep reading but this book almost reached that level for me. Even if I overlook the improbabilities (and there are many) of how society functions many years into a zombie outbreak, I have so many questions about plot points that went nowhere.

The narration bled from a succinct descriptions of what was happening/what had already happened into an attempt to wax poetic about life, God, and the universe.

I kept waiting for the characters to develop further, especially Temple/Sarah Mary Williams, but that didn't happen. The ending seemed like a strange cop-out. =\

I both loved and hated this book. It is both intelligent and dumb. It feels very profound and yet is about nothing. You can tell a lot of thought went into this book, yet at the same time there is so much that is inexplicable - like literally everything still working (cars, electrical grid, etc.) 25 years after the collapse of society because of the zombie apocalypse. The zombies are...not frightening at all. They are, as described by the main character, slugs. They are slow and dumb and easy to outmaneuver. Yet they are inexorable.

I do take strong exception to the mutants - not zombies, but mutants. Their inclusion in this story adding nothing and was just dumb.

A beautifully written dystopian horror story about a young woman surviver during a zombie plague and the burdens she carries through her travels. Bell creates a grim, deadly United States were people are locked in a battle with, or fleeing from, the "slugs" as the zombies are called. Temple ends up on the wrong side of a battle worn man with an Old Testament eye-for-an-eye code and is forced to run through the country with a mentally challenged man whom she saves from the slugs along the way. The ending may or may not be satisfying, depending on your preference for happy or sad endings. It didn't quite meet with mine, hence the four stars. Nevertheless, it is a great read.

This is a beautiful book, and I read a lot. Apparently it has taken some negative reviews? Can't please everyone I guess. I found myself quoting passages of it to my wife while I was reading in bed and we were blown away by the author's use of language - entire tracts of it are poetry.

I initially picked it because I was looking for a zombie book, and this is that, but more than that, it's a literary view of survival. The characters are vivid and relatable.

Book two, "Exit Kingdom" is arguably better but only because it takes characters we met in the first book and gives them greater context.

Very much looking forward to reading more from Alden Bell (aka Joshua Gaylord).

It's alright. Bell's prose is solid but it sometimes veers into the overwrought and it's not as controlled as I would have liked, and in general the religious allusions he weaves into the story rarely went deep enough to be intriguing. I liked Temple, but her only somewhat complex relationship was with Moses, and I just didn't get enough of his perspective for it to be deep. The episodes in the book's second half were generally more interesting than the episodes in the book's first half, but it was a bit too little too late, and I think the ending sacrificed any philosophical conclusion for a cheap emotional gut punch.

I recommend A Canticle for Leibowitz instead.

The Reapers are the Angels is one of the first books that has made me cry with pure sadness. I enjoy reading this book and it has left me with my mouth open a lot of times. This fiction book has amazing characters and teaches you many things and wonderful lessons too! I don’t know how to explain this but the book feels like you are in the story with the characters, traveling, laughing, and having a great time with all of them. The book takes major plot twists and goes fast and slow, but I would recommend reading this book if you enjoy suspense and it might change your way of thinking about some things. This book has inspired me to read more and to enjoy what I'm reading :)

This was very weird and I ate it up. Was very clearly inspired by many things, such as The Walking Dead, The Road, and The Last of Us to name a few. It did a great job of using those as jumping off points and reference points, but did not copy things so blatantly as to be boring or predictable (in fact Part 2 of this book, it goes in a surprising and freaky direction, which is never fully explained...).
I had never heard of this book before finding it on a library shelf, so for any zombie story fans, I would highly recommend! It's going to at the very least keep you on your toes.

Holy cow. I've been reading zombie books for months now, most I finish with zero satisfaction and other I just can't finish.
It was a dry spell.
Then this little treasure of bliss pops up in my recommendation and I have to read it. I but it and wow. It's good.
I could have used with a little less wordiness, but it was worth it. I do think I'll be reading part two since it seems it jumps back in time rather than forward and I do t want to read about Moses brother.
I'll call it a day with a tilt of my hat.
Good work.

This book is SO beautiful. I have always had this soothing fascination with a world overrun by a disease that would render it bare and empty. Alden Bell makes that world come to life for me in this book, exactly as it should be; as it is, calm, beautiful, full projectors on the wonders of the natural world. Suffering does not and could never kill wonder. Death is poetic in this story, and I can't help but imagine Todd as Death itself, giving it a good name, a name of respect, justice and salvation. It's death as beautiful and amiable as I have ever seen it. I loved this.

Honestly, I don’t even really know how to describe this book, but I loved it. It was so poignant and well-written, and I expect it to stick with me for years to come.

The descriptions of the post-apocalyptic US were stunning. I also thoroughly enjoyed how “southern” the characters, story, and landscape of this book felt. Being from the US south, this book felt familiar and frightening in a way I never expected, but wholly loved.

The only reason I gave it 4 Stars is because I found the ending a little disappointing.

This isn't the scariest zombie book or the most exciting or the most realistic but it is the most beautifully written zombie book I've ever read. I absolutely loved the author's writing and the characters voices, I loved the humour and I really empathised with the main characters, the story jogs along at a pretty fair pace and there is an inevitability to it which gives a undercurrent of sadness throughout the book.
I didn't particularly like the ending and the mutants but will be thinking about Temple and her journey for a long time to come.

I both loved and hated this book. Set approximately 25 years after the zombie apocalypse, it follows a young woman who understands the world she has inherited with a very clear eyed perception that she shouldn't have. While it is a great story, it showcases the skewed morals and forced adaptation of people trying to survive in this world. The differing psychological responses to it. I only hate it because I think it was written very well in a sad raw way and I the fact that there is no clear "winner"

Ahhh, this is an amazing book. The writing is lyrical and gorgeous and the characters are damaged people looking for redemption in a barren America which is infested with zombies. A 15 year old girl wanders the wasteland, killing zombies while being hunted by a man intent on executing her. It doesn’t sound like an emotional story….but it IS. This novella broke my heart with its beauty and horror. Fantastic, one of my favorites and top book of the year!!!!!! (I loved this book so much that I hunted down the sequel-can’t wait to read it!)

I thought this book was so good. The main character was strong and independent. I love to see a character who can take care of herself. There was not a point in this book that lulled in my opinion. I never felt like, come on just get on with it. I do wish it ended a bit differently. It’s definitely made me have to take a minute after reading this book to get over it, but it definitely doesn’t detract from my love for it. Even though it didn’t end the way I would have wanted, it was still fantastic.

This book has one of the best protagonists I’ve ever met. I love her. She reminded me a stitch of Dancy Flamarion for those of you who’ve read Caitlin Kieran that might be a familiar name. Set 25 years after a zombie outbreak, this book tells the story of a girl named Temple and her strange adventures throughout the post apocalyptic American South. Temple has a beautiful mind, a sharp knife, and a bigger heart than she thinks. It’s not the zombie post apocalypse story you think it is. Highly recommend.

I have probably read thousands of books across a range of genres (fantasy, science-fiction, war history, classics, horror,...). This book is unlike anything I have read before, it is beautiful, mysterious and emotionally involving - I implore you to ignore the incomprehensible bad reviews and treat yourself to a read which in all likelihood will be different to any other book you have read!

What this book is not:
1. Typical Zombie-fare (anything but)
2. Targetted at teenagers - it is adult fiction through and through

This was an incredibly atmospheric and character-driven horror novel set in a post-apocalyptic world full of both zombies and survivors. Our main character is 15-year-old Temple who was born into this current world and knows no other way of living. She’s alone and she’s a badass because she has to be but the interesting element here is her internal conflict in spite of what survival requires of her. This is not a young adult novel and it’s certainly not your typical zombie story either. The writing is beautiful and there’s an old-world western vibe going on. The book has much more descriptive gore than I prefer but overall I enjoyed this one.

I absolutely loved this. Gore, violence, sympathy, empathy & even a little bit of... romance??? Okay, so that romance was "wrong" but it is what it is. It took me a while to get over the lack of quotation marks. At first I thought it had something to do with my Amazon Kindle format/download but when I renewed it & used the ePub format it was the same. Oh well.

The ending didn't turn out as I was hoping but I wasn't disappointed. It ended well. I almost wish it was longer. Almost.

At first I was conflicted on how this book ended but the more I thought about I'm glad it ended the way it did; there was a savage beauty to it. In most zombie horror books you see the polar opposites of humanity playing out but in this book there is a believable middle ground. The dynamic between Temple and Moses reminds me of the age old question of what you should feel about the lion hunting the gazelle. Great read overall!

This book is a quick and easy read. For someone who has never been a fan of zombies, I was quite pleased by the storyline of the novel and how the author illustrated the protagonist, Temple, in a new light. Alden Bell carefully creates various communities in the novel to portray various views on morals and the downfall of society. The novel has a fairly short exposition so it is quite easy to get interested and hooked to the book.

To start off, this book had so many logistical errors that I almost couldn’t take it seriously. 2+ decades into the apocalypse and they still have running cars? Gasoline easily available? Cheese crackers in convenience stores?! It’s complete and total bull%!?$.

If you ignore those issues, I guess it was “just okay”. It wasn’t terrible. It wasn’t necessarily good, either.

I did like the ending however. I’m in a sad mood so it was perfect for me.

I want to say so many good things about this book that I'm speechless.

It's overwhelming. This is a zombie book--a zombie book--and yet it's one of the most lyrical, poetic and moving pieces of modern work I've come across. And it's a zombie book.

Bravo to the author. Thank your showing that creativity and elegance can be weaved into a genre like zombies (my favorite, BTW). I already bought your follow-up.

Just because the prose is pretty doesn't give you an excuse to ignore basic quotations for speaking or to have every single line of dialogue sound like a thesaurus was shoved down the character's throat. With how old-timey everything feels it just kind of feels like this story should have been set in the wild west times.

Ignore the snobs giving this 4 stars because the prose makes them feel smart and skip it.

This is a story about resilience, survival in the apocalypses, and a
pandemic turned to zombie infestation. Now those serve as a background
and unlike other zombie or apocalyptic novels, the characters have
internalize their fate and stories are more about living than
surviving.

A philosophy of life blossoms under the most dreadful and depressing
circumstances very moving with amusing moments as well as sad and
terrifying ones.

Very satisfying.

This was pretentious, ridiculous, and so religious it verges on hyperbole. The book was written in dialect that was strange and annoying, the world building made little to no sense (cars would not run 25 years later with no maintenance), the character motivations were paper thin, and when you finally become invested in the characters the book ends in tragedy. The only reason I rated it 2 stars was for the excellent narration.

Un libro sobre zombies con una historia muy entretenida y atrapante.
Lo que más me gustó fue la personalidad del personaje principal, Temple no es la típica protagonista débil en apuros y en espera a ser rescatada, es una chava con mucho carácter y fuerza y eso me gusta mucho en una protagonista mujer. El libro es muy ágil y de lectura fácil se la pasa uno muy bien leyendolo. Y como dato curioso los diálogos son libres. Algo que no es muy común en las novelas. Buen libro.

Can a thing be a horror and a source of beauty?

This book is. It is full of zombie horror but also contains some of the most beautiful passages i have read in awhile.

The main character is both a demon and a saint, able to deal with the horrors of her world and appreciate the miracles all around her.

Her journey through an America that we don't quite know, but is all she knows, is a tale well told.

Highly recommended.

Even though I just finished reading this for my college English literature and culture class and think it has a great ending. I think the real audience for this book is the high school-level age range. I do think that it is a good book up to a point but it only really gets good at the last 4-5 chapters for me. Definitely not a college-level literature book in my opinion because it does not challenge me as a reader.

Southern gothic with zombies - this was scary and gory (in a good way) and then starts meandering and then gets weird and then picks back up (but with fewer zombies) and then ends in a way that you see coming but hope you’re wrong about. There was something missing for me that I can’t quite put a finger on, but still a good zombie story (oh how I love a zombie story) and Temple is a great character taking us through it.

Removing a star since Temple died at the end and I'm still mad 😠
This book made me lose track of time it was so interesting. I've read a lot of zombie books and this was a great new addition. I really liked the focus on the new societies being built and how the zombies were more of a nuisance than an unending wave of death. I really wish Temple would've survived tho. It completely ruined the end for me 😔

I loved this story so much but you definitely have to gloss over a lot of ridiculous inaccuracies around the practical points of being 25 years into a zombie apocalypse. Finding vehicles that will run, working gas pumps, edible food on store shelves, abandoned towns with working electricity… come on. FYI gas will go bad in a vehicle not being driven in as little as a year. A bit more research on this type of thing would have increased my ability to fully buy into the world.

This was probably my 10th reread and each time I revisit this book I’m reminded why it’s my favorite. It’s just such a beautiful and moving story. Temple is a poetic and brutal narrator in the zombie wild west she navigates.

I decided to try the audiobook version this time around and I couldn’t have been happier with the narrator. She did an amazing job perfectly encapsulating Temple. 5 stars every single time. I love this book. I wish there was more.

I’ve read this book multiple times after getting it for free and judging it based on the title alone. Initially I was put off by the style it was written in, at least the structure itself as the dialogue does not use quotation marks. However, as I read it and reread it one or two more times it really grew on me. The writing itself is simple but it’s also so detailed at the same time. There are some beautiful scenes and quotes within the books and made me do a lot of thinking.

Good, ish. Well written but the story didn't quite make sense to me on contemplating.
Why did her hunter continue to try to kill Temple after learning why she did what she did to his brother? He admits he knew his brother was a wrong un. He also becomes fond of Temple, respects her, and even explains that he knows why she did what she did. But he wants to kill her anyway?
Just didn't make sense, and in a story that I rather liked its kind of unforgivable and indigestible when the author writes (and bases the story almost entirely on) something nonsensical.

I really like the journey Temple went on both physically and mentally. I think the writing was beautiful as well.

Has anyone else noticed the similarities to The Rising series by Brian Keene? The "dumb" character a main character takes as their charge, a woman being hunted by a man with a connection to another man she murdered, human settlements that end up being crazy. Not saying that's a bad thing! If you like this book you'll probably enjoy The Rising.

A zombie tale with a determined young heroine combing devastated America looking for wonders. While others have given up or denied reality, she dodges or kills "meatskins" as she travels, finding safe enclaves occasionally, but unable to settle. At one point she is pursued by a man who admires her but has pledged to kill her. Wonderful heroine, and interesting characters she meets.

The best part of this book was the writing. Oh my god, it flowed so nicely and the imagery was incredible to me. I felt like I was really there! 10/10 book.
The ONLY annoying part was the lack of quotation marks when characters were speaking, but once I got ahold of the style it was fairly easy to follow.

Though I am burnt out on zombie novels ( still am to be honest) I am so glad I read this. Vivid and beautiful while still horrific, Alden Bell has channeled the writing spirit of Cormac McCarthy for this trip across the southeastern United States. Fast paced and engaging on multiple levels, a solid winner.

This is such a haunting story. I find myself thinking about the main character days after finishing. I hated that she died in the end because I would have read so many books about her! And even her enemy, I am so curious about that whole situation.

She was one of the most likeable and interesting characters that I have come across in a book. I will definitely be re reading that one.

A pleasant surprise and well written novel about a young girl making her way through a zombie apocalypse. Bell blends the genre of the southern gothic with zombie horror with such ease that it seems like to the two were made for each other. I definitely recommend this to anyone interested in either genre.

Haunting, beautifully written tale of a girl trying to find redemption in a fallen, dying world. Temple is bad-ass, she it not afraid except of herself and what she is capable of. I liked her a lot. Her heart was much bigger then she gave herself credit for. I wish this was a longer story and that her journey didn't end just as the book did.

I wasn't expecting much but as I read I found beautiful style. It's a short read so I recommend reading it to know what I'm talking about, I have a high personal standard in books and never go for zombie books but I was very pleasantly surprised with this. Simply beautiful, for once the quotes on the book saying how amazing it is are right.

Beautiful little book. I appreciate the unconventional punctuation. So many little turns of phrase and unexpected contemplative gems that I paused and reread just to savor. I appreciate the biblical reference in the title as well. A zombie book that actually makes you ache for the beauty of the world.

A beautifully written novel. A zombie novel may put some people off - not a genre that everyone wants to read, but the zombies are not a focal point of the tale, which is about a 15 year old survivor, a young girl, who is tracked by a man who wants to execute her. I can say this is the only book of its genre that brought me to tears when I finished it. Highly recommended.

Excellent story.

The sentence structure for around half of this book though is odd and doesn’t read right, it reads as if those parts weren’t proof-read before printing.

But having said that, I still enjoyed this book.

Recommended? Yep
Read again? No. As much as I enjoyed this, it just don’t have that “read more than once” feel to it.

Well it was a good story, that is until I got to the end, only reason I've given this book 3 stars instead of 5 is because I finished it wayy too fast, yeah it says 300 pages but my ebook reader (moon+ reader pro) only shows the % and not the pages because I tend to decrease the font size, I really felt like this book would last me more then just 4 days but hey at least it was good😊

Well written and compelling

I'm a fan of post apocalyptic novels - and trust me there is some pretty dismal fare in that genre - fortunately not this book. Very well written -almost poetic in places. At times quite gritty - this novel will drawn you in until the last page. A fantastic find and well worth the purchase price

Ça aurait pu être un coup de cœur si l'histoire avait été moins rapide et l'héroïne moins jeune (et vulgaire)... En tout cas, on est bien loin d'un roman pour fillette ! C'est sombre, déprimant, violent et brutal, du survivalisme post-apo pessimiste qui pousse pourtant à l'optimisme et la réflexion. Ça méritait vraiment plus d'approfondissement.

Why did I spend so much time on this book? I won't spoil it for you, but it felt like the author couldn't think of a good ending. Plus they seemed very confused about the genre. The whole thing seemed like some weird YA zombie novel until you get to a random sex scene with the sixteen year old protagonist.

Honestly I can’t decide how I feel about the book. It’s not easy reading, though the writing is atmospheric. The lack of punctuation drove me batty even after getting used to it.

It loses points for ‘men writing teenage girls and sex’. If you know what I mean. Also I couldn’t take it that there was power in places 25 years post apocalypse.

The narration was really hard to take- overblown lyricism that was just over the top. I think I hated that way more than the weird way city infrastructure was in tact, electric grids and water worked, roads were clear, gas was not expired, but no one was communicating with phones or internet. However, the main character was great and so was the dialogue.

I wanted to like this, and for the most part, the journey of reading the book was entertaining. It felt a bit like tourism in a post-zombie reality. I also usually am all for endings that aren’t necessarily happy… but the ending to this particular read was so unsatisfying!

I couldn’t help but wonder if maybe that was the point?

The book was quite boring, you were waiting for the "ok heres the BIG, INTERESTING twist" the entire book, and while the world building was super cool and well thought out, its sold as a "post apocalyptic / Zombie" book. The Zombies aren't focused on and the actual building of how post apocalyptic society would work. The book dragged on and was not worth the read time.

This was another assigned Post Apocalyptic Sci-Fi novel. I enjoyed this novel relatively because it was fast paced & the story progressed along very well. Although, towards the end it became a little more dull in its telling. The Reapers Are Angels focuses on human survival, trauma, tropes of violence & trying to navigate this zombie driven apocalypse.


3/5 ⭐️

I really liked this book. It was paced perfectly and Temple’s character was very well done. The adventure, insightfulness, and descriptive writing style makes it one of my favorite end-of-the-world books I've ever read. My one complaint is that I wish it was set up to be a continuing series so I could have read more about Temple as she grew up. Pretty mad about that.

This was a really great zombie book. It follows a 15 year old as she survives zombies and non zombies. Due to the nature of survival, she seems older than she should be though we get peeks of her innocence every once in a while. One thing though is there is a sex scene between her and an older man which I found completely unnecessary but aside from that I did enjoy this!

Devastating and Beautiful

This story is told so beautifully, it almost seems wrong for it to be about zombies. I was not expecting the end. And it is devastating. And yet, for all the death and tragedy, it does leave me with a sense of hope for the human experience. So well done. I think I might put the novel in the same category as Jack London and Felix Salten. Unforgettable.

3.5 stars. Overall the book has some good messages, it’s very southern and had quite a few religious references in there but it’s pretty good. There are some weird parts though as some older men hit on her and she’s like 15-16. She also has sex w a 25 year old??? idk weird to me. If it had none of that it’d be a 4.

Good book. Not at all what I expected. It was a coming to age kind of read. Following and reminiscing a young life and journey. Not at all gory. I like that the zombie world was very very different from the typical standard. It was almost a "faith of humanity" feel. The main character was funny and relatable. I enjoyed this read.

Unlike any zombie novel I’ve ever read. Following a murder machine of a 15 year old girl as she navigates a dystopian zombie hellscape. But it’s all she’s known, and we are just along for the ride.

The writing is some righteous southern gothic kinda shit and I loved it, paired perfectly with descriptions of meandering corpses. A fun one.

I enjoyed this book far more than I thought I would. I had seen some of the criticisms and they are warranted but, overall, this book keeps you intrigued and the heroine is a likable character making her way through a zombie infested world. Much like the Last of Us, the zombie apocalypse is just the background to this coming of age novel of survival and redemption.

Another post-apocalypse zombie story. There were some problems with the story but overall the main character, Temple, is very engaging and there are sections quite poetic and moving. Good book overall.

Ok so this book was real good up to the ending. my favorite parts involved the abominations. Has this been optioned yet for a film..we all know that's coming right? Still not on the level of the forest of hands and teeth series. But I did enjoy it.

Beautiful! Probably one of the BEST zombie books I've ever read. I love that it wasn't as bleak as some of the other books of it's genre. It had hope and that's what makes it so good. Also very lyrical and amazingly well written!

I loved this. It is a quiet book set in a post zombie apocalypse world & I really liked that it was character driven. Highly recommended for those who like this genre. The writing was excellent & I would definitely read other books by the same author. 3.5 stars.

Huh... Well that was interesting.

I know some people, like me a lot of the time while reading books, just can't stand the suspense and have to know what happens before it is revealed in the book. For those of you like me, here you go-

Temple, a teenage girl, lives in a world where the dead come back to life and have been since before she was born. Her blasé attitude towards slugs and the living is fascinating. It is a wonder if anything can scare her. Perhaps real fear is finding out who you truly are.

I wasn't expecting to be wowed by the prose of what I thought was just another zombie apocalypse book, but then again, for some reason this genre does seems to attract writers that look just a little bit deeper into life, into beauty, into death.

Pretty ok book with alot flaws in the story.

There was no story focused line but it kept on changing whole book and made me think this book as travel journal rather than story. Lot of unnecessary time was invested in random characters which appeared as writer trying to fill up pages.

You have to just accept some things but if you can just accept the world as it is presented the story is enjoyable. Don't know if I will continue the series but this was better than I expected after the first couple of chapters.

This book has devastated me in the best possible way. What even is the world?! How will I move on from this? What can I possibly read next that won't utterly disappoint and frustrate me? The only other book that has done this to me was To Kill a Mockingbird. I will never forget Temple or Moses.

It's mostly the personal story of the main character, Temple, that happens to involve zombies. I enjoyed the personal reflections on motivation/survival, but there was a lot of questionable stuff like electricity, gas, cars, etc. still working after 15 years.

I don't leave many reviews, but this one i had to, as it was that amazing of a book. I read lots of zombie fiction and this book is like no zombie book I've ever read before. It is more abt surviving the "end of civilization", then it is abt crushing in zombie skulls. I couldn't put this book down! The ending i wasnt expecting either. I highly recommend this book!

Was enjoying the story of the post apocalyptic world and Temples role within it until it came to the mutant people. Then I found the book a chore and couldn't wait to finish. I totally lost interest when they came along. Pointless and boring.

I loved Temple. In general, I'm pretty much spent on Zombie stories for a while, but people kept singing high praises for this book. Well, they were right. It's a damned good story, not necessarily for the zombies but for the main character.

Unexpected

Poetic. So much better than I expected from a zombie story but it wasn't really about zombies. Lyrical and life affirming. I loved the unusual connection between Temple and Moses. Highly recommend.

The ending was fucking terrible. I feel like it might be a well-drafted story, but it's not enjoyable and it has too many corny developments (hillbillies injecting zombie brain juice to get swole) to be literature. Seemed like author was trying to have it both ways - pulpy and high literature.

It was a really good southern horror story, with great imagery in word choice. All the way to the end it kept your attention and had a very deep meaning throughout. Although one thing that I didn't like was that in general it was hard to read without proper punctuation or segways.

If Mattie Ross, the teenage heroine from True Grit, found herself in a zombie apocalypse, this is the story.

Wonderful main character that kept me reading even though I am very much done with zombie stories.

3.5
Steady going throughout, with areas of intricate prose—the pacing is good, the passage of time well constructed. It reads more like a new adult type of novel, and I had a few issues with the lack of speech marks, but a good zombie novel all the less!

This was just fantastic. It was beautifully written. We follow the journey of a 15 year old girl crossing the country of a zombie filled world. It’s was so gruesome I loved it. Temple will stay with me for a very long time. Didn’t expect that ending but it was just so good.

My wife and I fired up this audio book on a round trip drive from New Hampshire to NYC for a wedding. It filled the drive time almost exactly with a short and original take on the zombie genre. Exactly what we needed - something right in between thoughtful and brainless.

What a sad little story. I’m quite upset by the ending. I won’t say, but nooooo!

I found it odd that the author didn’t use speech marks. There were times I found that really confusing.

I’m going to sulk over the ending for a few days noooooo!

Soft 4/5 stars. More like 3.9 but it doesnt matter. A post apocalyptic zombie book that doesnt focus too much on the zombies nor the survivors. Good balance for both and it has a sad ending. It also seems like it is set up for a sequel.

A gift from my beautiful bride. Story of resourceful young girl being tracked by a red neck who's knownly jack ass brother earned his death at the hands of our young girl. The back drop is a zombie apocalypse. Great story from beginning to end.

Temple is very thoughtful and good-hearted for all she's gone through at such a young age. Seeing the zombie apocalypse through her eyes was refreshing. This was definitely more a story of people and who we become when worse comes to worst.

I overall really enjoyed this very unique zombie story. It wasn't perfect, but I had a great time with it. This story is more about character development versus action. Also, the audiobook narrator kind of distracted me as she sounded much older than the character was supposed to be.
Not bad for zombie pulp.
A dreamy novel, with a bit of nebulous plot. If you like literary fiction too, you'll probably enjoy this unusual zombie novel.
There was a memorable description in the book, where temple is bathing in a river, and the blood and her golden hair is reminiscent of the sun.

Enjoyed the story very much. It's sometime gory, personal and desperate. I loved Temple the main character, fearless attitude, she kept me reading.
I hope this is a stand-alone novel
A grim and confusing at times read.
meh
It's Catcher in the Rye with zombies and a protagonist I didn't want to strangle.
Very bleak, terribly sad. But awfully well written.
uhh, ok... the book is well written, but it feels like there is no beginning and no ending. what was the story really about?..
Loved it had an amazing story!Highly recommend it.
Just not interesting enough for me.
Couldn't put it down. But with the ending, I'm not looking to read the second book which is all about a character I hated at the end of the first book. Great read overall though.

RATING: 3.5 stars

Noo, that ending. Why?

But, finding beauty in small things and in a ruined, post-apocalyptic world was pretty cool.

I'm not even sure what to think of this book. I can say for a zombie book it has only a few seriously descriptive portions featuring zombies so it's not gore the whole time.
It's a quick read.
3.5 actually
The best zombie novel. Ever. Beautifully written.
This books started out well. Fast paced and entertaining enough. Then they wrote “should of” instead of “should’ve” twice within a page. I couldn’t finish it after that.
Very intriguing take on a zombie apocalypse. It is more of a road thriller book with zombies as a backdrop. Took me a minute to get into it but then it moves at a pretty good clip.
The characters are devoid of personality and I found it difficult to relate or empathize with any of them. I did not finish the book.
The voice of this zombie story is different. And the ending is not what you expect. It's worth a read.
I hate zombie stuff. It scares me. But I can't deny that this book was really good. If blood and gore doesn't work for you, don't read this book. It's graphic af.
Why do I do this to myself.
Surprisingly literary for a novel about the zombie apocalypse. Compelling narrator, and narrative. Enjoyed it considerably.
Standard road trip zombie book. Told from perspective of young woman. She meets a mute along the way and tries to get him home.
The audiobook version is phenomenal.
Some of the best Zombie pulp I have read. Rich language and builds on the tropes in an unexpected way.
Extremely intense.
The zombie novel as literary fiction. Well done. I'd like to see this translated to film that stays true to the spirit of the book.
Loved the main character. Hated the ending.
Ooh I liked this so much! It's lyrical and dreamlike and sad.
Excellent read. Moody, gothic, poignant, and surprising. Akin to Walking Dead episode
Love, love, love this book
Flannery O'Connor would be proud of this southern gothic novel with just a sprinkle of zombies.
Great main character and interesting story.
DNF
I was unexpected delighted with this book. Not your basic zombie plot. Loved Temple
Great book read it along time ago have been waiting for more.
This is the first “zombie book” I’ve read that was actually a novel. Very good read. Simple, beautiful story of a narrator living in a zombie world, the only world she’s ever known.
One of the best zombie books I’ve ever read. More literary than genre, with a strong, female heroine and generally well-drawn characters.
1.5/5 Two words: Southern Gothic
Easily one of the best zombie books I’ve read. Still feel some type of way about her only being 15 but... still worth a read if zombies are your kinda thing!
When zombies are all you have ever known this is how to live, a great quick read, would have been happier if it was twice as long
One of the most fascinating moral messages I've ever read, a brilliant realistic southern teenage girl, and a zombie plot that doesn't feel overused or redundant
Neat little zombie book with some touching literary flourishes. Can’t recall how this ended up on my to-read shelf, but I’m very glad I got around to it.
Read this book a while ago and enjoyed it; didn’t know it was part of a series. Just added book 2 (Exit Kingdom) to my TBR list.
Fantastically written, one of my favorite reads of the year so far. I really liked the protagonist, and her companion Maury; I liked their dynamic. Definitely would recommend.
Absolute favorite zombie/contagion book. Very unique relationship between the protag, a fifteen year old girl, and an older antag. Will forever love this story.

3½ stars.
This story didn't have much of a plot, and I was expecting much more up until the very end.
very good book

Who would've thought that Southern gothic paired so well with zombie apocalypse? I usually cannot stand the writing style that has no punctuation, but it really works in this novel. It's creepy and moving.

An eloquent and heartfelt look into the Apocalypse.
Beautiful. I'm going to be thinking about this one for awhile.
Do not read this goddamned dumpster fire of a book!!!
I loved this story. Highly recommended.
I never thought I’d find a zombie book so devastatingly beautiful, but here we are.
I really liked this road trip zombie book.

Excellent zombie novel that is well-written. This book is popular among readers, even though there isn’t much horror. There is, however, really good character development. Short and enjoyable.

Written in the present tense which I found jarring. The plot is like True Grit with zombies, but everyone talks like Mattie Ross. Beyond annoying.

perfect Pool book

It's alright, but doesn't seem to have much interesting to say. Also, the mutant subplot was just outright clichéd and silly.
Only real issue with the book was the amount of outward friendliness the world still has despite having experienced an apocalyptic event. Otherwise was a great dive into loneliness.
I really appreciate it the description of the apocalypse and emptiness in the world. Definitely my top five favorite dystopian books now.
I struggled with the prose style in this, and found it hard to connect with the characters because of it.
There are little nuggets of prose throughout this book that are breathtaking.

I… this… wow…
3.5 stars. Good read! I cared about the characters and I love that the author surprised me a few times.
Super fun fast read. Loved the language and the main character.
Read most of this a few years back and then forget about it. Reread it all the way through this time, reminds me alot of, Of Mice and Men, but a Zombie Version
This was a highly ranked zombie novel. As an avid consumer, it doesn’t take much for me to pick one up and enjoy. But this, did very little for me
A decent zombie book. I had no idea it was a series when I finished which is always a good thing. However, I don't think I loved it enough to continue.
A pretty good zombie book
One of the better “zombie” books available. Recommend to any zombie book fans and even those who aren’t…
Not great but not bad, would not read a second time. But the main character and her nemesis were both endearing. So it was a pleasant enough trip through the first time.
the pinnacle of post apocalypse
Took a chapter or two to get into it but once I did, I couldn't put it down. Burned through it very quickly. Wonderful post zombie apocalypse book with a young lady lead. Recommended.

Beautiful writing and great story. Unexpected ending. Perhaps too “unrealistic” given circumstances but still absolutely captivating.
