I'll be the first to say I'm a lightweight when it comes to horror books. Since I read one maybe once a year (and that's only in recent years), it's not really my place to say where an author or book stands in the genre, but dang, I must say that this book was great. It stressed me out, but I couldn't put it down and I didn't want it to end. It reminded me of The Road meets The Grapes of Wrath meets I Am Legend, but it wholly held its own as well. I liked that the book is a right balance of contemplation and action and that the two are not mutually exclusive. Man, those discussions especially between Temple and Moses Todd. It's great when a zombie apocalypse novel can really make a genuine stretch into discussions of humanity that ask you to regard these notions in the context of your life and not just of this particular world. Of course, I couldn't help thinking of The Walking Dead comics, which I thoroughly enjoy, but dare I say got me thinking in terms of my reality.

There were a couple spots that upset me, at least initially--the mutant "inheritors" for one. For an inexplicable reason I'm super picky about sci-fi/fantasy to a point where I can accept flesh-eating cadavers, but not 10-foot-tall skeletal semi-zombies. Bell didn't give me chance, though, to dwell on that point because the story kept on moving and shit got REAL. And I am still SO MAD that Temple freakin' died at the end! What the what?! I love that girl from the bottom of my heart. And by Minnie? I can't tell yet whether that ending will work itself out for me after it's had some time to settle...whether it's ludicrous in a good way or a bad way. It appears that perhaps this is the start of a series. However, as much as Moses Todd was a great foil to Temple, I feel cheated that Temple won't be in a potential sequel. I mean, don't get me wrong, Alden Bell is a great writer and I'm going to absolutely read his next novel (apparently, yes, following Moses and Abraham), but I just wish Temple could be there for it.

I'm so glad that this book won an award--it should win more awards--though seeing as it's an Alex Award, I'm not sure how comfortable I'd be giving it to a teen considering the type of violence and sex contained here. At least a younger teen. Or the repercussions of their parents finding out that it was my doing putting it in their hands. It certainly is moving though, and I'm pretty sure I would have loved it when I was 17 as much as I do now. Do yourself a favor and read this book. It's a doozy and well worth it.

Irgendwann in der Zukunft haben sich die Menschen in kleine abgeschottete Enklaven zurückgezogen, denn die Welt wird von Zombies überrannt. Temple, ein 15-jähriges Mädchen, zieht auf sich allein gestellt durch ein ödes Amerika. Als sie Zuflucht in einer menschlichen Gemeinschaft findet, währt diese nicht lange. Sie tötet in Notwehr einen Mann, der sie vergewaltigen wollte. Der Bruder schwört Rache und jagt sie. Aber beide sind sich ähnlicher, als sie zuerst wahrhaben wollen.

Die postapokalyptische Welt, die Alden Bell in The Reapers are the Angels (Nach dem Ende) beschreibt, ist wirklich furchteinflößend und schaurig. Das Buch hat einen gewissen Ekelfaktor, wenn zerfledderte Tote durch die Straßen schlurfen, verzichtet aber größtenteils auf plakative Gewaltdarstellung.

"Und die Horde in der pechschwarzen Nacht, nur beleuchtet von den Scheinwerfern, wimmelnd und aneinanderstoßend wie Maden im Bauch einer toten Katze, die grimmigste und degenerierteste Offenbarung der vernichteten Menschheit auf dieser vernichteten Erde – Bestien unserer verlorenen Vergangenheit, die herausquellen aus der von uns geschaffenen Hölle wie eine Armee der Verdammten, erstickt und würgend, verrottet und verkrustet und unglaublich kläglich, ja auf grausame, greifbare und grelle Weise kläglich."


Leider wird über die Ursachen der Auferstehung der Toten geschwiegen. Aber das ist okay, weil Temple nur diese Welt kennt, denn es begann bereits 25 Jahre zuvor. Und wenn sich das Leben in eine stinkende Hölle verwandelt, ist es auch egal, warum dies geschah. Weitaus störender sind logische Fehler. Es gibt noch Städte, die Strom haben, und in Supermärkten finden sich auch noch genießbare Lebensmittel, ebenfalls lassen sich immer noch funktionstüchtige Autos und Benzin auftreiben.

Es ist oft von Gott die Rede. Wenn ich Gott lese, dann ist das für mich nur ein Wort. Und ich habe auch hier nicht verstanden, was damit ausgedrückt werden soll. Ob eine bedeutsame, religiöse Botschaft transportiert werden soll. Ob Gott Erlösung schenken kann. Ob Gott eine Instanz ist, die über Gut und Böse, Richtig und Falsch entscheidet. Oder ob Gott Alles ist. Es wird hier nicht wirklich klar, es kann alles Mögliche sein. Die Suche nach den schönen Dingen, die auch eine zerstörte Welt noch bieten kann. Die Fähigkeit, dies noch sehen zu können, ist Thema. Und vielleicht ist das ja das Göttliche.

Der Stil ist zuerst gewöhnungsbedürftig, im Präsens geschrieben und wörtliche Rede nicht in Anführungszeichen gesetzt. Das Buch liest sich aber sehr gut und Temple ist eine Romanfigur, die sehr präsent und stark und in Wirklichkeit uralt ist. Doch es ist in erster Linie Horror-Trash, guter.

This is a tough book to review. It's definitely got things I really love in books- namely- it's at times brutal, beautiful and brilliant. I can't say that I *enjoyed* reading it- there's a horrific intensity to it that definitely makes it the complete opposite of a light, enjoyable read. But there is a really good story in there- and moments that are incredibly thought-provoking. I can see why people hate it- and why others love it. And I'd recommend it without reservation to a specific subset of people who are the kind of people who would love it (if that makes sense.) I would 100% recommend this to my book club, especially during October when when we pick something dark- because this is a great book to discuss with other readers.
The style is reminiscent of southern gothic- which works well for the story being told. It's sort of a zombie story and sort of a horror story- but the most horrifying characters are the humans in the story, not the zombies- which are essentially just a part of nature in this particular world. It's set years after a zombie apocalypse and told from the perspective of a teenage girl who has never known any other world.
The main character- Temple- isn't truly likeable- and she's incredibly broken (which is something I usually like in characters)-but there's not really an arc to her story- she is the same person throughout and there's not just no kind of redemption for anyone here, but not really any possibility of it. There is no real possibility for anyone in this tale- they are all driven to remain exactly as they are at the start.
And there lies the big problem I have with this story- the utter hopelessness woven through the world. That, perhaps, is more disturbing than the zombies, than the human monsters she encounters, than the choices people have had to make to survive in a world that outlasted human survival.
I don't necessarily need happy endings- there are books I love that end with the characters I love broken more than at the start, or that end with the character having a chance at something better and choosing to eschew redemption- or even trying and failing miserably. A narrative steeped in hopelessness is a different kind of story, though.
Essentially- I would recommend reading this if you're into zombie stories- it is an important contribution to that genre. But it's not going to leave you with hope or leave you feeling energized. If you're not looking for redemption arcs or meaningful character development throughout a story- then this might work well for you. If you're not into zombie stories or dark tales with unsavable people doing horrible things to each other- then this probably isn't the book for you.

The Reapers are the Angels by Alden Bell starts off like a lyrical melody that both fills your head and packs a wallop all in the same breath-a spicy Southern feast wrapped up in soft vowels and a wayward twang. For such a small tale (a mere two hundred and twenty or so compact pages) Reapers has more punch than The Passage, simply because of its soul and its enigmatic lead, and for its finality.

Reapers tells the story of Temple, who grows up in the aftermath of a global epidemic that lays waste to the world and morphs a portion of the population into zombies. While she has no recollection of any world before the epidemic, she has mastered a life for herself and has done so from an early age. For Temple, it has and always will be, a struggle to survive, to keep moving and to keep slaying. And it appears she has an affinity for it. But Bell has managed to build many layers to Temple. Underneath that steely exterior lies a vulnerable girl who, when peeled back, is surprising, and troubling.

There are remnants of influences from other sources, in Bell's work...it has a familiar feel of "The Stand" and "I am Legend" but the creation of his heroine is what makes The Reapers Are the Angels a truly amazing piece of work. Temple is a tragic lead and those who are pulled into her sphere know that the outcome cannot be good but will go along for the ride anyway.

It does not have the overwhelming derivative feel of Cronin’s piece. The difference between The Passage and Reapers is that Temple, Bell’s heroine is the lost heart and soul of humanity and even she does not know it. Temple, sometimes, an uncompromising stoic, is also an unknowing angel of death in the vacuum of a forgotten wasteland. Her ferociousness coupled with her fragility, is what makes her engaging to readers. We cleave to her vulnerability as much as we embrace her ferociousness, which has singularly been borne out of guilt.

Temple is endlessly running from herself, and from her humanity. Bell’s grisly tale of gore and zombies serves as the backdrop, the purgatory she must endure as she races from one corner of the abandoned country to another…shunning a home, real companionship, endlessly engaging in the “meatskin tango”. It is why she welcomes the chase from Moses. As long as she is fighting the slugs and winning, she staves off the feelings. In Reapers, those who have survived, struggle with going on, persevering. To what end? Never has this been more pronounced by Temple’s journey-The Reapers are the Angels reads like a hell-bound Natty Gann and Temple cannot help but be its incandescent slayer. Unforgettable in its finality and riveting in its soulfulness.

Having read this for the second time now, I think that if I were to have a favourite-book-ever-that-I-love-deep-down-to-its-core, it's this one.

--------

The Reapers Are the Angels is a book that you need to be in a certain frame of mind to read and enjoy. Though there are are a number of fight scenes, it's not an action book. Though some of the things that people say or do will amuse, it's not a humourous book. Except for the small uncovering of Temple's past that haunts her, it's not a mystery. There's no romance, except in the descriptions of desolate landscapes, lit-up schools of fish, and an appreciation for the power of the Niagara Falls.

Temple is a character that faces death as deserved and inevitable, though this wars with her indomitable compulsion to survive. She's rough and illiterate, though also intelligent and questioning. The novel is slow, it's contemplative, it's hopeless, it's grim. It follows Temple's journey across the American landscape as she travels for the sake of travelling and survival more than to reach any sort of destination. In fact, she quickly becomes uncomfortable in any sort of static environment, whether it be in a place or with a person.

I'm actually quite surprised at how much I liked this book. There's something about the character and her journey that compelled me to want to keep learning more of her story, though I was constantly afraid of a tragic end that seems inevitable for a character that is unable or unwilling to find any kind of happiness or salvation.

As for my thoughts on Moses:

This is definitely a book that will stick in my head for a while.

A fin he encontrado un libro acerca de "zombies" el cual haya amado de inicio a fin.

Este libro lo leí porque soy una amante de los libros así y cuando vi la sinopsis me dije que tenía que darle una oportunidad a ver qué tal, pero no fue eso lo que me hizo leerlo, fue el hecho de que todas las reseñas que leía de este libro eran positivas. Así que ahí me animé y lo leí.

Temple es una chica de 15 años que se la pasa de solitario de un lugar a otro lidiando con sus demonios personales.
Un día se encuentra con este grupo de sobrevivientes y decide pasar algún tiempo con ellos, hasta que uno de los hombres de ese grupo intenta violarla. No tiendo más opción, Temple lo mata y es forzada huir del lugar ya que Moses, el hermano del que intentó abusar de ella, quiere cumplir el propósito de su vida: obtener venganza.

Y básicamente ese es el tema central de la historia. Obviamente en el camino aparecen otros personajes, hay sangre, acción y ¡zombies! Pero eso si, tengo que decir que el libro no se centra en eso. Más bien ocupa un papel secundario. Lo importante es el viaje que emprende Temple junto con Bobo (personaje que aparece en el libro), su huida de Moses, y el descubrimiento que tiene ella de si misma y del mundo en el que vive.

Lo que más me encantó del libro fueron los pensamientos de la prota. Para ser una chiquilla de 15 años, se me hacía que estaba leyendo a una mujer madura de unos 28 años debido a la complejidad de sus pensamientos. Al inicio no entendía bien cómo alguien con esa edad tenía pensamientos muy profundos pero conforme avanzan las páginas se te hace un poco obvio. Temple nació en un mundo de caos, oscuridad y muerte, no conoce nada más, y , desde su infancia tuvo que pasar por situaciones muy fuertes que la hicieron madurar antes de tiempo... pero ese ya es otro punto.

Al inicio la lectura se me hizo muy complicada (no voy a mentir) puesto que el autor escribe de una manera muy peculiar; no utiliza signos de narración, pero como la historia era muy interesante, como que después de un tiempo te acostumbras y ya se te hace fácil distinguir pensamientos, hechos y narraciones (si lo leen, entenderán lo que quiero decir)

Ahora, puese que a mi me haya encantado el libro pero definitivamente no a todos les va a gustar. Si lo que buscas es un libro con una prota fuerte y zombies por doquier, armas, acción y más zombies, pues de una te digo que este no es tu libro.


El final me dejó con un nudo en la garganta pero no lo odié. Más bien me hizo amarlo más (dios, suena a que soy muy masoquista!)
Sé que hay un segundo libro, y ya que amé mucho la escritura del autor, definitivamente tengo en mente leerlo.

15-year-old Temple fights zombies and flees captors in this post-zombie-apocalypse story of survival, but her real struggle is against her own inner demons. After learning how to fight and kill in order to survive in a world with man-eating monsters, she also has to learn how to live with herself as she starts to feel like a cold-blooded killer.

I found the writing style rather jarring. The story is told in the present tense third person, which would fine if it weren’t so quirky. Temple’s illiteratacy and limited vocabulary (which could make third grader look like a Rhodes Scholar) makes the dialogue very twangy, while the narration wields unusual diction and leaves out any quotation marks on the dialogue (similar to The Road; apparently quotation marks are now banned in post-apocalyptic novels). The dichotomy between to Temple’s 400 word, slang riddled vocabulary and the thesaurus-wielding narration was kind of hard to swallow, especially when quotation marks may have helped let me know where Temple’s talking ended and the narration began.

On the other hand, there are several useful things that I learned about what the world will look like after the zombie apocalypse.

1. Gas will be free for the taking, widely available, and will last for YEARS and YEARS. No need to worry about being able to start your car. In the current world I have to make sure I empty my lawn mower of gas before winter so it has a full tank of fresh gas in the summer, but the same change that makes people rise from the dead and hunger for human flesh also makes gasoline last forever. After the zombie apocalypse, gas is in unlimited supply, provide you can find a gas pump that has power.

2. Although all commercial business (stores, gas stations, movies, TV, etc.) will be non-existent, and major cities mostly empty, diesel trains will still be running between major cities. This is not a plot hole; we already noted above that there is plenty of gas.

3. Don’t worry your little head about weapons; guns and ammo will be widely available for many, many years after manufacturing has shut down.

4. In spite of all the above, beware of plot twists. They are not your friend.

All that said, this was a rather unique (if twisted) take on what zombies would do to run the country. If you want to participate in the meme of reading about zombies, this book would be good for your repertoire, if you can stomach it.

Well, this is certainly one book that I couldn't really decide on in the end. Is it a wonderfully written, heartbreaking and at times allegorical story of a post-apocalyptic world, or is it a novel lacking punctuation, but full of plot-holes and rip-offs?

I liked the characters. Temple is a kick-ass character, who saw the beauty in a world full of terror because it was all she knew. Moses is a contradiction, an enemy to Temple, yet a kindred spirit at heart who understood her better than anyone else she'd met. There was a host of interesting supporting characters, as well.

Add to that the language, the fact that the descriptions were so well-done and Temple's voice was a wonder to read, and you have the makings of a very good story. I'm guessing the choices to put the speech throughout without the correct punctuation was to highlight Temple's upbringing and lack of education, but I don't know for sure. It annoyed me at first, but I got used to it.

The bad things? Well, we could start with the plot holes. How was the electricity working, or the water still running? How was there still trains and cars running on diesel? How could someone drink cans of coke twenty-five years old and not get poisoned? How come the infrastructure wasn't over-run with plants and weeds and just nature in general? How did the "slugs" manage to survive without food? How did Temple drive so many miles in a car and not have to fill up? How were the cars still running after standing still for years (as most with a car will know, you have to start them up frequently if they are off the road for a while, or the batteries run down)?

Then there's the fact that some of the plot (and characters) seems to be inspired by other books and movies of the same genre. At the end I was struck by the similarity to 28 Days Later (if you've read to the end of The Reapers Are The Angels and gotten to that part, you'll know what I mean). I kept thinking, this is Jim's story if he'd been brain-damaged by the accident and some kind soul took him back to his family. I've read other reviews that note the similarity to another well-known post-apocalyptic novel. The fact is, any novel of this genre is going to sound familiar in some ways, as there are only so many things you can do with such a plot-line, I guess.

Other than that, the story was good. I read it in the space of three days. I would probably recommend it to others, but with reservations. I imagine there are better novels of this genre to start with.

"God is a slick god. Temple Knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe."

This is a truly beautiful novel. I found the tone and style of the narrative absolutely entrancing.

The Reapers are the Angels (the title is a bible quote) follows Temple, a young woman in her mid- to late teens, as she makes her way alone through what is left of a zombie (or meatskins as Temple calls them) infested world. 25 years ago some sort of apocalyptic event caused the dead to rise from their graves. The reader never gets to know what exactly happened, and it doesn't matter as it is totally irrelevant to Temple's story.

Rather than a classic zombie survival story set during or shortly after the zombies start to rise, this book focuses on the events and people Temple encounters as she travels through the remnants of human society. The zombies, at this time, are part of everyday life and serve more as a backdrop for the story to unfold against than as a driving plot device. Since Temple was born a decade after the catastrophic event she has never known the world 'before' and has a rather unique outlook on life and the world in general, seeing things of beauty and wonder in places where few can.

Temple is a great character with a rich and deep personallity. She is strong, independant, wise beyond her years, jaded, and completely convinced of her own wickedness. The dynamic between Temple and the main antagonist, Moses, is what makes this book really shine though. Their perverted father-daughter like relationship is what drives most of the plot forward.

For me, one of the biggest strong points of this novel is the writing itself. There is some truly beautiful and poetic prose in this book. Alden Bell uses a rather unique writing style (no quotation marks, some odd sentence structures) that took me a few pages to fully get into. But once I did I was firmly hooked and read the book in one long afternoon. Once the style had 'clicked' with me, I actually started from the first page again so that I could read everything in that mindset.

The style and tone of the writing serve to create a rich atmosphere that permeates the narrative. A bleakness that wanders a fine line between despair and hope, between dread and wonder. The feeling stuck with me for days after I was done reading. This, for me, is the sign of a truly great book.

Why is no one talking about this book?? It's SO GOOD, the sort of story that'll stick with you for a long while. Calling it a zombie story is doing it a bit of a disservice because it's so much more than that...it's a gut-wrenching tale of desolation, despair and redemption. Yes, zombies are what brought about the end of the world as we know it, but really, you could substitute any mass extinction event (nuclear fallout, a deadly virus, whatever) and the story would still work. It follows a girl who was born into the wastelands of our post-apocalyptic world and knows nothing beyond how to survive. And she is one badass character - she slices and shoots her way through this landscape, rarely afraid of what she's facing and never hesitating to get her hands dirty. She tries to keep to herself, consciously shunning human companionship because she feels that she's unworthy of it (based on an event that is alluded to throughout the story and is finally explained in its entirety at the end), and her interactions with fellow survivors prove to be both her undoing and her salvation.
For being as philosophical as it is, it's surprisingly readable...it didn't get bogged down in its own greatness, like "Zone One." I thought the author's decision to not use quotation marks was interesting and gave the story a dream-like feel. The only gripe I have, and the reason I'm not giving it 5 stars, is the mutants. Their appearance and subsequent story arc was so abrupt and unnecessary that I was jarred back to the real world thinking, "WTF?" Making a zombie story believable isn't easy, and up until this point, I was completely sold. This is exactly how I imagine things would look 25 years after the dead rise. So throwing in hillbillies shooting up zombie brains in some demented meth lab and turning themselves into gigantic monsters with exoskeletons just seemed silly. Why not just have the characters encounter an army of hillbillies minus any monstrous enhancement and have to fight and strategize their way through that situation? It would have gone miles to maintaining the realism.
All told though, this was a gorgeous story, haunting and evocative, and even the grisliest scenes (and there really aren't that many of them, so when they happen, they stand out in high relief) are made into things of beauty. It's rare to come across a book that has this much meaning and soul, let alone one that features the zombie apocalypse. Loved it.

I thought I would be a fan of this book. I really did. I like zombie books, and I like a good survival story in a post-apocalyptic setting. Combine that with a strong heroine, and I thought I had myself an enjoyable novel. Unfortunately, I was wrong. I did not like this book.

It started out well enough. Actually, scratch that. It started off with me wondering how I received an e-Book with such broken formatting. I quickly realized that it was another of those stylistic things. I’ve been taken aback by this before in Blood Red Road and Shatter Me, so I moved past it and did my best to move on. However, I think it does bear mentioning that you should be prepared to find zero quotation marks in this book. In a book that uses dialogue and inner thoughts to drive the plot, it sometimes becomes difficult to muddle through exactly who is speaking, and if Temple is speaking aloud or in her head.

That aside, the book started off on a pretty good foot. It was a book about a young girl making her way in a country defeated by mindless zombies. She is thoughtful, considering God and the way things may have been before — when there were enough people to keep civilization running smoothly. But Temple knows that God works in mysterious ways, and that nature will always win. She moves on from place to place as the zombies or nature itself force her out. Pretty soon on from there it becomes apparent what the problem with this book is. At least, what I consider to be the problem.

That is, the author. Trying far too hard. This novel is chock full of purple prose and leading situations. Alden Bell has tried too hard to craft a literary zombie novel, and to me it shows. This is a book the author clearly intended to be analyzed in an English class, with students pain-stakingly examining between the lines for evidence of allegory, symbolism, motifs and themes. In my opinion, this is not a book written to be enjoyed, and it was not. I stuck it through to the end, because I hate leaving a book unfinished. But by the last few chapters, I was sorry I had done so, because the forced literary elements just piled on at the novel’s conclusion.

I’d only recommend this novel if you consider yourself a person that enjoys the kind of work that goes with reading a novel not just for enjoyment, but for hidden messages. Perhaps you will find yourself a good match for this book.

Okay, so this definitely ranks as one of my all-time favorite books ever. The caliber of writing, thought, and emotion that this book contains is a rare treat in the horror genre. It is thought provoking and gut-wrenching. To say I loved this book would be an understatement; it was simply literature at its finest. “Reapers are the Angels” is less a zombie novel and more the tragic story of Temple, an orphaned teenager who was born into a decaying "meatskin" (zombie) riddled world. Decades ago zombies decimated the human population and all that remains are clusters of survivors. In her journey we get to see that even in the darkest days beauty exists (within man and nature) if you are willing to keep your eyes open. We also get to experience Temple's struggle with her primal "fight or flight" existence, her inability to save those she loves (and the guilt associated with those failures), and where the boundaries lie between what makes us good versus evil. Temple is so philosophic and well developed that you connect to her plight so deeply, and your heart breaks over and over for her. Her world is so damn grim but yet she continually is pointing out the wonders still left to see.
I only have one beef with this book, and that would be the section I like to call “how did I end up in The Hills Have Eyes”. If you have read the story you know what part I mean. This story had this amazing flow, and then you get to this part and are like “what the hell?” I understand that to believe in zombies in the first place requires a bit a reality relinquishment, but this took it too far. It just seemed so terribly out of place with the rest of the book. I tell myself it was a necessary section of the book as a means to provide a platform for the jail conversation between Temple and Moses (which is simply brilliant), but it still has an awkwardness in context with the rest of the book. But the rest of the story was so exceptional that I am more than willing to forgive this odd little detour the book took.
As a warning, this is a heavy dark read, but it is so brilliant that you shouldn't let that stop you! It was not "make you want to puke" graphically violent (when compared to other zombie books) but just really REALLY emotionally is draining (if you have ever read "The Road" you should know what I mean). You attach to the characters so deeply (even some of the "bad" ones) that the never ending tragedy is excruciating

Wow. I just finished reading the book a minute ago.To begin with, this is not what I expected nor was it what I was looking for but it turned out to be something I would've regretted not reading. I read this book thinking of only zombies in my mind. I decided I wanted some zombie action and came across this book and thought I'd give it a shot and I'm glad I did. Forgive me if this review seems to be all over the place. I needed to get this out as soon as I read the book, because, the book gets to you.

Okay, so this book mostly revolves around a 15 year old girl named 'Temple'. She's a strong girl, surviving in a world loaded with zombies whom she refers to as "Meatskins". But it isn't about the zombies. It's about her journey, as she moves from place to place, the people she meets.It is about death, redemption, your beliefs.While on her journey, she comes across this place where an incident occurs and she makes an enemy who vows to kill her. But the man,Moses, and Temple are connected somehow, deep within, it feels like they're the only ones who understands this world.He grows fond of her which he reveals, in the end although it is quite obvious.

The writing, oh, the writing is lovely. It has these amazing prose and stuff in it,sometimes, you have to put the book down and think about it. In the end, all you can say is, the book gets to you. It is thought-provoking and those are books that have a special place.

Some of my fav lines:

“Some people, he says, they hide themselves away from the eyes of the world. They hunker down and shiver. They find four walls high enough to put between them and everything else. Those people, to them the world is a frightful place. See, you and me, we're different. When we are called on to move, we move. It don't matter the cause or the distance. Revenge or ministration, reason or folly - it's all the same to us.”

"Sometimes when there’s no light to see by, that’s when everything comes sharp and clear."

“Beyond the pursuit of meaning and beyond good and evil too, she says. See, it’s a daily chore tryin to do the right thing. Not because the right thing is hard to do—it ain’t. It’s just cause the right thing—well, the right thing’s got a way of eluding you. You give me a compass that tells good from bad, and boy I’ll be a soldier of the righteous truth. But them two things are a slippery business, and tellin them apart might as well be a blind man’s guess.”

I'll start off by saying I'm burnt out by post-apocalypse stories. They're melodramatic, bleak, and fundamentally unpleasant. I can understand their purpose--they're a push back to a frontier-like time, and represent both the bleakness of today's economic realities and an escape from them, to a state where your survival is entirely within your own hands. But generally, I think I'm done with reading them. Or rather, thought I was done, because The Reapers are the Angels is really, really good. It suffers from all the things I just complained about and more; the lack of quotation marks combined with the general mood and plot make a reasonable case that it's a McCarthy-clone. But damned if it wasn't done so well that I liked it anyway.

Temple is a teenage girl who's made her peace with the post-apocalypse. It happened before she could remember, and now, she's a loner who keeps to herself, a darkness in her that keeps her from what remains of civilized folk. (see, even in describing it, I'm slipping into melodrama.) The story is a series of vignettes, with two main constants: the mentally challenged man she tries to save whose presence gives her meaning (it's a Of Mice and Men situation) and the brother of a man she killed, who was sworn to kill her (it's a Javert-Les Miserables thing, if Javert was more bloodthirsty). It's the vignettes that really make the story: the settlement where the men are worse than the zombies; Belle Isle and a decaying (but not in the zombie sense) old southern family; religious hillbillies that have gone whole hog into monsterdom; and a tense showdown.

They're somewhat trope scenarios for zombie stories, but the pleasure's in the execution. Temple, thanks to some oddities of her upbringing, Temple's POV is a mix of high vocab words and less than high grammar, which is a hard note to hit without sounding disorganized, but Gaylord pulls it off. I think what I found most appealing was the tone; post-apocalypse stories tend towards protagonists that are either nihilistic or bent on rebuilding civilization. In contrast, Temple is... even just "resigned" is the wrong word. She's accepting that the world she lives in is unchangeable. And her certainty that the world is as she believes it is much more effective in creating a sense of melancholy than draping everything in bleakness. The plot is sort of a remix of familiar zombie things, but the way it unfolds makes the difference.

A zombie novel. A Western Gothic (not Southern Gothic) (okay, maybe a bit Southern Gothic) novel about a young women who is wandering a planet that is infested with the shambling, reanimated Dead. It has flavors of Faulkner and Flannery O'Conner, but didn't seem derivative.

Not only is it a gripping story, but the words are a pleasure to read, too.

Sample: "...it's a daily chore of tryin to do the right thing. Not because the right thing is hard to do -- it ain't. It's just cause the right thing -- well, the right thing's got a way of eluding you. You give me a compass that tells good from bad, and I'll be a soldier of the righteous truth. But them two things are a slippery business, and tellin them apart might as well be a blind man's guess."

Sample: "You Griersons are a touchy bunch. One minute it's biscuits and model ships and the next minute it's outrage and horror. Your family is livin at the poles when everyone else has gotta make do in the wide middle of things."

Sample: Some mercenaries who floundered without an economy to exploit, opportunists who, having gathered piles of cash, found themselves at a loss for anything to spend it on that couldn't be taken for free and with the world's permission. America having changed to benefit them, their accounts suddenly cleared, they reverted to the only actions that still seemed mercenary in this topsy-turvy landscape: they rode the countryside like desperadoes, helping people.

Sample: "It don't matter, she says. It just comes from thinkin too much. That's why you can't slow down for long. You gotta keep your brain tired out so it don't start searching for things to dwell on."

This is NOT a Young Adult novel, despite the fact that our protagonist is 15. Temple's only 15 chronologically but never had the 20ish years that most of us have as a childhood buffer before adult realities set in. Temple was born into a world irrevocably altered, were the remnants of humanity survive in tiny, fortified enclaves, and where the Dead shamble about mindlessly eating anyone slow enough to catch. Despite this, Temple is not hardened, bitter, or cynical. She's a realist, and a survivor, but also aware of everyday beauty, and retains her own humanity and empathy.

Really, really good.

Plus, you know, zombies.

I found this title on a list of "Best Adult Books for Teens" and began reading it to see if we could possibly use it as an independent novel choice for our honors freshman English classes. After about 30 pages I realized there was no way this would fly; I am pretty liberal and unfazed by things like sexuality, language, and violence, but even I was uncomfortable about putting this on an "Approved" list for 14 year olds. I don't believe in keeping things from kids, but there is just a lot of profoundly adult stuff going on in this novel, which is interesting considering the main character is only 15. I would suggest it to older students in a heartbeat, but it wouldn't work for my initial purposes.

However, I kept reading and truly enjoyed it. The story is haunting, the protagonist is damaged but likeable, and the style is masterful. In what we are made to believe is the not-too-distant future, American civilization has been overrun by "meatskins," as the main character, Temple, describes them - essentially, they are the classic horror-movie zombies, humans who have died and now walk the earth eating the living. For a zombie novel (which is absolutely NOT a favorite genre of mine,) there is a surprising amount of depth here.

Temple is on the run from something, both literal and figurative, and we follow her through a 3rd person limited narrator that creates miles of distance between the girl and the reader. Bell writes without the traditional quotation marks that denote conversation, and you become used to it quickly; in fact, I came to enjoy the way this stylistic choice added to the chasm between the myself and Temple. As a reader, I have never felt like more of an intruder on a character's lonely, isolated world; given the fact that Temple, too, feels isolated and disconnected from all of humanity (because of the meatskins, yes, but also because of the crimes she has committed) there is no doubt that this was intentional on the part of the author, and well-executed, too.

With an unexpected ending for which I applaud the author, I found myself quietly moved by this story of good and evil drawn in such an unconventional way. It blends style and beautiful language with a compelling plot, so if that's your thing, you'll most likely truly enjoy this novel.

Zombies, I'm willing to suspend my disbelief for. That the country still has gasoline, electricity, and working railway lines 25 years after the zombies appear, not so much. REALLY bugged me the whole time.
This is a road novel, and a good one, but the zombies are unnecessary to the plot and should have just been left out altogether. The story would have been equally powerful if it had been set in current times, no zombies or mutants in sight. That way when Temple pulls over and gasses up the car, or finds lots of canned food still on the shelves of well-lit convenience stores, I wouldn't have to roll my eyes.
Also-- Temple is supposed to be haunted by the blood she's spilled, but it's hard to "go there" with her and believe her emotions, because she's only killed one would-be rapist, zombies, and mutants, and it's hard to believe she'd feel guilty about that. As a reader I certainly felt nothing but empowered when she gets away from these creeps! Now if she'd killed a "real person," then I might buy into her sense of guilt and supposed need for personal redemption. But she doesn't, which makes it hard to truly identify with what the author wants to use as her motivation as a character.
One other thing-- many reviewers here have either LOVED or HATED the writing style. I found some brilliant passages that made me stop and say, "wow" and reread. I found some passages that made me think, as one reviewer mentions, that Bell (a pseudonym, by the way) just opened up a thesaurus and dropped words in so he could sound literary. This isn't really the problem, though; the problem is that there's no clear line between the narrator's voice and the character's voice, and so I find myself wondering how illiterate, uneducated Temple would know half the words she uses. In addition, the southern accents Bell employs should be reserved for the characters, and not used by the narrator, and the characters should have the same accent throughout the story. So these are some issues that should have been picked up on by the editor if not the author.
All that said, I still loved the book and would definitely recommend it--I know I haven't mentioned the good points here. It really is worth reading and full of great writing-- but be prepared to find yourself pulled out of the story by the above-mentioned inconsistencies.

Wow. Just wow. I am not worthily of this book. I did not know how good it really was until i was finished. The twist at the end was phenomenal!!
Alden Bell had me at the edge of my chair until page 225... which consequently is the end, and let's just say I've lost penalty of sleep staying up to read this book, and then trying to fall asleep after it-trying to get the vision of Temples Gurkha knife getting stuck inside a slugs head. I still have Millie's words "I'm gon kill you" on reply inside my head.
GOOD (there are plenty more)
a.) first of all I'll start off by saying how in love I am with Temple. She is by far the coolest, bravest, most kick-ass girl character that I have ever read. I love how she's just sixteen-and is still SO independence. There was no point in the story where she showed weakness.
b.) Thank you Alden Bell for writing it in third person. I had to five up on The Knife Of Never Letting go due to the sole fact that he narrated using words like: "ain't, "got", "gonna", ext. See I have no problem how Temple used those words- It just would've drove me up the wall if the narrator spoke in that improper language.

So if you up for anything but a light read, a book to keep you up all night previous days from finishing, a book to make you cry from the best/worst twist in the history of books... then you got a book right here.

I have to admit that the writing style threw me off a bit at first, with all those nonexistent quotation marks and everything. That being said, pretty much every other aspect of this story more than made up for the occasionally confusing speech patterns.

Temple is a perfectly well-written character, developed in a way that makes her easy to empathize with even when she's making objectively bad decisions. She's still a kid, after all, and she's doing the best she can to stay alive in a world that should have chewed her up and spit her back out by now. Despite everything that gets thrown at her, she pushes through, and somehow manages to do so without losing a single ounce of the spunk that characterizes her from the first time the reader hears her speak. I'll be completely honest and say that even though I had a feeling which way the ending was going to go, and I understand how it makes sense and fits in with the rest of the story, I was sincerely hoping for things to go in a different direction. I just really loved seeing the world through Temple's eyes.

The writing in this book is pretty great, too. I know some reviewers have said that the vocabulary is so extensive that it feels forced at times, but the way Bell describes his characters and their world felt very organic to me every step of the way. It felt like the reader was given living descriptions of living things, rather than being handed a 2-dimensional photo of a cactus and expected to bleed just from the image of the spines. The writing moved the story along in a very beautiful and enjoyable way, and was an excellent method of supporting the plot, which in my opinion is actually the weakest element of this novel. Not saying the plot is bad- far from it. But the characterization and writing are just so good that the actual plot seems to kind of pale in comparison to either one of them.

I loved this book, I would definitely recommend it, and I would definitely read it again. It's dark, it's intense, it's got a protagonist that the reader can honestly root for, and it's like the zombies are thrown in just as an added bonus. All the elements of this story combine very well for a really great reading experience. If you're still on the fence about whether or not to pick it up, let me give you a shove in the right direction- Do it.

Once a well trodden platform for political & environmental polemics from both earnest aspiring sci-fi authors and crotchety literary outcasts, over the last 2 decades, the post-apocalyptic genre has become completely saturated by chancers, ne'er do wells and genre hacks trying desperately to conjure up a facsimile of 'The Stand' or some zombie based scenario which can gain traction on the NYT bestseller list.

In contrast to the mass market hearse chasers there's the literary post-apocalypse sub-genre. Spear-headed by Cormac McCarthy and the most unlikely Oprah book of the month. These generally eschew genre convention and attempt to eke something worthy from well worn tropes - Emily St. John Mandel's 'Station Eleven', Jeff Vandermeer's Southern reach trilogy, 'After the Apocalypse' by Maureen F. McHugh, Richard E. Gropp's 'Bad Glass' - all spring to mind, though the most successful in recent memory must be Peter Heller's sublime 'Dog Stars'.

Heller has discussed in interviews how he wasn't entirely happy when he 'discovered' he was writing a genre novel as he (rightly) feared comparisons with McCarthy's book which he describes as a 'masterpiece of late 20th century literature'. Gaylord has no such compunctions. Citing Faulkner as a major influence, readers will nonetheless highlight the subject matter, sparse dialogue, lack of punctuation and semi-baroque descriptions of the natural world as evidence rather of McCarthy's more recent forays into the bleak. In fact, despite an admirably original, (if sparsely sketched) lead character, a healthy disregard for the undead threat (or 'slugs') as a driver of narrative and some sporadically inspired passages of prose, McCarthy's influence is so strong as to push us almost into pastiche territory, especially when combined with continuity errors which prick the realism of this world. This is even more evident in the sequel, which is essentially a post-apocalyptic Blood Meridian.

That said, this man can write. There is more meat & gristle & blood & shit in this short volume than in 100,000 words of mainstream post-apoclyptica, and if you're going to pastiche someone, it may as well be one of the most talented authors on the planet. Given a bit more time to develop his own voice, better editing and a loosening of the noose of influence, he's heading for the big things.

31/2 stars

The Reapers Are the Angels has some good stuff going for it: there’s a strong female lead (even if she is a bit of a [scruffy, angry] manic pixie dream girl); the zombies are just one part of the long cross-country journey; and the prose is full of pretty, literary phrases like

“you can’t put nothing past these southern boys. They just sit around waiting for somebody to kill their brother so they can get started on some vengeance. It’s like a dang vocation with them.”

The first chapter could survive alone as a short story.

However. I hated the author’s use of a nonverbal, disabled character as a plot device. This character, Maury, only exists a) to be the connecting factor between Temple and the man she’s trying to escape, and b) to make the audience like Temple even more because she takes care of this “dummy.” (He is also referred to as a “feeb” by the unlikable Albert in chapter 8, when Temple-- in comparison-- finally starts making a habit of using Maury’s name, instead of just referring to him as dummy.)  

Maury is an important character to the story, but the author doesn’t actually bother to write him into it. He’s a passive character, and things happen to him/people speak to him, but we never see him do anything or get past his “slow, heavy-lidded eyes”/"sad, thick eyes”/"dense, flat eyes” to his perspective, experiences, or desires. Author Alden Bell seems to enjoy pointing out Maury’s uselessness to Temple, and over-describes Maury’s body in every passage he’s in. He writes that Maury is a “big slobbery mess” who, in one passage, chews on nothing but his jaws “move in small slow circles like the jaw of a cow.” He makes sounds “inarticulate, like a mewling baby” or a “long wail, absent of meaning.” (It’s worth noting that his wail ‘absent of meaning’ occurs when Temple stops the car to yell out the window at a giant figure “human but disfigured, part of the skull exposed, one eye crazy wide and the other sleepy lidded, a pallor the color of moss or rot” in the hopes of drawing the figure out of the bush so she can get a better look.)

I could quote more but I’m annoyed and you get the picture. This book may be full of pretty little southern gothic phrases, but it’s no good to me.

I love zombie books, and this one grabbed me right away. I couldn't put it down, and really liked the main character Temple. Even though she was a cold-blooded killer when she had to be, she could also be a sweet fifteen-year-old girl, and a grown woman. Whatever the situation called for, she could handle it. And I loved that about her.

Temple is a young girl who starts out alone in a zombie-infested wasteland. The undead have been walking the streets for years, and she was actually born into this shitty world. So she's tough, knows how to survive and depends on her trusty gurkha knife. She also has no problem destroying zombies when she has to, and leaves them when they're not in her way.

She survives better on her own. But when she meets a pack of men who take her to some sheltered buildings, she captures the eye of one particular pervert. One she's forced to kill or be killed. Which begins the chase. Because now his brother is hunting her down and won't stop until he kills her.

Along the way she meets some really strange people. Ranging from a bunch of friendly hunters, a family that lives safely inside the comforts of their home, a pack of inbred, deformed psychos, a train that actually works, and a mute man called Maury. Which she actually goes out of her way to help.

As I mentioned above, I really enjoyed this book. It was a great story filled with a vivid and ugly future where the dead are still roaming the streets and the living are pretty much nuts and desperate. Still, Temple survives above all that and even though she's pretty rough around the edges, she also has a kind heart and I wanted to see her survive. Which is why I didn't like the way her life ends.

I think it's always risky to kill off the main character in a novel--it can work, especially in short stories--and this is one of those books where it didn't pay off. IMO, having Temple killed in such an easy manner didn't fit her struggle. And having someone else carry her story after her death didn't make up for it, either.

I was very disappointed with the ending of this book. After all the time I invested in Temple, I should've been saddened by her death not angry. I felt like her death wasn't justified.

It's such a shame because I was loving this book... :(

There are hundreds possibly thousands of post apocalyptic novels. The best I’ve read, McCammon’s “Swan Song,” King’s, “the Stand” and Cronin’s, “the Passage,” all deal with worlds that have been ravaged by something and focus on the human element of survival.

It is very hard to find a decent zombie novel though. Some of Brian Keene’s efforts have been enjoyable and Max Brooks does an interesting take on the genre but I have yet to find a zombie novel that I’ve really enjoyed....Until now.

The Reapers are the Angels is set roughly 25 years after the dead started returning to not so dead. The book focuses on Temple a young girl roughly 15 years old but with the experience of one who is much older.

Temple knows what it takes to survive. At the first sign of trouble she moves on. She has no emotional ties, just takes what she needs and goes. The story follows her progress across America. The people she encounters and the incidents she endures. Each of these episodes are intriguing and well portrayed. Whether it be communities in denial of the world around them, or mad mutants who feel they are superior you get the sense of desperation and loneliness of Temple’s plight.

Running alongside this survival, a carefully revealed back story is revealed that hints of a past family where Temple was happy.

Temple herself is a great character. She is hard and cuts herself off from getting close to other humans but at the same time displays a good sense of loyalty and at times subtle tenderness. It keeps her character fresh and the reader interested.

If surviving the zombies (slugs) wasn’t enough. Temple is also constantly looking over a man determined to kill her. It is this relationship that is the strongest part of the novel. Despite their hatred for each other, the two begin to recognise that they understand each other better then anyone else they have come across. The dynamic is interesting and plausible and concludes in excellent fashion.

Overall this is the first zombie book that I can say is really good. Others have been enjoyable but Alden Bell has struck the correct balance between portraying the horror or the situation and concentrating on the human elements of the story.

My rating: 8.8

It is a bleak and desolate world, with pockets of humanity scattered around the country. The world is inhabited by both humans and zombies (referred to in the book as "meatskins" or "slugs"), although these zombies really aren't quite as terrifying as in most zombie stories. They're sorta slow and meandering, and relatively easy to defeat. I'm really surprised at how many people get killed or attacked by them and how feared they are, all things considered!

In this desolate world, it is the humans that are far more dangerous than the zombie population. And alone in this world is a young, tenacious fifteen-year-old girl, being chased by her own demons.

I love Temple. She's haunting, but strong and courageous and smart and sympathetic. There is really something of a kinship between her and the character of Moses Todd. They really "get" one another. It's as if they are playing by the same rules in the same game, while everyone else in the world is playing by a different set of rules. The two of them are the reapers in a world of saints and sinners , and Temple is a little uncomfortable with her role in this world.

I also love the cover of this book! It transfixes me everytime my eyes fall on it.

Oh, please someone make this into a movie! What a fun movie this could be! I can see the scenes playing out in my head. However I also have a bit of an alternate ending playing out in my head as well.

There is definitely some "suspension of disbelief" required, beyond that required for a basic zombie/post-apocalyptic story. For instance, the fact that this is supposed to be something like 25 years after zombies appeared on the scene and the breakdown of government and society and life as it was known, and yet there is still gas available in working gas stations, and the gas hasn't gone bad after sitting for decades. Shoot! The gas can go bad in a weed-eater or lawn mower after just sitting for one season!

I really enjoyed this story! If you like post-apocalyptic, give this one a tumble. It's a quick and easy read, very well-written, with some fun, rip-roaring moments. I look forward to more from Alden Bell!

I figure if you can 'suspend belief' enough to go with the premise that the world is overrun by zombies, everything else in this book should be within your reach to accept as plausible.

The young female protagonist had me thinking initially I'd somehow ended up with a YA title.

I assure you, this is most-certainly not a book for young adults, in that sense. Definitely it belongs to the horror set more than anything.

Temple, the aforementioned protagonist, is a very likable character. Actually, most of the characters have some attractive qualities to them. The only thing is that the dialog rings really false for me, almost as if the author was scripting a melo-dramatic film (actually, there is a bit of a film-quality to the way this was written), rather than attempting realistic discourse between people. Then again, in the world created by this book, who knows how people would talk.

Like I said, once you accept the premise, you may as well just go with it all.

And, go with it all I did. I really enjoyed travelling along with Temple running from her demons and, potentially, a dude who wants to kill her. For all the gore and misery in the world portrayed, there are actually some sweet moments that aren't so cloying you'll roll your eyes or anything.

Also, small point here, I liked that the story was set in the wasteland left when zombies have destroyed civilization. Seems to me like zombie stories are always set in the time when they are just becoming an issue and people are evading them. In this sense, Bell took a much more interesting tack for me, just because I'm not used to thinking of that angle of the whole zombie mystique.

Oh, but there is some gore. Oh my...and I couldn't quite get my head around some other creatures who pop up along the way. Something about the way they're described didn't sort it for me.

Still, pretty solid book with some nice language. Wouldn't kill Bell, I don't assume, to use some more punctuation, but I guess that's a decision you make and roll with it, innit?

Read it. It's short. You can close your eyes in the few spots where it gets pretty bloody. I assure you you'll like Temple, at the very least.

It took me a few chapters to settle into The Reapers are the Angels because of the writing style. There are no quotation marks for dialogue, which made it sometimes confusing to know when someone started speaking. However, Temple, our main character, has a very distinctive, Southern voice, so she was relatively easy to pick out but not as clear on her meaning. I found it very hard to relate to her and to care about what happened to her. I was more intrigued by the world than I was in her, but it was enough to keep me reading.

I'm not sure how things got to where they are, but the world (at least the US from what we witness) is overrun with zombies aka meatskins aka slugs. Temple has been living on a small island for a few years, but at the beginning of the novel she realizes it's time to go. She ends up at a relatively safe place, a community of people held up in office buildings, but she makes enemies with the wrong man and is forced to leave. From that point on she's on the run, since that man, Moses Todd, is out to get her. During her journey she meets up with some very interesting characters and even picks up a traveling companion. Moses is never far behind though.

Even though Temple is on the run, I never felt a sense of urgency. The narrative was very detached and it seemed as though Temple didn't even care that a man who wants her dead is following her across the country. It was almost like the events were happening separate from her rather than to her, another reason why I just didn't care where she ends up.

There are some very disturbing scenes throughout the book and there is a lot of gore. Temple is good with a knife and takes down many meatskins, and a few...I'm not even sure what they are, mutant humans, I suppose. We're not spared any of the carnage. I kept reading in hopes of learning more about how the zombies got there, but we're basically told it's been that way all of Temple's life, and that's that. Overall, this book just was not for me.
