A friend lent this book to me; I have been aware of it for years now, always meaning to buy it and always ending up reading something else instead. I have to say, this book was not what I expected at all.

I originally found it searching for books similar to The Passage, which I had just finished and was waiting for the second book to be released. Although set in post-apocalypse America - some 20 years or so after the initial disaster - with zombies roaming the wilds, they are not really much of a problem. Certainly they are dangerous in the traditional zombie sense, but they are slow and dumb. After two decades of sharing the continent with them, the majority of humanity has simply adapted to their presence as they would any other wild animal. In particular the main character Temple, who was born in to this world and has known nothing else, bears no real fear or hatred towards them - they are the way they are, as God made them, she believes.

This book is not really a survival thriller at heart. Although Temple certainly has a few close calls in her travels, this is not really a story about finding a safe haven from the zombie threat. Temple travels the continent quite freely in fact, wondering at God's marvels and pondering on the meanings of good and evil, right and wrong. The main 'enemy' comes in the form of Moses Todd. After an unfortunate series of events, Moses has decided that killing her is the only thing that makes sense anymore - it is this constant fear of being hunted that plagues Temple as she travels on her own mission.

As I said though, this tale is more of an exploration of the human condition than a survival thriller. In between the fights for survival are beautiful descriptions of landscapes and emotion, and almost philosophical thinking in a way that only a wide-eyed 16 year old child that has seen and been through too much can achieve. I think it will appeal to fans of the general genres of zombies, post-apocalyptic landscapes, The Walking Dead, Fallout, etc, who are looking for the things that make those genres great - but also have a more deeper and emotional side to them.

This is a great read for those looking for zombie/horror-themed fiction that is both beautifully written and completely unique, and yes, truly terrifying. Having just finished "The Forest of Hands and Teeth", I found it interesting to compare this novel's young female protagonist, Temple, against that in the other book ("Mary"). Temple is truly a protagonist unlike I've come across before: super street smart, tough as nails, crafty, funny, kind, and unflinching in her protection of herself and those she cares about. "Mary" on the other hand alternates between MacGuyver-smarts and being too obsessed with her own romantic relationships. In a battle between the two, Temple would certainly win (though "The Forest of Hands and Teeth" is a good read too!)

"The Reapers are the Angels" follows Temple while she navigates the wasteland the United States has become since the "meat skins" or "slugs" have taken over (honestly, I forget what the inciting incident was, but it doesn't matter in this book which starts many years after the fall of civilization). She's tough and in charge of her own life, but has a lot of questions about the world -- does killing to survive make her evil? Is there a god if this is what his aim is?

The book takes Temple on the road while she travels around trying to survive both zombies and a man named Moses who is hell bent on retribution (as well as other ne-er do wells, etc.). Through her journey, we meet a whole assortment of characters, one of which, Maury, gives her a final destination to travel to but the route is paved with many unexpected twists and turns, both physical and metaphorical.

I agree with other reviewers who were a bit disappointed in the ending, as I could see several ways it could've panned it. I think the author chose correctly though, and the powerful ending of this book seems to match the idea of bleak eventuality that comes with all post-apocalyptic novels.

The epigraph at the beginning of the book says (with kudos to "Pet Sematary"): "Sometimes dead is better." It's up to you after you read this book to decide in this context if that's true or not.

Where to begin with this? I'll only start by saying this is one of the greatest pieces of zombie fiction ever written. As I've read a lot of that stuff, I would know. Is it better than The Walking Dead? Actually, yes it is. Much better. Is it better than Pride and Prejudice and Zombies? Oh, definitely. Is it better than World War Z? Maybe. I'm letting it sink in. It's certainly at least as good as World War Z. What this novel represents is a fusion of literary fiction and zombie fiction. It is truly post-apocalyptic more than it is mundane zombie horror.

The Reapers Are the Angels follows a 15 year old girl named Temple who has never known anything but a world overrun with the dead. She is illiterate, drinks a lot of whiskey, has questionable grammar and a coarse diction as she provides the gruff point of view for the novel that is sort of sophisticated in its crudeness, and is a complete killing machine. Temple backstory is a tragic one, unfurling slowly through her memories as the reader follows her journey across the entire southern united states. She encounters a variety of different human settlements (and even more inhuman ones). What is startling about the Reapers Are the Angels is not the zombie action or realism, though that is there in spades.

What is startling about The Reapers Are the Angels is the sheer poetic beauty of its language. Temple manages to find amazing things about the sites she sees in the overrun world in its rusty museums, abandoned towns and cities, even in glittering fish swimming in a river in the moonlight. Despite the violent brutality all around her, Temple's perspective is skewed and jaded but still maintains a sense of wonder at so many things. All the characters are well-sketched, even some that only occupy a few pages as Temple runs across struggling settlements and other wanderers such as herself out to explore the wasteland they inhabit. This approach keeps Reapers visceral and lyrical all at once, unique in a book about zombies.

What is it with English teachers making the transition to writing tales of horror? It must have something to do with seeing the darker sides of humanity as exhibited daily by children in classrooms across the world. Swelling the ranks of the likes of Justin Cronin (author of The Passage) is American High School English teacher Alden Bell and his debut novel, The Reapers are the Angels, a horror tale set in a post-apocalyptic America, plagued by zombies and beset on all sides by the more chilling side of human nature.

I think it is clear that this novel is not primarily about the undead menace that lurks around every corner but more about the survivors and how they are coping with the situation, with the primary focal point being that of Temple, a fifteen year old girl born into the torn world that Bell has so ably created.

Stylistically, Bell writes very much like Cormac McCarthy and the imagery is similar to that found in The Road. The tone is dark and bleak; and Bell himself has described The Reapers are the Angels as being more Southern Gothic than a tale of a zombie apocalypse. The zombie plague provides the backdrop to the narrative but it's Temple's flight from her pursuer that drives the story on and for me, evoked memories of Frankenstein and the Doctor's pursuit of his creation.

As I'm sure you can guess from the title, there is much discussion of religion and God throughout the novel and Temple's moral compass is very much tested throughout the book. Temple sees the beauty in much of the world that remains and believes this is all a part of God's plan and her background of having never known a world without "meatskins" (zombies) gives her an interesting perspective and makes her quite a compelling protagonist; her attitudes towards society and other humans gives the novel further depth.

In short, The Reapers are the Angels is a real surprise. Bell manages to pack an awful lot into just under 300 pages and succeeds where so many horror stories fail and has created a compelling character-driven horror tale.

I don't usually write reviews immediately after finishing a book or make a habit of writing them at 12:30 at night from my bed (thank you, Goodreads app), but I don't feel like waiting on this one.

First, let me say that I did *not* see that ending coming. I'll keep this spoiler free and not say more, but color me surprised.

This one's going on my favorites list, I think. Definitely my 'to ponder more' and 'to read again someday' lists.

It's a post apocalyptic book and a zombie book about a 15 year old girl on a journey across America a quarter century after the dead began to rise. She's running from a man hell bent on killing her and also maybe a man more like her than anyone she's known. It makes for an interesting conflict to say the least. And like most good books, it's not really about the zombies or the wasteland that America has become so much as just about the people in the story. Because as Temple herself asks, born after the 'apocalypse' as she was, what's really changed? Happiness & sadness look roughly the same whether you're being bitten by pesky mosquitoes or zombies (I'm paraphrasing here).

The fact that there was no punctuation for dialog took a bit of getting used to but not too much. For an illiterate teen Temple often thought and used pretty advanced vocabulary, but it works somehow. Maybe because she's advanced beyond her years or because her dialog and thoughts blend with the narrative because of that lack of punctuation. Regardless, the writing style worked for me.

I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys post-apocalyptic stories, or zombie stories or even literary stories. Maybe to those who were less than blown away by Zone One. This book does what I think that one was trying to do only better.

I'm really looking forward to the November (UK) release of the sequel though I have *no* idea what it will be about. Nothing was left hanging here. It's a totally self contained book. And that actually makes me even more curious about what might happen next ...

Review: Temple is simply trying to survive in this world where zombies, slugs, whatever you want to call them, roam. She wanders from place to place, meeting people then moving on. We find her coming in to a small community. After one of the men there tries to rape her, Temple kills him and runs from his brother, Moses. Further on in her travels, she picks up Maury, a man she must take care of, and plans to help him get back to his family. They carry on travelling, running, from a man who wants revenge.
I like the fact that the zombies weren’t the focus of The Reapers are the Angels. Instead, they’re the world builders, providing a reason for Temple to keep moving and the occasional big action sequence.
Here, the horror comes from the characters. Abraham, who thinks he’s entitled to have the new young girl have sex with him. The mutants. Even Temple, in the way that she detaches herself so easily.
I like the range of characters. There’s people who remember times before the undead started rising and there’s people who don’t know anything else. Everyone deals with the undead in different ways.
I couldn’t really connect with Temple, despite being given access to her thoughts and method of thinking.
The events in this book seem quite disjointed. Once we met a character, for the most, we don’t see them again. This is perfectly in keeping with Temple’s lifestyle, but as a reader, I didn’t really enjoy it.
It’s all written in third person, closely following Temple and her decisions. There’s simple punctuation, and a distinct lack of speech marks. This and Temple’s strong accent do well in showing her upbringing and lack of education. I did miss the speech marks. A lot.
The relationship between Moses and Temple is the most interesting one in the novel. There’s the whole wanting to kill each other, but when their meetings become more and more frequent, they start to understand each other, understand their difference, and similarities.


Overall: Strength 3 tea to a character driven post-apocalyptic novel.

Temple has been on her own for a long, long time. She's been living on an island lately, but the season is changing and it's only a matter of time before the will have to move on. The zombies will come. So Temple takes off. She starts off attempting to stay with an established community, but accidentally kills a man in the process of defending herself from his advances. She is then forced to flee before the other men retaliate. Temple decides it's better to move on her own. She picks up a companion, a man with special needs that she finds and feels compelled to help care for. Together, they embark upon a journey that takes them across the American South. They'll meet a variety of other people and groups who have all adapted (or not adapted, as the case may be) to this post-apocalyptic and unforgiving landscape. All the while, the brother of the man killed by Temple is determined to track her down to exact his version of justice.
This book was amazing, particularly for a zombie novel. I've read a fair amount of zombie-related fiction, but nothing has ever had quite the same emotional impact that this book had. Of course, it's really not so much about the zombies in the first place. It's definitely Temple's story. Temple is tough, street-smart and has the soul of a poet. The book opens on a moment that captivates Temple and fills her with a sense of wonder. Moments later, she's smashing in the head of a zombie with a large rock. She's compassionate to an extent, but survival is her primary motivation. And then there's the fact that this book starts years after the zombie infection has taken hold. Temple doesn't know who her parents were, she's never seen the inside of a school. She doesn't know how to read. She does, however, know how to survive. There's also a running theme of religious imagery that is both poetic and thought provoking, particularly since it shares space with a setting that seems almost entirely devoid of happiness and hope. Highly recommended.

This wasn't just a novel on the zombie apocalypse, or an allegory. It was a picture painted with words. Beautiful writing that goes beyond the usual blood and gore that comes with zombies.

By all means, there was gore., but it was not what made the novel. This book left a lot to think about, especially in regards to faith and what truly defines evil.

Vom Schreibstil war ich sehr enttäuscht. Er wirkt distanziert, wie abgehackt. Wörtliche Rede ist nicht gekennzeichnet. Alles fügt sich wie ein Bericht zusammen. Wenn mich die Geschichte hinter Temple nicht so interessiert hätte, wäre das Buch wohl ein Abbruchkandidat gewesen. Aber durchhalten hat sich für mich gelohnt. Stellenweise gab es im Laufe des Romans sogar schöne Sätze, die mich wirklich erreichten. Auch das Ende hat mich berührt.

Die junge Temple wird in eine Welt hineingeboren, in der Menschen der Minderheit angehören. Unsere Erde ist zerstört und jeder kämpft ums Überleben. Zombies spielen hier eine große Rolle, Temple nennt sie Schaben oder Fleischsäcke. Die Hintergründe der postapokalyptischen Szenerie bleiben unklar. Der ganze Roman ist eher eine Pilgerreise durch eine Mutantenwelt. Temple wirkt dabei sehr erwachsen, selbstbewusst und kampferprobt. Sie schreckt vor nichts zurück, weil sie sich das nicht erlauben kann. Für schwache Nerven ist der Roman nichts, wer aber ein wenig Splatter mag, ist gut aufgehoben. Für mich passte das zur Geschichte und es war dosiert, nicht übertrieben.

Manche Details darf man nicht hinterfragen. Erstens wird man keine Antworten bekommen und zweitens merkt wohl jeder Leser schnell, dass sie absolut unrealistisch und die Elemente nur der Effekte wegen vorhanden sind. Mühelose Autofahrten durch halb Amerika, Tankstellen mit Benzin auf dem Weg, verlassene Läden mit gut sortierten Warensortimenten ... und das geschätzte 20 Jahre nach einer Katastrophe ... *hust*

In der Beschreibung vorn im Buch wirft Heyne Alden Bell mit Justin Cronin und Cormac McCarthy in einen Topf. Ein absolutes Unding. Ich gebe zu, die Geschichte hat mich gefesselt, aber der Roman ist eher Trivialliteratur unter den Dystopien. Bell wird jedoch auch seine Anhänger finden, keine Frage.

Für Unterhaltung ohne Nachdenken: 4 Sterne, im Vergleich mit Cronin & Co: 1 Stern

The Reapers Are the Angels is a stunning horror novel, part Southern Gothic and part Western—Flannery O’Connor meets Cormac McCarthy. Although it is set amidst the zombie apocalypse, the zombies are merely the background against which larger issues such as balancing compassion and survival, finding morality in an amoral world, and defining humanness are examined.

The setting is a brutal, bleak America where anarchy and violence reign and through which the main character navigates a physical and metaphorical journey. The rough dialogue and gritty, visceral prose are streaked through with lovely poetic descriptions and philosophical ruminations.

She remembers again the Miracle of the Fish—the silver-gold bodies darting in circles around her ankles as though she were standing in the middle of another moon—the way things could be perfect like that on occasion—a clear god, a god of messages and raptures—a moment when you knew what you were given a stomach for, for it to feel that way, all tense with magic meaning.
It has become something to her, that memory—something she can take out in dismal times and stare into like a crystal ball disclosing not presages but reminders. She holds it in her palm like a captured ladybug and thinks, Well ain’t I been some places, ain’t I partook in some glorious happenings wanderin my way between heaven and earth. And if I ain’t seen everything there is to see, it wasn’t for lack of lookin.
Blind is the real dead.

The writing is evocative and haunting, but the real strength of the novel is the anti-heroine, Temple. She will make you laugh and break your heart with her fearless self-sufficiency, her innocent wonder for the beauty of the world, and her tormented sense of guilt. The Reapers is the story of Temple’s search for belonging and redemption. It is about finding simple beauty and meaning in a world full of conflict and chaos.

The Reapers are the Angels changed a part of me. I have no idea why I picked it up in the first place, I think I was piqued by the title. It is about a 15-year-old girl's journey across a zombie infested post-apocalyptic land. Doesn't sound interesting? I admit, I never cared much for zombies or even read a book with zombies featuring prominently in it. If I had known this would be one such, I would have passed. Thank goodness I did not because it turned out to become my favorite book. It's surprising really because it has none of the elements I usually enjoy (require!). Romance? Not hardly. Happy ending? Let's just say I bawled my eyes out.

Temple, our young protagonist, is not a teenager in a young adult novel. She has seen much, done much and still LIVES much. That is what I loved about her. Her story is not one of zombies and a ruined world-- it is about the human spirit, finding beauty wherever you can and being in the present world. I was moved by Temple's unwavering connection to the earth around her and her need to be free to move along its surface, seeing all there was to see.

The Reapers are the Angels is not a horror novel nor is it typical science fiction. It stands on its own. I can't even describe how deeply the words and descriptions pull at you. At its conclusion, I was dazed, emotionally wrung out-- and I wanted to read it again! From the last chapter backwards. It also reignited the burning desire within me to see all the wondrous corners of our world. Before reading the book, I had been wanting to travel for a while, but kept pushing that dream back to a later time. Afterwards, I solidified plans and finally set things in motion. A few months later, I quit my job, bought myself a one-way plane ticket to explore other countries and hike along the most amazing landscapes. Perhaps you will too, once you've known Temple and her way of living fiercely, unfettered by fear.

I'm conflicted about how I feel. On one hand, Alden Bell has a very poetic form of prose and his characters dance from scene to scene in the best circumstances. He omits quotation marks and blends dialogue with action in a way that at times feels very fluid and seamless. It has hiccups, particularly near the end, but for a long while he had a righteous groove pushin' his story forward.

On the other hand, the world building leaves a lot to be desired. He needs to sell it to the audience, which in my opinion he completely failed to do.

Alden Bell takes a pretty standard setting for zombies-- contemporary America-- and adjusts it ever so slightly to give it some...I don't know what. He turns the dial twenty-five years into the future, but he doesn't actually utilize all that gives him. He doesn't sell it.

Sell it: Give the audience a reason to believe that convenience stores still have Coke and cheese crackers, that cars run mostly fine, that roads are clear enough to drive on, and that the occasional power grid is still operational all in sunny storm-prone Florida and Texas. Some of that is easily verified-- you can look on YouTube to see that, yes, twenty or thirty year old Coca-Cola is still drinkable, albeit flat. You can look on the streets now and see thirty year old cars clanking along. But a lot of the other stuff... it needs work. Work in tying it into the time frame. A near apocalypse would've been a much more believable setting than an apocalypse +25 based on all of the information given.

I'm not exactly sure where I stand. It was fun to read, but at times I had to brush aside my questions and just "accept" things, which in my opinion, isn't a great thing to have in writing. If you like zombies, and adventure novels with female protagonists, this is probably worth a read-- as long as you don't question the author too much about his timeline, or can ignore it altogether.

This books marks one of the few 4+ star reviews I find myself giving each year, and as such it deserves a commentary to correspond with my review. The concept of the novel is nothing unique or original (humans surviving in a post-apocalyptic zombie wasteland), but nonetheless I found the prose of Bell's work to be unique and at times poetic. As a result Bell's take on an otherwise tired genre stands above most of the rest. A synopsis of the book reads like a YA novel, but I believe this to be more a work of adult fiction. It's hard to describe why with any clear logic, but the main reasoning for me was that the main character (a 15-16 year-old girl), didn't fall prey to the tropes of most YA novels (i.e. pining, love triangles, cringe-worthy internal monologues, over-valued sense of self-importance, dependency on the males in their peripheral social circle, etc.). Of course there are many YA novels with heroines that don't fall prey to the aforementioned stereotypes, but in my opinion this novel did not read like a YA novel (it's just something you feel while reading I suppose).
The novel isn't perfect of course, and no book needs to be in order to receive a 5-star review (and I would have loved to have given it one), but there were a few minor issues that I felt could have been addressed with some basic editing. No spoilers will be given here, but I can say that if civilization ended 25 years ago, the gas in the gas station tanks would have spoiled (or been depleted) after the first few years; apparently there is an abundance to be had to keep cars driving on the road. Furthermore (and I'll be vague here to avoid spoiling anything), Moses' means of tracking Temple would not in any way have been possible 25 years after civilization ended. And it is because of these simple oversights that I couldn't in good conscience give the book a perfect review. Nonetheless, it's still a fantastic read and makes the top 3 of my favourite zombie novels.
Actual rating: 3.5
Actually great. All star cast. Brutal.

This is a post-apocalyptic zombie novel that is unequivocally influenced by William Faulkner, from its style to its themes to some plot points and the names of its two main characters, not to mention most of the bit parts. When I noticed the names Temple and Maury in the review, I knew the author was up to something. I might go so far as to call it a mash-up, IF there weren't so many of those floating around after a certain zombie mash-up became a bestseller. And I'd argue that it's better than all of them.

Temple is a great character, and there is a long journey to deliver a body -- in this case a living one -- through a landscape of walking dead, to a family that may or may not still be there. She grapples with her identity, with her baser instincts, with her perceptions of God and duty and right and wrong in a broken world. History is a living, swirling thing, and "The past is never dead. It's not even past." In fact, it's still walking around. Aldon Bell also channels Faulkner when he describes so lyrically the bits of beauty that are always ensconced in decay, and the broad sweeping descriptions of the horizon and the road and the land.

"She raises her gaze and her eyes blur teary in the cool wind and all the lights of the city go wild and multiple, and she wipes her eyes and sits in one of the chairs and looks out beyond the periphery of the power grid where the black rolls out like an ocean."

Despite the fact that it borders on derivative much of the time, I found this book to be enjoyable, thought-provoking, smart, and occasionally really beautiful. I would have never thought that I'd read a zombie novel, but look at that, the pigs are flying.

It felt pretty episodic, which is neither here nor there. And I didn't like the last two sentences. But oh well. It is totally worth reading.

Make a note, Carrie Ryan. This is how you write a zombie novel.

Actually, in all seriousness, I can't call myself an expert on zombie anything. I'm a chicken about scary movies. I've only seen the re-make of Dawn of the Dead once. I read Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (thought it was pretty funny). So, I guess I can't really say I know what makes stellar zombie fiction. But what I feel more qualified to talk about is good writing, and knowing it when I see it. That brings me to this book.

So often, it seems like teen novels are just a means to an end. "Oooh, I've got an idea about a clique of really pretty, rich girls; kids will eat that up", or "How can I hop on this whole vampire cash wagon?". The writing is barely capable, the plot lines are irritating, and the story only really delivers the bare minimum, the most obvious cliche. Not so with this one. (Note: my library has this cataloged under Teen Fiction, but almost every other area library has it under regular fiction. I myself first heard about it as a YA novel, so that's how I'm considering it.)

The writing is stark, the emotions surprising. The re-imagined American south is familiar and terrifyingly new all at once. The invention here is terrific, I guess is what I'm saying. But most of all, the writing is excellent. The sentences don't "leak"-- you really understand what Bell is trying to describe because of how well constructed they are. The characters aren't annoying. The story is honestly heart-breaking. Have you noticed how often reviews use the word "heart-breaking" these days? Often enough to render the phrase meaningless. But believe me about this one: it really is a story that will give you that sad little pull at your heart.

Well done, Alden Bell. This is a beauty.

A cross between The Road, The Stand and the recent slew of zombie-apocalypse books.
I loved The Reapers Are the Angels.
It's another book (like Feed) that has the library's little "horror" sticker on it's spine - but was actually so.much.more.
Temple is 15 and alone, traveling the post apocalyptic country in the Florida area. Her view of the world (and the zombies who now make up the majority of the population) is intensely pragmatic...and oddly hopeful. Temple sees beauty all around her. She was born into this new, torn down world, and she doesn't see it as horrible or terrifying - she just sees it as reality. And there are still little miracles everywhere.
Honestly - I never knew a book about zombies could impart so much hope to the reader, but this one did. Even when Temple is running for her life and calling her companion "dummy", The Reapers Are the Angels managed to be beautiful and inspiring.

Speaking of Maury...
I found his character to be a super effective way of getting to know Temple better. Very well done.

Bell's writing was reminiscent of Cormac McCarthy's - but reads as more authentic, less egotistical. When McCarthy shoves made-up words down your throat, Bell sticks to the sparse storytelling and uses words that you can actually find in the dictionary.
"Bell" is actually a pseudonym, of course. I loved this book enough, however, to check out his other novel Hummingbirds: A Novel, and I will be looking forward to another Alden Bell installment.

This was a really solid, gritty, apocalyptic zombie novel. If you're into the traditional, serious horror version of this subject you'll love this book. The characters are very unique but realistic and the plot is straightforward but has a desolate beauty. The scene with smacks a little too heavily of 28 days later, but everything else was surprisingly original. I was particularly impressed by the horrific imagining of .

Pace:unhurried. The pace is slowed by the descriptiveness and the lack of quotation marks. It gave the whole story a dreamlike feeling of being in the main character's head. Luckily there are still paragraph breaks or I'd probably lose my mind.
Characterization: well-developed, realistic, distant, introspective. I really liked the character of Temple. She was strong but had a depth of emotion and appreciation for beauty that she didn't quite realize. I wasn't entirely convinced by her supposed fear of her own rage, however. Moses was also interesting, driven both to kill Temple and admire her. While I enjoyed the strange mutual animosity and respect they had for each other, I didn't quit understand why Moses couldn't just let go of his brother's death.
Story-Line: explicit violence, open-ended, character-centered, thought provoking
Frame: futuristic, post apocalyptic
Tone: bleak, menacing, gritty
Writing Style:direct, polished

Red Flags: graphic violence, sex, language

Read Alikes: I've seen many zombie movies that are similar to this story but I'm just beginning my foray into zombie lit. I'll probably come back to this in a few months.

Quand on commence la lecture, on rejoint Temple sur son île avec un phare. Elle s’émerveille de voir des poissons lumineux dans l’eau et prend conscience que le monde a sans doute d’autres merveilles à lui montrer. Mais voilà qu’on se rend compte que le monde de Temple n’est pas si beau qu’on pourrait le croire, car il est peuplé de zombies (appelés “limaces” ou “sacs à viande”).

On accompagne donc Temple à travers ses voyages. Elle rencontre d’autres personnes, qui ont réussi à se protéger du fléau. Ils sont gentils/méfiants/méchants/évolués, ils veulent ou ne veulent pas regarder le monde tel qu’il est devenu.

Les points positifs de ce livre sont qu’on se laisse balader par Temple. On découvre, par ses yeux, ce que sont devenus les Etats-Unis après le début d’un fléau dont on ne sait finalement rien. Et on ne saura jamais comment ça s’est produit. Mais on connaîtra Temple jusqu’au bout des ongles. Cette petite héroïne a beaucoup de peps… et elle a beaucoup d’humanité en elle.

Sur sa route, elle croisera un certain Moïse Todd, qui voudra la tuer à de nombreuses reprises. Elle rencontrera aussi Maury, un benêt dont elle s’occupera, prouvant ainsi qu’elle reste humaine, même si elle dit le contraire.

Ce que j’ai trouvé de négatif ? Les scènes sont parfois très crues. Mais c’est aussi ce qui fait le charme du livre. Par contre, j’aurai aimé en savoir plus sur le fléau qui a fait revenir les morts parmi les vivants. Rien n’est dit à ce propos, car dans l’histoire, on est projeté 15 ans après le début du fléau. Temple n’a d’ailleurs connu que ce monde-là, pas celui d’avant. Mais elle continue à le voir, avec des yeux d’enfants parfois.

En résumé, je vous conseille vivement la lecture de ce petit bijou. “Les faucheurs sont les anges” devrait vous faire passer un très bon moment, je n’en doute pas.

Review on: https://novabookreviews.blogspot.pt/2...

This is a special book. Made to be appreciated and devoured, no doubt. It's not for the week of heart people out there because it shows no compassion, it doesn't focus on a pretty love story to ease the loneliness of a world infested zombies.
It doesn't have the biggest action or the best scenarios. What truly matters is seeing how a 15 year old girl born and raised in that world manages to survive relaying only on herself, being the protector of a big Dummy while on the run from a hunter that promised "an eye for an eye".

It's a dark, twisted world that will make you feel all the emotion hidden beneath the words. It's creepy and awful while still being imperfectly perfect.

Temple or "Sarah Mary" carry's such guilt from past errors and lost loved ones. That's why she doesn't allow herself to care for anyone anymore. This girl "woman" is an inspiration She's the best written character i have ever read along her southern accent and thriving personality. The author did a wonderful job finding such convincing young world in this grown up world.

There is only two characters that become consistent in her life during the course of the story and those two will help enhance the credibility of the whole story as well as portraying this new surviving but desperate and mad civilization.

Along her journey we meet passing strangers that become friends never sticking around for long but somehow manage to leave their footprint, broken family's that struggle to remind themselves of the old world while maintaining alive and odd monsters and humans that switch the food chain giving the Zombies a run for their money.... It's not the best zombie movies but it's a book that it's going to leave it's mark.

I really enjoyed this book. It is only lately that I've actually got into the whole post-apocalypse world (not trying to say the idea hasn't been around for a while, it has, I just haven't considered it before now) and in doing so, this book came into my path and I've really really loved the journey it's taken me on.

'The Reapers Are the Angels' is beautifully written and describes a world that I could completely believe in, zombies and all!

It is what I like to call (but don't know if there is already a sort of genre name for it) a journey book. An adventure of sorts, but mainly just following a character through both a physical and emotional journey of their life. I really love those kinds of books - this is a warning for you if you don't!

The leading character, Temple, was realistic and what I would imagine a girl her age would be like if born into a world like the one described.

I want to note on the way that Bell has Temple talk about her 'God', not an all benevolent one or of any particular faith, but more of one that makes sense in the world she's living in - I really liked that aspect of the story.

I can understand if some people wouldn't like this book, 1. because of the ending and 2. because of the slight anti-climax of how her journey ends with no hope of a sequel (the kind I would like anyway).

However, the fact that I, all the way through the book, didn't know where she would stop or who she would meet next - the complete unpredictable nature of the story line - was a complete breath of fresh air for me; especially since finishing Wither by Lauren DeStafano (a VERY VERY VERY BAD BOOK - do not waste money on THAT ONE!) just before starting this one.

Anyway, I loved it! If you like zombies/adventure/action/relationships (not the true-love kind) then this is the book for you.

WHAT! No one told me what I was getting into when I started this book. I can't even remember what drove me to put this on my to-read list, all I know is that its been there for a while and I finally got my hands on a copy.

But lord almighty I wasn't prepared for this. This is certainly not the average zombie book. This straddles the line somewhere between Warm Bodies and Of Mice and Men. The whole while I read this, all I could imagine was that it reminded me of the classics that we read in high school. The setting, the characters, the metaphors are all that well written.

This book is about Temple, a 15 year old southern girl who has grown up in a time when zombies are a regular occurrence. She lives on her own. Temple travels around depending on the kindness of strangers where she can get it, but certainly not relying on it. She's fierce and no nonsense and can take care of herself.

This book is so well written and mind consuming that sometimes I felt like I could actually see the settings, feel what Temple was feeling. I very rarely can get sucked into the setting of a book like that, but its just that good. Bell doesn't try to paint a pretty picture of a world with zombies or the people that inhabit it. There are terrible things that happen, people die, people kill each other, and don't even get me started on the inbreeding mess. The characters are all terrible, flawed people, the world is a torrent of misery, but it's believable. And god damn it, I'm a sucker for a southern setting that isn't fake. As gross and as terrible as it is, it felt truthful. I applaud you Bell, but I will be hesitant to pick up the next volume. Honestly, I can't even imagine why this is a series, the first book closed so beautifully. I might just need a break from zombie books for a bit anyhow, they're pulling at all my feelings.

It's not often that I will give a book 5 stars since nothing is perfect. But coming to the end of this book, it felt like a shame to fault it on what I can only class as minor flaws.

Born alone into a world gone to shit, how far would you go to try and make sense of it all? For Temple, a 15 year old girl with the baggage of someone with a life fully lived, it takes protecting the only bundle of innocence - Maury, a mentally challenged grown man who doesn't speak - as a way to create purpose in a life which has none. Is that what she is supposed to do? Is that her ticket to heaven? Hell, are the meatskins' the angels and those left alive the one's that God left behind?

Alden Bell does a fantastic job of exploring all of this. In a niche saturated with horror and action, Alden Bell spins the genre on its head and creates a truly moving and compelling experience.

Not perfect due to some inconsistencies in the world (how is the electricity still running?), but a damn good read all the same.

Perhaps Bell was foolish in writing this, as it seems almost impossible to follow up with some as meaningful.

So I should note, first off, that this book is solidly 4 1/2 stars, but it was closer to 5 than it was 4. It would've been a solid 5 if it hadn't been for the obnoxious mutant interlude.

This book clearly takes some notes from The Road, but becomes its own fairly solid creature from very nearly the beginning. See, there are zombies (do we ever find out why? Nope. Doesn't matter. But. Digression.) And there's a 15-year-old girl named Temple who has a knife and a couple guns and a worldweariness that she doesn't deserve. And she soldiers through this zombified wasteland, attempts to do the right thing, constantly pays lip service towards being a pragmatist, and decidedly isn't, even though she'd never admit it. Her sentiment binds up her destiny, which is bound with a dark, dangerous man named Moses Todd (one of my favorite new characters; anytime he's on the page, he's absolutely spellbinding) and with a mentally handicapped mute. She's trying to get Maury to safety, and Moses is trying to kill her. Along the way, there's Southern gentry, hunters who have figured out how to eat the zombies, mutants (the weak portion of the book), dates with sheltered 15-year-old boys, falling in love with a man we'd say is too old for our protagonist, a secret that drives everything, sparse prose, and even sparser dialogue.

Of course, that's what's on the page. There's a world, though, between what's on the page and what's going on, and that's what you're going to need to read this book to discover. Like the best stories, I can't even hope to sum it up for you. I can only recommend that you read it and say that it will almost definitely be worth your time, if you want to read something that will make you think.

• The protagonist (Temple) is a teenage, zombie-slaying machine. She travels across the country to complete a mission while spilling “slug” blood along the way. The reader learns early in the novel that Temple is filled with some sort of desire to kill the slugs, but doesn’t fully understand the rage until the abrupt conclusion of the story.
• This is a very dark and very suspenseful tale of what the world would be like if zombies inhabited the earth for many years. The zombies are not your typical “horror movie” zombies. They are slow moving and easily out maneuvered. Though the author never comes out and says that they are more like “end of days” type zombies rather than “viral infection” zombies or “chemical spill” zombies, the reader can infer that they are. People become “slugs” minutes after death even if they are not bitten by a zombie.
• I would recommend this to a reader looking for a suspense novel that has dark undertones, someone looking for a story with a troubled character trying to find her way and discover her purpose in the world around her.
• This is not really a book for the hard core zombie action movie buff. There is little violence or zombie action. It is more of a novel about Temple living in this zombie-infested world rather than about the zombie-infested world. The focus is more on Temple and how she reacts to the world around her. While the back cover says it is “soaked in all the blood that any horror fan could desire,” I disagree. Yes, there is blood and some violence, but I think horror fans would be disappointed with this title.
• I liked it and would be inspired to read more Psychological Suspense books.
• Readalikes: The Passage by Justin Cronin (recommended by Amazon) and possibly Stephen King novels.

Enjoyed the book. Very satisfied with the writing style, simple introspection, and setting surrounding the characters in this book. My complements to Mr. Bell.

The 16 year old protagonist has grown up in the aftermath of a zombie apocalypse and does not yearn for a return of civilization or morn all that has been lost. Instead, she lives in the moment and sees beauty and miracles all around her... and she carries a big ass knife and wields it like a ninja. Even still, she maintains a sense of unity with nature and her surroundings, including the "slugs" that inhabit the world she lives in.

I'd have given the books 5 stars, but it seems to just miss its mark. For some reason, the protagonist is illiterate, but seems to have a wealth of knowledge and intelligence that goes way beyond street smarts. She is a fantastic character, but it was hard to buy into her inability to read street signs. And, its been 25 years since the world fell on its face. Bridges have collapsed, buildings have fallen, and yet there are many working cars and an amazing amount of the buildings and towns still have electricity, even the ones abandoned for decades. Frankly, I get tired of apocalypse fiction that feels like it has to explain to death every crumbling detail of the setting in order to make the story believable; so I'm willing to give a little. But it is still hard to swallow the idea of a gas station still operating on electricity (not to mention the light bulbs) 25 years after civilization has collapsed.

If a few of these pitfalls had been sidestepped, it would have been an almost perfect book. It is about time we have some simple philosophical spirituality and humanity soak into the same old zombie tale. Very satisfying.

Age is nothing but a number, and if there was anyone who exemplifies this adage best, it is Temple. She was born into a world ravaged, but not overtaken, by darkness. The dead have risen and in the carnage of her self-defense, she finds the tatters of her soul, drenched in the blood of the men and meatskins alike that she had ended with her own hand.

The Reapers are the Angels initially caught my attention with its haunting cover and original title. I knew it rang a bell somewhere in my head, but didn't have time to explore that notion before I decided, right then and there, that I must have this book. It was only after I read the first chapter that it came to me that "the reapers are the angels" is a biblical verse (and a beautiful one, at that). It set the tone for the lyrically decadent vision of the narrative, mostly as seen from Temple's mind.

With every instance of hope that Temple happened to stumble across, I knew she would move on... [spoilers removed] The descriptions of the world are every inch as eye-catching as the title and cover. Although some parts of the story could easily be spotted from a mile off, in that they were predictable [spoilers removed], certain other aspects of it completely threw me for a loop... some pleasant, some not-so-pleasant [spoilers removed].

It's not so much a zombie book as it is a book about fear and hope and the design of life coinciding with the design of death. And kickass to boot. Even without all the supporting characters, Temple (and Moses) can carry the story with the tip of her disembodied, pink-nail-polished pinky finger.

This book is a little hard to describe. It's a... quiet novel. There's no edge-of-your-seat excitement, or anything very sensational, but it has a kind of mellow intensity - which probably sounds like a paradox until you've read it for yourself.

The main character grows up in a lonely existence in a zombie ("slug") infested world, and struggles with her sense of morality. She dispatches the infected with little more concern than one of us would give to whacking down poison ivy on a walking path. Life in this world is, for most, one of acceptance and resignation. The story follows Temple through her travels, changing companions and landscapes, and leaves you feeling glad it is only fiction.

The first thing you'll notice about the writing is the lack of quotation marks. Usually this drives me bayshit crazy, as it often seems like an attempt at being artistic or original and instead ends up being a distraction. But I have to admit, it kind of works in this book. This world isn't like the one we know. It is quite a while after the initial outbreak (at least 20 years I gather), and life is harsher, people are harder, the smooth edges on civilzation are now made jagged from years of struggle. People worry less about social niceties and luxuries like proper grammar, especially people such as Temple who grew up without a refular adult influence. The unusual way of speaking gives a slight feeling of being in the past despite the opposite being true, and sometimes sounds more than a little like wisdom:

"Ain't no problem, Temple says. Sometimes you gotta bust apart to get yourself put back together."

Memorability Factor: 4/10 (no real "hook" and not painful enough to stick)
Follow this author? Probably only if someone recommends something specific to me.

First review! Whoop, whoop! *Spoiler Alert!!*
Alright, let's see, where to begin...I loved this book. That's right, loved it. It's so rare to be able to say that but this book was refreshing, gruesome, and wonderfully descriptive. Temple, the main character, was easy to support. She was a strong feminine character with moral continuity, especially when handling the "dummy" Maury. I was surprised when she drove away leaving him to fend for himself but even more so when she turned the car around and went back for him. Temple has a badass disposition (as she was born in the world of zombies) and isn't afraid to chop the hell out of some zombies and get dirty. Which, to put it plainly, is awesome.

Now, concerns. When I first opened this book and saw the deliberate lack of quotations around dialogue I was taken aback. I wondered how on earth I was to read a book without quotations? It was surprisingly simple and reflected the loss of the society in the zombie apocalypse. The book was written in such a manner that I had no trouble with continuity.

The ending was very refreshing. I had grown use to Temple's character. She grew on me, with her improper grammar, missing pinky, and crazy knife, and her sudden and unexpected death was surprising, even with Moses chasing her throughout the book. I wasn't sure what I was expecting, perhaps she would outwit him and escape - again. But no, her death was shocking and the book shifting from Temple was Moses was interesting. Moses was a good guy clinging to a social construct that resembled order in a world of chaos.

The Reapers Are The Angels is a great book with vivid detail that's great for an easy summer reading, if you don't mind blood and severed fingers.

This is a zombie book that is not about zombies. Sure, they are there, but they are so secondary to the story that you feel like Temple does about them, they're just there, part of the world and nothing particularly bad.

Temple is a 15 year old girl, born long after zombies, slugs, came into being. The world has always been the same to her and she doesn't understand the need to hole up and hide away when there is so much to see. She kills when she has to, but doesn't see the world as a bad place. It is her home and always has been.

No, the story here has nothing to do with zombies and everything to do with a girl coming to grips with her own violent nature and the mistakes she's made in the past. As she puts it to a man she meets, she has a chasing problem. She's always being chased or chasing something. And so it goes. When she causes a man to come after her to avenge his rotten brother, there is a unique interplay between the two. Temple doesn't want to die, he doesn't want to kill her, but they both acknowledge that that's just the way things are.

There are many secondary characters in this book, each rich in their own way, making their mark in just a few pages. Bell knows how to write people. Even the mute Maury, "the dummy" she finds beside the road and feels responsible for, has his own special presence.

For those who find it odd that an illiterate girl would have such an expansive vocabulary, I think it's because Temple is an observer. She listens. She watches. She learns. She picks up words from people she's known over time, even though she never learned to read. It's who she is and I thought it fit very well.

In short, read the book. It's worth it.

Summary: A young girl, grown up in a post-apocalyptic zombie world; travels America meeting its inhabitants and finding her own brand of philosophy.

Things I liked:

Style: The style is a bit like the Adventures of Tom Sawyer, very lyrical (possibly purple prose at times), but a refreshing contrast to the violent world of zombies and survival. The style underpins the beauty that the girl, Temple, sees in the world despite her survival driven existance.

Story elements:

I liked Temple and the Dummy; Temple and the Mose; Temple and the Cowboy. Great character pairings. I liked the choice to make this a road trip story with significant stops along the way.

Pace:

The story moved at a good pace, not slow, not frenetic, the style helped with this. It just made the character seem really laid back.

Ending:

Bold choice it felt right, but wow, did not really see that coming in the way that it did.


Things I thought could be improved:


People seemed a bit to nice: Maybe I'm a big fat cynic, but everyone they meet seems to be basically come on in and share my food and shelter and they're all, sure thanks for having us. I didn't really buy it. But it eased off as the story went on.

This seemed misplaced and I found it distracting from both the character and the story.

I gave this 4 stars because it's so well-written and heart-felt.

I've never read a zombie book before. It's not a subject I care to read about. But I've been on a sci-fi / dystopian binge lately.

This book is really sad. It's written in a really bleak manner, similar to "The Road" by Cormac McCarthy. It even omits the quotation marks for dialog. The characters are very interesting, especially the main character, Temple. I had such high hopes for her.

I want to comment though on the battle of Temple vs Moses. It was hard for me to believe that an adult would really go to such lengths to exact revenge on a child. It seems so ridiculous to me. Doesn't he have anything better to do? Especially since he acknowledges that his brother was a bad person and deserved to be killed. So why his crazy mind-set? He should be happy that there are kids who are able to take care of themselves and have enough self-sufficiency to maybe build a better future considering the current chaos. I would have liked them to join forces and become and team that helps people and maybe figures out how to get rid of the zombies. That would have been interesting to read about. I did like the end where Moses takes care of Temple and shows his respect to her as a worthy adversary.

I thought it was YA, since it's listed that way on the side of the screen. But when I got it at the library, there was no YA sticker on the spine like they usually have for YA books. So I'm glad I read this before giving it to my teen daughter. Just because the MC is a teen doesn't mean it's for kids. There is a lot of 4-letter words, but that isn't necessarily a deal-breaker for me. The problem was the sexual content. It's just too explicit for teens, especially the near-rape scene.

Well Written Zombie World !

So this is my first Post-Apocalyptic-World read . Author had penned down a simple story which revolves around the protagonist Temple who left the island to discover far new lands . On the way she stumble into different kind of humans and meatskins aka Slugs(Zombies ) . After reaching mainland , Abraham misbehaves with her and end up losing his life . With Ruby's help , she makes out of the area but got tailed by Moss Todd , Abraham's brother , who stay concrete to kill her any how .While running away she came across Maury , usually called Dummy in the plot & decided to get him back to his family to earn some good points .
Temple is a difficult character to relate to. She's tough and hard. She handles herself in a way I'd like to think I would do when zombies take over the planet. She kills with precision, both zombie and human when necessary. But she's broken. "Am I evil? " is what she wants to know and shed her shame. The world that she lives in is a terrible place . She knows nothing else. Responsibility and honor guide her through a world with no rules. Moss Todd is portrayed as an enemy who sticked to his word and commands honour even during futile time .

The Reapers are The Angels is a mature book, the violence and gore are intense and the lessons in it are hard learned. It's the moral though; that I think takes an adult mind to truly grasp. Concepts of sacrifice, family, and morality are rarely conveyed as profoundly as they are in Reapers. Bell has managed to give us the perfect Anti-Heroine in a world without heroes in a time without hope. Temple takes us on a journey through the worst parts of human nature only to show us that in the end, all that matters is what you hold inside of you.

Well shit. This book changes my perspective on a lot of things. For example, every time in hear the saying "everything happens for a reason" when something bad happens, I cringe. I've never been able to understand why this bad thing just had to happen. But in this book, the world is desolate and infected with "meatskins". Essentially, zombies. But there are still great people left in the world that don't just try to screw people over just cause they can. Most dystopian novels have the only people left in the world being cruel and out to kill everyone, cause why not. But in this world, there is a form of camaraderie among the survivors. Sure there are still the douch bags, but most are generally good people.

When I first started reading this, I was wondering what the hell the title meant. Reapers hold a bad connotation, while angels have a good one. At first I thought it meant the angels were bad. But then, towards the end of the book, they say the bible quote that contains the saying, and I finally understand. It's part of that "everything happens for a reason" thing. The whole end-of-the-world thing meant to weed out the bad seeds. The angels chose who would stay, therefore becoming the reapers.

Now, this is just how I interpreted it. I could be totally off base on this, but interpretation is in the eye of the beholder.

Anyways, this book basically restored my faith in humanity, the ending not included, except in a roundabout way, it still kinda did. All I've been seeing is the cruel people in the work and I forgot that there really are kind, considerate people in the world. And hopefully, when the world finally goes to shit, they end up making it so the world isn't filled with assholes.

I always struggle with rating books between 4 and 5 stars hahaha, and this was one of those tough ones. I want to rate it a full five, though something is holding me back and I'm not quite sure what. I loved this one from beginning to end, it hooked me right from the beginning, and it's been a long time since I've read from the POV of a main character that I respect so much! This book basically falls right in the middle of a zombie apocalypse story, where you're following Temple, a 15 year old girl surviving along the way - and this world is all she's ever known. She's honestly badass as hell, I had no doubt that she would survive this story...

I'm normally not a huge fan of zombie stories, maybe that's why I can't rate it a full 5 - there's just something about the walking dead that doesn't catch or hold my interest in the least bit. Maybe because it's been done so much? and each zombie story, book or tv show is relatively the same plot? Even this one - the setting, outside characters and even parts of the plot were all something I'd read or seen before in another zombie flick. There was just something about Temple and her personal journey that made me fall in love with her I think; her conscience, her reasonings, the feelings she experienced and her drive for survival kept me wanting to keep reading because I wanted to see where she'd end up.

The place where this story started and where it ended were perfect, I like that we were kinda thrown into her life one morning and then the book ended where hers did, but the stories still assumed to have continued with Moses and Maury. I heard there is a second book, though not as popular, about where Moses and Maury ended up - I would love to read it!

This is a strange and wondrous book. It reminds me of True Grit, but with just the girl and no Rooster Cogburn, plus zombies. Also the chase is in reverse - in True Grit the girl is hunting down the man who killed her father, while in this book the girl is being hunted down by the man whose brother she killed. That girl, 15-year-old Temple, was born post-zombie apocalypse, so it's the only world she knows. She's tough as nails and slices and dices the "meatskins" (and anybody else who threatens her, for that matter) like nobody's business. But even with all the action and brutal violence, this is in incredibly thoughtful and achingly beautiful novel. It's full of big ideas (What does it mean to be human? Is it enough to survive? Can there be beauty and magic and light in a dark and broken world?), plus the pacing is flawless and the prose essentially the brilliant love child of Faulkner and Cormac McCarthy. I have a feeling this book isn't for everyone, but it's easily earned a place in my top ten.

A snippet:

"And she turns her back on the lost and the dead and the trampled down, she leaves them to their airy graves, and she and the big man next to her look upward at heaven and find there not just gates and angels but other wonders too, like airplanes that go faster than sound and statues taller than any man and waterfalls taller than any statues and buildings taller than any waterfall and stories taller still that reach up and hook you by the britches on the cusp of the moon, where you can look and see the earth whole, and you can see how silly and precious a little marble it really is after all."

I'm not much for the "zombie apocalypse" fad but found myself enjoying this book a lot more than I thought I would. Indeed, this is artfully written. In the story, 15-year-old Temple lives in a world that is fast dying due to the rise of zombies. How the zombies came to be is left very much up in the air, but Temple has known no other life than the kill or be killed existence she has eked out. Ironically, through the story, the zombies never are more than a background, lurching and overshadowing threat- one fairly easily avoided by the street smart orphan. It's the human survivors that are a bigger threat. After Temple is forced to escape from a safehouse after one of the men tries to force himself on her, the man's brother pursues her seeking revenge. While on the run, Temple comes across a mute man and decides to undertake a journey to find his family - and possibly redeem herself after a terrible tragedy - which she blames herself for -results in the loss of her adopted brother. The trip and book ends in a way I -- and I suspect most readers - did not expect. What really makes this book is Temple- she is a fascinating character who is mature well beyond her 15 years. She is a strange blend of spiritual and pragmatic, and she keeps an ice cool head under pressure. The dynamic between her and Moses Temple is well crafted. My one nit is I would have liked to have known more about how the mutants came to be- vague hints are given, but little else. Otherwise, for those who like a bit of a different twist in their horror, this book is for them. I'd save this for older teens due to the violence and mature themes.

This book was an excellent book to read. If you're a type of reader who likes to read about the apcolypse or the dead coming back to life then I definetly would recommend "The Reapers Are the Angels". I would give this book a four star review, only because I was disappointed with the ending. However the rest of the book from begining to the end had me visiualizing the whole story in my mind and giving me a feeling as if I myself was in the book. The Reapers Are the Angels will keep you reading till the end and wonder if there will be a sequal. This book will give anyone who reads it so many personal connections such as: losing someone close, or having to deal with something that you shouldnt have too. I relate to the main girl in the story since I have grown up feeling like I push everyone away from me because of things that have happened in the past. I dont like dealing with other people since Im very selfdependent and don't want to have to deal with others drama or problems. However I do have a couple people who I would protect and help in anyway possible as would Temple. I did not relate to Temple in this story because I would never be able to kill anyone, zombie or not. Im great at fighting and being quick on my feet like Temple but I dont stratagize things before I do something. Temple does and she thinks of solutions very fast. I beleive the theme of this book is " Not to let your past burden your future". Everyone makes life changing mistakes but you should learn and be stronger. It wont help if you isolate people who care about you and try too help you. You arent alone in the world so dont make your actions define if you are evil or not.

This book will stay with me for some time. I was unprepared to love this book when I randomly grabbed it and several other books from the library shelf. My skepticism grew when I realized I had chosen a rare novel written in 2nd person point of view. There was another strangeness to the text, and that was the lack of quotation marks around the dialogue. I read the first short chapter and put the book down for a day, thinking the stylistic choices of the author and the subject matter (zombie apocolypse) just weren't my style.

And yet...

The next day, I wondered what Temple, the 15 year old narrator, was talking about in her believable, uneducated, and yet foreign-sounding narration. I wondered where she was, how she got there, and what she was doing, and as I do when reading any good science-fiction book, I wanted to know the definition of these unfamiliar words she spoke of. So I picked up the book again, and from that point on, I was hooked. The last half of the book I read into the early morning hours to finish. And what an ending.

Temple was violent, heroic, loveable, and entirely unforgettable. Her journey touched me, and I think it'll touch other readers as well. Although this novel fits into the trendy zombie genre, it's not like any other zombie movie I've seen. (This is my first "zombie novel.") Yes, it takes place in the future after a zombie apocolypse, and yes there are some violent scenes, but they are woven effectively into this beautifully written novel which almost reads like poetry, like a melody that plays on in your head, carrying you on waves of emotion and thought.

I loved this book. Well done, Mr. Bell

The Reapers are the Angels is a story that follows a teenager named Temple on her journey through zombie-infested America. Using flashbacks, the book describes Temple's experiences with a man she came to accept as her uncle, and her younger "brother". Temple is not like a normal teenager-instead of thinking about school stress and family drama, she she is in a constant fight for survival. She has learned that, in this world, it is the choice between killing or being killed. Sometimes, however, this mindset has gotten her into trouble. Her survival-of-the-fittest personality occasionally leads to wrongdoings, resulting in her having to move around often. Throughout the story, the reader learns about how she became this way, and how she feels about her life in the current moment.


While the book depicts violence in a very gruesome fashion, it also goes into detail about her personal growth, explaining how she has grown as a person as the world is falling apart around her. Alden Bell managed to take a gory idea and weave it into a beautiful story of self-growth. He has written this book so that many people can relate to the main character's growth, even though it is set in a world no one has experienced. I felt that this book was incredibly well-written, and went into issues that one would not think about during a zombie apocalypse. The intense contrast between detailed violence and Temple's personal growth continued to remind the reader that Temple is living in a very different world than us. Her relationship with others changes greatly throughout the book. Overall, I loved the book.
