Ever since I read World War Z: An Oral History of the Zombie War I've been moderately infatuated with zombies, and have read as many zombie novels as I could get my hands on. Most were decent, but nothing really resonated with me the way World War Z did until I encountered Alden Bell's The Reapers are the Angels.

The Reapers are the Angels is an atypical zombie tale, in that Bell (the pen name for Joshua Gaylord) doesn't bother explaining how the outbreak occurred or what the immediate aftermath looked like. Bell starts several years later, on a lonely island, where we meet Temple, a fierce teenage girl living on her own and driven by the urge to see as much of the new America as she can. Her travels keep her primarily in the South, and she encounters all variety of survivors and enemies both human and undead.

With a tone similar to Cormac McCarthy (I'm reminded of both No Country for Old Men (Vintage International) and The Road (Movie Tie-in Edition 2009) (Vintage International)), Bell combines stark landscapes, vivid imagery and language that shows real heart and emotion without seeming forced or awkward. It's so beautifully written you sometimes forget that there's also a really cool zombie story behind the prose. As zombie yarns go, this is a bit unconventional, though there is enough post-apocalyptic horror to satisfy most fans of the genre.

The Reapers are the Angels is without a doubt the best zombie tale I've found since World War Z, and I'd absolutely recommend it to zombie aficionados looking for something new. It's appeal goes well beyond just the zombie arena though, and might just surprise some more serious-minded readers.

This was definitely unlike any zombie story I have read. There is so much more to it than just the dangers of being eaten by zombies; in fact, the zombies really didn't play much of a role and were only there to set the scene. The real story is about how Temple tries to survive in this world, and how the people living in this world have changed with the times. To me, this story was more about the evolution of humans in a time of apocalyptic crisis, rather than the actual apocalyptic event itself. And that made it a really unusual and interesting read. I liked that the story was told from the perspective of this teenage girl, who is so strong and so broken. The things she just assumes are normal, well....they aren't normal and it breaks my heart to see how she takes it in her stride. This novel has definitely got a Western feel to it, and this is further accentuated by the slang and lack of quotation marks (seriously, there are no quotation marks) so consider that a warning to anyone who is particular on grammar and punctuation! Overall,a gripping story that masterfully depicts the struggles of a teenage girl in an undead world!

If you're going into this book thinking you'll find an action-packed, zombie-mauling good-time, you're in for a surprise. THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS is literary zombie fiction (yes, you read that right), although it's not too literary it feels pretentious and stuffy, but it's not a totally light read either. There's violence chock full of blood and gore, a semi-solitary road trip, and God. Does it work? Yeah, in a way. The book was serious but there wasn't much depth and it didn't impact me as much as it probably should have. The plot is basically an odyssey, in which many diverse characters appear and we see how the main character, Temple, relates with them. One of these struck me as odd and took me out of the story. Before, the book showed realism and grit, then it came to giant mutants and turned into a sci-fi horror show. Frankly, it was just weird and didn't correlate with the rest of the story. Temple was an interesting character who told the tale well but was a contradiction; she's illiterate but knows words that few people do. Since she's always lived with "meatskins" and has never known the world before, her background doesn't support this and I found it didn't fit with her character at all. I got her but didn't care about her.

Honestly, I don't have much feeling for this book, I liked it but that's all, and while it's a good read, it's not great. If you like a thinking zombie story with philosophy and a stream of Christianity running through it, although it's not too deep, than you just might enjoy this book.

Admittedly, I enjoy the trashy vampire novel as much as the next Jacob or Edward gal, but I do not think I would have chosen to read this book but for the fact that it came highly recommended. It was a quick, sometimes grosteque (at least for those of us with queasy stomachs), but thought-provoking book that seemed somehow a bizarre concoction of A Clockwork Orange and Wall-E with its desperation and good versus evil themes.

While Temple, the main character, possesses the remarkable ability to find beauty in the darkest of situations and meanest of people, she fails to see any good in herself - a theme that is set at the very beginning of the book. Upon coming across a "slug," she reflects "... you can cherish a miracle without deserving one. We're all of us beholden to the beauty of the world even the bad ones of us. Maybe the bad ones most of all." She then spends the entirety of the book running away from yet seemingly running towards evil never stopping to acknowledge the way things were or should be and never slowing down to accept her own selfless actions or beauty. In fact, she cautions that moments that "let through the clear spectacle of life" are either not intended for her or are intended to break her heart.

Bell does a fantastic job taking you along on Temple's bleak and desolate journey, but I think he fails to provide a sufficient back story to certain aspects of the book. For example, how did this plight come to be and how will it end? And, why does Temple vacillate between two very different names that evoke very different religious connotations?

After a quarter century of zombie apocalypse, the world has learned to survive. Cope may be a more appropriate word. The protagonist in this novel, Temple, was born into it, being only 15 years old. Hence, her sense of the world is as warped as the world, itself.

Her physical and emotional journey are both far-reaching and somewhat episodic, with the accompaniment of a friend, which made me think of _Huck_Finn_. The characters she meets along the way range from very civilized to gruesome hillbilly. I wanted Temple to find happiness and rooted for her throughout the book. At one point, I had given up hope because of the situation she got herself into.

For a zombie book, there is very little undead action and that bothered me. Also, I grew quickly weary of Temple's inability to speak in any language but Southern Platitude. She was a bit too bitterly weathered to be believable, but it is a zombie novel, so I'll forgive her that.

Expect strong religious overtones; they are legion. Nearly every character will begin the putative inferences in one way or another upon initiating a conversation. The title, taken from a passage in the Bible, is perhaps the most appropriate one I've run across. Near the end of the novel, the reader figures it out.

That's what makes the ending the shocker it is. I had trouble processing it and still don't understand the motive, as complex as it was. The sense of honor, I suppose, is all a civilization has to cling to during a time like this, which is just as deformed and dysfunctional as the rotting dead roaming the earth. Three and a half stars.

So normally I stay far away from the "splatter" genre, whether it be zombie flicks or horror books. Would never have picked up this book based on the blurb. But after reading several positive reviews, decided that skepticism aside, I'd give it a shot.

Am very glad I did pick up this book, because it. was. amazing. The book is less focused on creatively gruesome ways "brain eating zombies can take over the world", but more on the journey of the young protagonist, Temple,and her self-reflections along the way. (Think Wizard of Oz, but with a knife wielding Dorothy who can hotwire cars, and has insights well beyond her age, and instead of munchkins, flying monkeys and a wicked witch with a dead sister you have flesh eating zombies, more flesh eating zombies, and a post-apocalyptic cowboy hell bent on avenging his dead brother... so not really Wiz of Ozzy at all, really... except for the road trip part!)

The prose flowed beautifully (and I'd imagine it takes skills to put a poetic spin on bashing walking corpses), the villain had just the right amount of heroism to make it hard for you to hate him, and the poignant ending will probably have you tearing up. Despite growing up in this harsh horrific world, and dealing with all the crap that life has thrown at her, Temple could still find and appreciate the beauty in the places she visits, the things she sees. Her thoughts on religion, god, and the value of life were thought provoking, eloquently written, and certainly gives you much to ruminate over after you turn the last page.

Alden Bell’s The Reapers are the Angels is a surprisingly great read. So many books and films take on the same premise with far less finesse. The concept will sound familiar. The world has been overtaken by the undead, and a young girl, Temple, tries to both survive and find her place in this world.
But, man, this book has something others don’t. It has Temple, one of the most likeable, memorable characters ever written. Temple is fifteen and reminiscent of a weed that’s been stepped on a million times but keeps growing. She is childlike but resourceful and independent as well as uneducated but wise beyond her years. She is a complex, gurkha knife wielding vagabond whom you won’t stop thinking about even after you put the book down.
The language of the book is sort of a McCarthy-esque, bare-bones poetic prose, filled with religious undertones, and coated in a southern dialect. At times, it teeters on the fence between profound and pretentious, but because the story is from Temple’s point of view it usually falls into insightful.
If there were one thing this book could have done better it would have been the amount of fear I felt, which wasn’t nearly enough for being in a world immersed with zombies. Frankly, Temple has a stronger will to live than the Aspen grove in my backyard and much better survival skills. So even though she’s being pursued by a nasty villain through a world of moral-less creatures who devour humans any chance they get, it’s really hard to feel scared for her. But you’ll love her so much you’ll keep reading anyway.

Everything you've heard is true: this is the most beautifully written zombie novel you will ever encounter. That's right — beautiful. Because while there's certainly plenty of horror to be found in the book, it's wrapped up and relayed in such elegant, mannered and imagery-rich language that the whole thing takes on a really strange and lovely glow. Initially it's kind of an unsettling combination, but as things proceed and we find ourselves seeing this post-zombie apocalyptic landscape through the eyes of a preternaturally composed, capable and perceptive girl named Temple they begin to take on a kind of steady, masterful rhythm and tonality that in many ways call to mind McCarthy's The Road... only with a fully-realized, exceptionally lyrical and indelibly Southern voice. (Which, considering that Bell (a pseudonym) is actually a teacher in NY, is especially surprising.)

Is the novel perfect? No. There's one significant detour (both in terms of Temple's journey and Bell's choices as a writer) that rings strangely forced, and a deux ex machina moment close to the end (I'm biting my tongue here so as not to reveal a spoiler) that strains credulity even in a novel about the living dead. But the great bulk of the novel is tremendous: the characters (particularly Temple and her shadow, a man named Moses) are richly drawn and memorable; several scenes are truly haunting; and the language... by God, does Bell have a way with words.

In the end, this is probably the most beautifully written novel I've read in any genre in almost two years.

This was a phenomenal book! I am definitely putting it directly into my favorites list. I think that the concept is wonderful, and the writing is beautiful ( Very Cormac McCarthy!) I could rant and rave about how much I love this book for hours, more importantly though I am going to tell you about why you ( points haughtily) must read it.

The Reapers are the Angels depicts the story of Temple, a sixteen year old girl all on her lonesome during the zombie apocalypse ( If your not ready to pick up the book and add it to your Amazon Cart please keep listening.) Temple is being chased though by more then just the undead. She is also being pursued by a man bent on murdering her after she killed his brother. On top of that Temple does not know if she wants to die or not. She contemplates whether there is beauty in the world and whether it is a world worth living in. She engages in violence and wonders if what she is doing is right or whether she herself is twice as evil as the undead ( slugs) that surround her.

Temple's journey is perilous and littered with tons of brilliant characters and plot twists. Along the way she picks up a mute named Muray who she then becomes attached to despite the fact that he does not seem to acknowledge her support or existence.

Overall this is a beautiful book. The Dialogue is incredible, and I loved all the recurring themes. The power behind the authors words where completely numbing. I ordered his next book off Amazon just a few minutes ago.

If you pick up this book I guarantee you that you have made a good choice!

When it's good, it's brilliant. When it's bad, it's a head scratcher.

Temple is everything a character should be in this type of novel. She's tough, brutal and realistic. She's not pretty, she's doesn't rely on others, she does what she wants and depends on herself, she can handle things just fine on her own. Which I love. There were other little things, such as her not being able to read or write, details that I hadn't thought of before.

Overall? Good. Not perfect, or earth shattering. I am a zombie fan so the fact zombies played such a non-important part did leave a lot to be desired. Not that I need action packed escape scenes but considering that these same zombies wiped everyone out and set humanity back a few thousand years,I was expecting a bit more. Temple even lolls about on a beach stark naked drying herself off and is in no hurry, even when she sees them coming for her. They pose no threat, besides being in the background.

The writing style became quite grating. Maybe it's because I'm English and the whole book is written in a south American drawl made my hackles raise immediately.

The plot is...not too good. I have to admit that most of what happened came out of nowhere, but it wasn't unpredictable or surprising in a good way. I spent most of my time confused, not really knowing why the author thought half of what he'd written was even appropriate. The was a ridiculous idea. It did ruin it for me, since there is such a thing as too stupid.

30-40 years ago, post apocalyptic books took place after a nuclear disaster. Then came the Andromeda Strain variety - man made medical or scientific development gone very bad and most of humanity is wiped out.
Now we have zombies, I keep asking myself why zombies? And as mentioned in the book, how did these mindless undead beings manage to take over the earth?

What makes this book so wonderful isn't the zombies at all, just like it never was about the actual disaster in any of these books. It's a way to empty the world and deal with a very small group of people who suddenly become very important - since there are so few of them.

Our protagonist is Temple - she would never consider herself a hero. What I found so appealing about her is her relationship to God, not to the few other people she comes across. It is her humanity in relationship to God that makes this story so compelling. The other characters, Moses Todd, Maury- Dummy, the different people she meets on her journey - all are well fleshed out. They all show the many different ways that people cope with tragedy, either by building community - or retreating into a self imposed fortress. By turning the tables and becoming hunters or more vile monsters than the zombies themselves.

For me, it was very much the presence of God that fascinated me. God is only present in Temples' mind, but he is so much a part of her world view - that it was a 'lightbulb' moment to why her name is Temple. For that is what she is in this book.

I picked this up from the library because of a recommendation by a fellow Reddit user, and I was not disappointed in the least. The back of the book carried s review saying it was like "Flannery O'Connor with zombies", and while I would agree, I think "Cormac McCarthey with zombies" might be more accurate.

The writing style was bleak, introspective, and brutal, as was the protagonist and the world she lived in. We follow the journey of Temple, a 15-year-old girl who is old beyond her years. She is haunted by the things she has seen and done, and thinking herself evil and beyond redemption, she still holds on to a sense of wonder about the world around her.

The apocalyptic world is the background rather than the focus of this novel, and I think that was for the better. Rather than building pages of description on the ruined world, Bell used his pages to build characters and a sense of thoughtfulness about the meaning of life. I read this book in about 6 or 7 hours, not just because it was short and sweet, but because it was fascinating and enthralling.

If I had a complaint, it would be that I don't follow how certain areas would still be on the power grid and how some gas stations would still be operational over 25 years after the zombie outbreak. If the purpose of the book had been to explore a post-apocalyptic world, I might have a big problem, but as I said, that wasn't what this book was about.

Overall an intriguing, gritty read that I feel lucky to have found. I'm surprised I'd never heard of it before.

I had heard that this was one of the best zombie novels out there. It might be, but it’s still very lacking, which doesn’t say much for the subgenre. Alden Bell isn’t a bad writer, though, I’m not sure about his style. It seems to me that he has been very much influenced by Cormac McCarthy, from the lack of quotation marks to the characters’ personality (especially Temple). The whole thing kind of reminded me of McCarthy, actually, except not as good. I feel like, if pressed, Bell would list him as a major influence. This is not necessarily a bad thing, Bell just isn’t as good at it…but if he keeps working and decides to keep the Southern Gothic tone down the line, we might have a semi-competent alternative once Cormac heads to the great hereafter.

The biggest problem I had with this book is the convenience factor. The story takes place 25 years after the zombie apocalypse started and, not only is there still plenty of gas…but the pumps are working. There is electricity everywhere…even in deserted ghost towns. People have ice and refrigeration and all kinds of food. This just completely threw me off and kept me from enjoying the story as much as I could have because it just seemed stupid. The meat of the story, though, was pretty good. Temple annoyed me and I kept hoping she’d die throughout the whole thing. If you like zombies, you’ll probably enjoy this, but it’s not going to be a classic or anything. My advice would be to pick it up used or at the library.

3? ..4? i don't know how to rate it, i'm torn. i was gonna give it 1 star and dnf it after i'd read through the first few dozen pages. and look at me now...
i still have a lot of complaints (the world building was rubbish, and the mc's thoughts sounded like those of an old academician, when she's supposed to be a fifteen year old illiterate (albeit pretty bright) orphan, born and raised in the middle of a zombie apocalypse), but the second half of the book really did get to me.

some quotes (there's two, eh) because why not:

they're not the deepest ones of the bunch (i screencapped quite a few) but, come on, check that imagery.
Didn’t finish. Bad bad bad. Shocked at the positive reviews.

This would be more of a 4.5 stars. As I read in a post by someone else, this is more of a literary book. The story has moments of thought and introspection while still having action and intensity.

This is like I Am Legend (movie version, i have yet to read the book) and The Book of Eli somehow had a love child and this came out. I Am Legend because of the zombies and the solidarity she feels she needs and The Book of Eli because she reminds me of Eli with the way she believes in God and how badass she is at killing. And she believes in God, but he's slick and she believes she's evil because she enjoys the killing. However, she only kills when her life or someone she cares about (even if she tells herself she doesn't care) is in danger. She's done things she's not proud of.....

Also, there are zombie killings and a man (Moses) who sees the world in the same way that she does is after her to kill her because she killed his brother (he completely deserved being killed though and Moses knows this). She wont go easily and she will run, but she understands completely why he will kill her and is okay with the reasoning. There is a person she is trying to return home, but it's difficult because he is slow mentally and doesn't talk.

This book has so many aspects and I really did quite enjoy it and was sad and riveting and realistic in a sense (maybe except for the Hills Have Eyes/Deliverance part).

This is such a weird, beautiful, cruel and wonderful read! I've always had a fascination with zombie stories, but this I'll tell you, this is something new. I mean; How often is a book about zombies described as beautiful?

But this story isn't about zombies at all. It's about a young girls journey to survive, both in a physical and a more spiritual sense. The zombies just happens to be there. And the zombies aren't her greatest fear; it's the other humans, or maybe even her own thoughts?

The book has a feel of a magical western (does that even make sense?). And I couldn't help to think about "No Country for Old Men" (I've also heard other people compare the feeling to "True Grit") that might sound odd, but really, it isn't. It's a magical western road trip in a world that has turned into a total wasteland (yes, it's as brilliant as it sounds!).

And let me tell you about the main character Temple; she's just such a weird, smart, broken, strong, wonderful, confusing and awesome character! I can still hear her voice in my head (I love the fact that everything she says is written exactly as she would say it)! And most of the other character she meets on her way are just as weird and brilliant as her (Yes, brilliant is a word that needs to be used in this review).

So yes, I recommend this book to everyone! Even if you're not a zombie fan. Because this my friends, this is such a intriguing, different and beautiful read!

If someone told me I would enjoy a book about zombies infesting the USA, I would have laughed, but here I go: Alden Bell has crafted a haunting, gruesome, but also touching book about living with your past. He just happened to craft his story with zombies as the supporting cast.

Meet Temple, a 15 year old girl who is on her own in an apocalyptic version of the USA. Flesh-eating zombies (are there other kinds?) roam our country. One bite and you’re an automatic zombie. On the other side are humans trying to survive and create their own place to live. Temple makes her way across the country, where she comes upon other communities of humans, some nice and some ultra-creepy! All the while, there are hints of flashbacks from her recent past. Something bad has happened, but we only get glimpses. She meets a mute, whom she names Morey. Morey has a piece of paper in his pocket with an address. Thus begins Temple’s ‘quest’ to return Morey to his home. Along the way, she comes to grips with her past and a slew of unusual people.

The first half of this book is a strong contender for Most Depressing Book of All Time. However, the second half makes up for it and the story becomes quite touching (so hang in there!). With the exception of a few bad choices that the author makes (in my opinion), the story has a true ring to it. You will feel for Temple and what she is going through. The ending might not be what you expect, but that makes it all the more believable.

Say hello to a zombie novel with heart, depth, philosophy and, of course, horror. The Reapers are the Angels by Alden Bell is a gem of a book that deftly bridges a gap between YA and adult literature, writing horror reminiscent of Stephen King's Cell, but with much more emotional connection.

Temple is a fifteen year old orphan surviving as best as she can in a world full of "meatskins". She see's miracles in the small things, and feels the weight of God's judgement in everything she does. She is a teenager much older than her years, wracked by the guilt of a secret she keeps, and accepts the violence necessary to her survival as a manifestation of her own "evil".
When the meatskins find a way to her safe island haven, Temple knows it is time to move on, and as she treks across America she meets a host of eclectic characters, each suffering their own secrets.
In one of the safe communities Temple arrives in, she wanders across a group of "hunters" playing cards for pills. Here she meets Abraham, a man whose eyes "creep under her clothes". It is after the game that Temple is subjected to the man's violent lust for women, and ends up killing him. This act sparks a cat and mouse subplot when the man's brother, Moses, hunts Temple to exact revenge in her death.

It was a little hard finding this book, but when I finally did find it, I started reading it and didn't put it down until I reached the last page.

Where do I start?!

Well, the hero, Temple, is a weird choice for a main protagonist, but she is one of the best characters I've met so far. She's not your normal 16 year old girl, lost in a world of undead. She's though, without being cruel, and caring, without getting attached. She understands how things work in this infested world and she makes the most out of it.

I really enjoyed the vocabulary and the idea that the zombies have been around for 20 years or so. I really loved the insertion about the mutants and the supporting characters. Having Temple's story unfold at a slower pace was a good thing, because it keeps you motivated to go on (even though the outcome is what you expected).

Moses was a good archenemy, until he wasn't. I loved his determination and his appreciation for Temple, making him a simple character with a whole lot more to offer once you get to care about him.

The Griersons were a stereotype, but their presence was put to good use. Maury filled in the need to care about something or someone really good and the author got me to care about him too.

The book is written in a simple manner, with words and actions that could describe a future only so grim. I would give it 6 stars, but unfortunately I have only 5.

Teen Review

Genre: YA Sci-Fi/Horror

Summary: The world is infested with zombies. There are a few groups of people fighting against them, and hoping to survive. Temple, a young girl, is on the run - from her past, from the zombies, and from a vengeful killer. She travels restlessly from place to place, killing zombies and looking for some place she can settle. This is a story of her journey through the only world she's ever known.

Review: I rated this book a 3.5 because it was a good read in some aspects, but it fell a bit short in others. There was no real plot to speak of - it was more like a series of diary entries with a few smaller plots built in. The ending was very disappointing; it was almost as if the author didn't know how to end the story so he resorted to the ending that he chose. However, not everything in this book was bad, and it has some good merits. Temple was a good believable character, a strong heroine with a fatal flaw. This book dealt a lot with big, philosophical ideas, and I think there are a few passages and ideas in this book that are worth reading. I don't think you should read this book for an exciting story, but more for the life lessons and ideas and bigger questions that are asked. You can learn a lot from this book.

People might like this book if they liked: A Forest of Hands and Teeth, The Walking Dead

Reviewed by Ashleigh

I did not finish this book, so I cannot give it a full review.

I like zombies, but am not particularly fond of dystopias. I guess I'm okay with the zombie outbreak, but only if the humans win. If the humans lose, it moves into a dystopian future.

From the 40 plus pages I did read, I saw that the author writes well. Descriptions are good, and there is a beautiful opening scene with a lighthouse and seashore. Strong writing. The non-standard dialogue did throw me -- kind of Cormac McCarthy style. It felt a bit like someone recounting a conversation rather than me hearing two characters converse. That's just me and I wouldn't let it put you off.

For me, the protagonist and her actions were the problem. She made two distinct decisions in the section I read that did not make sense to me, or that I didn't think a rational person would make. But perhaps I should have read further to understand her. Perhaps she is not a rational character? But the decisions jarred me out of the story.

The biggest thing was that I just wasn't enjoying the book. And if I'm reading for pleasure and the book isn't fun, I stop.

I saw that the ratings on this book are quite high (3.9), so I am in the minority on this. If you like zombies, dystopias, and tough YA style writing, you may really enjoy this book.

Great book, almost gave it 5 stars. Very unforgettable, kind of what you'd expect to see in a post-apocalyptic zombie novel that is NOT about the gore and the horror. I'm not going to summarise for you what the book is about; I suggest instead that you go read it for yourself in stead! :-)

One little thing irked me though, something that I found to be very unrealistic, and that's why I didn't give it 5 stars:

How can the main protagonist (and others) be driving around in cars more than 25 years after the apocalypse took place? Where do they get the gasoline from? Surely, in a real life situation where the unthinkable happens and where your supply chain gets cut, because people die and there's virtually no one to work on the oil rigs, distribution, etc., gas would run out relatively fast, wouldn't it? Surely people don't get around with cars more than 25 years after it happened? Surely the world would succumb to a more primitive stave of development? Yeah yeah, I know, zombies are not realistic either, why do I make an "issue" out of the continued use of gas when zombies don't exist in real life either, but you see, my point is that when you add a fantastical element (zombie) in a "real world" environment, you must make that world realistic and credible in order to make to book come to life and make it "real", at least that's how it works best for me.

3.5 stars.

It's kind of incidental that this book involves zombies. Certainly none of the plot points around the onset of an apocalypse and subsequent demise of the civilized world make any sense. And in this book, its kind of irrelevant that the evident antagonists are zombies, they might as well just be man devolved into his most primal state.

But those parts of the book are really just set design, setting up for the heart of the story, which is -- philosophically and experientially, what does it mean to be a girl whose grown up in a crazy upside down world where she's had to hone her survival instincts on the razor edge of human/inhuman every day of her life? How does she maintain hope and optimism in her life? How does she reconcile what she does to stay alive with her desire for basic goodness?

The book is an interesting experiment: a style reminiscent of (though less successful than) mccarthy's the road + true grit.

5 stars for the strong, unforgettable female protagonist. for the dialogue, which flows with a lyrical cadence. There are some lines in this book that are outright beautiful, like poetry.

2 stars for the plot and related character motivation.

But for me, it was still worth reading because I'm a sucker for surrealist metaphysical lyricism.

I think this book is going to have people either loving it or hating it. It's not quite like any other book I've read, zombie or not. There isn't a lot of action yet there is a lot going on. Like my favorite zombie tales, this one is about the characters making their way in an altered world and not about the gore. The fact that the outbreak took place many years before the story is interesting but not much about the origin is discussed.

Other reviews have mentioned Huck Finn and I think that's a great comparison. The story is about a teen making her way through some exciting and unsual challenges while having to be more mature and matter of fact about life than she should be at her age.

I was somewhat surprised when I looked at the back cover again after finishing the book to see that's it's aimed at a YA audience. I know my YA self would've liked this book and probably picked it up again later in life as I'm sure there were things I just wouldn't get about the story in my youth. And what I'm saying here is that for a YA book it deals with some slightly more mature themes and relationships between the characters.

The ending was a bit disappointing after going on this journey and it's not necessarily what happens at the end but the way it happens. I felt a little cheated, but on the other hand it does allow other things to occur that otherwise could not.

I'm not even sure where to begin rating this book. Probably 3.5. Probably going to review it on the good vs. bad scale.

Good
It was beautifully written. Very descriptive and I was completely absorbed into the world.
I also LOVE Temple's character. Her empathy for the "slugs" and her strength was admirable.

Bad
Things went downhill for a bit when the giant hillbillies came into play. "Mama" reminded me of the fat female character on "Squidbillies" who lays around, so it became more comical to me. It took on a completely different element for that part of the book and I grew annoyed.

The other part I didn't like was the ending. That stupid giant hillbilly girl... are you kidding me?! Did Moses kill the hillbilly girl because he wanted to kill Temple or because he thought of her as his daughter? Was Moses actually planning on really killing Temple?? I just didn't get it, I suppose. He HAD to kill her throughout the whole novel, then he feels sorrow for her after she's dead? I didn't understand it! I was left confused, unsatisfied, and heartbroken. If I was the author, I think I would have ended it where Moses' gun was at her forehead - leaving the reader to guess what he would do.

All in all, I liked the book and won't forget it. It's been on my mind days after finishing.... just don't know how to deal with the ending.

What I loved about The Reapers are the Angels is the language. It is lush and descriptive and poetic without weighing down the plot. It’s a zombie book that dares to be literary in its delivery.

Alden Bell has created several unique vignettes, demonstrating the various forms of regression and evolution that people have experienced in this post-apocalypstic landscapes. From mutants to a family wasting away in their mansion, The Reapers are the Angels features several mini stories within a straightforward plot. Bell doesn’t shy away from the more sci-fi aspects of the post-apocalyptic genre, but he also manages to ground the story with character moments, both dark and sweet.

The novel is written like a western. Temple, our protagonist, is a strong, fiercely independent teenager who is damaged by her tragic past. She is torn between the savage feral world she knows and the pockets of civilization remaining, which tempt her to stop running. Bell has created a strong, female character who is not hyper-real (she doesn’t have any special abilities, snark, or unrivaled intelligence. She’s simply a girl who knows how to make her way through this broken world.)

If you’re looking for a literary narrative that delivers the darkness and gore you want from a zombie story, give The Reapers are the Angels a shot.

Yes siree, I got surprised by this one.

So, one day, I'm out of books to read and I'm trolling the bookstore looking for something, preferably apocalyptic to read. I saw this book, read a few paragraphs and knew it was the one.

I found Temple to be one of the most compelling characters I've seen in a while. I love character driven fiction, and seeing the zombie ridden world through her eyes was fantastic. The writing was wonderfully lyrical, and consistent which I find is lacking in many books attempting to be so these days.

Perhaps the most interesting thing about the novel, is seeing the world from the point of view of a person who grew up in a zombie infested world with few memories of the world before. I don't claim to be an expert on zombie fiction, but most of what I have read is centred around people who lived the bulk of their life in a zombie free environment, and this was absolutely refreshing for me.

One criticism, because it was so compelling, and I finished to quickly. One read, bam, done and left needing more, so hopefully this will become a series because I needs me some more Temple.

Edit: So there is another one... Exit Kingdom. Doesn't look like there is any Temple, but still going to get it.

This was a cute book. Well, I guess cute may not be the appropriate word but it´s the one that comes to mind when I think of the writing style and voice of the main character. The heroine of the story is fifteen year old Temple, a supremely capable young girl who has a go getting attitude and no time for nonsense. Only problem is that her very ´capableness´ has now gotten her into trouble. After years of living and, arguably, thriving, in a zombie infested post apocalyptic world Temple finds a community of other survivors who have managed to create their own relatively peaceful sanctuary. Here we see, as we so often do in literature, that of all threats man faces, whether they be mundane or supernatural, man is his own worst enemy. As I mentioned the voice and style of the book is kind of cute in its own way but this is contrasted by the darker elements of . However, it is the contrast between the light, yet eloquent, tone of the writing with the violence and with such themes as spirituality, purpose of life, and existential angst in a post apocalyptic world that make it poignant to the degree it is. So... cute probably isn't the word I want to use.

In short the book is well written and is a shiny raft on the sea of the zombie apocalypse genre.

Listened to audio version. Pros: Love anything zombie, and really liked the rich descriptions, which would've much better absorbed/appreciated in print than audio. Cons: Incredibly distracting that the author chose to make most of the characters speak in a really specific, Kentucky hills kind of way, especially the 15 year old protagonist that was born post-apocalypse. My grandparents used many of the same colloquialisms, but this manner of speech was old even in their time (born circa 1920). I don't live in Appalachia, but I do live in the deep south, and I'd be shocked if many young people speak this way. It just seems totally bizarre to suppose that this highly specific speech pattern would be resurrected in the face of an apocalypse and survive as the mainstream dialect. It was completely distracting, couldn't focus on the book for it.(Note that the characters were travelling freely via car, train, etc. across states, so the story wasn't set all in one tiny community or anything.) This is also the first post-z-apocalypse book I've ever read that has electricity still running all over and gas pumps still stocked up with gas for the easy taking, and the story's supposed to occur 18-20 years post-apo...plus, how this is happening is never addressed. Also very different is the idea that people would be generally friendly to one another rather than dog-eat-dog.

Plan to stay up all night and call in sick to work - this book demands attention. It is a compelling and beautifully written story of a Temple, a young woman surviving in a zombie-infested world. Temple is a self-sufficient woman, strong, skilled at survival; action abounds as she takes a journey across America, fighting zombies along the way. The road-trip action story is satisfying on its own, but at a deeper level it is absolutely enthralling because Temple is a unique and contemplative heroine who ponders the meaning of life and searches out beauty even as she kills zombies. Her story raises questions about the difference between good and evil, human motivation and satisfaction, and ultimately death itself. There are several reasons that this book stands out from others in the crowd of zombie literature: the writing is beautiful, lyrical; Temple has been born many years after a zombie apocalypse, and zombies thus are simply a part of life; and the emphasis of the story is not on horror and despair but rather on beauty and hope. For these reasons, and the tightly woven plot, this is a hugely satisfying read which deserves to be considered one of the best books of the year. Alden Bell is a newish author, and I hope he has a long and productive life because I am waiting to read more from him.

For the record, this is a 3.5, ad the .5 comes from the last three pages of the book which were sweetly haunting. I did like this book - it reminded me of Huckleberry Finn, except there are zombies - meatskins. The voice of the main character, Temple, is a strong one. She is one badass 15 year old an if there is a zombie apocalypse, I want her on my team. She is very much like Huck in her travels across the zombie-scarred US. She encounters some unique people and some dangerous people. There is an adventure theme in this book, and Temple is a memorable leader. There were some inconsistencies, however, that puzzled me in this book. Temple cannot read and has never had any formal education. She manages, however, to use words that are advanced and might be found on some ACT tests. I couldn't figure out if Bell was implying that she had picked these words up from adults or what his intent was. At any rate, that didn't work for me. I also didn't quite buy the explanation for what made Temple so tough and blase about her lifestyle. It wasn't developed enough for me. I have read quite a bit of zombie fiction, and at times the edges blur for me. Bell's ending made a lasting impression to me, however. I will remember this book because of it.

Just as vampires are the reigning poster boys for paranormal romance, zombies seem to be the in thing for horror these days, the go-to guys for a post-apocalyptic gorefest. The reapers are the angels doesn't do much that is new with the basic material - unspecified 'zombie plague' type event, small pockets of survivors, tough hunters guarding the borders - but instead of trying to answer any questions about the undead menace, it chooses to focus on it's central character, 15 year old Temple.

The prose is poetic and follows Temple's musings as she concentrates on surviving and finding the odd moment of grace in the ruined landscape. She is a great character - brave, honest, and unflinchingly true to her moral code. Her relationship with the man hunting her - who also lives by a code that is, in it's own way, honourable - is fascinating, and reminds me of the relationships you sometimes see in old Westerns between protagonist and antagonist.

A bit of a tough pick to recommend - it was plenty violent, but the violence wasn't really the point of the story, more the fallout from living in a harsh world. What stood out to me more was Temple's ongoing delight in the presence of 'God', redemption through natural miracles, present even in the worst of situations.

This is a beautifully written novel about the beauty of life even while death crawls at the edges. Temple, the main protagonist is 15 years old and exists in a world overrun by slugs, humans destroyed by a virus that turns them into cannibalistic monsters (in other words, zombies). She has spent some time living a solitary life in a lighthouse on an island off the coast of Manhattan. One day, as she realises that the slugs are getting closer, she decides its time to move on and head back onto the mainland. From there, the story takes her through her dealings with a range of people, both nobel and not. The slugs she encounters are not nearly as menacing as some of the humans she meets, particulary, Moses who is bent on exacting revenge on Temple. As she traverses the wide desolate landscape of a ravaged America, Temple finds a quiet beauty in God's handiwork. Temple is as much searching for salvation as she is trying to escape what she sees as the monster at the heart of her soul. I wanted this story to end in a different way, to have Temple find what she is searching for but unfortunately she does not. Despite this, the story is still beautiful, hauntingly so, like a tree, stark and beautiful against desert landscape.

I'm not a big zombie guy (though Shaun of the Dead is one of the funniest movies I've ever seen). But the premise seemed a bit different than any zombie story I've heard.

To quickly sum up the book, the protagonist is Temple, a fifteen year old who has been on her own for a few years, and she's basically the most kick-ass girl you'll meet in this post-apocalyptic world. Zombies, known as slugs and meatskins, have taken over the world for the past 25 years, so Temple doesn't know any other kind of world. When she accidentally kills a man who attempts to rape her, she is forced to run west from the dead man's brother who vows vengeance.

The writing is amazing. Turn the page, and you're bound to find a one-liner that will give you chills or give you philosophic pause. This story has gore, murder, mutants, and brain-eating. But, honestly, it's not so much about that. The book, to me, is a story about how evil is in the world, regardless if there's a zombie takeover or not. But despite that evil and the darkness it can create, beauty can be found if you want it. It's a dark and sensuous book that forces you to reflect --- right after your stomach settles from reading about eye-gouging.

I was skeptical about the rave reviews I read. The title didn't help. But boy, am I glad I began reading the book itself. Because this is a cut above all other YA fantasy out there. It's beautifully written, lyrical phrasing and poetic turns on almost every page, starting from some beautiful descriptions on the first page itself. It's amazingly tough to the point of noir. Action-packed. Fast-paced. But most of all, Temple is a true hero to follow. One of the many rave reviews I read compared this book and its protagonist to Justin Cronin's The Passage. That's true, but The Reapers is a much leaner book, an epic post-apocalyptic chase thriller stripped down to the bone. And Temple dominates the whole books. I'd have bought every single book in the series if this were a series. But sadly, there seems to be no sequel in sight even several years after its publication and the author doesn't seem to be very prolific. Oh well. Even if Alden Bell's reputation were to rest solely on this one book (not counting the previous book he'd published which wasn't a YA fantasy) that rep would still be well-deserved. The Reapers Are the Angels is everything it's cracked up to be and then some. One of the best YA thrillers I've ever come across and a terrific novel in any genre.

This is a somewhat different take on the "zombie apocalypse/future dystopian civilization" sub-genre. It begins 25 years after the dead have started getting up and, of course, eating the living. We follow a 15 year old girl/woman/warrior named Temple who has been surviving on her own since she was (five? eight? ten?) very young. Her backstory is slowly illuminated over the chapters and she first meanders through the blighted landscape and, eventually, is presented with an address and a destination. The story is basically a road book with the various vignettes--wacky Gothic Southern family, rough hunters, mutant family, etc. etc.--providing the fuel. Overall, the writing is quite good, and it is clear the author (Joshua Gaylord) is also trying to work on some bigger themes via the Temple character. Some of the interludes work better than others--I felt like the author was having a bit of trouble imagining and bringing to life the mutant family group, and the entire train bit seems to be kind of shoe-horned in to speed up the climax--but overall this is a very well-written take on an extremely familiar trope, so it should please both fans of these types of books and folks looking for something with a little more "mean on its bones."

In one of my favourite books of 2012 we follow 15 year old Temple across a devastating wasteland as she runs not just from zombies, but a vengeful man determined to see her dead. Temple is brilliant, and broken. Growing up post-apocalypse has made her tough, and she does what it takes to survive with a hardened calm which masks the terrors of her past. Although written in third person, the narrative carries Temple's distinctive voice, which is part of what makes the book so memorable. You can see what I mean from the very first line:

“God is a slick god. Temple Knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe.”

I was hooked from there, and even once I finished the book her voice seemed to linger in my head. This quote also leads into another thing I loved about this one: Temple's ability to see the beauty that exists even in her ravaged world. It's a reminder that no matter how dark your situation, the sparks of light are always there if you look for them.

A beautifully written book, with a protagonist I adored and some memorable supporting characters. I had to give it 5 stars.

An amazing read!

I set myself a challenge in January 2012 to read more horror and Zombie realted books, along the way I have encountered some really awful pieces of literary garbage, but what kept me going was finding gems like The Reapers Are the Angels.

It's beautiful and savage all at the one time. While it has the horror of the wandering 'Meatskins' Alden doesn't rely solely on horror to forward the narative. Temple's character is insantly likeable, she's bold, she's the kind of smart you don't learn at school, she's tough and vulnerable all wrapped into one. There's a line late on in the novel where Temple regards a deceased couple, the result of suicide, she hates them for giving in, 'at least the meatskins found somethin woth desiring. They keep on keeping on till the very last minute when they fall over in a pile of dust.' And that's how she intends to be, even if her reason for 'keeping on keeping on,' is to be pursued by someone out to kill her in a deadly game of cat and mouse, or traveling to see Niagara or a giant Iron man, she chases for a purpose that's always over the horizon.

I will certainly be looking out for more books by this author as I start into another reading challenge for the year ahead!

I really liked this because there was more going on here than your standard zombie story and in that way really distinguished itself from some of the other monster apocalypse stuff I've read recently--specifically I'm thinking of The Passage series with its (well-executed but) standard lets-go-on-a-quest-to-fix-the-world trope and Zone One beating you over the head with its "I have met the zombies and THEY ARE US" thing. In this one, the post-apocalyptic world is just a setting...our protagonist was born into it and accepts it and so the book is much more about how she finds beauty and tries to do right in a world that to us is very ugly and very wrong. As she says, "Blind is the real dead," and "Stayin alive ain't the hard part. The problem is stayin right." I was a little thrown by the characters' voices at first (not sure why a zombie apocalypse would make everyone talk like old-timey prospectors?) but it grew on me. Really really REALLY graphically gory in spots too, but not gratuitous. Great book.

Alden Bell’s apocalyptic tale of zombies, is a breath of fresh air. The protagonist, Temple is a young girl of 15, born into the world of the undead. An orphan who becomes a warrior. Although we don’t know the time frame in the story, we do know that it began some 25 years ago, a short enough time for the remnants of a world now passed can still be imagined by Temple as she travels across the country looking at God’s miracles. Although there is plenty of blood and gore when she encounters the undead, the story is basically one of survival and self-discovery.
Bell’s uncanny descriptive power makes for an amazing story. He doesn’t just tell, he shows us the life of young Temple as she seeks to do the right thing in a world gone wrong.
Not for a long time have I enjoyed a book so much. This copy was on loan from the library, but it’s one I will purchase for myself. Some books you can read over and over.
Although there’s no good guys and no bad guys per se, you’ll find yourself siding up with one against another. A truly good and fascinating read.
Alden Bell is a pseudonym for Joshua Gaylord. The author a teacher, has a truly awesome gift for words. His first book “Hummingbirds” was released in 2009. Look for more from this guy, I certainly will.

4,5 Sterne

"Nach dem Ende" ist zwar vordergründig ein Post-Zombie-Apokalypse-Roman, jedoch fühlte es sich für mich mehr wie ein Western an. Temple ist die einsame Hauptfigur, die sich zu perfekt auf das Überleben eingestellt hat, und sich deswegen bei alltäglichen Dingen, wie sie auch vor der Apokalypse stattfanden, fehl am Platz vorkommt.
Wir folgen ihr auf dem Roadtrip durch ein zerstörtes Amerika. Im Gegensatz zu vielen anderen Zombiestories interessiert sich der Autor dabei überhaupt nicht für die offensichtlichen Themen wie Ressourcenknappheit (trotz vieler Jahre seit der Zombie-Invasion gibt es noch Treibstoffreserven und teils auch Strom). Stattdessen muss sich Temple mit einem Rächer herumschlagen, der ihr beharrlich folgt, um tödliche Rache nehmen zu können. Die Zombies sind in dem epischen Duell hingegen nur Statisten, die nichtsdestotrotz gefährlich bleiben.
Das fand ich wie gesagt sehr westernmässig.

Das Buch liest sich sehr flüssig und ist stets unvorhersehbar. Warum man auf Anführungszeichen bei den Dialogen verzichtet hat, erschliesst sich mir nicht unbedingt - besonders anfangs ist das etwas irritierend.
Definitiv ein Highlight im Genre! Erinnerte ein wenig an Cormac McCarthy's The Road - aber weniger deprimierend.

I loved this book a lot, even though I have some problems with it. It's kind of like if The Walking Dead had a soul of beautiful shining light and hope, instead of horribly gratuitous goreporn. It's beautifully written, so thoughtful and full of heart, and really got under my skin. The characters are deep and touching, and the descriptions are breathtaking (sometimes in unpleasant ways, as well as gorgeous ones).
My big problems with it are in the internal logic of the world. The author seems to massively underestimate the amount of decay would occur in 25 years, both of the physical objects as well as the infrastructure of society. And the things he thinks Temple would recognize or know about, despite her upbringing, are pretty bizarre I think. I know it would be terribly limiting to write a book entirely from the point of view of someone with her life, but he made the choice to make her the narrator and so it's on him whenever I'm popped out of the world by thinking "wait, when would she ever have seen one of those?!"
If someone could have given him a brutally honest edit for those sorts of issues, this would be a perfect book. Maybe the second one addresses some of these things - I guess I'll have to hunt a copy down somewhere!

First line: "God is a slick god."

I've had this on my radar for a while and am glad I finally made the time to read it. It is in fact a zombie novel, and as plenty of blood and gore and a few nice twists on the standard myth to appeal to horror fans. But it goes beyond that in many levels. Temple is an amazing character, well rounded, innately strong but also fearful of her abilities. She was born after the zombie apocalypse occurred, and as such perceives the zombies to be part of the natural order. Their only threat lies in their mindless and constant hunger. She understands true evil does not come from nature (or zombies) but from humanity, and she fears that evil in hear self. Even with all the zombie fighting, the story generally has a mild pace with lots of introspection. It is also set in the Deep South and the setting is very detailed. Reviewers have likened this to Flannery O'Conner with zombies, and that's pretty accurate. It reminded me strongly of No Country for Old Men - which is an odd pairing, but one that just kept jumping to mind. It was a great read and could be enjoyed by many types of readers.

Whomever said this book was "Southern gothic with zombies" pretty much had things correct. The story explores some of the tropes (real or fantasized) of the South while guiding the reader through a post- (zombie-) apocalyptic world.

At the center of the story is a girl named Temple who is only 15 years old, but has already learned the rules of survival in this new world, and is already more of a woman (and sometimes more of a man) than those who remember a time without zombies. She takes a very existentialist view of her life and the walkers. This is the story of her interactions with the people she meets while winding her way through the southern U.S. in search of a safe place to rest.

The language is simple and occasionally poetic. Bell mixes succinct sentences with page-long Faulknerian rambles, both of which are sometimes too passive. My tastes run toward very active language and story that moves and does so quickly. The Reapers is a scenic walk instead of a sprint. Nonetheless, I enjoyed it. It picks up and gets more interesting in the second half, so if you find yourself struggling, stick with it and see what happens on the other side.

Holy Cow.

This one is a ride from start to finish. i read the entire thing in 48 hours (that's a feat when you work 16 of those hours). i couldn't put it down. the language is beautiful, Bell's non-use of quotation marks had me from hello. and the diction of the main character Temple is at once alarmingly hillbilly and Harvard professor in word choice. She is engaging and lovable from the first moment.

i think that my favorite part of the novel was that the zombies and apocalypse take a backseat to the story. it's just the background. The zoms are dangerous but Temple has always lived in their world and she behaves accordingly. there isn't any sappy nostalgia for the "old times" and most of the periphery characters act the same way.

my ONLY qualm with this book are the mutants. where did they come from and what purpose did they serve??? There are other ways to have imprisioned Moses, Temple and Maury and had them escape. But other than that, this book is an ace. i would recommend it to anyone who likes southern gothic, or as a friend put it, slightly toned down Cormac McCarthy

I hate to be the voice of dissent here, but I didn't like this book.

Yes, it's well written. Characterization was ok. Midway through the book I found myself rolling my eyes at the character of Moses Todd, which seemed like a rip from the Anton Chigurrh character of "No Country for Old Men." And then there's the plot itself, which seemed to be full of gaping holes. Assuming that the zombie plague happened 25 years ago and that 3/4 of the US population has been wiped out, why is Temple able to find basic working amenities such as viable gasoline, working cars, and running water? It would seem to me that a world nearly devoid of people 25 years later would seem more like a "Life Without People" (courtesy of the History Channel) scenario. And how are zombies able to survive for years with little to no food? That seems to, well, defy every sense of zombie logic I've encountered.

And then there's the ending. I won't give it away, other than to say it was quite predictable. I didn't want to leave Temple, I wanted the story to keep going until it found a better ending.

All in all, I'm dissatisfied. I got this book from the public library and I'm glad I did.

First off, I've read a lot of zombie fiction in the recent past. This is the first I've read in a while to be a little different. Instead of the "BRAINS!!" zombies of late, Bell (pseudonym) describes them as being more than just hungry for human flesh. They are creatures of instinct now. Lust and desire and fear and hunger and rage and joy are all wrapped up in that one instinct to consume. I liked that. It was interesting.

I also liked that the whole zombie aspect is old news in this world. People aren't living in abject terror. And for the ones like Temple who were born into this world, the "meatskins" are simply another fixture doing what they were "born" to do.

Now Temple. The story is really about a fifteen year old girl but I'd hesitate to say it's a "coming of age" tale. There is nothing about Temple that seems as though it needs to mature further. She doesn't need to "come of age". She is fiercely, heart-piercingly capable. A force to be reckoned with.

There's more to say and there's a lot more that I feel about it. But nothing is translating so it's time to stop there.

I am not really sure what to say about this book. It was beautifully written and deftly plotted. The characters are layered and interesting. I was able to be emotionally invested in a tough-as-nails young woman fighting zombies in a post-apocalyptic wasteland. I am giving this book four stars because of the gorgeous prose, the skillful allusions to other well-written literature, and the grotesque geniusness of the story.

What I liked:
-Temple and her love of beauty, optimism, and search for everyday miracles in a hellish setting.
-Allusions to well-written literature including but not limited to: Of Mice and Men, The Road, Gone With the Wind, etc.
-Plot twists and surprises
-Moments of "WHAT JUST HAPPENED?"
-Beautiful descriptions of settings throughout

What I ddn't like:
-The ending seemed in vain--the author took us on this epic journey only to end it like that
-The strange, obsessive, cat-and-mouse relationship between Temple and Moses
-Lack of quotation marks for the dialogue made it confusing at times
-Gore/detailed violence
-The book was labeled YA when it could have easily passed for Adult


Overall, I feel the positives outweighed the negatives.

This book is now one of my favorites and it has been awhile since I have been able to say that about anything I have read. It is just wierd, it is gross and it is human. The author does an awesome job of creating the characters and describing the scenery and surroundings. I loved the zombies, totally believable. I loved the fact that the author gave the human race a chance to survive. In most zombie movies or books I hate the fact that almost always the human race is over run and has not a chance for survival. I loved the main character Temple, I mean who can say anything negative about her. She is just kick ass. I loved the way the author made her dominate but then still made her human so that we could learn to love her. I have not read a book in a long time that the secondary characters also rocked. I have read many books that when I finish the final page I could not remember the name of the supporting cast. I loved them all every single one of them were perfect. I would love to live in this place zombies or not, it was just cool. The whole time I kept reading I kept thinking "Of Mice and Men" and "28 days Later". I would highly recommend this book.

I would recommend this book only to people who are really into the zombie apocalypse genre.

What the book does right: The book starts sometime after the onset of the zombie apocalypse. This gets things started right away and avoids the tedious explanation/description of the cause when it's really not integral to the story. I quite liked the ending

What the book does wrong: Unfortunately there is not much of a plot. It's mostly a set of events around the traveling of a teenage girl, Temple, who knows how to take care of herself...not quite an original concept. Also, the main characters have this odd morality code that didn’t seem at all believable to me and often makes them do really dumb things. Temple is supposed to be so smart and savvy, yet if she didn’t make a few painfully obvious mistakes the book would have no story at all. Finally, with a couple of exceptions, the book is also fairly predictable for anyone who has read this kind of story, or even seen a horror movie before.

Overall it's not a bad book, just not one of the better zombie books and certainly overrated on Goodreads in my opinion.

I absolutely love this book. It's like Cormac McCarthy's 'The Road' with zombies. It's every bit as lyrical, beautiful, brutal and haunting as The Road.

Temple is a 15 year old girl trying to navigate her way across an America in the grip of a zombie apocalypse. Along the way, she encounters other human travelers each trying to make their way as best they can. She eventually find a large, organised settlement, where she hopes she might find a place to stay. But a pretty young girl on her own doesn't just have to worry about zombies.

Fleeing from her soured haven, Temple comes across Maury, a docile, mute, mentally retarded man who is holding a piece of paper asking anyone who finds him to try and take him to his family. To ease her conscience at some of the things she has had to do, Temple decides to take Maury home. As the pair continue on their journey, dangerous enemies are following them, seeking revenge.

This is one of those books that I found myself reading with tears in my eyes and my jaw hanging open. It's pretty brutal, it's set in a harsh and alien landscape, but it's also tender, full of honour and unexpected kindness and totally unforgettable.

This is NOT what I was expecting....in a good way.

"Amid the hot stench of fresh offal, she rises to her feet like the dreadful ghost of a fallen battlefield soldier, her hands tacky with the thick pulpy dregs of death splayed wide.
The echoes of clamor having died on the puddled ground, the only sound in the room is the thin insectoid buzzing of three exposed bulbs suspended in ceramic sockets from the seiling overhead."


Lots of gore, explicit scenes, and kickass scenes. Although Temple is very young, this post-apocaliptic world has forced her to mature and harden.
She's a survivalist. But also a realist. The demons of her past haunt her, and this makes her keep to her self. To not get attached. Or so she thought.
She gets another chance to...redeem her self. To help another person, and heal her own wounds in the process. But its just not that easy.
Her decissions and actions have consequences, and she finds her self on the run, while still trying to help another soul.


Another story that keeps you on the edge of your seat, with an action packed story and great unexpected plot twists.

I found "The Reapers are the Angels" in the young adult section of the library. I was drawn in by the very first paragraph and once hooked, could hardly put it down. The book has a both a strong plot and very strong characters. And no, that last sentence isn't to be read with the silent trailer: "for a zombie apocalypse". It's just a strong story, fullstop. I would have been equally entranced by Temple (the fifteen year old girl-warrior protagonist) in a quieter setting.

The book is truly more like an Old-West movie, with Temple and her pursuer Moses playing out a morality tale (not like good guy vs evil guy, more in the sense of "using allegorical characters to portray the soul's struggle to achieve salvation") in a setting that just happens to have lots of zombies in it.

I think the question it asks is, which of us are truly the living dead?

Don't worry, there are plenty of for the gore-hungry among us. I'm not one of those and I really enjoyed this book.

Ok...this is a gem. I rarely get to say that, but I actually loved this book.

Although this is a story about zombies, or Slugs, as main character Temple likes to call them, they really just provide a reason for the characters journey rather than an obstacle impeding it.

The main character Temple is a simple person that has a funny,unique and insightful way of looking at the world that she was born into. Her views are honest and often hilarious. She is brave and caring even though she doesn't want to be. She is content with the hand that has been dealt and doesn't complain or over analyze things.

During her travels through the deep south of the U.S. she comes across a whole slew of remarkable characters, some good, some not so good, and some down right freaky, but each thing she takes in stride.

This book is an entertaining,witty, fast read that had me cheering for Temple and then left me completely devastated at the end. And while the ending of this book had me livid!!! Livid I say! And I wish that it had turned out differently, in way it was a means to an end, and though I was devastated, I was not disappointed.

Five giant stars!!

Det här blev lite av en överraskning för mig, jag hade förväntat mig en ungdomsbok utifrån temat postapokalyptisk undergång med zombietema. Istället fick jag en välskriven, utmanade och stark skildring sett ur ett barns perspektiv. Barnet är 14 år och heter Temple, hennes erfarenheter och visdom gör henne mer vuxen än gemene man. Ensamheten i ett land drabbat av The walking dead har gjort henne stark och hon har en överlevnadsinstinkt som kan jämföras med Wolverine. Medan den övriga världen försöker skapa små fungerade samhällen, föredrar Temple att gå sin egen väg, hon vill upptäcka världen och möter därmed en mängd olika människor och platser. Hennes mål är att nå Niagarafallen och få uppleva underverket med egna ögon.

Det är en riktigt bra bok som hör hemma i postapokalyptiska zombievärlden, den är inte en ungdomsbok utan passar mer i vuxenvärlden. Den är hård, grym och bitvis vidrig, även om det inte blir alltför ”splattrig”. Författaren är noga med fantasifulla detaljer, Temple plockar gärna med sig föremål från en svunnen tid. Hon grubblar mycket kring vad de är och vad de kan ha använts till. Boken rekommenderas för dig som gillar en kort exposé inom denna genre.

This is the third time I have read 'The Reapers are The Angels' and I enjoyed it as much as the first and second time I read it. The only difference from my last review is there was a sequel but not about Temple.

Review from January 2012:

This is the second time I have read 'The Reapers are The Angels' and as always with most of my re~reads I enjoyed it more the second time. Temple is a wonderfully vivid character, her strength, her confidence, her outlook of the world, her vulnerability shine through, she is only 15 years old and has learned to survive the best way she can by constantly moving, isolating herself and dealing with her own past, her guilt.

With my second reading, I found myself focusing more on the character of Moses Todd, a man who is pursuing Temple for his own reasons, which to his credit he sticks to throughout the book, despite whatever happens, like Temple, he is looking for redemption and they both find it.

Also with most books I usually see the potential for a sequel, this would never had worked with 'The Angels are The Reapers', Temple only has one story to tell and its hers.

A book I know I will read again and again.

For twenty-five years, civilization has survived in meager enclaves, guarded against a plague of the dead. Temple wanders this blighted landscape, keeping to herself and keeping her demons inside her heart. She can't remember a time before the zombies, but she does remember an old man who took her in and the younger brother she cared for until the tragedy that set her on a personal journey toward redemption. Moving back and forth between the insulated remnants of society and the brutal frontier beyond, Temple must decide where ultimately to make a home and find the salvation she seeks.

I hated this book! Spoiler alert- read no further if you plan on reading this book. I was invested in Temple and her plight, the people she meets and her ongoing feud with the brother of the man she has killed. Then the freakin' author ups and KILLS Temple at the end of the book. It wasn't even a logical ending. She is blown away by some mutant girl who doesn't like her - shot in the chest and buried by the man whose brother she killed, who had come to kill her as well, but didn't want anyone doing it but her. It was also pretty gritty- I wouldn't recommend the book in any case.

Devastating and beautiful and so very sad.

I worry about Maury.

And no, just because the protagonist is a 15-year old girl doesn't make this YA. It most decidedly is not, at least not in the US, because I am sure the dogged protectors of the CHILDRUN would have a conniption at the idea that a 15 year old might initiate sex with a 25 year old man. *sigh*.

It's not really about zombies either. Or about plausible scenarios -- somehow the people who whine about the unlikelihood of Alden Bells survivors still having the use of electricity despite 25 years of the zombie apocalypse are not bothered by the zombies at all. Sheesh. The book is about us. Whether or not we can still have ice in our coke, something we would damn well really cherish in that world isn't particularly important.

I can't do it justice because I lack sleep and therefore my brain might as well be zombified. But I really, really liked this; Temple is a fantastic character who will stay with me longer than she has been in Alden Bell's apocalyptic world. I have no idea whether Faulkner would be proud but I am. 4 stars, not 5 because of the ending. Damn you, Alden Bell; I was hoping you would not go there.

Meatskins- may favorite name for zombies yet. Not sure what to write about this one yet..I'm still in the what to think about it mode. The story follows the journey of Temple a 16 year girl surviving on her own, several years after the zombie Apocalypse first happened, she's pretty badass, she has a kind heart but also a dark violent and it's something she struggles with. Throughout the book she's kind of trying to avoid her ultimate fate, which you never really sure is going to play out in the end. While she's out to protect herself in order to survive, the reader sees that she definitely has a soft spot for others in spite of trying not too. There are other characters she encounters but you don't get to know them very well and you don't really get to know Temple well either because there's a lot she doesn't know about herself. It's a fast read, there's action, some gore and also parts where Temple is introspective and flashes back. It's a -good- book and if you're looking for a zombie read it's worth picking up- it's a quick read too.

(This is found in the young adult section of the library but is really not a YA novel. I don't know why stories with teenage protagonists are often automatically marketed as such!)

15/16-year-old Temple wanders the desolate landscape of a post-apocalyptic America, fighting off zombies and the unwanted advances of unsavoury men. There aren't many people left, and the natural beauty of her country is lain out for her sole appreciation. Temple dreams of the Niagara Falls, but doesn't really have any set goals in the way she meanders around the country, getting sidetracked into sending people back where they belong.

Alden Bell's lovely prose - reminiscent of Cormac McCarthy in some parts - makes this dystopic setting somehow spiritually enriching. I can see how criticisms of him being too derivative hold true - I do take issue with the many Gothic characters who appear in the book (the mentally handicapped giant, the creepy entombed family in a mansion) - but these seem quibbles in the face of the unusually, heart-achingly beautiful America he creates.

I thought The Reapers are the Angels was an interesting read. I chose this book for an Alex awards challenge I signed up for. It was written for adults but has elements that will appeal to a mature teen audience as well. Zombies have infested a fallen America but it is so much more than just a zombie book. Set in the South, it has western elements along with some stereotypical Southern characters. There is horror and violence but it is certainly more character driven. At 15 years old, the main character Temple (who only knows the world since the zombie infestation) definitely has a strong and unique voice. She really draws you into the story. She meets lots of strange characters on her journey that impact her and definitely leave their mark. The story raises some interesting questions and will most certainly leave you thinking. The ending was a surprise for me which was a good and a bad thing.

The Reapers are the Angels is not your typical run of the mill zombie book. So if you are looking for something different within the genre I would recommend this book.

I bought this yesterday and finished it today, though I needed to linger over certain passages just to parse out their loveliness. With multiple allusions to classic Southern Gothic works (the Griersons echo that most infamous of Southern ladies, Miss Emily Grierson, and there's a Caddy/Maury Compson dynamic going on as well), this book moves well beyond the corpse-strewn highways of zombie pulp and into the ranks of true literature. Oh yeah, did I mention it's about zombies? But not really--no, the zombies don't stand for capitalist greed, as they do in "Dawn of the Dead," "Sean of the Dead," or WORLD WAR Z; they're just...um...zombies. But the book is really about the way the "Caddy" character--15-year-old Temple--views the world through a peculiarly Southern prism. Gorgeous passages pile up like bodies waiting to burn. It also reminded me of Cronin's THE PASSAGE, arguably one of my favorite books--but that may be just because there's a train in both. I will definitely re-read this at some point.

This book really surprised me. It presents itself in an unassuming, quiet way; the first few pages introducing a world a reader might be familiar with from other stories. The zombie apocalypse is trending right now but this story was made true by the main character, Temple, who often went around calling herself Sarah Mary. Temple is tough and she is a serious survivor. Hidden beneath that rough exterior is a young girl of fifteen years that has learned to staunch emotion almost immediately. A back story involving a young boy named Malcolm is revealed to us slowly through her very erratic memories, but once we learn the whole truth we can see why she is the way she is.
