I don't want to give too much away. There are other characters that are as thought provoking--Maury and Moses Todd--but Temple constantly surprises the reader with her mature mentality, deep thoughts on life and death, and the inevitable end for everyone. I highly recommend this book to anyone who would like something a little different.

After reading The Passage, this book seems like a YA novel or something. Maybe I would have liked it more if I hadn't read that first, but this book just seemed to gloss over a lot of the realism that The Passage had. I guess I just can't seperate them and not compare them, and that's my problem with it. A little too much god talk too. I mean, seriously, if you were born into a new world with zombies in it, and had no recollection of the world before, and can't read and stuff, how would you have any concept of god and religion, and what you think gods plan or whatever is? It just didn't make sense that someone would have taught her about god and not taught her to read, because I think knowing how to read sounds like it may help a little better in a zombie apocalypse. Just saying. Also, probably my biggest problem with this book was the fact that the writer chose not to use quotation marks or italics when people were speaking. It made it confusing, and I couldn't see the point of why an author would choose to do that.

A small book about big ideas. If you are going to buy into the zombie apocalypse craze, this is the way to do it--you create something beautiful and strange, you make your heroine brave and clever, and you find the dignity of the living rather than the horror of the dead.

Channeling the voices of Cormac McCarthy and William Faulkner didn't hurt, either.

But the fact of the matter is, Alden Bell, with lyrical language and musical pacing, tears apart all expectations by finding the beauty in a world that has past, by finding the sorrow in monsters, by picking up the concept of grief like a precious stone and casting a light at it until it sits there gleaming in your palm. The quiet moments in this barren wasteland will break your heart. In a world full of walking dead, Bell leaves kindness and joy like breadcrumbs toward an inevitable and heartrending end.

"The abundance of gone things, it'll bury you," Bell writes. "The Reapers Are The Angels" is about a world full of gone things, and the small points of light left behind.

This was quite a beautiful novel to read. Unusual, when you consider that it is a zombie novel, and has its share of gory death (though this is by no means the main emphasis of the book). But the way it is written is very evocative, and you fall a bit under the spell of Temple, the protagonist of the book.

What keeps it from getting the 5 stars? Well, a couple of things jar. Mostly it is the occasional reference to things that belong to a world 25 years old being as good as they were so long ago (coke not losing its fizz?), and places in not that out of the way parts of America not being completely picked clean over that length of time (especially with cars still roaming freely, and there being some decently sized settlements referred to). That, and I get that Temple, having been alone for most of her life, wandering the world, would grow up fast. but even so there are some things that seem just a little too advanced.

However, these are little things, in what is otherwise a lovely - yes, lovely! - read.

Definitely a 4.5 star book.

I read this entire thing in one sitting because I couldn't put it down. It had everything I look for in a book: depth, internal struggle, beautiful writing, heavy subjects and grittiness. I was completely enthralled in the atmosphere, the world itself, the characters. I even cared about the side characters no matter how briefly they appeared in the book. That's true talent.

Temple.. that girl, I swear. What a bad ass. I really liked her, how fierce she was, and her edginess. A wonderful, strong female character.

I thought I'd point something else out. The lack of quotation marks around speech was, at first, a little jarring. Then it became part of the book's flavor. It really matched with the quietness and desolation of the book, if that makes sense. As if the quotation marks would have made it too "loud" or would have disturbed the overall feel of the atmosphere. Without them, it makes the world in this book a lot more lonely. It was a nice, surprising touch.

I highly recommend reading this book.

After i finished i came directly here to write something. I actually searched for "googlebook" for some reason.. This illustrates my state of mind right now. I loved the book. Can't seem to think about anything else except after that ending i'm left thinking... 'Wut?'

Also this is a 4.5 stars because i wish there would have been something more.. This is one of those books i would have liked to be in more then one tomes. Maybe a tome dedicated to those secondary characters that lack something in comparison to Temple.

In a world full of zombie novels, this one is really unique and strangely beautiful - despite being pretty grim and gory. The back of the book describes it as Southern Gothic zombie. It is that, with rotting mansions and an old wealthy family with secrets, but there's also a wild west element to the story. It all leads up to a showdown between the protagonist and her sort of fated antagonist, in an apocalyptic landscape. I don't know how I feel about the ending yet, but I can say that I think it was as unique as the rest of the book...and that this story will linger in my memory for a long time.

Another thing I really liked about this book was the lens through which the main character sees the zombie infested world - it's still a place of "crackerjack miracles" and things she wants to see and learn and be. She was born into it, it's just how the world is for her. All of that adds a layer of painful, tender hope to a hopeless, violent, bloody life, and that makes the whole thing ache a little bit, in the way that makes a story stronger.

Ok, yes, the punctuation thing bothered me for about 15 pages. But then...

What a great book! Loved the way the story unfolded, and the relationship between the two main characters becomes surprisingly complex. Told in close first, it is a very nice perspective on a world gone to hell, and the people trying to rebuild.

I'm more of a genre junkie, and read things that easily pass the time on the bus going to and from work. But every once in awhile, I want something with substance. The Reapers delivered. The language was used beautifully, the story was well-paced, there was plenty of suspense interspersed with introspection and philosophy, the characters were (for the most part**) quite engaging.

** I wasn't crazy about the mutants, but they did serve for an interesting change of pace and helped push the story in an interesting direction.

So. If you're looking for quick to gobble pulp, The Reapers isn't the right book. If you're looking for a very well-written, very human story in a post-apocalyptic world that will leave you very satisfied when you're done, you'll love it.

This is not a zombie book. This is a drama about a young girl navigating the apocalypse and making it her own. It is lushly written. Parts make me feel I emerged from a long Faulkner paragraph.

There ARE zombies in it. And a bad guy hunting our hero down for reasons that are good only his mind (and yet understandably so). But it is not a zombie book.

It's a book about us, and about how much fun we will no doubt be if anything even close to an apocalypse (no internet, cheap crappy food no longer easily available) ever happens to us. Things like this DO happen in other parts of the world, where "apocalypse" isn't an entertainment genre.

The book surprised me, it even shocked me a couple times (and that's hard to do). I loved the hero, for all her 13-year-old flaws (or was it 15? can't remember now). I loved the setting. I loved the token scene that was a nod to "The Walking Dead". I read the sample on Amazon and was so delighted by the setting (a lighthouse) and the hero that I purchased it immediately.

Really this is a 4.5 star book only because I didn't care for the end. This is not a spoiler.
The Zombie plague happened a long time before the main character was born. A life with Zombies is the only one she knows. She has glimpses of the past through houses, people who are much older than herself (she's 15 if I remember correctly), magazines, etc. She is a tough loner girl who has clearly had a hard life. She is so kick ass you just can't help but love her.
This book is about her journey encountering & killing Zombies, & the trials of dealing with her own non zombie kind.
Even though I didn't like the end, others who read this might think it goes perfect with the book & suits it well. I was hoping for a happier ending. One that felt more hopeful for the fate of the human race. Another may have the point of view that it is hopeful, but it just made me sad. Aside from that, I loved this book!
If you like Zombie books, then I think you will like this too & decide for yourself how you feel about the end.
Happy reading! And remember a Zombie only loves you for your brains.

I went back and forth about giving this one 5 stars, but since I haven't been able to stop thinking about it and read almost all of it yesterday in one sitting....

Just an illiterate BADASS of a teenage girl living in a zombie-filled world.



I only have a couple quibbles:

1) No quotations for dialogue. I realize this is a stylistic choice of sorts, but to me personally it just ends up looking messy/disordered. It messes with the rhythm of how I read in my head and 'hearing' the inflections, etc of how things are said.

2) THAT ENDING THO.

3) The fact that there is a ghost third book that exists but might never get published so that's lovely that I KNOW THAT AND CAN'T GET MY HANDS ON IT.

The writing is just... If it were a type of food? I would want to eat so much of it that I made myself sick. So I will keep my eyes out for two of his other books I've added to make sure I get my hands on them ASAP.

Curious to see what #2 is like since it's a prequel/sequel.

I picked this up because an article online called the author the Cormac McCarthy of zombies. Once I was able to dispel the notion, I actually enjoyed this book. I'm tempted to make my own comparisons, but the book jacket's call on Flannery O'Connor is pretty close. The novels, not the short stories.

On its own merits, the novel is flawed but deeply enjoyable. Bell seems to have acquired some animosity from the die-hards incensed that this post-apocalyptic world has a semi-functional power grid. That doesn't bother me (and even seems more probable than the alternative...we really like electricity). Rather, my only complaint was with passages that tried a little too hard. Like using the word "residuum". I mean. Come on. Clever, but narrative interrupting. Great authors interrupt, but with a purpose besides innovative prose. Thus, Bell is a good writer, not great. Yet. But a good writer with an eloquent voice taking on a "crackerjack" heroine in the zombpacolypse? How do you say no to that? How do you not revel in that?

What makes The Reapers are the Angels a beautiful read is the author's skill with language. Gaylord's imagery and personification of nature is unique, and it's been a while since I read a book that drew me so deeply into the story. Temple is a unique main character with an inner strength that I think any of us would hope to have when facing a worldwide apocalypse. But she doesn't just fit the "kick ass" mold. She's also kind and thoughtful with some of the best lines in the book. The story is fast paced and definitely a quick read, you're not going to get bored with it. And it's more than a zombie slasher story. Rather than the creatures taking front and center stage, it's the humans that Temple encounters along her journey. And through their actions and words we learn that it's not the undead that become the sole monsters in a post-apocalyptic world. Readers of The Reapers are the Angels will experience a story filled with beautiful detail, fast paced action, and revelations about our culture that has the potential of making anyone see the world a little differently.

I am a big fan of the southern gothic style of writing and also love zombies and the Apocalypse style end of the world books. This book came heavily recommended and really didn't disappoint. The story telling is well done and you can hardly stop yourself from turning page after page as you get deeper into the story and head towards a well done ending.

As you would expect from this gothic genre the characters are rich and deeply flawed with grotesque elements. The lead character is a young girl which makes a refreshing change from the norm and the writer does a good job of writing in her voice and conveying her personality. On her journey she meets some fantastical and macabre characters all coping with the new world order in their own interesting ways.

The story is interesting and in many ways resists many of the cliches of both the zombie and apocalypse genre. We meander through a number of well described locations and the story keeps a good pace. The book is well worth a read and is vastly superior to the average Zombie fest.

Disclaimer: I really I don't think this is a bad book. It's just one of these cases where a reading quirk I have is interfering. Tell me if I'm the only one here, but the (perfectly valid!) stylistic choice on the author's part to not add quotation marks when a character is speaking drives me up the wall. It's honestly all I can pay attention to when I'm reading the story.

I first came across this last semester when a required text, The Brief Wondrous Life of Oscar Wao had this same technique. I didn't really have a choice, so I read the book and yes, I did get used to it. But it bothered me. It didn't stop bothering me, even when I read it through multiple times when I did a term paper on the novel.

I guess every reader has little things that piss them off: plot devices, tropes, writing styles. And this is just one of mine. It's sad though because it sounded from other reviewers that this was something awesome.

3.75 stars

A zompocalypse story that's a little different, both in content and in delivery. I kind of felt sometimes like I was reading The Odyssey in that the main character goes through a series of bizarre and seemingly unrelated events while wandering around the country.

If I were still a member of the Alex Awards committee, I'd be nominating this adult novel as soon as possible! It's creepy and deliciously good. It's suspenseful, but not choppy. It's beautifully written (a little too verbose for me in parts) and very, very descriptive. And it's about zombies.

Temple is on her own wandering around (think The Forest of Hands and Teeth) and she reminds me of River Tam from Firefly. Temple can kick some booty, especially dead booty. But her internal struggle is like that of River's. Sure, Temple can kill and protect the weak. But she's still killing zombies, and even some alive humans in the process. She's searching for salvation, wandering across America searching for a reason to live.

Now, why didn't I give it 5 stars? I'm sorry, but no paragraph should ever consist of one sentence that is 16 lines long (as seen on page 177). I don't care if I'm reading a fun novel or high-fa-luting literature, that just isn't necessary.

Wow! This book is easily the best zombie story I've read in a long time. It's not really about the zombies, which are mostly just in the background. Instead it's about the journey the main character, Temple, is on. I kept picturing her looking like a younger version of Starbuck in Battlestar Gallactica, a little blonde thing who is not to be underestimated and could totally kick your arse.

It was refreshing to read a zombie story that wasn't about the breakdown of society. Temple was born after the dead rose and doesn't know any different, and is rightly sceptical about the stories she's told of how wonderful the world supposedly was before. She accepts the world as it is and just deals with the challenges it presents as they come up.

I can't really put into words just now what it is about this book that affected so much but I have a feeling that it will stay wiht me for a long time.

What a powerful and unassuming book. Alden Bell has an uncanny strength as a writer to curl up inside your thoughts, showing you his imaginative world with grace and poise. I have not been touched emotionally by many of the recent books I've read, but "The Reapers Are the Angels" is a quiet book filled with silences of emotional orchestral beauty.

Bell's protagonist, Temple, is a delight to befriend as she travels the lost world in hope of the search that we all have--finding who we are, coming to terms with our humanity, our darkest impulses and why we choose (or don't) to rise up toward the light and what is right.

Without pretension, explanation or wasteful exposition, Bell weaves a tale that's harrowing and thoughtful. If you're not into zombie and horror, do not allow the topic to scare you off. You'll be pleased that you read this book as Bell's novel will stay with you long afterward.

Someone wrote that this book is like Flannery O'Connor with zombies, and while I haven't really read anything by her, the language style did remind me of Kaye Gobbons' "Ellen Foster." Temple is a shrewd, tough-as-nails fifteen year old trying to survive the "slugs/meatskins" (slang for zombies), traveling north from Florida while managing to survive. Just as often she has to protect herself from the living, but she seems to be drawn to trouble (even if she manages to hold her own), in a way that makes you think she sees it deep down and some sort of penance. As hardened as Temple is, I found myself rooting for her, as best as one can for a girl that shuns reliance on anyone and suspects kindness from anyone. Redaers who take to her will follow her in the book, rooting for her to find a satisfying life somehow. At 225 pages, it's a quick if gritty read. It appears some people have a love/hate thing going on with this book--I loved it.

This is a distinctly different zombie book. The zombies have been around for centuries and the young heroine, Temple, knows how to deal with them. Picture Summer Glau in the movie,Serenity, and you have an idea of the methods Temple uses. She travels around the United States, like so many people during this time, trying to stay ahead of the zombies and of her memories. As she travels, Temple ponders God and His grace, right and wrong and whether or not she is good or evil. Warning - if you don't like Southern-speak or William Faulkner, you will probably not enjoy Temple's "pondering" but if you have a tolerant attitude toward sentences like "See, it's a daily chore tryin to do the right thing. Not because the right thing is hard to do - it ain't. It's just cause the right thing - well, the right thing's got a way of elduing you." (p. 167). This book is short, only 225 pages but you may find yourself savoring the sentences and rereading them for a while. I recommend it.

I would never think that prose and philosophy could be included in a zombie book, but here it is. I don't think I've read many books in my life that have such beautiful use of language. I'm a believer in the power of words, and boy, does Alden Bell know how to manipulate language and weave a fabric of incredibly strong and gorgeous narrative.

I consider this book largely allegorical, and for a book with zombies (or "slugs" as they're called here), zombies have very little to do with it. This is a book about how children feel the need, and are forced by society and nature to become adults before their time. To abandon their innocence, to grow up and try to make sense of the crazy and confusing adult world. Temple is a girl with a wisdom way past her 15 years, with courage and strength unseen in many other book characters.

This book is tragic from beginning to end. But the knowledge of hope resting between the lines is resonant and dauntless.

"God is a slick God. Temple knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe."

How can you read this first paragraph of Alden Bell's book and not immediately pick it up and finish it? This is a more literary take on the current zombie apocalypse craze. Though I would agree with a previous review that it is more of a character study than a zombie story.

Temple is just a fantastic character with a fantastic voice. The plot is a classic Odyssey/road trip, but is well executed. My favorite random detail involves Temple's flashbacks to a pivotal event taking place in front of Tulsa's "Golden Driller" statue (thanks Google), which is a supercool landmark. I hadn't thought of it in like a decade, but her memory made me think back to a day when I was driving along in Tulsa, and just happened on to this random, awesome artwork. I know how she felt when she saw it.

Solid work. If you like the genre, give it a shot.

I really enjoyed this book. It was a quick read and it took no time to get me into the story. It took me a chapter or two to get used to the fact that Bell did not use quotation marks for the story's dialogue, but once I figured it out it was easy to adjust to.

But I'm not really sure how I feel about the ending. With most protagonists, you want them to typically live. I don't like how Temple got killed, and I really don't like the fact that she got killed at all. I was expecting Maury to come up behind Moses with that paperweight and clobber him in the back of the head. I was really hoping that Maury would end up saving Temple since she ended up doing so much for him, but unfortunately, that never happened. I also wanted to know more about the strange mutants that they came across. But overall it was a fantastic read and I think anyone that is into zombie/post-apocalyptic books will enjoy it.

Got about 3.5 stars. Lost a half point for not using Third person to its full advantage, may as well have been in first person as i didnt get any additional info from it which you really needed for Moses. Altho its nice not having to read about a characters every thought. And the last star is lost because of the mutants... why?? And what the heck... feels like they were chucked in for some random reason. It also seemed like Bell didn't know how the book was going to end, it's like he got to page 300 or whatever and decided okay lets wrap it up i've done enough.

All the other poor points were okayish to overlook such as the lights, gas, never ending bullets/coke/ice/crackers, Temples knowledge and language use for things she would have never experienced, weird crap about god, using an elevator, the dumb ending, the lame drawn out revelation about Malcolm (it wasnt worth building suspense for) and the random remark about birth control and the reason not to use it.

Well this was a really good dystopian tale, despite having zombies in it. Don't be put off by them by the way, they are do not feature too much and don't get in the way of the story.
I enjoyed the characterisation and the rawness of emotions, particularly Temple and Moses. The hunt/chase between these too is excellent, I could feel them battling with their emotions and respect for each other. I did expect more from the Malcolm storyline - that was a bit of a let down. There are some gory bits and it's sometimes bleak reading but the author isn't scared of being unpredictable and thankfully didn't take the easy option with her characters.
The only downside is the lack of speech marks, I found this unnecessary, annoying and sometimes confusing. The negatives pointed out by others about the readily available crackers/petrol/electricity didn't really bother me but they are silly inconsistencies that should have been better explained.

The Reapers Are the Angels utterly surprised me. Most post-apocalyptic books follow a tirelessly predictable pattern: loner hero goes on a journey that somehow enables him or her to bring the world back from destruction. I picked up this book thinking it would be a quick and easy read.I was only partially right. It was a fast read, but mostly because I was engrossed in the story and the language. The Reapers Are The Angels is not what I would call an easy read. For most of the novel, I was at the uneasy place that is the crossroads between disturbed and intrigued. Alden Bell captures the nature of a dystopia and the the people in it. You'll like Temple, even as you struggle to figure out her motives. The language Bell chooses fits perfectly if you're trying to explain God in such a dark and distressing place.

There are zombies, but its not a zombie novel - it's a compelling story of a human journey to reconcile faith, life, and ever-present tragedy and danger.

(Book club book) Loved this book way more than I expected! Loved Temple's voice, loved her attitude, loved her strength, loved her way of looking for miracles in a world that would otherwise seem void of all hope. Also loved that there was no need to explain how things got to be this way. No long explanation of how the world came to be inhabited by zombies. It's just how it is. Now, I'm usually looking for a "happily ever after" in my favorite books and this one does not have that at all. But the end seemed right and in a strange way was satisfying in a "this is the way it had to be" kind of way. No wondering what happened later on. This story seemed to sum up life in a way - you come into the world as it is, you find your way in it, you wonder if you're doing the right thing, there are little miracles among all the day to day stuff, and in the end something finally gets you. Hopefully not zombies!

This was a beautifully written story about one bad-ass girl who grew up in a world overtaken by zombies, abandoned by mankind. It takes place decades after zombies have pretty much messed up the whole world, and it's all she's ever known. So to her zombies are a way of life, and killing them is as normal to her as washing her hair. Still, something inside her knows it isn't right, despite it being all she knows. There are some other characters, but it's mainly a story about her wrestling with her own inner demons and trying to survive. Lots of great paragraphs, definitely approached as a literary work and not just a shock-fiction-horror novel. Sometimes the author goes a bit far in his verbosity which got annoying over time. But not that annoying, I still appreciated the attempt to make the sentences so beautiful when describing things so horrifying. And for the most part the author succeeded in threading beauty into this gritty narrative.

Surprisingly I really enjoyed this book. I'm usually not a very big reader of zombie books but I thought this one was done with a lot of taste. I didn't feel like a syfy nerdy zombie book. The author had unusual writing technique (he didn't use any quotations) but one thing a liked about his writing was his characters. Every character you met was in great detail and popped from the book. Temple, the lead, was born into this world so she had never seen anything different. She always found good in a situation, she always found her God doing something for her, and I thought that was something everyone could take from this book and apply it to their lives. On a side note, the author (Alden Bell) is married to big time Edgar-writing crime author, Megan Abbott. That fact was practically his whole bio, which made me feel a little bad for him.

I made it to Chapter 13 out of 16 and couldn't force myself to continue. There were just too many things that don't work. Temple's dialect was only annoying in that she was uneducated and spoke like she stepped out of the old west rather than Florida. Add to that her casual use of words like cartograph and it got under my skin.

In addition, the timeline was so ... off. 15 years old 25 years after the apocalypse and never ate in a diner but remembers airplanes. Never saw a record player except in movies? She was watching movies? Can't read and is only 15 but knows guns by name and identifies a "mid size Honda". The mutants were more insane than zombies and she never even mentions them to anyone. She just randomly "found" working gas pumps. She leaves her island because of a single washed up zombie and then singlehandedly takes on adult men, zombies, mutants and wins. Every time. Usually with a knife or no weapon at all.

My disbelief can only be suspended so far.

3 and a half stars. Okay where to start on this one. I liked it so don't get the 3 stars confused, actually 3 and a half! It was a storyline I haven't read before. It was about a young girl who is making a life for herself in the often barren wastelands of America after a zombie or meatskins outbreak as she calls them. Temple (14) was born into this life and doesn't know of *former* america before the attacks.
It was about life-coming-of-age (kind of) and survival - hopes and dreams and the stark reality of the often desolate areas Temple treks through trying to find the one beautiful place she keeps hearing about , Niagra Falls.
It was a good tight read and the only issue I had with this book was when Temple meets Maury the backwards loveable guy on her travels. I really took issue with her continually calling him dummy. I just found it offensive and the term overused. Call me sensitive but yes it was off putting to me in that I nearly didn't finish the book because of it!

Que ce soit clair : ce petit bouquin mange à tous les râteliers : un Walking dead mâtiné de La route de Cormac Mc Carthy (avec un style d'écriture beaucoup moins marqué) et saupoudré d'une pincée du Fléau de Stephen King. Alden Bell connaît ses classiques et sait s'en inspirer. En même temps, difficile de faire dans l'originalité avec un thème comme celui-là, déjà maintes fois traité. Un monde post-catastrophe, des zombies, des survivants endurcis par la situation... Quoi de plus classique?
Il n'en reste pas moins que le charme agit. Au bout du compte, pour moi, ce livre vaut bien ses 4 étoiles.
Le plus décevant, finalement, c'est que contre toute attente, j'ai trouvé ce livre beaucoup trop court, presque un simple prologue. A mon sens, il est dommage qu'Alden Bell n'ait pas eu plus d'ambition. J'aurais bien vu un pavé de 800 pages ! Il y avait matière.
Et non, le fait qu'il y ait une (fausse) suite ne change rien à l'affaire. :-)

About 1/4 of the way through this book I recognized certain elements that reminded me of other modern zombie fiction, namely World War Z and The Walking Dead. I resisted the urge to figure out which came out first until I finished the book because I thought that once I knew the answer one or the other would be ruined for me. While Reapers came out after both of them, I was able to view it more as a companion story than a ripoff. This is because there are also elements that are unique (or stolen from something I'm not familiar with).

Every form of zombie lore has it's own unique blend. Some are fast, some are slow, some starve, some don't, etc. Bell's "meatskins" have a couple of qualities that I haven't seen before and at times the main character borders on sympathy for them, and I did too.

Beyond that it's a quick read, and surprisingly fast-paced despite chunks that are beautifully verbose. It's well worth the short time it takes to read it.

it's gotten to the point of the market and my brain being oversaturated by Zombies and things that go bump in the night but this is not your run-of-the-mill zombie stories. Thank God. (God is slick)

The complete immersion I got from this story and the the characters is so rare that I have tried to read this book over the span of a week instead of one hour. But it's not pretentious and it's beautiful and lyrical and incredibly awesome.

"She thinks about the people she's known, the things she's seen. She thinks about the nation she's traveled since she was born, the derelict landscapes, the rain that washes the blood and dust into rust-colored puddles."

But down to earth and accessible: "God is a slick God. Temple knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe."

HELL YES. Read this. There are two more in the series and I am eager to read every word. Thank you Alden Bell!

If you're looking for a unique and thought provoking zombie book I definitely recommend The Reapers are the Angels. If you're looking for action packed horror, I don't.

The zombie genre is known for its at times overwhelming cynicism, which makes this book and its protagonist a big breath of fresh air. All about appreciating beauty and hope even when terrible things happen/have happened

I can see how the style, particularly how the dialogue is done could be off putting, but it succeeds in creating a dreamlike quality, almost like it's all just happening in the narrators head which makes for a very interesting read.

There is one major part that I'm not sure how to feel about. It didn't seem to quite fit in with the world or the rest of the book, and seemed like it was just sort of thrown in there because it seemed cool. But that may just be me, and without that part it's definitely a four star book for me.

Maybe nearer a 4 star. Through circumstances I ended up listening to this in disjointed chunks which probably distracted from the experience.

There were things I really liked about it though.

It was not your common or garden zombie apocalypse fare with zombies bad - humans good, or even humans 'backs against the wall' - more a challenging lifestyle where the canny survived.

The heroine - Temple was a wonderful character, neither beautiful and charismatic or kickass (though there is some of that). She is capable and thoughtful and very pragmatic. To a certain extent the 'baddy' (though he isn't really) is a similar character. Their unifying characteristic was to be comfortable in the world they inhabit and able to accept the good and the bad of it.

In that respect it reminded me somewhat of the Girl with all the Gifts which was another book that advocated living in the now - however bad - rather than trying to regain the world of some idealised past.

I read this book two years ago and still think about how awesome it is. Alden bell wjho name is really Joshua gaylord. It follows the life of a girl named temple who is fighting desperately to survive in a world wrought with zombies and crazy humans who will kill you for whatever you got.l it's obvious that temple has been through alot at the beginning of the story. In fact as it progress you notice how she recalls long forgotten memories of her younger brother who we discovered is kill earlier before the novel. While on a pit stop things go awry for her and before she know it she is being chased by men who want revenge on her for something she didn't mean to do. Along the way we get to see how other humans adapt to their new surrounding since the apocalypse began 25 years ago. In the end this is a heart felt novel of survival and perseverance in a world where you lost everything but still want to live. This book is well worth the read in my opinion. Especially for fans of zombies.

Hmmm What can I say? i have to give it a 3. I enjoyed the content as I am a massive horror fan and the story content was interesting.
Except the giant zombie people, didn't get that not thought it was really relevant to the story to be honest!

BUT.......My MAIN issue with this book is the lack of grammar and punctuation, making it exceptionally difficult to read.

In primary school we are always taught that when someone is speaking we use " "
This book doesn't have any making conversations between the characters hard to read and as a consequence I was unable to fully submerge myself within the book because I was constantly thinking about is there a a new rule to writing about doing away with speech marks that I don't know about?

Then I am even more baffled by the fact that the author has a Phd in English and actually teaches it!

To sum up. Poor writing spoils what could potentially be a good book.

The Angels are the Reapers (Holt pbk, $15.00, 225 pages, ISBN 978-140-134133-6) by Alden Bell.

It was described to me as a “quirky book” before I read it. All I can say is it’s in fact a quirky one. If you like the works of writers like H.P. Lovecraft, Brian Lumley or Stephen King at his goriest . . . The Angels are the Reapers has more decapitations, blood and guts than a sausage factory at stuffing time. The author’s flesh-craving zombie-vampire fest ignores the what and the why and the when to focus on the who and where in the form of a fifteen, “I’ll be sixteen next week,” year-old girl with a mission, a quest, and a ghurka knife. Should you choose to read this southern gothic, I can promise you’ll be entertained and you won’t soon forget the protagonist, a girl named Temple. All this comes from the pen of a high school English teacher in New York City who moonlights as a creative writing instructor at The New School. It’s not for the faint of heart however.

While the plot felt constructed and some of the characters felt flat, overall, it is a good book with some key themes that would make a good book club discussion.

Starting off with what I didn't like. The plot felt like it was moving through a series of constructed events, each with a mostly new set of characters that I didn't get to know well. Overall, it felt a bit flat and dull.

While I wasn't the most impressed with the plot, it does have merit with critical analysis. Temple's character is well built up and I can think of some central themes that this book explores well. I would enjoy having conversations about this book and the characters in it.

Overall rating 3/5 stars
1 star: Terrible book, didn't finish it
2 stars: Fair book, finished it, but didn't really enjoy it
3 stars: Decent book, finished it, but probably won't read again
4 stars: Great book, would recommend to friends/reread
5 stars: Phenomenal book, would reread right now

Of all the books I've read so far this year, THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS is one I keep coming back to. I can't stop thinking about Temple, a young girl in the barren wasteland that is America, who can't remember a time when she wasn't trying to outrun zombies and stay a step ahead of would-be predators. Temple forges ahead against all odds, sometimes with only faith to keep her going, encountering character after character -- a wealthy family holed up in their estate, a "dummy," post-apocalyptic cowboys, and a man named Moses, who will follow her to the end of the earth in the name of revenge. REAPERS is a striking novel, as creepy as THE ROAD but also as artfully written and emotionally intense. With a fiery female protagonist, a twist around every corner, and enough monsters to keep you awake all night, Alden Bell's novel isn't one you'll soon forget either.

A curiously underwhelming tale of the Zombie Apocalypse. It's far less bloated than Justin Cronin's similarly-themed post-apocalyptic epic The Passage, clocking in at only 225 pages, but after a strong, eerie start it just goes from too many plot-holes (why 25 years after humankind has been nearly wiped out by the living dead are there gas pumps with gas still in them and running water and working electrical outlets all over the place?) to too many tired thriller tropes (every time the main antagonist has the heroine at gunpoint he begins to monologue, thereby providing her, of course, with the means to escape). The folksy religious musings of both the heroine and her antagonist ultimately became rather tiresome as well. Author Alden Bell has a sure hand with prose and there are some inspired passages throughout, but not quite enough for me to recommend this one.

I'm not sure how to review this book. I guess the most succint way is to say it's in the top ten books for me in the last five years. The writing is just staggering in its sincerity, its perfect clear simplicity and the talent of the author is overwhelming. I've read some really good books of late (lucky me!) and this outshines them all.

This reads old school southern classic and if you say zombies, it might make you laugh. I've never seen anything close to The Reapers Are the Angels. I'd never dream of anyone doing a zombie novel this way. Ever.

I'll be looking for more from this author. I'll also be tucking this book lovingly on my shelf. Reading and rereading it and then some years down the road rereading it again.

Kudos and thanks to Alden Bell for what I consider a literary work of art.

Published for adults, this is a perfect crossover for teens: Creepy, gothic, exciting, and thought-provoking. And it's all about zombies! Temple is a kick-ass heroine: she does whatever it takes to survive in her zombie-infested world. But it causes her a real moral dilemma: is she evil for destroying God’s creatures, no matter how monstrous? And then there are the pockets of civilization filled with people who aren't entirely good either. In one, a man tries to take "unsolicited liberties" with her. Temple takes care of the situation the best way she knows how: she kills him. Now the man's brother, Moses, is after her, too. The funny thing is, Moses is the only one who understands her. The tortured landscape feels real. The author has created fully dimensional characters and the dialogue is rich. Even if zombie lit isn't your thing, give this one a try.

Overall, I did like this book, but I was somewhat disappointed. Parts of it are beautifully written, and it is easy to become fond of Temple, the main character. However, there is a section of this book that just ruined the entire story for me. I realize it is important to suspend disbelief when one is reading a book about zombies, but when an author sets the framework for a book like this, and then drops something in the middle that is completely outside of this framework and just seems too fantastical, even with a willing suspension of disbelief .... well, it ruined the entire story for me. It went from good story to bad B (or C) movie back to decent story -- only made less decent by the descent into cartoonish violence. So, I couldn't rate this more than a three because of that but, overall, it's not a bad read.

This book is more like 4.5 stars than 4, but the system is not subtle enough to handle the distinction. I just finished reading it ten minutes ago, so these are a first impression before I write a more detailed review on my zombie blog (http://zombieparentsguide.blogspot.com/)

This book had a very similar feel to Cormac McCarthy's The Road, describing a journey of discovery and self-discovery through an apocalyptic American landscape. The main characters wander through byways and people's lives with a bigger goal in mind. Some people are good and some are evil, and the protagonists of both stories struggle with which categories they belong in. But the similarity ends quickly. The Road is pretty bleak and unrelenting; this book has moments of grace and joy throughout.

The 19-month old just had a major late night meltdown, so you'll have to wait for the review on the blog!

This is a beautifully written book. I just devoured it. Temple is an amazing character that I loved getting to know. I had so much hope for her in this tragic Zombie filled world.

Temple was born into the Zombie infested world so it was the only way of life she knew, she didn't think it was that bad. She had learned to survive and had grown up a lot faster than she should have.

This is an Amazing Zombie novel. While I was reading it, I kept thinking why is this book so short. I just thought that Temple had so many stories that could be told. I didn't want it to end.

The ending is hard to except.

The Zombie post-apocalyptic genre has been for want of better word done to death in TV, movies and books. The Reaper Are The Angels is a remarkable book in the fact that it manages to add something a little different to the well know story of humans fighting for survival against flesh eating monsters.

It follows the story of Temple, a 15 year old girl who has spent are whole life in this godforsaken nightmare and drifts from one place to another.

What works so well is the relationships she forms along the way, the people she meets and enemy she manages to make in the form of Moses Todd. Everywhere she goes he sure to follow but their conversations and promises to kill one and other reveal the desperation and dreams of two damaged people.

I really enjoyed this book and look forward to further novels by Alden Bell.

Pretty damn cool. I've actually never been a fan of the zombie genre but decided to give this a try. The zombies themselves are more of a background threat while the real threat is the host of characters she meets on the trail.. Think The Road, Mad Max, etc etc. The main character is a bit like the girl in True Grit - definitely one of the more lively, colorful characters I've come across. This book has a fair amount of forward plotting, first she goes here, then she does that, but another driving force is the subtext about how people create their own sense of morals to survive in a lawless society. This is a zombie story that quotes Updike's Couples and king's Pet Cemetery with equal significance. One final note: dialogue is without quotes, in the tradition of many fine novels I have never read. I can't say I'm a fan but after a while I learned to live without 'em.

One of my favorite zombie novels to date.
Loved the strong, yet flawed female character. She was engaging, well developed and her reveals were done impeccably. The novel itself gives all the gore and grittiness one would expect with a zombie novel, yet presents characters that the reader can care about. The author bravely goes to dark places with both the plot and his characters, adding to the tension and shock. In short, this novel was devastatingly beautiful.

Probably more than anything, I loved the cadence of the language in this book. It felt very much like reading an episode of Firefly. The back cover has short review blurbs that call this a cross between Southern Gothic and zombie novels -- I hadn't heard the term "Southern Gothic" but if the writing style is anything like this novel, I'll be searching out more "Southern Gothic" books.

I loathe the absence of quotation marks around dialog. I abhor it. I usually won't even read more than a page before abandoning the book. Reading such a book is like listening to an oral presentation by someone with a severe speech impediment.

However, I couldn't take a full star off for it. This is more than a four star book, even with its impediment. A slightly different take on the zombie dystopia, with a strong lead character who is easy to understand (unlike an impaired speaker, for example.)

The story description was intriguing enough for me to give it a few pages despite the problem mentioned above, and the story itself was good enough for me to finish it and to like it a lot.

But really, please, any future authors reading this: the odds of me reading another book with this particular disability are about 1 in a hundred. Don't do it. Hyphens are annoying, too.

This is quasi-Cormac McCarthy, [possibly] young adult zombie fiction, enjoyable enough, easy to read, but the pretension of the protagonist's diction drags the reader, unwilling and pissed off, into disbelief. Not enough to ruin the experience, but it detracts. And there are several things Temple comes across in her travels, or says, that don't make sense, given the post-apocalyptic state of the world and her own upbringing. But worth a read, good October fun, just don't expect too much. Oh, I almost forgot: an "idiot" mute named Maury? In the American south? Come on. This did not propel the narrative or make the reading any richer; just the opposite. This book shrivels up, dries out and blows away when compared to Faulkner, so any reminder of Faulkner just makes the author look that much worse.

But it's good. Really.

Meatskin tango

In the 50+ years that I have been reading voraciously, I have never finished reading a book - and then picked it right back up and reread it again cover to cover - until "The Reapers are the Angels."

I relished every word, every phrase, every description. I didn't think a LITERARY zombie book could be written and I was wrong.

This book grabbed me from the first sentence and kept me excited all the way through. Zombies, adventures, mutant giants, vengeance, a bad guy with his own set of ethics, a mute, a strong female protagonist who lives her life in a manner that makes sense to her as she finds beauty in every day - all come together to weave a magical tale.

And, be warned, this is not a wimpy zombie story - blood and guts and cringe worthy moments abound. Even though the protagonist is 15 years old, this is not a Young Adult book.

I really enjoyed this, though felt it was too short. I wanted to learn more about Temple's background rather than simply seeing the results of previous experiences.

The book does a good job of being more realistic as far as these stories go. Bad stuff happens and Temple behaves as an adult despite being 15. Gotta step up if you're gonna survive zombies.

The story is largely Temple being chased, which made me think of The Knife of Never Letting Go. I think the implementation is better done here though.

This is probably more of a 4.5/5 book, but I felt like we didn't get enough of Temple's story. We saw the girl as a consequence of things that had already happened, but we didn't get much of a view of those things. So she's more the stoic wanderer dealing with the world than the young woman who has developed because of it.

WOW!!!

Me encantó el personaje de Temple, por alguna razón me recordaba mucho a Michone de TWD. Esto podrá sonar un poco racista pero nunca pude imaginarme a Temple como una chica rubia, en mi cabeza siempre será morena.

El libro es fácil de leer y cada uno de los diferentes escenarios es creíble y emocinante. Las últimas 100 páginas del libro iban un poco lentas, pero de repente recupera su ritmo habitual.

Faktiskt en bok som jag tyckte väldigt bra om. Jag skulle gärna velat läsa mer om Temple och hennes äventyr så därför tycker jag det är synd att det är en helt egen bok. Men samtidigt är det också skönt att läsa en bok som inte är en del av en serie. En del berättelser behöver sina slut utan att man ska känna sig tvingad att läsa 10 uppföljare för att få reda på vad som händer med de karaktärer man tycker om.

Berättelsen är ganska rå och blodig och handlar om en typ 15-årig flicka som är på flykt genom en zombie-härjad landsbygd. I en del städer finns fortfarande mindre bosättningar med överlevare men flickan hör inte hemma där. Med sig på vägen möter hon och tar hand om ett stort "pucko" som inte klarar sig självt och det blir till hennes uppgift att hitta någon som kan ta hand om honom.

Kan rekommendera denna bok.

Not a bad zombie book. I loved Temple. She was kick ass. Those slugs did not stand a chance with her around. As is the same with most zombie tales. You have more to fear from the other people left than the zombies themselves. The plot was interesting enough, traveling around America, running into things along the way. Not just zombies but mutant hill billies, which I would love to see if they ever turn this into a movie. I imagened mama as a gross sight. I liked Maury even though he says not a word they whole book. Which was properly a good thing because there are NO speech marks in the entire book. And this was what ruined it for me. It was sometimes hard to follow who was talking or if that person was talking at all. But still it's worth a read and I won't spoil it but the ending was pretty bold.

The Reapers Are the Angels is a different take on a kind of apocalyptic event. Most of the human population had died off. But the dead, back alive again where there are two types of zombie creatures. The story follows Temple, a young girl and her journey. Along the way there are the odd communities of humans who have survived or just small groups of people. One community thrown into the mix appear to use part of the brain of the creepers and inject themselves. The results are very interesting, but we do not learn how this came about. We do learn a bit about the why. I felt this could have been elaborated. It was a good read, easy to follow but I felt that I only read the "middle" of a novel. To me, I would have enjoyed the book more if there was more events leading up to Temple. The end seemed to do just that, end.

Wow - this is really a powerful book! Anyone considering reading this should prepare him/herself for the fact that it has very little to do with zombies. Instead, it focuses on the internal struggles of characters who are born in/adapting to a post-apocalyptic wasteland; concepts such as duty to self/others, forgiveness, and freedom are central to the tale. I thought the author did an outstanding job developing characters I really cared about...even Moses, who technically I probably should have hated. Temple is an amazing character that will stick with me for sure. Overall, I rate this 4.5 stars. The only problems were a few inconsistencies that jarred me out of the story - power still on in abandoned areas after 25 years, gas pumps working/fuel is still good, etc. Very forgivable flaws in an otherwise remarkable book; I will definitely recommend this story to others!!

I always hate the books where the main character dies, because I'd have already developed an emotional bond with them; a deep understanding. I mean, you get this insight into their thoughts and feelings, like seeing someone's soul raw and transparent in front of you.
And then they just die. Like their life was meaningless, like it didn't matter. How easy it is to die and be forgotten...
I know,this is overtly emotional for a simple fictional character. But not when the characters are written so beautifully, so life-like and just..sad, it make for a very powerful impact.
Anyway, this was a light read, but each word carried a heavy weight to it. The story felt like just one big conclusion to a story long forgotten , like Temple was already dying, or perhaps the world as it was once known was dying, or dead, and this was a funeral.
I loved it, I love books that make me contemplate.

Basically, this book features a teenage girl travelling through the US around 25 years after a zombie apocalypse.

Good points:
Well written for a zombie novel; interesting characters, rather than stereotypes (except Maury maybe); enough action and gore, but not too much.

Bad points:
No use of quotation marks which makes it hard to read for no gain in my opinion; the main character is quite annoying and not particularly likeable; slightly unrealistic ability of a young girl to slaughter many foes with only a knife; half the story is given away by the blurb on the jacket.

All in all, not a bad story, and better written than most zombie novels. However, I didn't think it was as great as most people seem to think it is. To be fair, it wasn't just a series of scenes with people's intestines being ripped out, but it just wasn't that interesting.

Loved it!
But...
I was looking for a good book go get my mind off of Allegiant. This book was defiantly the wrong choice...I knew ten pages in his it was going to turn out, but I shrugged and said 'ah, whatever,' But when I got to that part I went through a great deal of stress. Don't get me wrong, the book was great! Not to mention that it's my first Zombie book. And I finished it while driving home from camping, in the car. I wanted to throw the book out the window. Of course, that would be stupid, I don't know which is worse, this or Allegiant. Hmm...this. But I still like it better than Allegiant. Reason being ha that with Allegiant you got a whole trilogy to inks the characters you love until you get shot. The Reapers are the Angels gave you a single book, therefore the ending was more expected. Well, onto another book...

Fantastic. This book is beautiful and thought provoking. Two things I thought I'd never say about a zombie novel. Really though, it's a beautiful and thought provoking novel period. It just so happens to have a few zombies in it.

We get just a brief glimpse into Temple's tragic life and in that short time we fall in love with the character. She is so young but is an old soul who has seen too much. Her apocalyptic environment is the only world she knows and its dirty and hard. Somehow she manages to see good in it and is truly thankful for it. Bell's prose is subtle and heartbreaking. Very refreshing to see in a genre saturated with superheroes and easy to hate villains. A short read but one that will affect you long after you close the cover. One of the best novels I've read in a while.

Literary zombie fiction is pretty rare. The story was compelling, but the writing felt like a weird hybrid of Cormac McCarthy and a western. Like The Road, There was no punctuation except for periods and commas. Not sure why the post-apocalyptic survivors always seem to lose the ability to punctuate, but at least words were spelled correctly (I'm looking at you, Blood Red Road). The plot line of Temple being tracked by Mose so he could get vengeance felt very much like a western to me. I found myself thinking of the zombies as "high plains drifters" (a term used in Rot and Ruin, a fantastic YA zombie series). By the end, so much had happened between these characters that it it felt a bit like a plot convenience that he was so determined to follow through.

Overall a quick, entertaining read.

Very nearly five stars. Terrific story, well told, and I'd love to go back to this world again. Think "No Country For Old Men" by way of "The Walking Dead." Tremendous.
The only thing...
(No spoilers here, don't worry.)
There's a tiny story within the story toward the middle of the book. The story is fine, and yet one of the trappings is enough to jerk me out of the story, my tongue running over the broken tooth description, and my mind trying to work out why. Why did it bother me so much. Why did the author choose to do this? Without this one niggling issue, the story was a five-star feast, an uninhibited recommendation. I'll still recommend it, but will always do so with a hitch in my step, a tension in my shoulders.
Great book, great read, good job.

Also, this book is written by Alden Bell, not Joshua Gaylord, as the top of this screen is suggesting to me.
Pudo haber pasado más.

This was a book I happened upon by chance, and as such I didn’t have any expectations going in. I was pleasantly surprised both by the engaging story and the author’s unique voice. I’ve read a fair amount of post-apocalyptic books, many of which focus on all the ways humanity as a whole seems to devolve into something animalistic. I enjoyed this fresh take on things, where the people have adapted to the new world while managing, for the most part, to retain a sense of civility and even optimism. The main character, Temple, was someone I rooted for from the beginning, and I was drawn to the way she thinks about things, and how she views the world and the part she plays in it. This is an interesting and easy read that I would definitely recommend.

Temple was born into a world of chaos. In all her 15 years, she has never known anything more than the dilapidated cities, ruthless citizens fighting to survive and the zombies that are the cause of it all--and how to kill both. Armed with her Gurkha blade, a childlike-faith in God and haunted by her inner demons, The Reapers Are the Angels follows Temple on a journey through a post-apocalyptic American South, where there's more to fear than meatskins, there's thugs, rapists and just plain crazy people. This is not a happy story—think The Road meets The Walking Dead—but it is so absorbing.

Continued here » http://www.read-all-over.net/fiction/...

Everything I originally wanted to say about this book is covered in the blurbs. Southern gothic, Cormac McCarthy, William Faulkner (I'm glad someone else said that one first, because it feels like a bit of a stretch), drenched in gore. All of these things are awesome. To that, I would add that protagonist Temple has a dash of Lisbeth Salander, a pinch of River Tam, and a splash of Buffy Summers.

Which is not to say that Reapers is derivative. On the contrary, I think it draws on this wide array of traditions while simultaneously creating its own world. Alden Bell creates a thick atmosphere - I say thick because the experience of reading it is so immersive, and the voice is so consistent. Really enjoyable, scary, bittersweet.

I read this book because it received good reviews here on Goodreads and because I'm a huge fan of "Zombie Lit." I was hoping it would be similar to The Forest of Hands and Teeth by Carrie Ryan and while it didn't disappoint it was a very different book. Temple is a tough as nails character who is near and dear to my heart now. I wished she had let people into her heart a little more but I understand why she didn't. She had lost too much and didn't have a very high opinion of herself. The relationship between she and her nemesis was a very interesting one indeed. I would have liked to have seen it end on a little more hopeful note but then again, I don't really like endings that are all tied up in a neat little bow.

This was, hands down, the best zombie book I've read since World War Z. It was, in fact, similar to WWZ in many ways: it describes not the panic and chaos of a zombie apocalypse, but the gritty realities of survival after a disaster; it presents a surprisingly calm portrayal of what is, objectively, a horrible world; and it shows how people deal with the horrible world in very, very different ways.

The writing of this book is more lush than one would find in a run-of-the-mill horror book, with passages that are so beautifully written that they seem at odds with the gruesome and bloody killings they describe.

My only quibble with this book is that Temple sometimes seems much wiser than her years -- but, I suppose, that's pretty much the point.

This book leaves me in a quandry. I liked it so much, and loved the voice of the young female main character so much that I was awfully sad to finish it.

It is, as others have said in reviews, a gothic-styled Southern tale featuring a young heroine and zombies in a post-apocalyptic world. And that premise is promising enough. But what really captured me about this book what makes it truly stand out for me is the voice, Temple's voice. The way she describes things, the way we see the world, as terrible as it is, through her eyes gives beauty to this ravaged land described. It is truly wonderful to read such a unique voice.

I will be reading this again, and probably picking out some of the more lyrical phrases for myself, to ponder the truth in the beauty.

Absolutely breathtaking. This is the most gorgeous zombie novel I have ever read. Bell describes grotesque, morbid, macabre and gory scenes with such artful perfection it makes me queasy at the thought of all those zombies. Yet, at the same time, he creates this beautiful, complex and deep main character whose thoughts seem like those of a living human being. The emotional turmoil in this book tore me to shreds, every feeling of anger and hatred captured perfectly. I feel in love with all of the characters, good or bad. Alden Bell's writing is stunning, allowing you to not just read the book, but feel it. This book immediately shot to the top of my favorite list. Just amazing. I would give it a million stars if i could.

Great book! I truly enjoyed reading this and following the main character, Temple, on her journey through post-apocalyptic America. The author used beautiful descriptions,metaphors and spiritual influences to make the book immersive and interesting. Temple is a strong character who makes you wish you could be just like her. There was also just the right amount of conflict in the story to make it interesting and relatively fast-paced.

There were a few things that bothered me, like the complete lack of quotation marks. Apparently all the characters could read minds? Some basic facts about the setting like people still having electricity and plenty of gas were also inaccurate for the setting, but I'm just nitpicking.

recommendFor: zombie fans, YA enthusiasts, open-minded Western readers
text:
I hesitated between giving this four or five stars, but I give five stars sparingly. Still, this is a really great book. It's written like a Western, which I say with great expertise since I read the The Sisters Brothers and I've seen True Grit. Like the latter, or like Winter's Bone, the protagonist of this is a extraordinarily capable and level-headed 15 year old girl, who is making her way competently through a difficult and perilous land. The language is poetic and lovely, and it's liberating to read a book with a female heroine who isn't afraid of anything.

I may be finally ODing on zombies and apocalypses, but this is one of the good ones.

I wanted to like this one more than I did (it's gotten rave reviews from some folks whose taste I trust) but I just couldn't connect with it. This is going to make me sound both pretentious and simple-minded, but I have a hard time absorbing narratives that don't use quotation marks to off-set dialogue. Also, the dialect felt slightly off -- it read very old west when the story was supposed to be taking place in the south, and (especially after reading Zone One, which is an unfair grade on a curve because this is a YA book and Zone One was adult lit) reading about a post-apocalyptic universe that had managed in 15 years to devolve into your generic future dystopia old west -- I don't know, I'm over it.

Faulkner meets The Walking Dead. Zombie literary fiction.
One of the best southern gothic novels, it just happens to be written after the zombie apocalypse. The luscious prose is enough to recommend this book, but then there's the protagonist, our anti-heroine Temple. What a fascinating character.
Like Temple, the book isn't without its faults. The last quarter of the novel, where Temple detours into a town of mutants, is the weak part of this story. In my opinion, there was enough craziness with the meatskin slugs and the exoskeleton mutants were unnecessary. That said, the novel as a whole is worth the detour. It really did remind me at times of Faulkner's prose - if Faulkner had written a post-apocalyptic tale of the walking dead.

WOW! The only word I can describe this novel with. Never have I read a zombie novel as adult and real as this one. If ever I yearned for a novel to be a movie, it'd be this one. If ever I had to advocate for people to read a book, it'd be this one. I won't go into detail about the plot, but the story is enthralling and the prose is Beautiful! And I'm not one to be all over the prose, I'm more of a story centric person, but there's no way I can deny the beauty of the story and the words that are specifically chosen to create an environment. This book is a five star for me, and it's a must read, everyone must read it for their own interpretation. A beautiful zombie novel, about life! READ IT!

My first "zombie book," if I read any others I don't think I'll find one quite as good as this.

Expertly written with wonderful Gone With The Wind-style Southern dialogue, this book takes the Walking Dead approach to tell a character-driven story who occasionally bump into the odd zombie.

Comparisons with The Road are inevitable and justified: The Reapers are the Angels is bleak and heart-breaking, but I found teenage protagonist Temple to be a ray of sunshine. Her unwavering optimism made sense despite the 25-year old zombie apocalypse (to her, it's natural that the world is full of animated corpses who want to eat your brains) and at just under 300 pages I only wish I could have spent more time with her.

4.5 stars I listened to the audio version of this novel. Despite what a few critics think, I believe it's an homage rather than a ripoff. Author Bell cunningly plants the zombie post-apocalypse seeds of his story in the dense, fertile loam of the Southern Gothic, and thereby grows a savory hybrid from established roots. The product is pungent with the flavors of McCullers, McCarthy, and Faulkner, and it's as weighty with grit as a Walker Evans photograph. And if its protagonist is as thorny as a Scout without an Atticus, that's all to the good. She has enough O'Connor-esque sardonicism to carry her through the grotesqueness and absurdity of this oft-trod landscape without falling into the pit of the Derivative. I loved it.

It used to be that nearly everything I read stuck with me...... even if it was terrible. Now my selective memory only allows for books that make a significant impact. This was one of those books. Be warned, it is brutal and lyrical and unflinching. It reminds me in many ways of True Grit and the heroine is one of the most original characterizations I've read in a very long time. The pace is driven and nearly perfectly plotted. I won't give away any of the plot or even a synopsis but there is nothing lacking, derivative or gratuitous here. Everything is measured,weighed and delivered perfectly. If you love the unexpected poetry of life's small and brutal moments then this is definitely the book for you.

What a unique writing style... Each character's personality comes across in the book. You can hear Temple's and Moses' voice in your head. While some will moan and complain about grammar or how it annoys them, then they must be easily annoyed. It's young adult fiction, not a masterpiece of literature. If you expected more, aim higher next time. I enjoyed this book much more than I thought I would. The author goes in depth with details and emotions, so you can easily get caught up in the story. There wasn't a single boring chapter in the book. I wanted to know what happened to Temple and Maury till the end. I was a little surprised by the ending, but I won't spoil it. The second book comes out this fall and will follow Moses and his brother. I'm looking forward to it!

I really really enjoyed this book. I actually wish it had been longer. The story was amazing and while I love zombie stories, I can't really say that this was actually about zombies. It was about Temple - the main character - and her voyage to try and find peace. Inner peace. I think that the writing in this book was so vivid but yet so simple. Something very hard to do. The book pulled you in right away and kept you locked inside. I can't say I loved the ending, but in a way, there was no other way for it to end. Temple almost had a predestined fate and no matter how far she ran or tried to hide, she couldn't escape it. Wonderful, thought-provoking book. Don't let the subject matter of zombies scare you away.

Most books in this genre are focused on civilization in the midst of an apocolypse (i.e., zombies running around in hordes, folks lamenting a dying world). This book's protagonist was raised in the post-apocolyptic world. Temple doesn't have a notion of creature comforts or the world that was. Her "normal" is constantly being on the move and simply surviving. Loss is a rite of passage and mourning is an afterthought. The book takes you on a ride through this tattered world with Temple as its frame of reference. Her journey introduces you to what "civilization" looks like 20 or so years post-plague -- demonstrating the stark contrast between those who were born pre and post-apocolypse in terms of how they see the world and live their lives.

I loved this book. I fell in love with Temple. She is the quintessential philospher. Her exchanges with Moses were deep water for a Zombie book. I found the book funny. I laughed out loud one minute and felt the despair of a world dying while trying to rebuild the next. I will say the ending was . . . abrupt. I think the author could have been a bit more creative. But all in all, I loved every part of the story. It was the perfect blend of post apocalyptic America, violence, and even hope. Understanding for Temple was beside the point. The point was asking the right questions. For the thought provoking dialogue alone, I give this book 5 stars.

This will be a book I revisit for years to come!

Although I have a "how to survive a zombie attack" poster in my office, it often takes me a while to get into a zombie apocalypse book. This book was on of the exceptions. I am not overly versed in zombie books, but the ones I have read often tell the story from the ones who are trying to survive a recent zombie outbreak. The Reapers are the Angels looks at the apocalypse 25 years after the start. Temple is 15, a girl who knows no other world but the devastated one she is living. This book is a very interesting commentary on human behavior and life, Temple suffers from what I would call survivor's guilt, and keeps on the constant move to escape it. I was yanked into the book from page one, and felt I was running right with Temple until the final pages.

This is a bit of an odd one to rate. The writing is definitely 4-to-5 level stuff, but the post-apocalyptic setting is something I'm weary of anymore. I was going to split the difference at about 3 stars, but in the last seventh or so (I listened to the audiobook, which was in 7 parts), I had begun to actively like it more. The book is just so extremely well-written, which many readers mention but which I didn't quite grasp until I listened to the book myself.

Audiobook note: I would recommend skipping the audio version and reading the print novel instead. I think the narration — which was not terrible by any means, but just didn't work for me and was a distraction at times — was part of my problem for a lot of the book.

As my first post apocalyptic fiction novel, The Reapers Are the Angels was a great introduction. It's made me want to branch out and read mroe genres of its type, something I shied away from for a while. Within its bleak exterior can be found the innocence of childhood that is rapidly taken away as Temple has to deal with a much more dangerous thing than the meatskins that inhabit her world. Highly recommended as a novel that defies convention and sets for itself a compelling character driven journey against the desolation and solitude of this new world.


Read the full review of The Reapers Are The Angels at Mithril Wisdom.

This book gutted me. Having just finished it, I'm struggling with the notions of duty and honor that play out in the story, but I love the heroine and her belief system and how her self-doubt is the same as anyone's, with or without a zombie apocalypse to grapple with. Don't fixate on the the third person voice and how it sounds like an inner voice but doesn't quite sound like Temple, how some of the references are ones she might not know as a post-apocalypse child. It rattled me at first but Let. It. Go. Just accept it as a translation of her impressions of the world and it works. The language is beautiful and the author masterfully reveals Temple's view of the world and her place in it through the other characters, even the ones that don't talk or are barely present. So good.

Bell creates a story that's both beautiful and haunting. He writes a novel where everything happens for a reason even if it may not make sense at the time. Only an author this skilled can make such a world like this real and believable.

The Reapers are The Angels is a mature book, the violence and gore are intense and the lessons in it are hard learned. It's the moral though; that I think takes an adult mind to truly grasp. Concepts of sacrifice, family, and morality are rarely conveyed as profoundly as they are in this book. Bell has managed to give us the perfect Anti-Heroine in a world without heroes in a time without hope. The protagonist takes us on a journey through the worst parts of human nature only to show us that in the end, all that matters is what you hold inside of you.

Vous avez aimé Rain Man, vous aimez les zombies, alors ce livre est pour vous! £Je n'ai pu m'empêcher tout au long de la lecture de faire le rapprochement avrec le film de B. Levison, un rapprochement ni en bien, ni en mal mais il m'a donné un sentiment de déjà-vu.

Ce fut une lecture facile et agréable même si certaines scènes sont assez dures et sanglantes et pourtant... J'ai trouvé l'écriture trop légère, voir un peu niaise en trop grand contraste avec le monde morbide de l'histoire. Le mélange ne m'apparait pas crédible et perd sa consistance. Trop d'extrêmes s'opposent dans ce livre que pour finalement créer un cocktail détonnant. Pour moi, la sauce n'a pas pris malgré la qualité des ingrédients, certes une bonne lecture mais sans plus!

Good fun read. Possibly the most well-written zombie book that I've read, although sometimes the author tries so hard to make a southern Gothic classic that it slows the pace, but I'm glad to see someone write a post-apoc story that actually cares about the quality of the writing instead of just exploiting the genre. The characters are original and have some depth, even if they are predictably McCarthian and their outlines a bit cartoonish. There was were some holes that were not too hard to gloss over with a little suspension of disbelief, namely that 15 years into an apocalypse there was still power to the buildings. That's it though- the book is a cool read on the whole. I'd recommend it.

This story was better than I thought it would be. I wasn't expecting a masterpiece in any event and more or less was looking for a light entertaining story and this was what I found. In many was the story was an inventive take on a zombie theme, but not so much that it pushed the genre. Individually the characters were interesting and district from one another. I thought that the interactions between the characters were lacking. The defining moments between characters were stated more so then told or illustrated, which in a sense made the story shallow. But what the hell. It didn't require much thought and I was lead through a story line that took me to an ending I didn't expect. Good enough for me.

This book certainly deserves the praise it has received, and stands a cut above most post-apocalyptic novels I've tried. The comparisons to McCarthy or Flannery O'Connor are apt, as there is a hint of that lyricism in the language. The book is a solid "4 Star" read, and I reserve that 5th star for one reason only: there is a disparity between the eloquent & lyrical narrative of the book and the broken, simple speech of the main character (Temple) that I couldn't ignore. Its certainly not a deal breaker, but I find that the writing style interferes slightly with the creation of a believable & relatable character... As though the book is not narrated by the main character at all.
I thoroughly enjoyed this book, though, and look forward to reading the next in the series.

So,I gave this book 5 stars so I feel like I need to write something about it.

This is an amazing novel. And definitely among my top zombie apocalypse stories.

Something that the author managed to keep in mind (that a lot of authors in this category forget) is that the zombies can only ever be the environment of a story, and never a character. This is a human story that happens to be set in a world full of the walking dead.
