It's written in third person present tense which was a little off-putting for me at first but the style really lends itself extremely well to the story. It felt like the entire novel was one long sentence (in the best possible way).

I absolutely loved this novel - and, whether you're into apocalypse-stories or not - you should definitely read it.

I don't usually read Zombie Novels. But this one was recommended by a number of people as a quality Zombie Novel.

It does indeed go a bit deeper into the effect of living with the Zombie Apocalypse on the human psyche and the ending is pretty good.

But in general things are a bit too easy, the Zombies are really useless and easy to deal with, there's still allot of electricity and fuel to go around, communities are eager to take in new survivors rather than hoarding their meager supplies.

In addition while the greatest danger from the Zombies is being bitten, our hero's favorite weapon is a large knife, rather than something with more range like a sword, ax or speer.

While the characters where interesting the badly thought out world took me out of the story.

Oh my goodness gracious this book wrecked me! Bravo to author Alden Bell who crafted a wonderful story set deep within a zombie apocalypse. We follow Temple, a bad ass 15 year old girl who is a survivor and that's all she's ever known herself to be. I see a lot of authors get compared or bucketed into a Cormac McCarthy "style" but Bell did a fine job of setting his own voice. I've read too many who try to BE McCarthy. As a writer this book was very inspiring. His development of the characters, and tension were perfect. He also threw in surprises you'd never expect to see in a post zombie apocalypse setting. I thoroughly enjoyed this read and wonder why this hasn't been pitched as a movie. Maybe it should be.

Part of the series where I review books I read a long time ago

An interesting thing about this book was that there was no dialogue/no quotation marks for the dialogue. And while that was initially a bit frustrating, as the book went on, I got quite used to it and I think it added to the overall bleak setting of the story. We are in a post-apocalyptic world and we follow the main character as she escapes from zombies, helps a boy get to the address scribbled in a piece of paper he carries with him, eludes capture from a bloodthirsty man who is after her for killing his brother in self-defence. I think the ending was not well rounded. I wanted to read more about what happened to the main character but the story just ended.

Awesome Read! I think the author totally rocked out the zombie angle in this one!

The story we follow is interesting because the main character, Temple, remembers nothing of life before the "zombies." She was a small child in an orphanage when the mess hit so it was a twist to follow a character surviving as she always has.

I have to say that I was really impressed with the overall storyline. I read this one in a day because I just could NOT put it down.

I'll point out that the ending did make me mad. I was expecting something to happen that didn't. That's probably what will make this one memorable for me for a long time.

The Reapers are the Angels is a zombie book with a hell of a lot more going than brain eaters! It's more about being human and being humane. About survival in a world gone mad and loyalty. Loyalty to family and to those you meet. Shades or degrees of loyalty. It's also about the search for family a determination to find them no matter what.
Then it's about vengeance, revenge and if they are truly worth the cost.

I don't care if you can't stand zombies, this is a book about so much more that you do yourself a huge disservice by not reading it. If Alden Bell can write this good now, who knows where he'll be next year. I, for one, intend to follow and find out.

I was initially resistant to reading The Reapers Are The Angels because I don't like zombies. There, I've admitted it; the very mention of the undead is enough to put me off any book or film that mentions them. However, I decided to face my prejudice as this book has been highly praised by many of my peers. Reading reviews by other bloggers indicated that the undead zombies in Alden Bell's novel are an incidental, background feature rather than the main event and so I settled down with a mug of hot chocolate and started to read.
Read my full review here.

My favourite book this year by far, and one that just happens to contain zombies. Like other great post-apocalypse novels though, the setting is incidental to the characters and their story. It's a book about people and the zombies are just a part of their life rather than brain munching hordes jammed into every scene.

It'll probably be overlooked by lots of people because it goes that one step farther than things like 'The Road', which is a shame since it really is a beautifully written novel. There are a few strange decisions like not using quotation marks, and the technology and food seems a little too well preserved but that aside it really is a great read.

This may be the first philosophical zombie book I've ever read. Its probably not easy to find a new twist to the zombie story, especially with them being so popular these days, but Bell managed to do so by showing a world from the point of view of a wandering teenage girl who never knew what life was like before. In this way, the story becomes more travelogue than horror story, the zombies are largely pests that don't seem too formidable, and survivors are somewhat plentiful if you know where to look. Bell writes a story where characters muse on right and wrong in a zombified American south and it makes for a compelling read.

Another novel of zombie apocalypse? Well, yes, "The Reapers Are the Angels" is that, and some passages in it are not for the squeamish, but it's also lyrical without being sentimental, and easily the most life-affirming and unexpectedly optimistic zombie novel you'll ever read.

There are graduate-level courses in philosophy that can't touch the heroine (16-year-old "Temple") or her nemesis ("Moses") for insight. Daily miracles are celebrated in this novel. I do not mean that Alden Bell favors the "magical realism" style that was once popular among South American novelists like Gabriel Garcia Marquez; I mean that Bell notices things other people do not.

4.5 stars. Could have been a 5 but the zombie giants (and their mother) was a bit much. The story was, surprisingly, wonderfully written - the desriptions were vivid and detailed without being too wordy. The dialog was simple and yet complex which gave depth to the characters that you rarely see in this type of story. The voice of Temple was hard to get used to at first but worked well for her character as you learn more about her - Temple is definetly an unforgettable character. Overall, I loved it. Although the main character is a teenager, I would not recommend this to anyone under 18 - very graphic scences involving drugs, sex and yes, of course, blood.

Humans who eat zombie flesh in stews seasoned with Rosemary and a 15 year old gurka knife wielding female protagonist...hell, I was totally prepared to give this 5 stars but like so many other wanna be modern fiction writers Bell leads us along the primrose path to the ever lasting bonfire with relish...the dear reader looks forward to it. However, once we cross into Texas the problems start, for the writer that is. And it spirals on down into madness...I've never understood why an author who builds hope for a whole novel wants to tear it down at the end...WTF gives with that? It's a complete crapout...just like in Cold Mountain!

This book was crazy good. Well written, pulled into the story mainly from the tone that the author conveyed and the strong visual images created. Best quote (paraphrased): "God is a slick god. Temple knows."
That statement pretty much sums up the bitter beautiful dirty world that is inhabited by this book.

Just re-read this. Still love it. I just can't even explain how vivid this world is when you read it. You know, you just know, there can't be joy in this place, but you keep reading with a vain hope. It's like McCarthy's The Road and Mad max, and for some odd reason I want to say Catcher in the Rye, made a strange, chaotic, visual, bitter chocolate mess. And I want in on it.

One of the best books read this year. Basic plot is a 15 year old girl surviving in a world ravaged by zombies, she travels the country with a found companion, being pursued by a man who seeks revenge. This book resembles more of a southern gothic novel then a horror story, its language flows, filled with detailed characters. Most reviews have commented on the ending, some people love it, some people hated it, which speaks to the power of the book, if it wasn't such a good book, people wouldn't be arguing so strongly about it. My one problem with the books is a weak and jarring episode in the middle of the book.

This book was crazy good with details. I loved all the gory descriptions, and the kills. It is definitely what I wanted in a zombie book! I overall got too involved with the main character Temple. Whilst I didn't want to put any emotion, she made me feel forever. I over all adored her and her lost innocence. She was so cleverly wished but only fifteen. What really pissed me off was how she died. She went to easily. Her long run in the book was ended by a mutant. She did not deserve the way she died, but I guess that's life. I enjoy this book, and will enjoy any other of Alden Bell's work. Hopefully more zombie books.

One of the most beautiful, horrific, gut wrenching and gorgeously written books I have ever read. Alden Bell tells Temple's story with such beautiful imagery and prose that you almost forget your reading a horror novel and at times that you are reading a novel at all ... I found my self equal parts frightened and heart-broken unsure wether I was frightened by the zombies or the fact that this simple, tiny, savage girl was traipsing around in a world so hopeless and scary that you could taste the depravity...This book decimated me... A note quick note... with out giving to much away, it ends as it should... and I love you for it Alden Bell, yet I hate you just the same.

Maybe I was expecting too much going in because of the rave reviews that I have read but I was a bit disappointed with this book. The prose was bit too much. The author seemed to be trying too hard to make this a deep book, but it is about the end of the world as we know it and it did not fit for me. Another thing that bugged me was that the main character was a 15 year old girl, born 10 years after the beginning of the zombie apocalypse, who is not educated, in fact does not know how to read, but has a very extensive vocabulary. Overall it was an okay read, but not the best zombie novel I have read.

I enjoyed this book very much. It's not a long read, so it was good to have in a three-book juggle. The author painted a picture of a strong, feral child who has seen more in 15 years than anyone would want in a lifetime. However, this strength is also a curse, as she can feel herself turning into something that she believes is dark and deadly.

The author stays true to the characters, which is a quality I look for, and presented an interesting dynamic between the main character and her nemesis. The book is also rife with possible symbolism that the cerebral types can pick apart and make into all sorts of interesting theories.

recommendFor: Anyone who enjoys a good book.
text:
"The Reapers Are The Angels" is the type of book that's literally difficult to put down. I read it in the span of a day and a half. It follows the (mis)adventures of a spitfire girl named Temple through the zombie-infested countryside with an autistic man she picked up by chance along the way while being chased by another man hell bent on vengeance. This is not your typical dystopian-slash-zombie novel and has a few surprises for the reader if they're patient enough to keep reading and wait for them. The twist at the end was the only thing I didn't like but even with that I still give this book a full five stars because I really did like it that much.

~Ami E. Bowen

I have to say I was unsure whether or not I would enjoy this book. I started to read it, and it took a while to sink my teeth into.
However, after the first 2 chapters or so, I was feeling better about it, and rather enjoying it.


I'm unsure whether it deserves more than the 4 stars I rated it, I can't fully make up my mind.
I enjoyed it, that's for sure. But having found it took me a while to get going, I feel I cannot award it any more stars.

Where I can usually identify with the main character of most books I read, it took a while to feel that way about Temple. But I'm glad I got there in the end.

All in all, I would say it was a good book and I like the way Alden Bell writes.

Yes, it's a zombie book, but it doesn't follow the typical zombie tropes. It probably feels so refreshing and different because the whole thing takes place at least a decade after the initial outbreak. People have settled into small colonies and have gotten used to surviving in the post zombie-apocalyptic world.

The narrative voice (third person, but definitely the voice of the protagonist, Temple) is very unusual. If you love flowery and poetic language, you won't like it. It's definitely a very character full voice. I think it added a nice layer to the story.

All in all, this was absolutely a fun monster-book read, but it wasn't the kind that lowers your IQ while you read it.

5 Stars

The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels.

This story of a young girl named Temple. Temple and her demons; imagined or not; move us through this desolate landscape and her repeated torturous memories. All of this, while being pursued by one man's sense of what is right and what is deemed wrong.

Truly powerful, dark, tragic and gritty. Not your average zombie story; the zombies, or slugs; are only background. This hearkens to the Autumn series by David Moody; in how poetic the story is; as well as, The Road by Cormac McCarthy with such a dark and almost hopeless tale.

Highly recommended.

So I finished reading this one. I almost gave up halfway through. I just couldn't connect with the characters. The narrator is Temple, a 15/16-year old girl who keeps looking at the beauty in her post-zombie-apocalypse world. Then she kills a man in self defense, and spends the rest of the novel meandering around avoiding the man's brother, Moses Todd. Sure, the narrator is deeply damaged, and that comes across well, but the whole novel just has this plodding sense of inevitability. Either Moses will kill Temple, or Temple will kill Moses, but it never really seems to matter, even to the characters themselves.

This book was amazing. I love books with a zombie element and this one also had a very deep human element to it which I loved. The story is about Temple who is wise beyond her years because of the zombie infested world she has grown up in. She comes across a ton of "slugs" throughout the book, but the real danger comes from the humans and Temple herself. It gets into what growing up in this particular world has done to her and the other humans she encounters. Some people have complained about the lack of quotation marks, but I think it worked for this kind of story. I highly recommend this book; it was beautiful in a zombie apocalypse sort of way.

It may not be an original comparison, but Reapers is a cross between Blood Meridian and The Road. The language is gorgeous - long paragraphs of simple, lyrical, descriptions that read like poetry.

Temple is like The Kid in Blood Meridian, and like that character it's best not to hope for the best. And Moses corresponds to The Judge, in the implacable and irrational pursuit of an inevitable end.

The zombies may turn off some readers, but they are really just a backdrop. You can ignore that aspect of the story and not miss much.

I finished this one a while ago but it was still a great book. It is billed as an adult book for teens but I would definitely not give this to anyone under the age of 15-16. The book follows Temple a tough as nails 16 year old girl who is looking for redemption and a new place to call home. The only problem is that for the last 25 years hordes of zombies have walked the earth turning America into a wasteland. Temple comes across various groups of people on her search for a new home and to forget about the little brother that haunts her soul. Some help her along the way while others have more sinister motives.

This is a slow and emotionally intense story. The main protagonist is a hard and simple young woman who is as kind as her circumstances allow her to be. I'll be honest, I cried over this book. The various people you meet through Temple are an interesting and varied lot and you get to see how vastly different people can turn out in a post-apocalyptic world. All of the characterizations made sense for the situations the characters were in, and the world building was excellent.

The only reason this got a four instead of a five from me was that I didn't find it believable that people and society would still have some of the luxuries they were shown to have in the story.

This is not your typical zombie book. From the fifteen year old teenager, who is anything but your typical teenager, to the way the author spins his story with beautifully written words, this is not your typical zombie book, it is something much better.

There are zombies in this book but they are not the star of this book, that would be Temple. As she wrestles her inner demons as she walks the land, looking for a place to call home. The book is deep, and at times not easy to read, but also a book I couldn't put down.

If you are looking for a post-apocolyptic book that is something different, something that stands out from the usual, then give this one a read. You will be enthralled.

recommendFor: Zombie fans, Southern American fiction fans
text:
Interesting novel. The back cover said it was like Flannery O'Connor meets zombies, and that is such an apt description. The story is beautifully written, although lacking in many elements of the back story that would have been nice to know. Like, where did the zombies come from, for example.

The strangest thing about this book for me was that I checked it out from the library a month ago, long before I knew we would end up moving to Lighthouse Point, and in the beginning of the book not only is the main character in Florida, she's living in a lighthouse! Spooky!

If you're into zombie stories, definitely check this one out. Such a unique take on the genre.

A strong entry into the genre of apocalyptic fiction. A zombie story, actually, although it never felt like a zombie story as I was reading it. That's because the focus here isn't so much on the zombies as on the astructural travelling lives that the plague forces upon the remnants of civilization. The prose was rich, although Bell is no Cormac McCarthy. There was an odd innocence that hung about this book, mixed in with the cynical qualities. The protagonist is a young, illiterate girl whose slang is mixed with vocabularic eloquence that she has no right to command, yet manages to enhance the story. Pretty good stuff, if a bit tonally inconsistent at times.

My friends here in GR probably know how much I love Blood Red Road. Temples of TRATA reminded me so much of Saba from BRR! The way she talks and her fortitude, all the other admirable qualities you can name. I love Saba, she's one of my fave book heroines, and Temples makes it to the list as well.

The cover art gives me the creeps, and the title is misleading. This isn't a book involving angels, it only has zombies... and mutated hillbillies! Bloody, brutal, & gory. I enjoyed reading this book!

This book was quite good for reasons I can't really figure out. Very different than any other "zombie" book I've read. It was sad, very sad. Terrifying. Dark. And wonderful. There were things that REALLY bothered me about it. Like the lack of quotation marks. But I couldn't stop reading it. It really sucked me in from the beginning. I hated the way Temple talked about or to Maury, but it was part of who she was, part of her character. I wish there would have been more about Temple's past. More about Malcolm. It looks like this might be turning into a series? I will be reading the next one when it comes out!

The book cover put me off but in the end I enjoyed this way more than I supposed I would. It was very decent for a zombie novel at least. Temple, the main character, was like a mix of Katniss from the Hunger Games and Daryl Dixon from the Walking Dead, so of course I liked her a lot. The male characters, Lee, James and Uncle Jackson were all quite similar to each other. I liked the bad guy, Moses, but there could have been fewer moments where they sit down and have a talk about life because those didn't make him feel threatening at all. Maybe he wasn't supposed to. <input type="checkbox" class="spoiler__control" aria-label="The following text has been marked spoiler. Toggle checkbox to reveal or hide." onchange="this.labels[0].setAttribute('aria-hidden', !this.checked);" id="6b09c022-6b98-4b08-a486-dc0431e7ad91" /><label aria-hidden="true" class="spoiler" for="6b09c022-6b98-4b08-a486-dc0431e7ad91">I also wish that the mutants had been left out of the story. They didn't make much sense. </label>

This book wasn't what I expected it to be, but it was still really great all the same. It was simpler, but I think that made it more poetic and was likened to the way the main character, Temple, was. She saw things how they were, there really were no shades of gray with her. I loved her sass, her strength, her loyalty to Maury. I loved everything about her. I like to think that if I grew up in an apocalyptic world taken over by zombies, I'd be her (with better grammar, I hope).

It's a quick read, but it'll ring down into the depths of your soul. Because if anything else, it's a point on the true beauty of the world, and those who can recognize it.

Wow I just loved this book from start to finish.

It uses the zombies as a normal part of the world as it is years after the zombie outbreak started. Temple a 15 year old girl has known nothing else and this is just the world she lives in.

She might be young but you don't want to cross her as she is fearless and inventive.As her story unfolds you root for her and care about what she does and where she is going.

I'm not saying anymore as I don't want to spoil it.

The book is short (I wish it was longer) and it was over all too quickly.
Its not your normal zombie novel and is all the better for it.

Hugely entertaining.

though there were parts that were beautifully written, and the story involved so many experiences of a post-apocalyptic zombie world, the pace wasn't consistent enough for me to really enjoy the ride. i admit i wanted a 'quick read' but with so many different interactions, i felt rushed instead of being able to immerse myself in any of the communities that i wasn't able to attach myself to. maybe that was the point - Temple's character didn't spend too much time getting attached to anything/one/place - then i agree that the point was well made, and this was simply not what i was looking for. i can see this easily becoming into a movie (that's the trend now anyway).

Compelling, vivid literary zombie novel, elegiac and poignant yet with plenty of the violence and gore the genre is known for. The young girl protagonist, Temple, is very, very well drawn.

When assembling some fall Halloween themed class reads, I had 3 blockbusters: the latest Stephen King (the very solid Doctor Sleep) , World War Z (meh) , and Dracula (too talky) . And then I impulsively bought this one that I was not familiar with at all but that seemed intriguing and had some good reviews. Didn't think I would arguably enjoy Mr. Bell's relatively obscure novel the most of the four (it was definitely better than World War Z and, yes, Dracula) but that is what happened.

I love Temple. She is tough, sure of herself, direct, and brave ...especially for a 15 year old. She was born into a world full of zombies. It is all she has ever known. She wants to wander the United States and see the wonders that still exist. She has heard about them from older survivors. She does not really want to be "trapped" in a "safe house." Instead, she would rather take her chances out in the world. The writing is good. Bell has an interesting story to tell. It is easy to read and has a lot of insight. At times, it is very introspective. I was not ready for it to end. I will look forward to reading more novels by Alden Bell.

4.5 stars

A gritty, post-apocalyptic tale with a main character who is tough as nails. Temple strongly reminded me of the main character in the Dust Lands trilogy, with the hardened attitude, twangy drawl manner of speech, and even dialogue without quotation marks. I found this story gripping to the last page, and my only criticism is that I found it hard to believe the power still worked in many places, the gas stations often had working pumps with gas that hadn't spoiled after 25 years, and there seemed to be plenty of food and ammo/weapons lying around in perfect condition. Recommended for fans of zombie stories and The Walking Dead.

What I Liked
I absolutely loved the poetic writing style of this book. The first chapter had me mesmerized. Bell is certainly a wordsmith. One of my favorite lines within the few pages were, "...she listens to the ocean wind whistling loud through the hollow flute of her tall home."

What I Didn't Like
There was some racy (and near-rape) content that left me feeling a bit uncomfortable, so I probably wouldn't recommend this to my friends or young readers. The descriptions of the zombies are exciting and realistic, but towards the end of the book, the science fiction got a little weird for me.

Overall, I enjoyed the writing, but not all of the content.

My god. This is one of the most beautifully written books I've read in ages. As in Zora Neale Hurston level prose.

The protagonist is a fifteen year old girl named Temple and her world is a quarter century into a zombie post-apocalypse. I won't give away any of the actual plot but this is a book far grander than mere zombie survival.

I would give this a solid five stars but I'm going for a final 4.5 stars because of a few minor details (gasoline still usable, random electricity etc) that pulled me out of the story unnecessarily.

Overall though, I cannot recommend this highly enough. It's simply breathtaking.

Most zombie books are about the outbreak of the zombies and the initial fleeing catastrophe. This book widens the scope considerably. It reminded me a lot of The Road, with zombies.

Temple is clever and strong, and her world made her that way. She's surely the most interesting character I've ever come across in zombie lore. It's a coming of age story where there isn't much hope of a better life, so there's no salvation at the end of the tunnel. Just more horror.
The prose is one of the novel's stand outs. Bell writes very well, and his words were a gift to the genre, I just wish the story had been slightly longer to give more pacing to all the things that happen.

I didn't care for the writing style of this book - it was too artsy for me. The lack of quotation marks especially was really annoying. I was also annoyed at the lack of thought about what the world would actually be like 25 years after the collapse of society really annoying. I know that modern snack foods have extraordinarily long shelf lives, but 25 years is pushing it way too far.

The main character was all right, but the writing style just wasn't able to hold my interest - it made everything into kind of dream state - she was floating through the world but not part of it. And if she's not really a part of it, why should I care about it?

I’m of two minds about Reapers. The writing and prose are first rate, drawing a southern sensibility to the pacing and the use of down home metaphors. Using this style gave the story a clear sense of realism, but there are times to weave an expository tapestry and times the action needs to be tended to above all. The impulse to over-analyze and dance along witty comparisons needs to be stowed away during the penultimate moments where the reader is dying to hear what happens. This small aspect pulled it down from a great book to a good book. Still, this will be a solid recommendation in my library.

It's drawn apt comparisons to William Faulkner and Cormac McCarthy. To those I'll add "It's the To Kill a Mockingbird of Zombie Apocalypse fiction." There's nothing particuluarly inventive or uniquely thrilling in Bell's survival/coming-of-age/road trip tale- at least not in the narrative sense. It's the elegaic quality of the prose that is surprising. Bell delivers terse, pointed dialogue punctuated with pithy, epigrammatic observations on human nature and the (post?) human condition. Almost makes one believe that they're reading littachur... but the ravenous, decaying revenants keep it fun. This will help tide you over until the next issue (or season) of The Walking Dead, at least.

4.5 stars

I came to this book hungry for the flight that reading fantasy (read anything non-realism) used to bring. That reading joy of teenage years before studying writing at uni managed to deconstruct and kill a lot of books. This is writing to fall into. This is unexpected and stunning - literary zombie fiction with a Southern gothic heart.

If you like your zombie fiction with strict genre conventions - you ain't gonna like this; you're gonna call the prose mauve or somesuch and whine a lot. But you strange litkids that grew up with Lestat and dragons and Harry and are wandering the high plains of literature lost and forlorn...come over here, tucker's up.

I relatively enjoyed this book. It was a certainly worth reading if you enjoy your 'horror' to have an moral core with an edge. However, if you are into zombie fiction, the zombies are just a way of creating a post-apocalyptic setting. Therefore, I wouldn't necessarily categorize it in as Zombie Fiction, other than the fact that there are zombies in it. Having said all that, I did rather enjoy the novel, it takes the reader on the journey with the main character showing us that even in a society defined by death that beauty can be found anywhere. Not a particularly difficult read, and worth a go for anyone who enjoys some semi-mindless pulp.

Sweet Jesus, Mother Mary, and all that is holy... it's like they were TRYING to make this the most painful book to read. Hell, you can't even tell what you're reading because there are no quotation marks. I repeat, THERE ARE NO QUOTATION MARKS WHEN PEOPLE ARE TALKING. I just... *mind implodes* I guess it's supposed to be philosophical or some bullshit, but I hated it. Absolutely abhorred it. Quotation marks were invented for a reason. Also, completely elementary grammar mistakes such as "wouldn't of." Wouldn't HAVE, people, geez. That's 3rd grade crap. Ugh, I can't. Judging by other reviews, this is apparently a good book if you can get past the awful writing, but I just can't.

Instead of your typical police officer/military man survival story, in this book you are told the story from the point of a 15 year old girl named Temple. Hearing the story from a hardened 15 year old girl makes it all the more terrifying and personal, every person is a threat and Alden Bell makes you feel every moment of terror and joy. The author even manages too keep it fresh with some new zombie ideas that I had not seen introduced. There are two very good side characters that are with you for most of the book, one holding a vendetta against Temple and another a mentally impaired man who temple has taken responsibility for. Great book.
This isn't a bad book, but it isn't a good book either. If you have 50 other books to read, go read them first.

My humbled opinion: This was an amazingly well crafted story! The author's style of writing makes you feel like it's an old friend telling you the tale. I really appreciated this experience, and hope many will take the time to read this without any preconceived notions of its content or quality. It is a brilliant piece of work!!!

What I learned from reading this book: We never know what kind of quality we would have in any situation being faced. My hope is that I would be one to help rather than hinder.

This book is perfect for reading by adults age 17 and above.

Decent zombie book. Follows a 15-year-old girl who is alone, and tough as nails, as she makes her way around America which is 25 years into a zombie takeover and sparsely populated by small pockets of humans. It's a pretty quick read, just over 200 pages, and is very easy to follow. I was a little put off by the writing style as oddly none of the dialog is in quotation marks.

Overall, it was a good story. There was just no big wow factor or excellent writing that made me feel that this was a really good book.

A southern gothic with zombies? Oh my, yes! Can I have I side of grits with that too?

This novella grips you from the beginning and takes you on a ride through the zombie-infested South. However, humans prove once again to be the real stuff of nightmares. The protagonist, Temple, is on the run from a (human) killer, and she is also running from guilt. She's is one of the more memorable characters I've read about recently. I'm still mulling over how I feel about the ending. That's the only reason this did not get 4 stars.

Side note - I believe the film rights have been bought.

It was good, very good especially for a debut.It is essentially the story of the well-rounded Temple rather than the Zombies.
A spot of fresh air in this zombie infected world.
I had a good feeling about this book from the outset. It seems this year is Zombie literature year.
I thought it was odd at first the lack of quotation marks, but it is something you soon get used to. And I believe it is how Cormac McCarthy writes.

I only give it 4 stars because I thought we could have gone on a longer journey with Temple. And that was the only thing that disappointed me.

I don't have enough praise for this dark, harrowing, smart, and blunt novel about a young but weathered girl named Temple who must travel the South, escaping from a vengeful man who wants her head on a platter. This book is a hard one to top for me because it is such an epic tale, full of colorful characters and heartbreaking emotion. Temple is my favorite book heroine of all time because she is not only tough as nails and afraid of nothing, she has a truly kind heart and is extremely funny and full of live in a dying world.

I cried when I read this book. I don't see how you couldn't.

Wow. I flew through is book, not just because it's relatively short, but because it's beautifully and simply written, and very, very good. The main character is 15 year old Temple, a tough, smart girl who carries a deep well of guilt for the many deaths that she has caused in her past. In spite of, or perhaps because of, the utterly fucked up world she has grown up in, she is incredibly profound, and her code of honor and clear-eyed way of viewing the world make her one of the most interesting characters I've read in a while.

Alden Bell’s The Reapers Are the Angels reminds me of nothing so much as True Grit with zombies. It’s plain spoken and profound at the same time, anchored by a tough girl who is trying to do the right thing in a violent world. Unlike True Grit, there’s no one to protect and guide Temple. She’s on her own, with a vengeful man on her trail. In that way, it’s sort of True Grit in reverse. With zombies...

Read the rest of my review at A Bookish Type.

Elegant zombie prose. I am not yet bored with zombies but I can see that eventually it will be a milieu that has been fully explored/exploited, but with something this good to read it may lived (or remain undead) a little longer.The Reapers Are the Angels by Alden Bellis a page turner that could be described as literary zombie fiction

Very unique! I loved the Cormac McCarthy's Blood Meridian/Stephen King's Desperation/zombie western flavor of it. I docked one star for the presence of the hillbilly mutants. I honesty could not picture them in my mind at all. Giants covered in bone plates? Men without eyelids? Functional limbs flayed down to the bone? Huh? At one point Temple describes the matriarch as a huge "white lobster." What?! The best image I could conjure up in my mind's eye is a cross between a burn victim and a triceratops.

It took me about 3/4 of the way through to really start liking it. Bell's writing was beautiful and haunting from the beginning, but the pacing felt off to me and I didn't feel like I really got to know Temple (which is, I suppose, the point). Also, I really wanted to know more about the zombie fallout -- I guess, really, I was looking for another World War Z, which this wasn't. In the end, though, I was won over by Bell's writing and the kind of full-circle conclusion that was really satisfying.

One of the most beautifully written books I've read in a long time. And it was about zombies. Although with Bell's clear, precise, yet poetic writing, the zombies were secondary to the heart of the story: survival. It's been awhile since a story gripped me in such a way I felt a part of that world. And it's because of this I wasn't completely happy with the ending. Not that the ending was poorly written or executed; I simply wished to spend more time following along with the characters. Highly recommended to anyone, regardless of your taste for zombies.

I really like sci-fi books so I thought I would love this book, however at some points, ai struggled to not roll my eyes at the cliche descriptions of the protagonist....maybe she was too familiar for.me, seems like every zombie story line contains a character like her.....

Buuuut I did find the sexual aspects of the book interesting and the writing was very good. I stayed interested and enjoyed it mostly.

The ending was a let down and didn't make sense to me. I didn't mind the final conclusion....just wish it had made more sense.

This book works, and I'll be damned but it's easily one of the best I've read this year. Bell smooshes a poetically beautiful coming-of-age saga onto a post-apocalyptic zombiescape, shakes it up a bit, and pours out an incredibly unique and worthwhile story. There are a couple of flaws (notably the, um, zombie growth hormone bit with the hillbillies...why?) and a too-predictable Dark Secret of the protagonist's past, but those are completely drowned out by the sheer awesomeness of the rest of this book.

Grotesquely beautiful, eerie and captivating.
I love finding little gems like this book and it's not very often I do, I haven't fell in love with a story for a long time. This book came out of no where and slapped me around the face and I'm so glad it did. The way in which the book is written left me in what I can only describe as dream like state, I believed every word of it and it takes a talented writer to put a reader in that position! It was dark and disturbing but amazingly heart felt.
You'll only understand how wonderful this book is until you read it and I recommend you do!

I have to admit I'm stunned.

If cheesy, cheap, Rage-Virus gore is your thing, this is NOT the read for you. The characters, the prose, the themes all put this eerily close to the realm of literature. I kid you not. If Flannery O'Connor ever deigned to write about the zombie-apocalypse, it would read a helluva lot like this. I would never expect a horror-genre book to be so poignant, so (forgive the pun) alive. And I certainly never imagined giving one Four Stars.

Well worth your time and money.

A lot of violence, but a wonderful heroine. So your world is full of zombies and your past is tragic; deal with it and find beauty where you can. I enjoyed this story, found the heroine's voice charming (if ruthless), and only the end disappointed me...but I don't know how it could turn out otherwise. If you like 'Hunger Games', you might like this. It's also similar to Cronin's 'The Passage' (which had vampires, instead of zombies) but WAY shorter and simpler. If you like your post-apocalyptic heroines plucky and poetic by turns, and don't mind wacked-out zombies, give it a read.

Best book I've read in a long time! When zombies are written about, the chances for things to be overdone and repeated are very high, but I feel like this book didn't go over the top with that. Great story about a girl facing a world of zombies. It does focus a lot on her introspection and how she grows and the apocalypse affects her, but I don't consider that a bad thing. Just wanted to give you a head's up in case that isn't your type of thing. That said, there are also some great action scenes in it and it's a fast read.

recommendFor: people who have time to waste on something TERRIBLE
text:
I finally finished this book! To be honest I couldn't even really enjoy it because of the absolutely IDIOTIC writing style!

I cannot stand it when authors do not use quotation marks to indicate someone is talking. I can't tell what is supposed to be narrative and what is spoken word and it completely changes the tone! I don't care if they think they are being "artistic", in all reality they are just being five shades of stupid.

The only reason I actually even finished this book was because I bought it and figured I had to. I would not recommend this to anyone.

This book was a new take on the classic zombie novels. I did enjoy the story of the characters and how they interacted with one another, especially Mose. He knew his journey to kill was wrong yet he had to do it. There is interesting moral dilemmas in the book that make you stop and think. The writing itself was wonderful and beautiful when it really should not be. The descriptions alone would make me read this book again. If you are looking for a survivalist tale like other classic zombie novels this is not it. If you want something that reflects humanity for it is, this is for you.

This isn't your typical Zombie book, in fact the zombies are barely in it. This book is about a girl named Temple trying to survive alone in a world where man is worse then monster. Along her travels she picks up a mentally handicapped man, and the story becomes a buddy trip book. Her and Maury treck across America avoiding all sorts of dangers from Mutant to a hillbilly swearing a blood feud because Temple killed his brother. My biggest complaint is that the book is very formulaic, it is quiet, then trouble, violence, then run until it is quiet again, then repeat.

To echo what other people have said this is a zombie book that is really nothing like a zombie book. The writing is reminiscent of Cormac McCarthy and very poetic. The protagonist, Temple is the enigmatic warrior. Although she is supposed to be 15 years old, this book certainly doesn't read like YA lit. It has very adult themes. It is the kind of book that wants to you to think. I didn't like the ending, in fact I hated the end, but at the same time I'm not sure it could have ended any other way.

The heroine of this story, Temple, is easy to like. The action in this post-zombie-apocolyptic world is fast-moving and interesting. Alden Bell's twists are pretty captivating. His prose is sometimes notable. However, the religious undertones of the novel were overdone and I had a very difficult time surrendering to Bell's insistence that there is something deeper and more meaningful in the zombie apocalypse than carnal desire. The "reaper" and "angel" dichotomy was played out to a nauseating extent for my tastes.

I have been reading a ton of dystopian lately and Temple is such a unique character. So wise beyond her years and such an amazing soul. Born into a world full of zombies and not really having anyone else around its surprising to see her content with her situation in life, very accepting and understanding of the way things are. Not that she likes it but she looks for the beauty in life and accepts the things she cannot change. Such a great way to be even in our times. A haunting and sad story but also so inspirational.

Wow, I really enjoyed reading this, I fell asleep trying to finish it. I don't read books about zombies, but I loved the character in this book. I usually read "pop" urban-fantasy and not too much "literature". I loved this book for the WAY it was written and how the author handled the other characters and the subject (so yes, for me, there are a lot of fancy words in it, but that made it all the more lyrical for the subject matter). Not the best way to describe it, but that's as good as gets.

I didn't think I was going to like this book. That is why it sat for so long on my list of currently reading. There was always one more book ahead of it. Then one day I decided I wanted to give a little horror a try. And I was honestly pleasantly surprised. First of this is very (to me anyways) YA. However I really enjoyed Temple and her adventures. The colorful people she met and the one that followed on her trail for ever. I cried when she passed and worried and fretted. For me the biggest negatives is sometimes she was WAY too old for her age.

I could not put this book down. We follow the journey of Temple as she journeys across the zombie infected landscape. The zombies however are merely a backdrop to the story and unfortunately the ones she has to fear most are not the bloodthirsty undead, but the living. The bad guy Moses is an ego driven ahole who is not someone you want as an enemy since he stubbornly refuses to acknowledge the stupidity of his vendetta and will continue on his mission rather than back down and thus, in his tiny mind, appear less manly.

Holy shit. I'm still kind of in shock, like what the hell did I just read, but in a good way. I will likely read the story again, and I don't do that very often for books across many genres. It also helps that it took about 3 hours from start to finish. If I had to describe it, I'd say it's like a strange-ass, macabre Western that artfully uses juxtaposition and delves into some deeper questions than what you'd usually find in these kinds of stories. You'd think Zombies would be the biggest fear here, but I think it's really a matter of who/what you've become by the end of your days.

This post-apocalyptic zombie novel revels in such illuminated poetry that it’s terrifying and heart-breaking at the same time. Bell shapes words into gorgeous images of loss and longing with effortlessly style and beautiful simplicity, tugging the reader across the ruined landscape of the American south. The fearless heroine of the story, Temple, is powerfully rendered; a touching and complex character of stunning depth and disturbing horror. This is a small book with profound resonance. Highly recommended.

"Flannery O'Connor with zombies" seems to be the most popular description of this book, though I enjoyed it far more than any O'Connor I've read. One would think it would be difficult to relate to Temple and her grim, businesslike attitude toward the violence that characterizes her day-to-day life. But her search for beauty, and meaning, and her adherence to her own stoic code of ethics make her a fascinating character to watch. She reminds me of Katniss Everdeen, minus the romantic dithering and talent for spinning a media narrative (as there is no media to spin).

I listened to the audiobook version of this book after seeing it recommended on this list: http://www.lawrence.lib.ks.us/news-ev... I really enjoyed the story-telling. It had great pacing and I found myself wanting to be friends with the main character, Temple. The story dragged a bit towards the end for me -- not enough action, too much philosophizing with a word soup of five-dollar-words that had me rolling my eyes at times. But all in all, an enjoyable book.

RATING SYSTEM
character 1/1
Page Turner 0.5/1
Writing Style 0.5/1
Plot 1/1
Feelings Evoked 1/1
OVERALL: 4/5

this book made me question some things. first of was moses temples father? and despite his obvious affection for her why did he still want to kill her even though yes she did kill his brother but then again she did save mose's life. and the setting was not realistic really, and the writing style flowed perfectly, in some places, however some places it was "iffy"

overall good read.

very entertaining and interesting story.
it seemed to be about a strength of spirit residing in a small girls body. a girl born in a world where zombies are a fact of life. she isn't burdened with memories of a safer time. nor does she bother thinking the world will return to how it was. there are more important matters to contend with. like surviving and trying to do right by her own reckoning.

obstacles that would overcome most any person don't seem to daunt this tiny amazing warrior. a girl who refuses to die and I personally would not wish to cross.

Absolutely beautiful writing, and an interesting narrative not just of survival, but of the unexpected wonders of this earth. Although, I was slightly suspicious of the seeming abundance of gasoline, twenty-five years after the rise of zombies caused the collapse of civilization <input type="checkbox" class="spoiler__control" aria-label="The following text has been marked spoiler. I really like zombie books 'cuz its a blend of action,adventure,thriller & obviously horror...the language is simple(though it made me turn the dictionary a couple of times,i liked it..mostly the native language),the character development is good,personally i dont care about grammar or whatsoever..'cuz i just want to know the story.It could've been more better if it included a litle more action & adventure...& i never expected the ending where the protagonist gets killed.
I read a lot of comics & manga,so was expecting an action-thriller story 'cuz its main theme is about zombies..

This tale follows a young girl born into a zombie-infected world. After a man is killed at a military outpost, she finds herself on the run from his revenge-seeking brother.

This book was better than I thought it would be. The young leading character is tough, but also interesting and believable. The people she meets along the way are well thought out characters, although the ending did ruin it for me a little. It was inevitable, and probably necessary, however it did bring it to an ineffectual conclusion for me.

Bell nos transporta a un mundo en el cual el apocalipsis zombie fue una realidad de hace 25 años por lo que para Temple, nuestra protagonista, la existencia de estas criaturas es algo de lo más normal y por ende, no las rechaza como diabólicas o malignas, sino las entiende como una criatura más en el mundo del Señor.

Es interesante la reflexión de carácter místico que enmarca el carácter de Temple dervado de ese, la habilidad de Bell para plantearnos una situación moderadamente difernte.

Lo recomiendo si les gustó la trilogía de "Dying to Live"

Told in the voice of an unschooled but sharp 15 year old girl, her world is overrun by zombies. She wanders trying to find small miracles while avoiding the dead and staying alive. She becomes responsible for a low IQ man. Her mission becomes to get him home. She is being chased by a man bent on revenge.The writing is excellent, the main character is interesting and stays in character throughout. The book is more about what it means to be human and what happens to people just trying to survive, and less about zombies. Beautiful, lyrical, and gruesome.

This little novel really stunned me with it's depiction of a nasty, brutal world being navigated by a teen girl who is as ruthless a human as she has to be to survive.
Temple is a girl full of contradictions and many flaws, but man did I fall head over hills in love
with this fictional girl and her journey.
This is a gem of a novel that covers a lot of emotional territory. It's equal parts hope and sadness
with an overall sense of dread throughout.
Read this book. It's not really enjoyable but you will be a better person for having read it.

More like a 3.5.

I read this at the insistence of my fiance. I don't usually care for zombie stories or involving zombie anything. It was not your typical zombie story though. It was about a girl who knew nothing else of life except a zombie apocalyptic world. It was an interesting view point and I liked her voice. The writing was beautiful.

The plot and story dragged for me though. I wasn't sure where it was going and the ending left me unsatisfied.

Very philosophical and poetic storytelling. I can see why my fiance loved it.

Southern gothic type, post-zombie apocalyptic world. Freaking awesome. About survivor types and the confusion of "good" people who are able to live and thrive in a brutal world without breaking, and are able to do what needs doing. None of it is easy, and the morals should to be different in a world like that, but everyone tries to live to the same ideal from before the end of the world. Not easy, not quick though only a little over 200 pages. Well written, fascinating and brutal, sad and lonely. Definitely makes you think.

Relieved as a 'First-Reads' - Thank You!

I had to settle on two stars for 'It was okay' rather than three for 'I liked it'.

I loved the story and the direction it went in etc.

I did not like the writing style. To me it felt clunky and long-winded in places. I didn't like that there were no speech marks when people were talking.

But it was a nice quick easy read. Would I recommend it? It depends on the person I guess and their preferences. Would I read it again? Probably not but don't let that put you off, after all you make like the style!!

If Huck Finn and Rhee from Winters Bone had a child and then that child was orphaned and dropped in the middle of a zombie apocalypse, it might very well be Temple. This book was pretty amazing- sparse, economical writing, totally creepy and gross and weird scenes and a really great protagonist. Very Southern. Two things nagged at me a bit- sometimes the dialect felt a little strange to me and the third (and last) section kind of went "clunk" but on the balance, this one will stick with me for a while.

"The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels"

This is definitely not a YA novel in my opinion. It isn't really about zombies. It has zombies in it sure, but it's more about the story of Temple or should I say Sarah Mary surviving whilst travelling from place to place. Kind of like a road trip; meeting people on the way with lots of bumps in the road.

The writing style is very beautiful and poetic. The relationship between Temple and moses was a wee bit odd for me though.

This novel is intense with genuine suspense. It is a zombie novel in the truest sense. Yet somehow it is written in an extremely elegant and intelligent way. It was like zombie art. The story is very unique, the main character so detailed, some of the parts uncomfortably engrossing and I say that as a positive. The ending. Wow. It will stick with you. Great read. Don't be turned away by the writing that some seem to feel is pretentious. It is worth the read and the occasional trip to the dictionary.

I dont think i can write something about this book that hasnt been written before in another review. This book has zombies but its not about zombies. A 15-yr-old girl 'living' (if you can call that living) in a world where zombies infestation has taken control of it. Ppl creating little communities here and there. And a guy that has his mind set in ending her life. The details very gruesome, that i liked. Think of this like someone is narrating a story, not much of conversations. Another thing that kinda bug me is that after 25 yrs of this, technology still exits, but it doesnt really. Weird.

There's a cadence to this book that's quite accomplished, a way with language that's engrossing. However, having recently read a lot of hard scifi, I couldn't help but be annoyed by the unscientific world building; in particular, somehow gas still works some 25 years after the apocalypse? How easily you can put aside believability issues like that may determine how much you like the book.

But putting aside those issues, the characterization was quite good, the plot had momentum (despite being somewhat episodic), and the language was excellent.

This is a different kind of zombie story than I am used to. There's plenty of the elements that you come to expect like different stages of zombies decomposition, pockets of survivors, & graphic fighting. I liked reading about Temple, a 15-year-old girl who has never known the world before zombies, and her mute companion.
Somehow this book has a much deeper meaning & moral tribulations, with a sort of romantic feel to it. It's hard for me to describe what I mean, but when you read it you'll have an idea of what I'm getting at.

I wanted to love this book. I picked it up off the shelf because I was in the mood for a good zombie novel. This wasn't so much a zombie novel as it was a survival novel, which was fine except that I never really got entirely invested in it. Yes, there was a bigger message and I felt like some of the emotional connection to the characters was sacrificed for that bigger message. I did appreciate that it showed many different ways that people survive and I loved bits of the novel, but not enough to make up for the feeling of apathy that the rest of the novel left me with.

This was one of those books I picked up and I didn't know why. Zombie-apacolypses are not my very favorite type of book. It was really good. The story has stuck with me, particularly the way in which the things some see as monstrous can be seen as simply part of the world. Temple is a great protagonist-she has a real personality and doesn't try too hard to live into her gender. This is a thoughtful book, more about the inner landscape of human meaning than it is about the outer landscape of adventures with zombies. Dark, sad, bleak, hopeful, and memorable.

Wow! This book was amazing and beautiful. The authors voice/tone was pure magic. A must read for any zombie fans!

Never has a zombie read hit me in the humanistic feels...this brought out a surge of emotion I never associated with a tale about the undead and the living who continue to do just that...live.

Because we have never been in such a situation, it is hard to fathom how the living would change/grow/react to all that around them. This read hits the nail so hard on the head it shatters!

Thank you Alden Bell! This was great!

Decent 'Zombie books' are my guilty pleasure and I have no idea why.

I got through this fairly quickly though admittedly, the first half of this book was a lot more gripping than the second half. Yes, this was a zombie book but it was quite intelligently written despite becoming a little dull toward the end. A bit of a disappointing ending but I really liked Temple throughout. I would have liked to have read more about why the 'zombie's' came about - instead the main focus was on this random man chasing Temple around the country for killing his brother which I found a little unnecessary..

Beautifully written unconventional zombie story

"God is a slick god. Temple knows. She knows because of all the crackerjack miracles still to be seen on this ruined globe." Thus begins Alden Bell's THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS, a heart-heavy story brought to 'life' by Bell's beautifully descriptive language, most-often brought forth in the musings of his 15-year-old protagonist, Temple in this 'Zombie Lit as Literature' tome. Highly recommended if you like your 'reads' to employ language that you can almost taste.

How is there electricity in seemingly deserted towns? Would petrol really last that long? Some of the things in this world didn't make much sense. Some parts of it reminded me just a liiiiiittle bit too much like a fallout fan-fic too. Also some of the language used by the main character was odd for someone with no education - not even some of my well educated friends use the vocabulary Temple does.

It was also not the book I wanted it to be; it is more the tale of a girl wandering about than anything huge happening. Eh, not really my cup of tea.

Infuriating. I kept hoping it would get better, or at least have a point, but no. Pointless. I mean, entertainment would have been a good point, but it wasn't all that entertaining. The thing is, when you write an apocalyptic novel, do your research!

Some twenty years have passed since the start of the zombie apocalypse, but the electric grid still works, houses and buildings are largely intact, abandoned cars still run, food in convenience stores is still fresh, and on and on.

I'm not going to get into the rest of it, but I have to say I hated the ending. Hated.

Pointless.

This is an intense book. The matter-of-fact way the lead character deals with the problem of a world overrun with pesky man-eating zombies is interesting and at times darkly humorous. The author really gets into the character's way of viewing the world, and tells a tale that is pretty bleak but has it's hopeful spots. You really end up getting attached to the main character, Temple, and hope that all works out for her in the end despite the odds.

It seems that paranormal/horror is becoming so incredibly popular, that even the literati are getting in on it. First, there was The Passage, a literary tale of vampires and the downfall of society. Now, there is The Reapers Are The Angels by Alden Bell, a much more formal take on zombies, than the urban fantasy and YA fare that I am used to.
Read the rest of my review here

Book 54 for 2010. This was an amazingly well written book. I found I couldn't put it down. To best describe it, it's a book written for adults but with great appeal to the upper teen market. It's king of like a cross between TRICKS by Ellen Hopkins, THE FOREST OF HANDS AND TEETH by Carrie Ryan, and lets throw a little GONE WITH THE WIND in there, too. Highly recommended for upper teens and above who like like dystopic/apocalyptic stories.

This a thoughtful and enlightening book that speaks to the beauty that can be found in even the bleakest and most brutal of surroundings -- disguised as a horror/post-apocalyptic novel. The book reminds me somewhat of The Life of Pi, or even the movie Pan's Labyrinth, in that the protagonist lives with an innocence and a steadfast belief in goodness that allows her to survive a nightmarish reality. Highly, highly recommended!

I enjoyed reading this book, and I like the risks the author took in the story. It's really unusual and interesting. It has all of the checklist items of a zombie story, and somehow defies the more irritating stereotypes. I would definitely recommend it to fans of dark fiction or science fiction!

Read my full review at my book review blog

I could not put this book down! Literally, I read it in one night! This book follows Temple, a young girl as she navigates through a bleak post-zombie world. Ultimately finding redemption, this book has a beyond tragic ending yet the journey made it a completely satisfying read! I would recommend to anyone who likes a well written, very philosophical book. Oh, and Temple can kick some serious Slug Ass!

I didn't think that "Zombie Literature" was ever going to be a real thing. This book delivers plenty of undead terror, no doubt about it, but at the same time it manages to humanize the Post-Zombie-Apocalypse world in a way that is slow and tender and gentle and completely different from the typical tropes that all the other zombie books and movies so delight in rehashing. This book makes me happy to be human.

There are many things I loved about this book. First was the setting. Many books describe the onset of the zombie apocalypse, but this one is a story set AFTEr, and its a fresh exciting stage for the story. I wish more books would come out in this setting. Second is the "Street Talk" of the main character. Her use of "Aerodynastics" instead of "Aerodynamics" made me giggle for a while after reading it. Overall, I have to say that I enjoyed this book a LOT more than I thought I would.

Wow. If somebody had told me this would be a postapocalyptic story with zombies, I might have anticipated something about the book - & I would've been SO wrong. Then after I read it, I saw references to it as being in the "horror" genre or the "southern Gothic" genre, & I wondered whether those people had read the same book I had.

An amazing book (imho).

I also question its being marketed as "young adult."

I am getting rather sick of zombies. It has been done. So, I reluctantly started reading this book. I will say I liked it. This book is like "True Grit" with zombies. The 15 year-old protagonist is a great character, and has a believable voice.

I will say that the ending bothered me and because of the end I am not sure if I want to give this book four stars, but the rest of the book was such a good read I guess it deserves it.

I would have given this 4 stars but the way the author wrote his dialog made me insane. While this takes place with the backdrop of zombies, they aren't front and center in the story. You have a young girl left to fend for herself in a world gone nuts and she gets by the best that she can. She's a hard nosed kid and you come to really connect and feel for her. I breezed through this, probably the fastest I've ever read a book.

The book reads pretty quickly and it's interesting, a lot of stuff going on.
Although, for me, the ending was not satisfying, to say the least. Also, the descriptions of places were a little too long for my taste. And the third and first person (the actual characters' thoughts) got mixed up a lot.
After saying that, I must add that I did enjoy it, I really like it, and the characters are easy to get involved with, to understand and sympathize with.

A great read!In this intelligent and affecting post-apocalyptic tale a fifteen year old zombie-killing orphan called Temple makes her way across a ruined American landscape on a mission to return a mentally handicapped man to his family, if they're still alive. She's pursued by a man sworn to kill her and haunted by a tragic past. Her story grabs you and refuses to let go until the shocking and heart-wrenching conclusion.

Horrifying. Simply horrifying. Most zombie stories revolve are about the time of the outbreak, and honestly only about the violence...

But the heroine of this story does not even know a time without the "slugs", she only knows *about* the time before from all the little artifacts she finds. It is pretty hard to add anything new to all the previously written reviews, so I will just leave with a clear recommendation that this is one of the zombie stories you really should not miss.

I found this book a page turner and more... It's sort of the Hunger Games meets the Graveyard Book. it's about a time in the future where the dead have returned to terrorize the living. sounds ridiculous and stupid but it doesn't play that way. the main character is a teenage girl who is attempting to survive. The author manages to work some pragmatic philosophy in to her story. I think a lot of adults might not love the book but older teenagers would.

I just finished reading this book and it is one of the best books I have read in a very long time - incredibly engaging from start to finish. Only 225 pages long it is a quick but intense read. I would have given this book 5 stars but I am petty and this book made me sad. I wish this book were a little more upbeat despite the Zombie wasteland it took place in (which says more about me then the book I suppose).

I loved every moment of this book about a lone southern girl surviving in a post-apocalyptic world. Rather than add my own commentary I will refer to this already perfect summary from amazon:

"The language is flawless. It is unobtrusive, but lush and almost lyrical. The pacing, too, flawless. Not a passage drags, nothing wasted. The characters are strong and believable; their motivations make sense; their voices are clear and distinct."

The writing bothered me a little, for that reason the story didn't quite "Flow". With the quotation marks missing, sometimes I wasn't sure who answer, said what to whom in a dialogue. I like to know when Temple is speaking and when not. I got used to it after a while but my mind keeps telling me it's not right.

Overall, the plot itself wasn't bad but I'm not sure I would recommend this book. The ending was ... unsatisfactory.

A story about finding Good/God even in the most dire and horrific circumstances and the struggle to stay good or believe you are good despite what life has required of you. I wasn't happy with the ending but I'm not sure happiness is what the author was expecting to elicit. I'm not a big reader of zombie stories so I don't know how this stacks up with others but my guess it is very different from the standard fare.

This may be the best zombie book I've ever read! The Reapers are the Angels is a rarity among the genre, in that the the writing itself was as gripping as the story. Everything about the narrative screamed quality to me. I was so compelled and super thrilled to be reading one of my favorite types of stories and NOT have to pause constantly to correct editing errors or decipher deficiencies in language. I loved it and wished it was longer.

I liked this book a lot. I say that as a person who is deeply into zombie literature but who also knows real literature. The problem with this book is that it seems very derivative of No Country for Old Men by Cormack McCarthy. It was an enjoyable read and I won't go so far to say "rip-off", but Alden Bell's novel seems a conscious clone of a McCarthy work. Sorry to say this but all the positive reviewers should reconsider this book.

This book was written in present tense that kept pulling me out of the story. I also found it very distracting that no quotation marks were used in conversations.

Apart from that I didn't like Temple and thought she wasn't too bright at times.
She gives people constantly a fake name, but used the same name everywhere, so the use of the fake name becomes useless.
The one character I connected with turned into the bad guy.

I put the book down about halfway through.

This is easily a very memorable book, the character of "Temple" makes you feel for her, everything she is going through,her sorrows, her guilt,fighting zombies and fleeing her enemy, over all just being a traveler, while still keeping the faith. You cant forget this character. The plot is well written the story line keeps you holding to your book till it ends, and even then makes you wonder. No boring parts at all, and alot of meaningfulness to the writings. by far a favorite in my list.

This was my first Zombie book, and definitely not my last!!! Love how Temple is the oldest 15 year old ever, Love how she handles herself with life. She's not bitter but powerful. She expects the bad to happen so she is always prepared. Such a creative story. My only issues with this story was the ending. Looking back I know it had to end that way, but I wasn't expecting it and definitely wasn't ready. I cant wait the second book to come out. I want to read more!!!

The Reapers are the Angels by Alden Bell is a dystopian adventure coming-of-age novel that offers some of the same insight and perspective of Butler's Parable, but with zombies. The main protagonist, Temple, is also more mature than her age, and navigates her radically altered world with a steely perseverance, while she processes the grief and trauma she has experienced by trying to help others. Also try The Book of the Unnamed Midwife by Meg Elison.

The story of a girl, Temple, and her survival across post-apocalyptic America. Along the way she meets Maury who needs help. A story of Temple's path, her ambitions, her animalistic way to survive and her deep, dark secrets keeping her going. Meatsacks and other dangers cross her path which she has learnt to deal with or adapts too quickly. It's like the frontier meets The Walking Dead. A story of hope, determination, personal battles, morales, fate and human nature at it's best and worst.

recommendFor: zombie lovers, strong female MC lovers
text: i really really liked this book a whole lot. the main character had such a passion for life and doing good by others. she held a deep sorrow for the things she has done in her life and the people she has lost but none of that phases her as she travels on her way to take a stranger she found back to his home in texas. She is a fierce Zombie killer who can do anything with her Gurkha knife. I loved the entire journey this book takes you on.

I devoured this book in about 2 hours on a cross-country flight. Don't think this is just another zombie-lit entry. The writing sucks you in until you are living inside the story and don't take a breath until the last page. Yeah, it's about a zombie apocalypse - but there are surprisingly few zombies driving the story. It's more a survival and character-study type book. Completely compelling and amazing character insights. I was very pleased with the ending as well.

This is a more literate version of the post-apocalypse, and is mostly pretty successful. There is plenty of action and lots of fascinating characters, though the protagonist was the least interesting, compelling, or believable of the lot. There are far too many digressions into hillbilly philosophy, which gives an almost almost comic tone to the book. This is in conflict with the constant undercurrent of fear, creating a mood that never worked for me.

Wow!

Here is Eddie Whitlock's review and he call it perfectly:
Just finished reading THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS by Alden Bell. It's a post-zombie apocalypse story about a girl who travels between pockets of surviving humanity. Bell succeeds at using the ZA as a symbolic backdrop without having the story become morally heavy-handed --- and without losing the excitement and "fun" of killin' zombies. Good job, Mr. Bell. Good job.

Amen, I add to that.

For those of you wanting to dip your toe into the zombie market but worried about over the top grossness or just plain poor writing, this is the book for you. Has a certain southern gothic charm, beautifully written. The heroine is something else, speaks like a hillbilly with the soul of a poet. She's truly captivating.
I thought Peter Coates' review was dead on:
http://thesecondpass.com/?p=6971

If you liked this book, you might also enjoy:

✱ The Road
✱ The Dog Stars
✱ The Age of Miracles

I'm a horror fan but not a huge fan of the zombie sub-genre. Here, however, Alden Bell brings a much needed poetic and literate take on the zombie apocalypse. After the first few pages, I was struck by how much I was reminded of the atmosphere and lyrical story telling of Cormac Mccarthy's brilliant novel, THE ROAD. Much like it, THE REAPERS ARE THE ANGELS has scenes that I'm sure will stick with me for a long time.

This is was my second time reading this book. Definitely in my top ten favorites. There is something so beautiful about the writing and I love the main character, Temple. She is 15 and has grown up in after the apocalypse. She goes on the run from Moses, a man bent on vengeance. They are enemies by circumstance but come to form a strange type of bond. Each has a strict moral code they live and are compelled by, yet there is a mutual respect. Definitely worth a read. (First read in 2012)

I read this unaware that it was a zombie book. This book was amazing. It is not your typical zombie book though. There's not a lot of gore. This is more of a reflection type novel. Thought provoking. Temple is wise beyond her years really. I forgot plenty times that she was only 15 years old. I did wonder what the heck was the point of the story at the end though. It did not end the way I thought it would.

Great book. Gritty and dirty and yet with a hopeful outlook on the world after a zombie apocalypse. Mostly a character study, the book tells the tale of Temple as she travels the ruins of the world and tries to make things right with herself. Exciting and at times very "gory", the book is unusually well written for such blatant genre-fare.

Highest recommendation for those who like zombie books, strong female characters or just really dug McCarthy's The Road.

Easily the most beautifully written zombie novel I have ever read - very reminiscent of Cormac McCarthy's The Road in its poetry - and with a plot that - though it veers close to Resident Evil extravagance in the middle section -defies expectation. Some might find the ending a disappointment, as it deliberately veers from its expected course, but that only adds to the melancholy that permeates the novel throughout.

I loved the beginning of this book so much i mean i loved most of it. The part that only earned 4 stars is the ending, its so surprising, and you wont expect it. I feel like this book had so much more positional. Really to be anything, a series or just a book that didnt end like that. I just feel, like a part of me has been taken, that Temple could have changed things, stayed with James and there could have been a so much better book. 4 STARS

Post-apocalyptic setting? Check.
Zombies? Check.
A fifteen year old girl, hard as anything, wandering through swarms of slugs, groups of survivors, trying to get a friend home.
The book was exciting and sad, Temple was a great character. Attempting find balance between morality & survival in gruesome situations, finding people who want to take care of her but fearing to depend on anyone. No teen-fiction, this.

This is...not a book about zombies. There are zombies in it, but this is a book about honor and pain and forgetting. For a book that takes on the rather lofty examination of the effect of constant zombie killing on the human condition, there's an awful lot of zombie killing.

The book feels like something Cormac McCarthy might write, and if you've read _The Road_ comparisons might be inevitable. It has its own story to tell, however, and is worth a (melancholy) read.

Good things about this book:
- it has a fun, slightly pretentious writing style
- it's a book about living in a zombie infested world without zombies popping up all over the place
- it has a strong female protagonist

Things that I could have lived without:
- weird mutants that didn't seem to have a real place or explanation
- an ending that was supposed to be a surprise, but wasn't really
- Moses Todd and his obsession that doesn't really make any sense

Overall a fun book.

An ok story line (enough to keep you interested) but the best thing about this book is the descriptive language used:

"Temple has forgotten how bad they smell - that muddy mixture of must and putrefaction, oil and rancid shit. She sees a faecal ooze sliding wetly down the back of the woman's leg. They must have fed recently, so they will be strong. And they are between her and the stairs".

How can you beat that?

So I went looking for a genre escape—I keep coming back to zombie books, for some reason—and found something lyrical and profound instead. Horrific, violent, gory, and upsetting, too, but still ... True Grit meets The Walking Dead through the prose of Faulkner or O'Connor.
